paragraphs.text: David dedicates the beginning of his prophecy to Christ, who was to be born of him. That is why, at the very start, he calls blessed those who have put their hope in him. [He calls blessed those who have not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of the pestilent. For there were three orders among the Jews that rose up against the Saviour: scribes, Pharisees and lawyers. These might fittingly be called ungodly, sinners and pestilent. Life is called a way because those who are born press on [?] toward their end.] Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly. By “the counsel of the ungodly” one may understand the assembly, or gathering, of the wicked. Since it is harmful to approach the gatherings of the ungodly, he calls blessed the one who does not join them to any degree at all. Joseph of Arimathea, who buried the body of our Lord and God, was such a man, for it is said of him that he did not consent to the counsel of those who betrayed Jesus. And in the seat of the pestilent he has not

sat. By “seat” he means teaching, as when it says, “On the seat of Moses.” The seat of the pestilent, then, is the teaching of the wicked. Day and night. This signifies constancy, for one must not meditate on the law of the Lord carelessly. [But his will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he will meditate day and night. “The law”: the angelic [?] law, clearly. It signifies constancy, for one must not meditate on the law of the Lord carelessly. One must not meditate at some times and not at others, but always and continually be fastened to the divine oracles; this is what “day and night” signifies. Fine is the reward of this achievement: for the one who devotes himself to the divine law and is watered by the streams that flow from it [?]. Christ too called his own teaching water, saying, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” He is likened to the tree by the waters, always flourishing, always laden with ripe fruit. For the athletes of virtue will receive the fruits of their labours in the future; yet even here they are shaded by good hope as if by leaves, and by this consolation they steal away the heaviness of their labours. For such a one all things will prosper. For he will do nothing contrary to the divine laws, since he brings his will into harmony with the intent of the law. Having first renounced every form of wickedness and shown the perfection of the divine laws, he then added: “All that he does.”] And he will be like the tree planted by the channels of the waters. In the divinely inspired Scripture Christ is described as a tree of confession, or of comparison [?], according to the saying: “She is a tree of life to all who hold fast to her.” He means, then, that those who have believed in Christ will be his body, for he will transform the body of our humiliation so that it is conformed to the body of his glory. By “the channels of the waters” he means the divine Scriptures, in which one can find Christ proclaimed everywhere. [The tree of life is Christ; the branches are the apostles; the fruit is the blood and water from his side, the one a figure of martyrdom, the other of baptism. The leaves are the words. By the fruit of the tree you are to understand right faith, and by its leaves the fulfilment of the commandments. The fruit is also those who are saved; the root is baptism; the husbandman is the Father.] Which will yield its fruit in its season. By the fruit of the tree you are to understand faith, and by its leaves the fulfilment of the commandments. And its leaf will not fall away: it will not drop off. And all that he does will prosper. For no deed done according to God is unprofitable. The season for giving is the fitness of the one who receives.
Therefore the ungodly will not rise in judgement. “Therefore”: because they have no root, but are like

the dust of the earth tossed by the wind. By the wind you are to understand God’s threat that says, “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire.” Those who hear this voice will justly fall, for they have not stood firm in Christ, who is the support and foundation of believers. He says “in judgement”, not “for questioning”. In the assembly of the righteous, he says, for he separates the righteous from the sinners. For the Lord knows the way of the righteous. “Knows” stands for “honours”, as in what God said to Moses: “I know you above all,” that is, I honour you, and you have found favour with me. PSALM of David. Among the Hebrews it has no title.

In the first psalm he declared the rulers of the Jewish nation to be ungodly, sinners and pestilent; in this one he goes on to show the deeds by which they came to share such names. [Having ended the first psalm with a mention of the ungodly, he makes this the beginning of the second as well, teaching that the end foretold for the ungodly awaits also those who raged against the Saviour.] [?] “Raging” is irrational arrogance. “Why” is to be supplied for both clauses, that is: Why have the peoples meditated vain things? [For how was their meditation not vain, since they did not receive the Saviour of the race?] [What, he asks, is the cause of such great hatred, that nations and peoples ran together to the same end? For “they raged”, meaning they were so arrogant, signifies being agitated and in uproar with a certain elation and boasting. The word is transferred from the irrational charging of horses at nothing that is needful [?]; and this is what happened to the Jews in the case of Christ. What is the reason that nations and peoples ran together? He calls either the Israelites both nations and peoples, or else Herod and Pilate and their followers, as gentiles, nations, and the Jews peoples.] [The kings of the earth stood by. “Stood by” stands for “set themselves apart for this”: the kings Herod and Pontius Pilate. So too the holy apostles interpreted it in Acts.] And the rulers gathered together. The orders mentioned earlier: scribes, Pharisees and lawyers. Against the Lord and against his Christ. For the plot against Christ reaches up to the Father himself. If the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, how could the outrage against them not be one?

Let us burst their bonds. The word “saying” is missing, so that the sense is: They gathered against the Lord and against his Christ, saying, Let us burst their bonds. For they did not want to be inside the holy net, of which it is written: The kingdom of heaven is like a net. And let us cast their yoke away from us. The weight of the law, of which he said, “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” [Their yoke: for the plot against Christ reaches up to the Father himself. If the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, how could the outrage against them not be one?] He who dwells in the heavens will laugh them to scorn. As men who have plotted foolishly; for the one they nailed up and handed over to death, being in heaven and holding all things together, shows their counsels to be empty and vain. And his Father, the Master of all, will exact from them the penalty they deserve. And the Lord will mock them. For he will set them at nought, it says, and hate them and turn away from them. [“Will mock” [?] stands for “will hate and turn away from”. He who is higher than the plotters, it says, will deride them, that is, will show their plot to be a laughingstock, as of men attempting foolish things. For mockery is breath let out through the nostrils in contempt of those who rage arrogantly. And the fact that these words are said with prepositions makes the laughter more intense. And not only this, it says, but they will also feel his wrath.] Then he will speak to them in his wrath. “Then”: when? Was it when they said, Let us burst their bonds? And what were the things spoken by him in wrath? Surely these: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees”; and, “The kingdom will be taken from you”; and, “Woe to you also, you lawyers.” [For a Roman army enslaved them. Anger differs from wrath in that anger is wrath fuming up and still burning, while wrath is the desire to pay back pain. Anger, then, is less complete than wrath, and wrath is its completion. The outcome of events teaches us how to interpret such words. For a Roman army came upon them, sacked the city and burned the temple; most of them it put to death, and those who escaped the slaughter it enslaved and delivered to servitude. The believer should note that he mentions two persons in succession: first the Lord and Christ, for he said, “against the Lord and against his Christ”; then the one who dwells in the heavens and the Lord: “He who dwells in the heavens will laugh them to scorn, and the Lord will mock them”; and again he kept the same pattern.] But I have been established king by him on Zion. Since the people from Israel have been rejected, he himself recounts to them the faith that arose among

the nations; and Zion signifies the Church. [The Lord said to me, You are my Son, and so on; that is: the Father’s nature declared me Son, not by the working of a command, but because his essence showed me to be the imprint of the Father’s substance. “You are” is fittingly added to indicate the birth before the ages, for he was always Son. He added “today I have begotten you” to show the birth according to the flesh, for “today” denotes [?] time, and so it is placed with reference to the birth in time. What follows, “I have begotten you”, likewise accords with his humanity. See how the Father makes his own the fleshly birth of his only-begotten, Christ.] And the ends of the earth as your possession. You will shepherd them with a rod of iron. That is, with the cross, for its material is wood but its strength is iron. Some say it signifies the rule of the Romans. And now, O kings, understand. That is, perceive, and turn to repentance. Be instructed, all you who judge the earth. By “be instructed” he presents progress, and by “lay hold of instruction” perfection. Lay hold of instruction. The instruction of the gospel, clearly. And you will perish from the righteous way. The way of him who said, “I am the way.” PSALM of David, when he fled from Absalom his son. 3.

The title set before the psalm runs as follows. This is what the psalm is saying: that the choir of the prophets is persecuted by the people of the Jews. For “David” is interpreted “beloved”, and this is the choir of the prophets. Just as Absalom sought to rebel against his own father, that is, David, so the Jews rose up against their fathers the prophets, not receiving God’s commands but opposing them. Lord, why are those who afflict me multiplied? “Why” stands for “exceedingly”. There is no salvation for him in his God. His God, they say, will not save him; for they looked only at the sin he had committed, knowing nothing of his repentance. This shows more clearly that the psalm is spoken of David. For “to rise up against” is properly said of those who were formerly in the rank of subjects and afterwards took up war. But you, Lord, are my helper, my glory. Since it has been said that the psalm is spoken in the person of the Lord, we must say that his head too is lifted up,

his head being God, when his divinity is made manifest to the faithful by demonstration. [But you, Lord, are my helper. These words befit the faith of the prophet, who bore such great trials unshaken and trusted that he would not be forsaken, but would be helped and exalted and would recover the kingdom; for this is how some have understood “lifting up my head”. The glory of the righteous man, then, is God, in whom he trusts; and the one whose glory is God has his head lifted up.] With my voice I cried to the Lord. The passage teaches that in trials we must turn to no one but God alone. [With my voice I cried to the Lord. He first set out the prayer, and then, after the diapsalma, the thanksgiving for having obtained what he asked. Now, however, he turns his face toward us and recounts how he prayed and was heard, saying: With my voice I cried to the Lord. By “voice” we must understand the mind’s spiritual supplication to the God of all; for he does not mean a shout, but the silent [?] prayer of the mind. “He heard me from his holy mountain” is said according to the prevailing belief, for God was thought to dwell in the Tabernacle, since it was from there that the oracles were given to the priests. Or “from his holy mountain” stands for “from heaven”, as also in “On your holy mountain” and “You drew near to the everlasting mountains” [?]. The holy mountain of God, from which God hears those who pray, may be his only-begotten, of whom it is said: “The mountain of the Lord shall be manifest in the last days”; this expression signifying his manifestation, which took place at his coming at the consummation of the ages. Or “from his holy mountain” means from heaven. The holy mountain of God is the supernatural knowledge of him. The diapsalma marks a change of musical melody or mode, or an alteration in the thought and force of the words. “I awoke” signifies this: that, having enjoyed the divine turning, I rose above what had befallen me.

I lay down and slept. He means the sleep of the mind, through which he also fell into sin. [For you have struck all who are hostile to me. “Strike”, “crush”, or “you will strike”. He urges on God’s rising up against them, that is, his retribution. In vain does a man have enemies who gives no pretext for hatred. By “the teeth of sinners” he means either the strength of those who sin against him, or their words against him and their blasphemies. Or the teeth of sinners are irrational thoughts that come upon us contrary to nature. For the adversaries, using thoughts as teeth, often draw near to us to eat our flesh, that is, the things that spring from the flesh. “Now the works of the

flesh are manifest,” says the divine Apostle. He says “teeth” by a metaphor taken from wild beasts, whose strength lies chiefly in their teeth, and which become contemptible once these are crushed. For murderers and the bloodthirsty are worse even than bloodthirsty beasts, or at least their equals.] Salvation is the Lord’s. Save me, Lord, he says. And I pray that this may extend to all the people. It should be understood that the whole psalm refers to humanity: humanity sinned and for that very reason was handed over to its spiritual enemies, but cried out in affliction and was heard by God, and was indeed saved, clearly through his rising from the dead and striking the demons who are hostile to us. For he is the Lord who crushed the molars of the lions. And salvation is his, that is, it comes from him. [Salvation is the Lord’s. I do not set my hope on man, he says, but I await salvation from you, and so does your people, who are warred against along with me.] For the end. PSALM of an ode, of David. 4. Argument. He dedicates this psalm to the giver of victory after winning the war. [In place of “for the end”, Aquila and Theodotion translated “to the giver of victory”, and Symmachus [?]] When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me. This is like: “While you are still speaking, he will say, Here I am.” In affliction you made room for me. Not only did you bring me out of my trials, he says, but you also set me in a broad and spacious place. [Ziba and Barzillai brought David much food and rugs when, having fled from Absalom, he was living in the deserts and in the mountains; just as with the three youths in the furnace, and Daniel among the lions. When we recognize the reasons for afflictions and temptations, it is then above all that we are enlarged. Spaciousness can also be understood in another way.] Have pity on me and hear my prayer. Since he said he had been heard on the strength of his righteousness, he therefore has recourse to God’s mercies. Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? This is addressed to those who trusted that they would capture the righteous man by the size of their army. But this hope, he says, is vain and false. And know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful. That is: Know, then, you who trust in numbers, that he has shown the one who trusts in him to be wonderful. The Lord will hear me when I cry to him. One tense is taken for another, for he said “will hear” in place of “heard”. Be angry, and do not sin; what you say in your hearts, be pierced with compunction for it on your beds. He says this as to his own people,

as to all people. Even if you give anger room, he says, make it ineffective by compunction in quiet. This is what “be pierced with compunction on your beds” means. Offer a sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord. He teaches how we shall overcome our enemies. And how shall we overcome them? By acting righteously and sending this up to God like a sacrifice. Many say, Who will show us good things? These are the words of those who make light of God’s governance. The light of your face has been signed upon us, Lord. Christ is the light of the world, who also taught us the things that are truly good, through which we have gained spiritual gladness in mind and heart.

The one who inherits is the soul that loves God, or the Church. And what does she inherit? What eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and has not entered into the heart of man. She also prays, doing whatever she can [?] to be heard, presenting her own uprightness and denouncing the wickedness of those responsible. [For to you I will pray. Having come to enjoy the spiritual light, it says, I will pray to you; and so I also trust that I shall be heard.] Give ear to my words. In the morning I will stand before you. It is a great boast of struggle to stand before God straight from one’s bed and to be ahead of the sun in giving thanks. For thus, it says, I shall look upon your divine and holy mysteries, which you have prepared for those who love you. For you are not a God who wills lawlessness. Therefore, it says, I am confident that I shall be heard, because I have practised none of the things you hate. These are lawlessness, wickedness, transgression, falsehood, envy,

You have hated all who work lawlessness; you will destroy all who speak falsehood. Those who stumble in their way of life he has called “workers of lawlessness”, and these God hates; but those who have fallen away from the truth, the heterodox, he has called “speakers of falsehood”, and these God will destroy. Observe the difference between “you have hated” and “you will destroy”. First, “you will destroy” is worse than “you have hated”; second, he put the one in the past tense and the other in the

[Speakers of falsehood: also those who call idols gods, and the demons themselves, who speak false and crooked and [?] words in the idols. The Lord abhors a man of blood and deceit. For God hates such a man and turns

away from him. But I, in the abundance of your mercy, will enter your house. The heavenly Jerusalem, the mother of the firstborn. I will worship toward your holy temple in fear of you. The temple of God is a virtuous and holy state, which those who possess it speak of [?] with boldness. And Christ as Son will rest upon his own house, and we are his house. For, enjoying your love for humankind and guarded by your right hand, I offer you continual worship in the temple dedicated to your glory, says the holy and pure soul; for, always carrying your fear within me, I will not let myself cast it off through presuming on your love for humankind. For the sake of my enemies make my way straight before you. The spiritual enemies, clearly. Their heart is vain. The heart of the wise of this age, or also of the heretics; for these do not know the word of truth. Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they have deceived. They make their tongue smooth and belch out dead doctrines. Let them fall from their designs. For they made all these designs against me, he says, opposing my progress toward God. [According to the multitude of their impieties cast them out, making them godly [?]. For those who persecute the soul that does what is pleasing to God embitter God, plainly fighting against God.] And you will dwell among them. For he himself will come, and the Father, and they will make their dwelling with him. And those who love your name will boast in you, for you, Lord, have blessed the righteous. For your blessing and providence are bestowed on your servants, who, having made themselves lovers of your name, will take great pride in your care as they recount your power. So too blessed Paul says, “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.” As with a shield of good pleasure you have crowned us. You will grant us, he says, the end of our labours as a crown, and with it, as with a shield, you fence us about. For the end, in hymns, concerning the eighth. PSALM of David. 6.

And what could the eighth be but the day of Christ’s resurrection, on which we shall enjoy the fruits of our labours? Our enemies, that is, will be turned back, with shame and confusion, clearly. He sings the psalm as one who has spent a long time in the repentance he offered for his sin. Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger. He does not refuse rebuke, but rebuke with anger; nor discipline, but discipline with wrath. Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak. For no soul falls into sin until it has given up its strength. [He hints at the weakness that arises from despondency and lamentation.] And my soul is greatly troubled. The [?] of the soul

[?]…of the soul, that is, the powers. “And you, O Lord, how long?” The phrase points to a repentance that lasted a long time. “Turn, O Lord, rescue my soul.” He speaks as though God had turned away from him, clearly because of his sin. “Save me for the sake of your mercy.” For the whole of our salvation must be credited to God’s mercy. “For in death there is no one who remembers you.” Since the time of my repentance, he says, has grown long, I am afraid that death may come before your mercy does, and in death there is no confession. That is why I ask you to hurry your mercy. “I am worn out with my groaning.” Let us hear what kind of repentance the king showed. He did not merely grow tired; he wore himself out with groaning. He did not merely weep; he washed his bed, and did so every night. And he looks not only to the past but also makes promises for the future, for the whole of his life. The time that most people make a time of praise [relaxation], he makes a time of confession. “Every night I will wash my bed.” For the one night, he says, in which I committed the sin, I spent many nights soaking my bedding with tears. “My eye is troubled with anger.” By “eye” he means the mind, since the mind is the eye of the soul. “I have grown old among all my enemies.” Here he indicates how long his suffering lasted. [? … and he also counts it as an achievement, because it was long.] “For the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.” As one who has already been heard, he puts together a long speech against his enemies. And this too is no small road to virtue: to flee and fend off the company of the wicked. For this is the fruit of repentance and the profit of tears. Or the phrase is elliptical, meaning: “Grant me to say to the enemies who attack me: Depart, for I have been heard, for I have been accepted, I who through sin…”

Hushai was David’s chief companion. David sent him to Absalom to work against Ahithophel, who was proposing plans against David. Hushai went and pretended to betray David. Absalom then put the question to both Hushai and Ahithophel. Ahithophel urged pursuit; Hushai urged against it, saying, “One must not rashly attack a man skilled in war.” By this advice he saved David. And David, as one who had not been saved by human help, sends up to God the song of thanksgiving for these events, crediting everything to God’s grace and nothing to any human being. “O Lord my God, in you I have hoped.” Since I do not trust a human being for my salvation, he says, even though Hushai’s words were good, save me from my present enemies, and above all from the spiritual lion that lies in wait for our soul.

“If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil.” He offers his freedom from grudges as a plea, and through it calls God to mercy. “Then may I fall away from my enemies empty.” The righteous man, having won, comes away from his enemies full; but the worthless man, having been beaten, falls away from them empty, with nothing to fill him. “Then let the enemy pursue my soul.” What he means is this: may I fall into the hands of the devil if I have done any of the things mentioned before; if I have done this or that, may I not be set free from sin before I die. “Be exalted in the borders of my enemies.” That is, among the strong ones of my enemies, for “borders” means the extremities. “And arise, O Lord my God, by the command you have given.” In these words he clearly announces the good news of the Savior’s divine appearing. “And the assembly of the peoples will surround you.” In these words he clearly indicates the Church’s faith in him. “And for its sake return on high.” That is, for the sake of this assembly. “On high” alludes either to the precious cross, onto which he carried up our sins, or to the ascent into heaven. For he went to appear before the face of the Father on behalf of…

“Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness.” Again he asks to be saved from his enemies, calling for mercy because of what they have done. “Who saves the upright in heart.” Since you know, he says, the thoughts of our heart, for this reason I ask [?] for help. “God is a righteous judge, strong and patient.” By such words he clearly sets forth God’s patience: God puts off our punishment, but does not grant complete pardon. “He has made his arrows for those who burn.” By “arrows” he means punishment; by “those who burn,” those who deserve fire. “Behold, he has been in labor with injustice.” That is, the enemy of our life. “He conceived toil and gave birth to lawlessness.” That is, he both made his plans and carried his schemes into action. “He dug a pit and hollowed it out.” For having prepared death against Christ the Savior, he is himself handed over to death. For the end, concerning the winepresses. A Psalm of David. [?]

In the old worship under the Law there was a single wine vat, namely the altar in the temple. But after the calling of the Gentiles there are many winepresses, and these would be the Churches, which receive the fruits of those who succeed in godliness. [It says “for the end” because the things prophesied reached their fulfillment at the end of the ages. For he is speaking of Christ and of the Churches after the incarnation, since the Only-begotten is also called a vine, and the

faithful are its branches. But if the Jew insists that the psalm is spoken about humanity in general, then let this too be understood: all things were made subject to man for this reason, that he had come into being in the image of the God who was going to become man.] “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!” He is amazed at the knowledge of God’s name that has been given to humankind. For God is no longer known only to those in Judea. “Out of the mouths of infants and nursing babies you have perfected praise.” That is, of those who in God’s sight are infants in wickedness. The Gospels clearly record that the Savior said this when the Pharisees were trying to silence the children who were blessing him. “Because of your enemies, to destroy the enemy and the avenger.” Either the visible enemy, or the spiritual one, or the Jewish people. For they persecuted Christ as an enemy, while pretending to do it in order to avenge the Father. That is why, depriving them of this excuse again and again, he said, “Whoever hates me hates my Father also.” “The enemy and avenger” means the devil. For after forcing people to commit sin, he also punishes those who sin, setting the greatness of their sin before their eyes. Or it means the Jewish people, an enemy of the truth, and an avenger in that they seemed to be avenging the Law. “For I will see the heavens [?], the works of your fingers.” They are indignant at infants perfecting praise; but I look upon something so great and so beautiful (I mean the heavens) as a small work of your craftsmanship. “What is man, that you remember him? Or the son of man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels.” Since Paul clearly took these words as referring to our Savior, we must be content with that interpretation. “You have put all things under his feet.” When God said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” he added, “And let them rule over the fish of the sea,” and goes through the rest one by one, and then adds, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it.” For he granted to the rational nature, as made like God, rule [?] over all things. And man, having received the power of the divine image, was appointed ruler of the things on earth, just as God is king of all. Now if it is said without limit, “And you set him over the works of your hands,” and elsewhere it says, “And the heavens are the works of your hands,” it is clear that he set him over the heavens too. Perhaps it signifies, in a hidden way, the life in heaven of those who are moved there from earth, when they are to inherit the kingdom of heaven, as has been promised. And Paul too says, “Heirs of

God and fellow heirs with Christ.” In the same way we must also understand “You have put all things under his feet.” For now, it means the animals. But since a life equal to the angels’ is stored up for humankind in heaven, man, once set there over the works of God’s hands, will be a spectator of the heavens and of what is in them. Yet blessed Paul took this too as referring to the Savior, as something that will come about in the age to come. That is why the Father says to him, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.” “All sheep and oxen.” He is alluding to those from Israel who believe. “And also the beasts of the field.” By these he means the Gentiles. “The birds of the sky” are those who are puffed up in their way of life and think lofty thoughts, the most irrational of all. “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!” Taking it up again, he repeats his wonder, amazed, as I said, at the knowledge of God that has come to humankind. For the end, concerning the hidden things of the son. A Psalm of David. 9.

In this psalm he reveals the things the Savior did in secret. Many were the things he did in secret: his birth in the flesh from a Virgin through the Holy Spirit, his astonishing and wonder-working powers, his death itself, his descent into Hades, and his return to life from the dead. All these he did in secret, for he hid them even from the rulers of this world. It is for these hidden things that the prophet steps forward in the person of humanity, giving thanks and saying, “I will give thanks to you, O Lord.” (Another manuscript:) The seal of the hidden things is the death and what was done in Hades, and the resurrection and the ascension. “I will give thanks to you, O Lord, with my whole heart … when my enemy is turned back.” He shows what the thanksgiving is for. He says that his enemy is death, which is turned back, that is, into nonexistence. “They will grow weak and perish before your face.” When death is turned back, he says, then every opposing power will also be abolished. For if death is abolished as the last enemy, clearly the opposing powers will have been destroyed before it…

“For you have upheld my judgment and my cause.” He gives the reason for his thanksgiving. “You sat on a throne” indicates God’s oversight in judging. “You rebuked the nations, and the ungodly one perished.” He means, of course, the spiritual enemies. “You blotted out his name forever.” He means the spiritual dragon, who is the devil. [“You rebuked the nations, and the ungodly one perished.” He means the dragon, that is, the devil. Since rebuke also means correction, one could say that when the nations were cor-

rected by the apostles, the ungodly one perished, since the smoke of his altars was put out and ceased. For when the nations were rebuked and turned to the Lord, the devil, who was at work in them as sons of disobedience, perished together with the idol temples, which like cities held fast those who looked toward impiety. And they perished so completely that not even a trace was left. This can also be taken to refer to the final judgment. For then, when sinners are rebuked, the devil too, the ungodly one in the strict sense, is wiped out. The cities, once the impiety that formerly lived in them had been destroyed, received the building up of godliness.] “The swords of the enemy have failed completely.” By the devil’s swords he means the opposing powers, through which he was strong. [The cities are the opposing powers, which, like strong walled cities, seized those they had captured by deceit and held them inside. And what cities could he mean but those of which it is said elsewhere, “You have made strong cities a heap, so that their foundations fall”? These, as has been shown, are the opposing powers.] “Their memory has perished with a noise.” [So that their destruction was heard far and wide. He means either their utter ruin, or the enormity of the evils and how conspicuous their destruction was.] For their destruction became known far and wide. “And the Lord became a refuge for the poor.” [He constantly calls himself poor and needy, even though he lived in palaces. For he knew that all human things are feebler than a shadow. By “timely occasions” he means the time of affliction. For we always need help, even in prosperity; but we feel the need of an ally more keenly in affliction.] “For the poor”: he means the spiritual people. “A helper at timely occasions, in afflictions.” As in, “At an acceptable time I heard you.” “Sing to the Lord who dwells in Zion.” In the heavenly Jerusalem, he says. “Proclaim his deeds among the nations.” He says this as though to the apostles and the heralds of the Gospels. What these deeds are he indicates in what follows. “For he who seeks out their blood has remembered.” The blood, he says, that was shed for him he will seek out, so as to grant them vengeance. [“He has not forgotten the prayer of the poor.” Again he calls “poor” those who became poor for his sake, who constantly make supplication to him, asking for vengeance for the wrongs done to them by the demons.] “You who lift me up from the gates of death.” For this reason you raise me from the earth of humiliation, so that I may join in the dance of the heavenly Zion. [“In the gates of the daughter of Zion.” That is, in the heavenly Jerusalem. “That I may proclaim” stands for “I will sing for a long time.”] “The Lord is known by executing judgments.” For it is truly [?] a just judgment that those who prepared for men…

“Arise, O Lord, let not man prevail.” He prays that the Only-begotten may shine on those on earth, so that the arrogant devil, whom here he also calls “man,” may no longer raise his brow. “Let the nations be judged before you.” He prays, urging on the calling of the nations to salvation. “Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them.” And who is the lawgiver but the one who brought us the law of the New Covenant? “Let the nations know that they are men.” Through the overwhelming deceit of the demons they had been changed into the likeness of beasts, so that it was said of them, “He was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them.”

“Why, O Lord, do you stand far off?” He prays that the calling of the nations, which was to come long afterward, may be hastened. It was the devil’s arrogance that brought this about. “While the ungodly one is arrogant, the poor man is set on fire.” The arrogance of the wicked one, he says, becomes a burning for your poor people. “They are caught in the schemes they devise.” This stands for “they will be caught.” For you, he says, are the one who catches the wise in their craftiness. “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul.” So great, he says, has been God’s forbearance that, because the ungodly go unpunished, their way of life has even come to be approved by some of the more foolish. “The sinner provoked the Lord.” He provoked him by mocking the teaching about his providence and judgment. For many people laugh at once when they hear anything of the kind. This is connected with “according to the greatness of his wrath,” so that the whole reads: The sinner, he says, provoked the Lord, storing up a great deal of wrath for himself. For “his” must be taken to refer to the one who provoked. Then the words that follow, “he will not seek it out,” must be read with a slight pause, so that the meaning is: Does the one provoke God, even while kindling a great deal of wrath against himself, and will the other not seek it out? Read with the pause, it means: Will God not seek it out, he says, and repay him according to the wrath he stored up for himself in the day of God’s wrath? “God is not before him.” The beginning of every evil deed is not to reckon God as judge. “Your judgments are taken away [?] from his sight.” For one who does not know that God exists does not know that he is judge either. “He will gain mastery over all his enemies.” This is like “I will seize the whole world in my hand like a nest.” “For he said

in his heart: I shall not be shaken.” That is: I shall not stumble, I shall not be overthrown from generation to generation, for I shall never be in trouble. [“God is not before him.” Having driven the fear of God out of his soul, he lives continually in wickedness. The beginning of every evil deed is not to reckon God as judge. “Your judgments are taken away from his sight.” He does not want to know that you are a just judge; for one who does not know that God exists does not know that he is judge either. “He will gain mastery over all his enemies.” Of temptations, some are brought against the soul, some against the body, and some against the things around the body. Those brought against the soul are called impure thoughts, which give birth to sins and false doctrines. Those brought against the body cause beatings, tortures on the rack, persecutions, imprisonments and deaths. Temptations involving what surrounds the body include losses of money and property, the loss of children and the taking away of wives. From this it is clear that Satan has gained mastery over every righteous person through one or another of the temptations listed; for Christ alone committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth.] “His mouth is full of cursing.” He has reckoned, he says, that his prosperity will last. That is why his mouth is full of bitterness and deceit; and he lies in wait for the poor to kill them with his own snares. And “with the rich”: what else could this mean but those who are rich in evil? For these work together with the devil, their father, against the poor. “He sits in ambush with the rich.” Sitting in gatherings and councils, he lays ambushes and plots against the innocent. “He will stoop and fall.” When [another manuscript adds: the devil] says, “I have won,” then he falls and is put to shame. “For he said in his heart: God has forgotten.” The devil says this not because it is so, but because he wants to deceive us, so that we may be tripped up, thinking that God neglects human affairs. “Arise, O Lord my God.” He prays to rouse God’s forbearance and goodness. For when God’s hand is not lifted against the folly of the ungodly, they become more reckless. [“Let your hand be lifted up.” Raise your hand and teach them that you care for those who are wronged; and as though risen from sleep, show that your punishment is stronger than their designs. Punish them, but spare the one who is wronged, being more sorely vexed at their audacity and blasphemies. “Why,” he says, “has the ungodly one provoked the
For he said in his heart: He will not seek it out.” This is the cause both of his being lifted up and of his fall.

“You see, for you take note of toil and anger.” You, O Lord, he says, know all things, and nothing that is done escapes you, nor anything that rises up in the mind and thoughts. You know precisely their toils, the anger of those who abuse others, and people’s provocations. For you take note of everyone’s thoughts, and you are the one who tests hearts and minds. And though you see all this, you are patient, knowing that all are in your hands and no one can escape anywhere outside them. “To you the poor man has been left; you have been the helper of the orphan.” That is, he waits for help from you. “Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked.” That is, the power of the enemy. “His sin will be sought, and it will not be found.” That is, because of the sin itself. The whole means this: If [?], he says, you seek out the sin of the wicked man, he will not be found; that is, the wicked man will perish because of it. [Those who are saved are found by God, as in “I have found David my servant,” and “The lost drachma was found”; and if it had not been found, it would have been lost. Those who perish are never found, for the judge remains and reigns forever in the future and new age.] “The Lord will reign forever.” In the future and new age.

“You nations will perish from his land.” For in his kingdom they will be thrown into the eternal fire. [He calls the unjust “nations” because they do not live according to the law but with the savagery of heathens and barbarians. He asks that they be cut off, saying, “You will perish,” and threatening them with utter destruction, so that the one group may breathe again and the other may come to its senses.] “You have heard the desire of the poor, O Lord.” For this was their desire and longing: to be found worthy of the good things to come. “Your ear has attended to the readiness of their heart.” For since they are ready for this, they prepare their hearts to endure everything. [Readiness of heart is a kind of pledge that the soul’s movements will follow God.] (a) Ambrosian manuscript: parastatikos is the better reading; supply “psalm.”

"In the Lord I have put my trust; how will you say to my [?]?" How can you tell me, he says, to flee to the mountains like a sparrow, when I have put my trust in God? "Move away to the mountains like a sparrow." Migrate, depart, flee to the mountains, that is, to the virtues. "For behold, the sinners have bent the bow, they have made ready arrows for the quiver." With these words they were urging him to flee, saying that unless he fled, the sinners would shoot him down. He shows, then, that evil thoughts are the arrows of the evil one. "To shoot in the dark at the upright in heart": that is, secretly. For such are the [?] of the spiritual enemies

"For what you established, they have torn down." The enemy, he says, brought man down into corruption, although he had been established for incorruption. "But what has the righteous one done?" Even if the enemies, he says, have done such things, yet the Lord, who has heaven for his temple, examines the righteous and the ungodly, and allots good things to the one and sends the others away to eternal punishments. "The Lord is in his holy temple." ["For what you established, they have torn down." That is: they are hastening to destroy your works through me; for they are eager to set aside the one you anointed king, arming themselves against your decree. And they do this having torn down within themselves the upright notions that accord with nature, which, of course, you established.] "His eyes look upon the poor." This signifies that nothing escapes God; and by "eyes" he means his beneficent oversight. "His eyelids examine the sons of men." By "eyelids" he means his judging providence, which examines all affairs. For the end, concerning the eighth, a Psalm of [?]

The eighth has been discussed under the sixth psalm. Here he prays to be rescued from the evil generation. This would be the generation of the time of our Saviour Jesus Christ, of which he himself said: "The men of Nineveh will rise up and condemn the generation [?]"

"Save me, Lord, for the godly man has failed, for truths have dwindled from among the sons of men." He is gathering together the plots against our Saviour. For the Jews abandoned the truth and carried out a lie against Christ. "Deceitful lips in the heart." Because, while they called him teacher and good, they were plotting something else concerning [?]

"The Lord will utterly destroy all deceitful lips, a boastful tongue." For how was that tongue not boastful which dared to say to the Saviour, "By what authority do you do these things? And who gave you this authority?" Those who said, "We will magnify our tongue;

our lips are our own; who is lord over us?" As though they had this in mind: to have authority to say whatever they wished against the Saviour. And this, "Who is lord over us?", is like the saying, "But as for this man, we do not know where he is from." "Because of the misery of the poor." By the poor and needy he means those who are poor in spirit; hearing their groaning too, he says, "I will arise. I will set him in safety; I will speak boldly in it." That is: I will make the salvation manifest to all, and I will see to it that it is heard far and wide. For it was proclaimed throughout the whole earth. "The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire." True, he says, are the words promised concerning salvation, like silver that has been refined many times. And he has put "sevenfold" in place of "manifold"; for this is customary in the divine [?]

"You, Lord, will guard us." You will guard us, he says, for this reason: because the ungodly surround us, plotting against our salvation. These would be the opposing and evil powers. "According to your height you have shown great regard for the sons of men." By "height" he means power, and by "great regard" length of time. So that the meaning is this: through your strength you have given us length of days [?] and eternal life. For after the saving resurrection, for endless ages, the things of the [?] … For the end, a Psalm of David. 12.
"How long, Lord, will you forget me? To the end?" [?] since the [?] that came upon him because of sin was long [?] of the approach to God in repentance. "How long [?]"

"But I have hoped in your mercy." I am confident, he says, that I shall receive forgiveness of sins, holding fast to your mercy, through which you have also given salvation to all men; and that salvation will make my heart rejoice, which has long been in pain because of sin. For the end, a Psalm of David. 13.

In the present psalm he sets out plainly the utter impiety and lawlessness of men's practices, in order to proclaim how necessary was the appearing of Christ. "The fool said in his heart, There is no God." Since, he says, they did not reckon that there is a God who watches over human affairs and judges with righteous judgment, they committed every kind of lawless deed; for this reason the Lord looked down from heaven. For this clearly signifies the Lord's coming forth to men. "There is none who does good, no, not one." When the Lord came, he says, he found not one worker of goodness, but everyone answerable for every wrongful deed. "Their throat is an open grave." For the demons held man in their own gullet like food, not realizing that God cannot forget his own creature. "Will not all who work lawlessness know?" This is to be read with a slight pause, and "the Lord" is to be supplied from outside, so that the meaning is: "And they have all turned aside, and have done this. They will not know the Lord." "They did not call upon the Lord, those who eat up my people as they eat bread." For they devoured his people by persuading them to worship the creation rather than the Creator. And these, he says, having become instigators of evil to others, will not call upon the Lord. For the future must be read in this way, in place of the past. "There they were afraid with fear, where there was no fear." The law of Moses, he says, brought punishment; but the fear of Christ is pure, for it prepared men to fear the Father as sons. At that time, he says, that is, plainly, the time of the appearing, they will fear with a fear where there is no fear: not, clearly, from the threat of the law, but rather the reverence that befits free men. "For the Lord is in the generation of the righteous": of those who are justified through his appearing. "The counsel of the poor is put to shame." This is said as to those who remained in unbelief and persecuted those who had believed in Christ. "Who will give the salvation of Israel out of Zion?" This contains a twofold prophecy: for it speaks not only of the deliverance that came at that time to the besieged, but also of the saving appearance of our Saviour, which came from there many ages later. "Jacob will rejoice." The holy [?]

He sings this psalm to teach what would prepare a man to attain that blessed lot; and so at the outset he says: "Lord, who will sojourn in your tabernacle?" Sojourning is a temporary way of life; it suggests not a settled life but one of passing through, in the hope of removal to better things. For it is the part of a holy man to pass through this life and to be led on to another life. That is why David too says of himself: "I am a sojourner with you and a stranger, as all my fathers were." Who, he says, will be worthy to be in those heavenly tabernacles? "Or who will dwell on your holy mountain?" For whoever is counted worthy of that blessed tabernacle will possess blessedness for endless ages. "He who walks blameless," and so on. He teaches by what means we shall reach that blessed end: first, if we travel the blameless way, which is Christ; next, if we work righteousness; third, if we make our heart a house of truth; fourth, if we do not acquire a deceitful tongue; fifth, not to do evil to one's neighbour; sixth, not to reproach one's neighbour in arrogance; seventh, not to show partiality; eighth, not to break faith with an oath; ninth, not to lend at interest; tenth, which is also the crown of all good, to be above bribery. Whoever has learned to accomplish these will have the gift of good things unshaken. An inscription on a pillar, for David. 15.

The prophecy before us contains the calling of the Gentiles, the charges against Israel for its disobedience, and indeed the very mystery of the resurrection of Jesus Christ, the Saviour of us all. Hence, I think, the song was named a "pillar inscription," since the prophet David set it up, as on a pillar, for those who came after him. The words in it are sung as from the person of Christ; for this is how Peter taught us to understand it. "Guard me, Lord, for I have hoped in you." Taking up, as it were, the common person of humanity, he addresses his words to God the Father: not indeed on his own behalf, but for our sake and on our behalf, as one of us, because of the dispensation. He therefore calls the Father "Lord" because he came to be in the form of a servant. And he asks to be guarded for the sake of the Church, which is his flesh. For the flesh

of Christ is the Church, and it is this that he asks to be guarded. Fittingly, then, the guarding may also be referred to his own person. "I said to the Lord, You are my God." Again he puts this forward too as one in the form of a servant; and at the same time he points to the righteousness that is in faith through confession. "For you have no need of my goods." By "goods" he means here the sacrifices offered according to the law; for the word of faith abolishes them. "For shall I eat," he says, "the flesh of bulls, or the blood of goats [?]"

"To the saints who are in his land the Lord has made wonderful all his wills among them." He says that the saints are those sanctified in the Spirit; Christ's land is the Church; "made wonderful" means "taught"; and "his" means the Father's; so that the whole runs thus: to those sanctified in faith he made known the will of the Father. That is why he is also called the Messenger of great counsel. ["To the saints in the land God has made wonderful." To those sanctified in faith he made known the will of the Father, "among them," that is, among those in God's land, the Church; or among some of those in the holy land; or because the saints, whose citizenship is in heaven, dwell in his land even while they are still in this land. The wills of God are the particular virtues, which God makes wonderful in his saints, since they have something more than other men in the practice of virtue. For the courage of apostles and martyrs is not the same as that of others who are brave, nor is the chastity of Joseph like that of others. And one who has been made wonderful in this way perceives his own weakness, as falling far short of the divine strength and greatness. For when the weaknesses of the righteous are multiplied, they hasten to God in repentance.] "Their weaknesses were multiplied": when they worshipped idols. "Afterwards they made haste." Though they were weak before, he says, being in sins, yet when they heard the preaching they quickly obeyed. For this is the meaning of "Afterwards they made haste": namely, to obey the preaching. "I will not gather their assemblies out of blood." Gathering assemblies from the Gentiles, he says, I will not gather them by means of blood; that is, I will not have them approach me through the worship of the law, but rather through praise and the unbloody Sacrifice. "Nor will I remember their names with my lips." They will no longer be called idolaters and godless, he says, but called and chosen. Formerly, he says, they bore titles that matched their deeds, being named idolaters and polytheists; but now I will no longer remember those names, calling them godly and holy, called and chosen. [?] for "righteousness" [?] "justification."

["Their weaknesses were multiplied." When they worshipped idols. Even if they are multiplied, they do not last; for they had them lasting only so far as to be felt, because they were strong in Christ who strengthened them. Or he seems to be speaking of the apostles and of those who believed through them, in whom the divine wonders were made manifest, since they kept all the divine commands. Their weaknesses, or to put it differently, their toils, were multiplied when many peoples, orators, generals and kings rose up against them; yet they overcame them all and finished the race. Or else the brevity and transience of afflictions shows the endless age [?]. "Not … assemblies." They made haste to obey the preaching; those who are to be gathered by Christ must be pure of murders and blood. Gathering assemblies from the Gentiles, he says, I will not gather them by means of blood, nor will I have them approach me through the worship of the law, but rather through praise and the unbloody sacrifice.] "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup," and so on. As if he were saying more plainly: My Father has given me the Gentiles as my lot and portion, he to whom I also became obedient unto death. For the cup signifies death, as it was said: "Father, if it is possible, let the cup pass from me [?]"

["The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup." He calls the kingdom of the Gentiles an inheritance. The portion of my Church, which is my inheritance, is the Lord, the Father; and he himself is also the portion of my cup, that is, of my death. The Church inherited the Father by fulfilling his commandments; and my death itself inherited the Father, according to the one who says: "Heir of God, fellow heir [?]"

"The measuring lines have fallen for me in the best places; for indeed my inheritance is most excellent to me." He means the bonds of love that he had toward the Church, which is also "most excellent," that is, pleasing to him. "I will bless the Lord who gave me understanding." The interpretation of this is found in the Acts of the Apostles. "And moreover even into the night my kidneys instructed me." It is the custom of divinely inspired Scripture to call hidden and deep thoughts "kidneys," and what is unseen "night." "I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand, that I may not be shaken." Insofar as he is understood as God, he is the one who supports and upholds all things; but insofar as he became man, it would also befit him to say that he had the Lord at his right hand so as not to be shaken. For everywhere he conforms himself

to the measures of humanity, and because of the dispensation he is not ashamed of what befits his self-emptying. See, then, how our nature has come to be approved in Christ. We who had been cast out because of the transgression in Adam have been brought before the face of the Father, and we have him defending and supporting us. ["He is at my right hand." This contains a plain refutation of the folly of the Jews. For Peter, the chief of the apostles, applied these words to Christ in the Acts. For insofar as he is God, he is the one who supports and upholds all things; but insofar as he is man, it would also befit him to have the Lord at his right hand, so as not to [?]

"You will not abandon my soul." Though he is himself life and the giver of life, he is said to be made alive by the Father because of the dispensation. "You have made known to me the ways of life." He who bears the person of humanity, as having become like us, offers up words that befit us rather than himself, insofar as he is understood as God.] "Delight is in your right hand to the end." This means that the saints will be in delights and gladness after they come back to life at the time of the resurrection. And this delight and gladness, which is incorruption, they say they will receive from Christ, who is among us and is also the right hand of the Father. That the saying is true is clear from the oracle that says: "Who will transform the form of our lowliness, to be conformed to the body of his [?]"

"Hear, Lord, my righteousness." The words are full of great confidence. He speaks of righteousness here not as boasting, nor as declaring himself righteous, but in this sense: as one who rightly asks your help and begs to be freed from what he suffers unjustly, persecuted by Saul without cause, both hear me and grant my request. [?] "Give ear to my prayer, which is not from deceitful lips." For God gives ear to a prayer offered not through deceitful lips but through a tongue that has been purified and is accustomed to meditate on the divine oracles. "Let my judgment come forth from your presence." He plainly prays that the Only-begotten be appointed his judge. "Let your eyes behold uprightness." He asks of the Son the just judgment which he gave for us. "You have tested my heart, you have visited it by night, you have tried me by fire, and no unrighteousness was found in me." Divine Scripture is accustomed to call blasphemy against God "unrighteousness": "For they spoke unrighteousness against the height," it says. "So that my mouth may not speak the works [?]

of men." He teaches that one must guard against this too, so as to utter nothing mortal or merely human. "Because of the words of your lips I have kept to hard ways." Because of your commands, he says, I set out on the narrow and hard-pressed [way]

"Make my steps firm in your paths." The verse teaches us not to trust in ourselves but to lean on God. [The paths of the Lord are the keeping of the commandments.] "I cried out, for you heard me, O God." "You heard" stands for "you will hear." Not in vain have I used these words, but because I have experienced your love for mankind; for you have often heard me when I called on you. "Incline your ear to me." God is wholly ear, since he hears all things. ["I cried out," and so on. I do not cry out in vain; but since you have often heard me, I ask to be heard now as well. A cry to God is also the intense [?]

["They shut up their fat." "Fat" signifies the enemies' very great prosperity.] "They set their eyes to turn aside to the ground." They had one aim, he says: to bring him down, as it were, to the earth and persuade him to set his mind on the things of the flesh. "Your sword from the enemies of your hand." Every righteous soul, and especially of those who draw sinners from impiety to godliness, is in a way a sword sharpened against the spirits of wickedness. This sword, then, O Master, he says, which you yourself sharpened against your enemies, rescue from the enemies of your hand. And who would the enemies of God's hand be, if not those who oppose faith in his Only-begotten, who is also his hand? "Lord, from the few from the earth, divide them." He prays that the ungodly be separated from the few, as it were divided off. And who are the few, if not those of whom it is said: "Many are called, but few are chosen"? "And with your hidden things their belly was filled." They enjoyed every precious thing, he says; which is why they kicked out so far as even to break the law. "Your hidden things" means: the punishments that you know in secret and I do not know, with these fill their bellies; "their bellies" being a periphrasis for "them." "They were satisfied with sons, and left the remainder to their infants." They were filled, he says, with every lawlessness, and handed it on to their children as well. [And they left it to the infants of their sons, that is, even to their descendants.] "But I shall appear in righteousness before your

face." I shall not be like them, he says, nor shall I be filled with the same things; but I shall be filled with your glory through righteous works. For the end, for the servant of the Lord, David, who spoke to the Lord the words of this song on the day when the Lord rescued him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul; and he said. 17. Argument. The psalm contains the uprising of enemies and an appeal to God for help, the descent of the Only-begotten and his ascension, and, after the ascension, what was done against the demons, the casting off of Israel and the calling of the Gentiles. And "from the hand of his enemies and from the hand of Saul" may be referred to the spiritual enemies and their ruler. "I will love you, Lord, my strength; the Lord is my firm foundation and my refuge." Perceiving God's benefits, he dedicates to him what is the greatest gift: love, I mean, which the Saviour also set first among the commandments. "With praise I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies." Here we are taught to give thanks for the good things already granted, and to ask again for what is still lacking. Then he recounts the many kinds of uprising by his enemies. "The pangs of death surrounded me." He mentions here, he says, no mortal war, but invisible powers encircling his soul within. "And torrents of lawlessness troubled me. The pangs of Hades encircled me; the snares of death overtook me." The torrents of lawlessness are lawless thoughts. These same thoughts are called pangs when they linger in us, and snares when they kill us through sin committed in act. "And the earth was shaken and trembled." He recounts what happened at that time, at the Lord's descent; for all who dwell on the earth were stirred, and every land was filled with the report about him. "And the foundations of the mountains were troubled." The mountains are evil powers that exalt themselves against the glory of God; by their foundations he means their deep thoughts. "And they were shaken, because God was angry with them": because for a long age they had deceived those on earth through the superstition of many gods. "Smoke went up in his anger." Being angry, he says, he quenched their fire, with which they had long set men ablaze; and he sets down the smoke as a symbol of this. "And fire will blaze forth from his face." For these things the Son of God works invisibly against the opposing powers, quenching their fire with another fire, better and mightier. [For when the demons saw the Lord, they were burned at his coming, from his face.] "Coals were kindled by him": those who were enlightened by sharing in the divine fire.

And he bowed the heavens, and came down. Acontius [?]: He prophesies the descent of the Lord. It would signify the saying: "He humbled himself unto death." And darkness was under his feet. This shows the hiddenness of his journey in the dispensation, and the invisibility of God, so that we may not be drawn by what he has said into bodily notions. He mounted upon cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds. By these words he shows his ascension. [?] By cherubim and wings of the winds he means the cloud [which took him up; or the swiftness of his appearing, the speed of his presence and help], about which it is written in the Acts: "And having said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him up out of their sight." And he made darkness his hiding place. That is, the invisible and hidden sojourn of the Saviour among men. Around him was his tent. By his tent he signifies the holy Church, in which he has promised to dwell. "Around him," he says, in accordance with the saying: "Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst." Dark water in the clouds of the air. He says this because the words about him lie obscurely in the prophets, who were also called clouds. From the brightness before him the clouds passed. The light of his appearing, he says, made the prophecies plain. [And since threats too are contained in the prophetic words, he hinted at these through the hail and the coals. Or thus: from the brilliance of the preaching, the apostles, passing before him, watered the world like clouds. And the hailstones are forms of punishment that repel the unbelievers.] Hail and coals of fire. By these he signifies what befell the enemies after his ascension, the spiritual enemies, I mean. Just as, when freeing Israel from the Egyptians, he rained down hail and fire, so also, when freeing all the nations from slavery to the demons, he rained down hail and coals of fire. These would be punishing powers, by which he brought down the spiritual Egyptians. And the springs of the waters were seen. After the destruction of the enemies the springs of the waters were seen: that is, the saving word of the Gospel, which has also become the foundation of the world, for upon it we have been built up. Or also thus: by springs you will understand the holy prophets, since they gush forth the saving word. For so it is written about them: "And you will draw water with joy from the springs of salvation." And by the foundations of the world, the Scripture of the all-wise Moses. For we have found in it, laid down first, the base of faith and of the knowledge of God, travailing with the mystery of Christ in types together with the prophets. So "were seen" stands for "were made manifest." Or else by springs you will understand also

and by foundations of the world under heaven, the holy apostles; for they too gush forth the saving word, and they laid down faith as a base for the world under heaven. Again, by springs of waters and foundations of the world you will understand saving baptism. At your rebuke, O Lord. We must supply: the aforementioned enemies were destroyed. At the blast of the breath of your wrath. God does not punish sinners immediately, for then they would perish utterly; rather, he announces beforehand the punishments of his wrath: "For I will chastise them in the wrath of their affliction." And this is his breathing out the breath of his wrath. He took me from many waters. By waters he means temptations. [From many waters. By waters he means temptations. David says: He took [?] me, that is, human nature; for on the day of Pentecost about three thousand souls were baptized by the apostles.] He will rescue me from my mighty enemies, and from those who hate me. He has passed on to what he did concerning his sin and his repentance. What he says is this: Already the Lord, having heard my confession, has become my support when I was about to be overturned and to suffer a great fall, had I fallen after my sin into total apostasy. But more than that, he will rescue me completely, granting forgiveness of my sin at the prophesied time of his coming; and the Lord will do this as my benefactor, because he desired me. For if he had not desired me, he would not have sent his prophet to me. And the Lord will repay me. I am persuaded, he says, that at the time of his righteous judgement he will not remember my sins, but will repay me according to my righteousness. For when he sets my other deeds, done in righteousness, against my sin as on a scale and weighs them against it, he will find them far outweighing the sin I committed. The passage teaches that one who has slipped through some weakness can recover himself through subsequent good deeds. [By righteousness he means virtue in general; by purity of hands, the practical life: practical activities that have become undefiled because they are performed from the best disposition.]

[For all his judgements, and what follows. Those who have slipped must recover themselves through subsequent good deeds. And even if his judgements are unsearchable and like an abyss because they are incomprehensible, yet all of them are before the one who loves God.] With the holy you will be holy. Fittingly you have deemed me worthy of your kindness, since, being just, you know how to be holy with the holy. For if I had remained in sin and suffered total perversion, I know that you yourself, the great judge, would have brought upon my sin a judgement to match it. But since I kept your ways, for this reason you, being holy with the holy and innocent with the innocent, have not dealt with me according to the perversion that befell me at one time; rather, according to my life afterwards and my conduct in righteousness you will grant me my reward in your court. For you will save a humble people. He refers this to the choir of the apostles. And you will humble the eyes of the proud. This points to the Pharisees and scribes. For you will light my lamp, O Lord. He means the mind. My God, you will illumine my darkness. You will scatter, he says, the ignorance that is in me. For in you I will be rescued from trial, and in my God I will leap over a wall. For my enemies surrounded me, he says, to shut me in. [By trial he means pleasures, and by the wall the devil.] My God, his way is blameless. Here, he says, he censures the senselessness, the wickedness, the disobedient mind and the hardness of the senseless, ungrateful and hard-hearted Jews, since they attacked our Saviour Christ as one acting against the divine law. And indeed they also reviled his words and slandered him

as a blasphemer, saying to one another: "He blasphemes. For who can forgive sins?" Out of an evil conscience and wicked reasoning they thought these things against the Lord and God of all, reasoning [?] what they reasoned. [His words are tried in the fire. And his words about this are like silver tried in the fire, pure of every reproach, tested and proven.] For who is God besides the Lord? Or who is God except our God? For the Word of God is alone true God, and for this reason also Only-begotten, because he alone is [?] as the Father is. Having spoken of Christ [?] as God by nature, he now says, "Or who is God?", saying that, besides him, there is only the Father. "But for us there is one God, the Father." For there is no other God, such that one might grant this request and the other that one. Perhaps he has also set out the two following verses in parallel. Thus, he says, the true God, as I trusted, girded me with power to conquer, and made my path unharmed in what had to be done.] God who girds me with power. Similar is the saying: "Until you are clothed with power from on high." And he made my way blameless. That is, through the Gospel oracles he has prepared me to run a blameless way. And setting me upon the high places. That is, he teaches me to set my mind on the things above. [Perfecting my feet. For the saints are destroyers of the venomous passions; for they received power against the spiritual serpents, and for this reason they are likened to deer, for deer too destroy physical serpents. Like a deer: for they received authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy.] Teaching my hands for war. For by stretching them out in prayer I overcome my foes. [?] And you made my arms a bronze bow. Having made the powers of the soul manly, like a bronze bow. By the bronze he shows their vigour and invulnerability, and by the bow the arrows symbolically shot from our arms. [Teaching my hands for war. Teaching me to be successful in battle, and setting my arms like a bow, as if making them bronze in strength. Or he means that he made the powers of the soul manly like a bronze bow. Bronze is a symbol of the practical life: "For he has destroyed your bronze," says Ezekiel to Jerusalem.] And you gave me the shield of salvation. You shielded me, he says, by your salvation. And this is the sojourn of the dispensation.

[And your discipline set me upright. By discipline he means the Gospel; or by discipline he means the instruction that comes from the law. It is as if he says: benefiting me in every way, you have also given laws, through which I was taught what is right. For learning from them that one must not do wrong, I refrained from it. But so that I might not be harmed again by such leniency [?], you surround me with sufficient help, granting me enlargement. Or by discipline he means instructive teaching, as in "Take hold of discipline"; or laborious training, as in "Do not make light of the discipline of the Lord."] And your right hand upheld me. The right hand of the Father is the Son. And your discipline set me upright to the end. That is, evidently, the Gospel teaching. And your discipline itself will teach me. "And your discipline itself will teach me" is Theodotion's rendering, in place of "Your discipline set me upright to the end," as the Seventy have it. You enlarged my steps. For you set my feet upon a rock, which is our faith. And my footprints did not weaken. For by removing the stumbling blocks and the snares that the enemies had prepared, he made our journey sound. [You enlarged my steps. By removing, he says, the stumbling blocks and the snares that the enemies had prepared, you made my journey free. He speaks of steps inasmuch as one steps across from vice to virtue. At first these steps are toilsome for one who walks the narrow way, but with progress they are widened. For when one receives rest after the labours of virtue, the footprints are strengthened; for he set our feet upon a rock.] I will pursue my enemies. As one prepared for the race by divine grace, he is confident of victory. I will crush them, and they will not be able to stand. Dispassion accomplishes the crushing of the enemies. And you girded me with power. Again he ascribes the whole of the victory to the one who gave the strength. And you made my enemies turn their backs to me. That is, you put them to flight; for it is characteristic of those who flee to turn their backs. Our enemies the demons turn their backs when they can no longer cast passionate thoughts into the soul. And you destroyed those who hate me. Saul, Ahithophel, Absalom and countless others. They cried out, and there was none to save them. He says these things about the physical enemies, as if in the person of the Lord. For neither did the foreigners, when they called on their own gods for help, enjoy any providence from them, nor did Saul and Absalom and Shim-

ei and the rest of the enemies of the Israelites have God as their ally. And I will grind them fine like dust. They will vanish completely, he says, since your grace works together with me. Rescue me from the contradictions of the people. The person is still that of the Lord, who turns away because of the disobedience of the Jews and asks for the nations as his inheritance. You will make me head of the nations. But we do not know of David ever reigning over the nations; therefore the prophecy is fulfilled through the one born from him according to the flesh. For the one born from him according to the flesh, who is himself also named David according to the divine Ezekiel, the Master, I mean, Christ, reigned over all the nations. As God he always rules over all things, but after the incarnation he also received the willing service of those who believed in him. A people whom I did not know served me. [This too is of Christ; for turning away from the disobedient Jews, he asks for the nations as his inheritance.] This does not signify ignorance, for as God he knows all things. It means that those who at various times did not obtain kinship with me would be aliens and strangers, far removed from kinship with me. Foreign sons lied to me. Israel, who was called the firstborn son, was called a foreign son because of his unbelief. Foreign sons grew old. All that grows old is near to vanishing. The Lord lives, and blessed is my God. He fittingly cried out, "The Lord lives," since he had mentioned the contradiction of the people, when they shouted: "Away with him, away with him; crucify him!" And let the God of my salvation be exalted. Even if he humbled himself, he says, taking the form of a slave, yet he is exalted. Similar to this is the saying: "God highly exalted him, and gave him the name that is above every name." God, who grants me vengeance. That is, evidently, on the unbelieving people of the Jews. And who subjects peoples under me. The nations, he says, were subjected to Christ. My deliverer from my enemies. He means the rulers of the people of Israel. From those who rise up against me. He means Judas. [My deliverer from my wrathful enemies. From the unbelieving people. The wrathful enemies are the Jewish people, who mocked him as a Samaritan. And the unjust man is Judas, or Pilate, who punished him without cause. Therefore, because of your benefits to me, I will give you thanks among all, whether Jews or nations, and I will keep your name in hymns.] Therefore I will confess you among the nations, O Lord. Since you have done such and such things, I, says the prophet, when you yourself, the Lord, call the nations,

will confess you through them [?], as they sing the hymns that I have made. And not only this, but I will also magnify, he says, the salvations of the king of these nations, the salvation that he wrought in the midst of the earth. "I will magnify" means: I will proclaim it splendidly to all. Since he wrought this too, he says, showing mercy to his anointed people; for we were anointed into a royal priesthood. And as you show mercy to the people and to me, David, you will cause it to come to him and to my seed. For the people from the nations is also the seed of David, since it has become the child of the one born of the seed of David according to the flesh. For the end. A Psalm of David. 18.

The present psalm contains introductory teaching addressed to the nations in the person of the apostles. Therefore they say that the heaven and the sun and the other elements, which the nations considered great gods, sing the praises of their maker. The heavens declare the glory of God. Similar is the saying: "For his invisible attributes, both his eternal power and divinity, have been clearly seen since the creation of the world, being understood through the things that are made." Day to day pours forth speech, and night [to night proclaims knowledge].
