The day and the night, he says, yielding their courses to one another in good order and harmony, proclaim their creator through the very facts. There are no speeches nor words. This is to be read with a pause. He meets an objection and cuts it short; the objection is: "But surely they do not speak?" So he says: Are there not some things which, though they utter no sound, proclaim their craftsman? Yes indeed; for the skill of the shipwright is evident from a well-fitted ship, and the same holds in other cases. So the works mentioned above likewise proclaim their creator by their size, beauty and harmony, so that their proclamation has run through the whole world. In the sun he set his tent. For the sun, he says, he set a tent, that is, a house. And where did he set it, if not in the heaven and firmament mentioned above? This house he also called a bridal chamber. Just as day and night proclaim the creator by their ordered concord, so also the sun, by running its course with a certain harmony, shows the power of the one who commands it. The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls. That is, evidently, the Gospel law. Those from the nations, having already been taught by the aforementioned elements that the creator is one, are next taught the Gospel law as well, so that the souls of all the nations are converted to the truth. The testimony of the Lord is faithful, making infants wise. That is, the testimony that the Only-begotten bore about himself: "I have come as light into the world"; and, "I came forth from the Father, and I have come"; and, "I am the [?]

[Making infants wise: confirming the apostles. Or by infants he means those who have become infants in Christ, [?] the foolish, and men inexperienced in wisdom.] The ordinances of the Lord are right, gladdening the heart. That is, the justification that took place at our judgement. For having judged our case, he cast out the ruler of this age, giving us gladness in our hearts. The commandment of the Lord is radiant, enlightening the eyes. He means the eyes of the understanding, since the commandment sends out its radiance from afar. The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever and ever. This is said in contrast with the fear of the law, for that fear was punitive. Our purity [?] is abstinence from sins. Therefore it is called pure fear, because it makes people pure; for through the fear of the Lord, he says, one turns away from evil. And this fear, being eternal, makes those in whom it arises eternal too. In keeping them there is great reward. For the reward of keeping them is what eye has not seen and ear has not heard, and [what has not entered] into the heart of man

[For indeed your servant keeps them. The new people, initiated into the mysteries by the Gospel law, having said that it also keeps the true judgements, sends up a prayer to be found pure in the reasoning of its understanding, and likewise to be rescued from the demons within.] [?] For the end. A Psalm of David. 19. Argument. The psalm is spoken in the person of David's companions, praying for David himself as he offers sacrifice. But it is also referred to the person of [?]. May the Lord hear you in the day of affliction. May [?] be added to you [?]; may he shelter you and guard you. May he send you help from the holy place, and from Zion may he support you. These things might be said for the consolation of one who is despondent, either by the Word dwelling in the soul or by the Holy Spirit. One who is afflicted needs prayer and must not cast away his hopes; in this way God becomes attentive. We will rejoice in your salvation. The Son is the salvation of the Father in the world; the cross is the salvation of the Son in the world. [We will rejoice in your salvation. The salvation, he says, that you have given to the human race you have made manifest to all through your resurrection.]

[?] May the Lord fulfil all your requests. What were his requests, if not "Holy Father, keep them from the world"? Clearly he means those who believe in him. [Or he means David or Hezekiah, for this is said of priests and kings; or it is said because of the Lord's dispensation in the flesh and his resurrection; or also because, when we are saved, he says that he himself is saved, since we are his members, being one body. This is why he also said "now": for at present we know Christ as saved, in that from now on we receive the pledge of salvation. And you saved by the might of your right hand. By right hand he means the deeds, the great powers, the help; he foretells the divine signs of Christ.] Now I know that the Lord has saved his Christ. He says this as one already enlightened by the Spirit about the things concerning the

In the mighty acts of the salvation of his right hand. He saved us, he says, by working great powers. For here he signifies the deeds, because [?] he stretches out the powers of his right hand to those who approach him. [They, he says, trusting in these things, fell; but we, armed in the name of the Lord, were saved.] And here again he speaks of a right hand in human fashion, giving this name to the divine activity. Some in chariots, and some in horses. Just as, when he saved Israel from the physical Egyptians, he cast Pharaoh's chariots and his army into the sea, so also, when he saved the race of all mankind from the spiritual Egyptians, he shattered their chariots. O Lord, save the king. Therefore, having enjoyed such great help, we beseech you, Master, that both we ourselves and our king may share in it continually. For the end. A Psalm of David. 20.

The king's companions mentioned before also send up this psalm, as he is already rejoicing because of the salvation born to the world from his seed. For this was what he longed for in his soul and prayed to receive. When it was given, it became for him like a crown of precious stone, glorifying his head; for David is glorified among all the nations together with his own Lord and son according to [?]

[?] …he will have, it says, unending gladness of countenance as well, that is, by obtaining your favor. And the cause of these things for him was his trust in you. "You will gladden him with joy with your countenance." The countenance of the Father is the Son. "He who has seen me," he says, "has seen the Father." With him we are to rejoice in heaven, like groomsmen with the bridegroom. "For the king hopes in the Lord, and in the mercy…" One who enjoys your grace is stronger than those who make war on him. And he enjoys it by trusting in no human being, relying on hope in you alone. "May your hand be found by all your enemies." These words are addressed to the Lord himself, because of what was done against him by the Jewish people. [He says that he will hunt down those who have sinned. For if the love of God is made perfect in the one who keeps the commandments, it is clear that the one who does not keep them hates; and such a one is also said to have perished.] "For you will make them like a furnace of fire at the time of your presence." That is, you will show them to be partakers of fire. For this is what they have stored up for themselves at your second appearing, when you render to each according to his works. "The Lord in his wrath will throw them into confusion, and fire will devour them." By "wrath" he means the punishment that will come upon them for their outrage against him. "Their fruit you will destroy from the [earth]." That is, their wicked words and thoughts. These are the plots they devised, which were also done away with through the resurrection. [He means their teachings and godless doctrines, which God, being good, hands over to destruction after their death.] "And their seed from among the sons of men." It is a kindness to be rid of sins and wicked thoughts. For a wicked thought is the seed of sin. "For you will make them a back." Symmachus translated it this way: "For you will make them turned away," that is, behind, following after the Gentiles. "Among your remnants you will prepare their face." You have left them, he says, a time for turning back to repent. And this is the calling and the turning back that comes after the fullness of the Gentiles. [You will make the Jews who disbelieved [?]. Those from whom God turns away he makes a back, unable to be a face, so that by perceiving his back parts through the things he has made they may again be brought up to him. For those who are unable to see his face, because they do not have a pure heart, he appoints to perceive his back parts, the created works that come after him, so that by contemplating creation they may gain some notion of him, and, drawing near to their God, may see the face of God. And the remnants of God are the things above the created things of the

…he prays that his coming may take place for this reason: "We will sing and make music to your mighty acts." For then every soul of the righteous, having come to the dwelling places above, sends up spiritual worship.] For the end, concerning the morning help: a Psalm of David. 21.

The present psalm is sung concerning the morning help. That is, the only-begotten Word of God freed us from a long night and gloom when he shone upon us as a dawn from on high, as it is written. Or else by "morning help" he means the time of the Savior's resurrection. For he rose at early dawn, opening for human nature the road to incorruption. Christ sings the psalm in the person of humanity. And he plainly sets out for us what was done to him by the Jews at the time of the cross. "O God, my God, attend to me; why have you forsaken me?" He asks for the Father's watchful care, transferring our condition to himself so that [?] [for we were the ones formerly forsaken, but now taken up and saved. He says these things so that, and so on] he might put an end to the curse and turn the Father's face toward us. For we are the ones who became an object of aversion and abandonment through the transgression in Adam. "Far from salvation are the words of my transgressions." Consider again, I ask you, the person of humanity in Christ pleading to be freed from its stumblings, that is, from its transgressions and the words concerning them. And it is clear that this concerns the righteousness befitting each [?]. {"O God, my God." The Savior says these things in the person of humanity, in place of: "My God,"

"My God, I will cry out by day, and you will not hear, and by night, and it is not as folly for me." This should be read with a pause. It signifies to us that the fruit of prayer is not without profit. For it says: "It is not as folly for me." That is, I know clearly that I will cry out, and he will hear. Since indeed, dwelling among the holy who have their minds fixed on you, you become their praise and glory. "But you dwell in the holy place, O praise of Israel." That is, the one praised by Israel; or the one who is himself praise. "In you our fathers hoped; they hoped, and you delivered them." He calls the patriarchs and the prophets his fathers according to the flesh. He also shows the gain that comes from hope. ["In you our fathers hoped." Those also who were before me according to the flesh, that is, the prophets, waited for you, looking for my shining forth, and they were not disappointed in their hope; and likewise the patriarchs.] "But I am a worm, and not a man." He teaches us to be hum-

-ble-minded, especially when we approach God. "A reproach of men and despised by the people." The evangelist plainly says that these things were done to him at the time of the cross, when those passing by wagged their heads at him and blasphemed him, saying: "If you are the Son of God, save yourself." "For you are the one who drew me out of the womb." He says this because he became man by the good pleasure of the Father. "For when," it says, "the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of a woman." For he also names his own Father as his hope, and says this as a man. For God drew Christ alone out of Mary; other human beings are not drawn out but come out. For "Esau came out," it says, [?] "whose skin was hairy." "Upon you I was cast from the womb; from my mother's belly," and so on. Again he prays as in the person of humanity. For the band of disciples had in fact abandoned him. Then he foretells the kinds of affliction. "Many young bulls surrounded me." He means the rulers of the Jews. "I was poured out like water, and all my bones were scattered." By his bones he means the holy initiators into the mysteries; for if the Church is his body, those who hold it together may fittingly be understood as bones. And we have heard from the evangelist that when he was arrested by the cohort of soldiers, the disciples were scattered. And another interpretation: The bones of wisdom are the holy doctrines of the Church, which the Jews were commanded by law not to break at the Passover: "For you shall not break a bone of it," it says. "My heart became like melting wax." What is said here is characteristic of grief; for it is written: "He began to be grieved and distressed." He grieved over the Jewish nation and over the betrayer, because they were being given over to destruction for their impiety toward him. ["And all my bones were scattered." Scattered and dispersed, he says, were those who until then, ranked as bones, made up the company around the teacher; for the disciples left him and fled, like water let loose over a plain.] "My strength was dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue has stuck to my throat." By these words he signifies the thirst that came upon him on the precious cross, when he asked to drink and they brought him vinegar mixed with gall. [That is why he says: "And my tongue has stuck to my throat."] "And you brought me down into the dust of death." For by the grace of God he tasted death for everyone. For Christ was brought down not into death but into the dust of death; for his soul was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. "For many dogs surrounded me." Again he means the rulers. "They dug through my hands and my feet." He says this because of the nails of the cross. [?]

"They counted all my bones." Presumably they felt over his whole body and measured each of the bones, to see where the nails should be driven. "But they looked and gazed upon me." That is, they mocked me. He says this because of the scarlet cloak, the crown of thorns, and the reed in place of a scepter. "They divided my garments among themselves." This was plainly recorded in the Gospels. "But you, O Lord, do not keep your help far from me." He turns his words to prayer. [With you helping and supporting me, he says, I will rise on the third day and show their plot to be in vain.] He became a pattern for us of how we must call upon God in temptations, and not fall into despondency or lose heart under afflictions. "Deliver my soul from the sword." By these things, the sword, the hand of the dog, the lion, and the horns of the unicorns, he signifies the malice and folly of the Jews. "And my only one from the hand of the dog." He calls what was done by this dog its hand, and calls the man himself a dog; for "It is not good," he says, "to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs." [The sword might also be the devil, who is always trying to wound. He calls his soul "only one" because it is set apart and separated from other souls; for all of those knew sin, but it did not; and because it alone always has union with God the Word according to the hypostasis, together with the flesh. For Christ is one from two opposites, perfect God and perfect man. Those other souls he visits only at intervals. Perhaps he also calls the Church presented to him his "only one," because it has no spot or wrinkle, being filled up by degrees from the blameless, from the sixty queens and eighty

"Save me from the mouth of the lion, and my lowliness from the horns of the unicorns. I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will sing your praise." For he taught us that his Father is God by nature and in truth, and of one substance with him. [?] Again, as man he is united through the Church. "You who fear the Lord, praise him; all the seed of Jacob, glorify him." For since the Church is made up of both Gentiles and Jews, he rouses both the one and the other to the hymn, naming the one group after their forefather, Jacob and Israel, and the other after their virtue, as being enough to adorn them in place of lineage. So too it was customary to call Gentiles who came over to the Law "Jews." The history of the Acts teaches us this; for the divine Apostle, addressing the people, spoke thus: "Men of Israel, and those among you who fear the

"For he has not despised." He clearly teaches what the Only-begotten accomplished for us through himself. "From you is my praise." By praise he means glorification; and this can be seen coming from the Father when a voice came from above saying: "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again." [Or else: just as I made you known to men, so you too surely render the same honor to me, at one time saying, "This is my Son," at another revealing it to Peter and the rest.] "I will pay my vows." In divine Scripture a promise is called a vow; so the fulfillment of obedience rendered by the Son to the Father even to death may likewise be understood as the vow paid by him to the Father. [In divine Scripture a promise is called a vow; so the fulfillment of obedience rendered by the Son to the Father, and that even to the death of the flesh, may likewise be understood as the vow paid by him to the

"The poor will eat and be satisfied." These words signify the proclamation of the calling of the Gentiles. "And all the families of the nations will worship before him." He is said to reign over those on earth, although as God he is King of all, because he turned them from the error of the demons to faith in him, and to right-mindedness and righteousness. "For the kingdom is the Lord's, and he rules over the nations." For God is not the God of the Jews only, as they suppose, but the maker of all human nature. The Apostle also says this: "Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also, since God is one, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith." "All the fat ones of the earth ate and worshiped." The spiritual food, that is. He calls them fat because of the rich nourishment of the divine oracles. "Before him will fall all who go down to the earth." He says this because those who believe bend the knee to him. And these believers were formerly those going down to the earth, that is, those who had fallen into ruin and corruption because they did not know the Lord. "And my soul lives for him, and my seed will serve him." For the life that Christ lived in the flesh on earth was holy and blameless. For he alone did no sin, though he became like us and took on flesh that is prone to sin. The seed of God may be understood as those called through him by faith. "The generation to come will be proclaimed to the Lord." These words too refer to the Gentiles.

"To a people yet to be born, whom the Lord has made." Similar is the saying: "Not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, but they were born of God." A Psalm of David. 22. Argument. The present psalm is sung in the person of the Gentiles, who exult that the Lord shepherds them. And they also describe a mystical feast, which the one who shepherds them has himself set before them. "The Lord shepherds me." Those whom the Lord shepherds take great pride in him. "In a place of green pasture, there he has made me dwell." He made me dwell amid the beauty of the grass, meaning grass for the mind. "By the water of rest he has nourished me." The water of rest may be understood as that of holy baptism, since it wipes away the burden of sins. [These things he provided for me, he says, first taking care of my soul and turning me from the trackless waste to travel the straight road.] "He has turned back my soul." Turning my soul back to himself from captivity to the devil, he guided it onto his commandments, from death to life. [As one who had formerly neglected his own soul, but had restored himself through the food just mentioned and was turning back from death, he says: "He has turned back my soul" onto paths of righteousness; he means the Gospel doctrines. "If I walk in the midst of the shadow of death" is spoken as to the Father. And he calls Christ himself the rod of power, the glorious rod, and the rod of majesty. As a rod disciplines, so too the practical life teaches moderation of the passions.] He means the Gospel doctrines. "Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me." He means Christ himself. Compare also: "The Lord will send forth for you a rod of power from Zion." And: "a glorious rod," and "a rod of majesty." The rod is the power that disciplines; the staff is the support given through comfort. "You have anointed my head with oil." This too is the mystical chrism. "And your cup, which makes me drunk." Again he means the mystical gladness. "And your mercy will pursue me all the days." For those who partake of all the things mentioned above will be in God's mercy for ever; and indeed they will also dwell in his house. ["You have prepared a table before me." He means the mystical table; the oil is the mystical chrism; and he speaks of the cup.] For the end: a Psalm of David, on the first day of the week. 23.
[?] The present psalm proclaims to us the ascension of the Lord, and also teaching for the Gentiles: how they too may become worthy of the heavenly tabernacles.

"The earth is the Lord's, and its fullness." By these words he proclaims the kingship that the only-begotten Word of God exercised over the Gentiles when he came to dwell among us. "He founded it upon the seas." So that none of the enemies might suppose that the earth belongs to Satan and that Christ has only now come to reign over it, he shows that Christ is its maker. At the same time he also reveals his power, in that so great a mass of earth has been made firm upon waters. "And upon the rivers he prepared it." That is, he set it in order. [For the Church gains a firm foundation when, though the waves beat against it, it remains unshaken in faith. "And upon the rivers": so that the rivers too make their courses unhindered, mountains and groves are allotted for life, and lands and plains are set apart for people as homes and farmland.] "Who will ascend to the mountain of the Lord?" Having set out the faith, he also explains the teaching about works, so that through both we who hear may attain the true inheritance. "Innocent in hands and pure in heart." This was discussed in the fourteenth psalm. "Who has not taken his soul in vain." By vanity he means arrogance. "And has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbor. He will receive a blessing." Whoever has become innocent in hands and pure in heart, and has not sworn deceitfully, he promises will receive gifts from God, namely blessing and mercy. "This is the generation of those who seek the Lord." He means the generation that has kept the things mentioned above. "Lift up your gates, O rulers." The angels who ministered to the Savior on earth, as he is taken up, tell the heavenly powers to open

["The Lord, strong and mighty." The powers are astonished to see him with flesh animated by a rational soul; that is why they ask.] "Who is this King of glory?" The powers above ask this, struck with amazement at the wonder of the dispensation. "The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory." The angels who ascended with him initiate those above into the mystery: that he who trampled down the enemies, the spiritual ones, that is, is himself the Lord of hosts. (8) The Ambrosian manuscript adds: "This has been spoken of in [?]"

In the present psalm the person of each of those who have been called is brought forward; that is, of those [?] gathered together to be directed toward the spiritual life. These words should be said at a time of martyrdom. "To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul." They say this as people who have already turned away from idolatry. "Nor let my enemies laugh me to scorn." The spiritual enemies, that is. The enemy is the devil, with the demons and impious people. Perhaps he also foresees the Savior's incarnation, after which the enemies' talk [laughter] has also ceased. [I became to the lawless as one lawless; for this lawlessness did not come about in vain.] "For indeed none who wait for you will be put to shame." He affirms this on the strength of those who have already trusted in God and become illustrious, because he is confident that he will obtain what he prays for. "Let those who act lawlessly without cause be put to shame." He says this about those still held fast in idolatry. ["Let those who act lawlessly be put to shame": on the strength of those who have already trusted in God and become illustrious, because he is confident that he will obtain what he prays for. "Those who act lawlessly without cause" [?] are strong. This is about those still held fast in idolatry.] "Make your ways known to me, O Lord." He means the Gospel doctrines. "Guide me to the truth." He says this as one who has not yet reached the truth. "And teach me that you are God my Savior." When the prophet prays this way, as one who has not yet known the ways of the Lord nor been taught to walk in his paths, not yet guided to the truth of God nor taught about God as Savior, who will not take heed of the saying, "Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and clever in their own sight"? "Do not remember the sins of my youth and of my ignorance." By youth he means folly. And the time of their idolatry was plainly folly. Another interpretation: the sins of the people in Egypt; for they practiced idolatry there. So do not now remember those sins, but remember your love for humankind, by which even then, when they were ignorant, you showed them kindness and had mercy on them. "For the sake of your goodness, O Lord." For I beg to obtain this not because of my own worthiness but because of your love for humankind. "Therefore he will give a law to sinners in the way." He will enlighten sinners; he will show a way to those who sin. "All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth." For those who are continually nourished on the divine words learn precisely through them that all the dispensations of the Savior Christ our God are in mercy and truth; and this is said in the person of the whole people, asking to be freed from captivity.

[?] are blended together. For to those who repent of their offences he holds out mercy and pardon, while the undefeated athletes of virtue he proclaims victors and crowns, delivering his verdict in truth. [?] And on those who have lived their lives in lawlessness and have not made use of repentance he brings punishments, according to the bounds of truth. [And his seed shall inherit the land. The deeds, he says, that won him the inheritance of the intelligible land will be the seed of good men; by these he means those who are begotten according to God. Look upon me. For we must not lie back and recline at ease, relying on God's mercy; we too must contribute the labour that comes through works

The Lord is the strength of those who fear him, and his covenant will make it known to them. The Gospel covenant. And what will it make known? The way of salvation. For all of God's legislation, he says, looks to this: to bring the good into the enjoyment of what they have chosen. For this is what he means by "will make known to them", that is, "will establish them in the enjoyment of what they have chosen." The afflictions of my heart have been multiplied. I am surrounded on every side, he says, by many sorrows. So weigh this humiliation and misery of mine against my transgressions; grant remission and bestow pardon. Bring me out of my distresses. Out of the continual

See my humiliation and my toil. For we must not lie back and recline at ease, relying on God's mercy; we must contribute the labour that comes through works. See my enemies, that they have been multiplied. He appeals for mercy on the ground of his enemies' injustice as well.

The innocent and the upright clung to me. This too is a mark of virtue: to hate the company of the wicked, and to keep as companions and friends those who honour fairness and practise uprightness. The prophet said that he had done this, since he believed that in this way he was serving the Master. For the end. A Psalm of David. 25.

The speakers introduced are those who have believed in Christ, who disown, and vigorously protest against, any established fellowship with the Jews who gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ
Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence. By innocence he means having no share in the wickedness and the madness of the Jews. And trusting in the

Lord, I shall not grow weak. I shall have a firm footing, he says, since I have entrusted my hopes of salvation to you. Prove me, O Lord, and try me. If you examine the depths of my soul, he says, you will find all the labour of my mind resting on your mercy alone. And by doing this I shall be well-pleasing to you, since I have loved your truth. I have not sat with a council of vanity. Before him who knows how to search hearts, he clearly disowns the council of the most lawless rulers of the Jewish nation. I will wash my hands among the innocent. I shall be clean, he says, of their bloodthirsty deeds. And I will go around your altar, O Lord. In these words he clearly proclaims spiritual worship. O Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house. [I long, he says, to see the divine house that shines with your grace.] The beauty of the house is those who are distinguished in the Church through godliness. Do not destroy my soul along with the ungodly. He prays to be kept clear of the punishment laid up for the Jews. In whose hands are iniquities; their right hand is filled with bribes. Either because they too perverted justice with bribes, or because they bought the traitor with gifts; or else because they grasped eagerly at lawlessness, and therefore filled their right hand with gifts. A Psalm of David, before he was anointed. [?]

The psalm contains a declaration [?] against his enemies, based on what he already knew he had received from God, and a request for further blessings, together with thanksgiving. The words "before he was anointed" signify this: having foreseen by the divine Spirit that he would be anointed king but would fall into trials, he girded his loins with courage [?] and firmly asserts that he will hold out very well against the dangers. The Lord is my light and my Saviour; whom shall I fear? He looks down with contempt on the opposing powers, trusting in the light of the Lord. Enlightened by you, he says, I despise all who make war on me together [?]

When evildoers drew near against me. They came, he says, wanting to destroy me, but suffered what they had hoped to do. That I may dwell in the house of the Lord. For the request was fitting for a saint and worthy of God to grant. That I may behold the delight of the Lord. In this house, he says, I pray to dwell for ever, the house in which I also obtained salvation. He has lifted me up on a rock. Paul clearly affirms that the rock is Christ. I will sing and make music to the Lord. He clearly proclaims the worship of the "Holy, holy, holy." Hear my voice, O Lord. That is: I thank you for what is past, and I will pray for what is to come. Give me a law, O Lord, in your way. He prays that the Gospel law be laid open to him; for He himself was also the straight way. And iniquity has lied to itself. That is, the iniquity directed against us has grown weak. I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. He means the Jerusalem above. A Psalm of David. 27.

He sings the present psalm in the person of those who have believed in Christ, calling on God for help through supplication. At the same time it contains a curse on the madness of the Jews and a prayer to be separated from their worse portion. To you, O Lord, I will cry ... and I shall become like those who go down into the pit. It is the custom of divine Scripture to call Hades a pit. Do not drag me away with sinners. By sinners he means the Jewish nation, in keeping with what the Saviour said to them: "If you do not believe that I am he, you will die in your sins." And they are also the ones who work iniquity, because they killed the innocent and righteous one, whom the law commanded them not to kill. Who speak peace with their neighbours. He says this because, while calling the Saviour teacher and good, they were plotting evil

For they did not understand the works of the Lord. That is, they did not want, he says, to accept their own salvation. And my flesh has flourished again. In these words he clearly proclaims the resurrection.

And the protector of the salvation of his Christ. By Christ here he means the people anointed into a royal priesthood. He himself, then, he says, the Lord, shields the one anointed by him, so as to save him, and for

And shepherd them, and lift them up for ever. For he himself will shepherd us, having sent us the Paraclete in his place and as himself. And indeed he lifts them up, that is, he makes them exalted for the ages to come that have no end.

clearly indicating to us their departure. Bring to the Lord, O sons of God. He calls the holy apostles sons of God, for he taught them to say, "Our Father who art in heaven." Bring to the Lord young rams. By young rams he means those called through the apostles from the Jewish nation to faith in the Lord; or else those who believed from among the Gentiles, since they were born of irrational fathers. Bring to the Lord glory and honour. One brings glory to the Lord by doing good, in keeping with the saying, "That they may see your good works and glorify your Father." And one brings honour, in turn, by practising good deeds, in keeping with the saying, "Honour the Lord from your righteous labours." Worship the Lord in his holy court. Through these words he clearly instructs us that one must not worship outside the church. He says this because of the assemblies of the heterodox. [Worship must not take place outside the church, but be performed in the very court of God. Do not, he says, devise private courts and assemblies of your own; there is one holy court of God.] Those who have climbed higher may also understand the court as the heavenly way of life. The voice of the Lord is upon the waters. By waters he means the multitudes of those saved through the apostles. The saints are waters; that is why rivers will flow from their belly, that is, spiritual teaching, with which they water those who hear them. Over such waters, then, is the Lord. But in the historical sense, Elijah after the drought heard a sound of many waters. He means the voice of God the Father that came at the Jordan, saying, "This is my beloved Son," which he also likens to thunder. The voice of the Lord breaking cedars. By cedars here he means the opposing powers. And the Lord will shatter the cedars of Lebanon. By the cedars of Lebanon he means the lofty ones of the Jewish people, because Jerusalem is often called Lebanon in divine Scripture. And he will grind them small, like the calf, Lebanon. The calf signifies the altar. And the beloved is like a son of unicorns. The beloved,

he says, the choir of the apostles, became a son of unicorns. The unicorns are the holy prophets and patriarchs, whose sons are the holy apostles; they are so called because they have their horn and their strength in God alone. The voice of the Lord cutting through the flame of fire. This signifies the very promise he made to the saints when he said, "Even if you pass through the midst of fire, the fire will not burn you." The voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness. "Shaking" is said here, once again, of something heard far and wide, as in, "When Jesus entered, the whole city was shaken." By the wilderness he means the Church from the Gentiles, which of old was a wilderness, empty of the knowledge of God. And the Lord will shake the wilderness of Kadesh. Kadesh means "holy"; and holy is the Church of Christ

The voice of the Lord preparing deer, and he will lay bare the forests. The deer are the saints; and "preparing" means "making ready." For he made the holy apostles ready and sent them out, in keeping with the words, "Go and make disciples of all nations." He calls the Church forests because of old it was the mother of fruitless trees. [And in his temple everyone speaks of glory. The Lord made the holy apostles ready and sent them out, so as to drive away the demons and bring the nations to the knowledge of God.] The Lord will make the flood a dwelling place. By the flood he means the multitude of those who have believed, in keeping with the saying, "The whole earth was filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as abundant water covers the seas." And the Lord will sit as king for ever; this is like the words, "For to him every knee shall bow." The Lord will give strength to his people. This is like the words, "I can do all things in Christ who strengthens me." The Lord will bless his people with peace. This is like the words, "My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you." A Psalm. A song for the dedication of the house. For the end. Of David. 29. The dedication of the house is either that of the Church, or the moment when, though our outer man is wasting away, the inner man is being renewed.

He sings this psalm after he has recovered from sin, his soul having been, as it were, renewed through repentance, the soul that of old was also a house of the Holy Spirit. He sings it about his forgiveness, offering thanksgiving and praying that he himself may remain secure in time to come; and he also gives others a lesson, that if anything of the kind should ever happen to them, they should lift up their prayers to God. I will exalt you, O Lord, for you have upheld me ... You saved me from those who go down into the pit. By the pit he means Hades.

And give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness. It is fitting, he says, to raise our hymns ever higher, remembering God's love for mankind. For wrath is in his anger. Not because he wishes to do this, but because each person brings it on himself through sin. For his will is life. In the evening weeping will lodge. These words signify how easily repentance succeeds. For there is no multitude of sins so great that repentance does not quickly turn it into rejoicing. But I said in my prosperity, I shall never be moved. He states the cause of his fall. Because I was proud in my prosperity, he says, I have been troubled. And this happened to me not because you thrust me away, but only because you turned away your face. Since, then, we cannot even stand without your strength, carry out your will once more and make the beauty of my soul shine forth. Adam too hoped this, while he lived in paradise before the deception, and Hezekiah too, when he had conquered the Assyrian. The book of Chronicles teaches this clearly when it says that the heart of King Hezekiah was lifted up. To you, O Lord, I will cry ... What profit is there in my blood, if I go down to corruption? I pray, he says, to be brought up out of the pit, since dust does not give thanks to you. If I go down to corruption, there is no profit whatever, either for me or for others. For I would be deprived of the life that comes from you, and others would in no way obtain the salvation that comes through me. But when you have heard my voice, turned my mourning into joy and girded me with gladness, no ordinary profit will come to me. For having recovered my former glory, I speak to you with it, and not with any bad conscience; this is what "that I may not be pierced with sorrow" means. You tore my sackcloth and girded me with gladness. He called mourning sackcloth, since those in mourning customarily wear sackcloth. For sackcloth signifies wickedness and ignorance, since it is made from the hair of goats, those that stand on the left, [?] and of the scapegoat. For the end. A Psalm of David, of ecstasy. 30.

He sings the present psalm as one still in a state of repentance on account of his sin, and asking to be set free from it. Yet he also offers thanksgiving as one who has already been heard, and he recounts besides what befell him during the time of his repentance. "Of ecstasy" signifies nothing other than sin itself, through which the soul was, as it were, driven out of its right mind, so that it no longer hoped for recovery and said plainly, "But I said in my ecstasy, I am cast out, then, from before your eyes." In you, O Lord, I have hoped ... Incline

your ear to me. Since our cry does not reach up to the height, incline your ear to me by condescending to me. You will bring me out of this snare that they hid for me. For they lay in wait for his soul and caught him. In what? In sin. You have redeemed me, O Lord, God of truth. He says such things as one who has already been heard. You have hated those who pay heed to vanities to no purpose. By vanities he means the distractions of the present life; when we labour at them we work at vanity. "To no purpose" goes with the one who pays heed to vanities. I will rejoice and be glad. Having trampled down grief and the other passions. And you did not shut me up in the hands of enemies. That is, you did not hand me over. You set my feet in a spacious place. Freeing me from affliction, you have set me in ease and spaciousness. My eye was troubled with anger, my soul and my belly. Just as he calls the mind of the soul an eye, so he calls memory the belly of the soul, in which, as in a belly, we store up our rational food. My soul and my belly. I turned my eye away from the people of the Jews in great wrath and anger. For my life has failed in pain. This shows the intensity of his mind. And my years in groaning. I spent my time, he says, groaning over my ills. My strength has grown weak in poverty. Having become poor, he says, in the help that comes from you, because of my sin, I grew weak. And my bones were troubled. By bones he means the powers of the soul. [For my life has failed in pain. The lack of necessities, he says, wasted my body away; for Shobi and Barzillai brought David wheat and barley and flour and beans and lentils and honey and certain other things, as well as rugs and bedding, and they offered these and the food to the people, for they said that the people were hungry and faint with thirst in the wilderness.] I became a reproach beyond all my enemies. [He who is bereft of virtues is dead at heart.] My enemies, he says, reproached me, my acquaintances were afraid of me, and those who saw me fled from me because of the extreme repentance I displayed, worn down by sackcloth and ashes and weeping day and night. Therefore, as they fled from me, I was forgotten, like a dead man indeed, and I seemed like a lost vessel. "Beyond all" is not meant as "more than all," but in the sense of "from all"; that is, I was reproached by my enemies. For Aquila too says this: "I became a reproach from all my enemies." For I heard the blame of many who dwell round about. By blame he means plotting. He says that the enemies surrounded him with their plots. They took counsel to take my life. But in you, O Lo- 2 Kingdoms 17:1–4.

rd, I have hoped. By the soul they mean the heart; for through anger and desire they put the mind to death. My lots are in your hands. Even if my enemies plot against me, plotting to take my life, yet my lots are kept safe in your hands, and you will give them back to me in due time, because I hope in you. That is why I pray at present to be rescued from my enemies. They, for their part, have gathered together and are stitching together my death; but I know you as God and ruler. Rescue me from the hand of my enemies and from those who persecute me. "Flee wickedness," says the Apostle. If wickedness pursues, then clearly adultery, greed, anger and wrath pursue as well; and the rest [?]

Make your face shine on your servant; save me in your mercy. For once your appearing has come to me, all that is gloomy will at once be dispelled. This, he says, is the only way of salvation for me: that you make your face shine. O Lord, let me not be put to shame, for I have called on you. From this we learn that sin differs greatly from impiety. That is why the great David asks that he himself be freed from the shame that came upon him through sin, but that those who live in ungodliness be sent off to death in shame. Let the deceitful lips be made dumb. I pray, he says, that my enemies may be struck dumb; and this will happen if you make your face shine. How great is the abundance of your goodness, O Lord! As one already enlightened by the Spirit, he gives thanks for what is to come. David often uses the word "how" in expressions of amazement, in the sense of "exceedingly." Great is your goodness, which you store up and keep for us. "You have hidden" means "you have kept," as also in "He hid me in his tent." He uses "you have hidden" for "you have kept" because what is hidden is kept safe. You have accomplished it for those who hope in you. That is, you have accomplished it at the fitting time. You will hide them in the secret place of your face. May your face, he says, become a shelter for those who hope in you. You will shelter them from the turmoil of men, in a tent, from the contradiction of tongues. You will cover them, he says, as with a shelter, so that they are neither harmed by those who attack them with words nor captured by those who make war on them with deeds. Blessed be the Lord, for he has made his mercy wonderful in a besieged city. Through me, he says, God was glorified; for when countless enemies had gathered around me and were trying to besiege my soul like a great city, my guardian threw a fence around me and showed his mercy to be wonderful. But I said in my ecstasy, I am cast out. When, he says, I was humbling myself in

…in the ecstasy that came upon me, when my eye too was troubled with anger, I wore myself down as one cast off because of my sin. "But I," [?] he says, "said this; yet you, lover of humankind, did not cast off your servant." Love the Lord, all you his saints. He turns his words to exhorting others on the basis of the benefits he received, urging the rest to confess. And he repays those who act with excessive arrogance. The Lord is patient with the arrogant, but those who act with excessive arrogance he also repays. A PSALM of David, of understanding. 31.

Setting forth the great suffering he endured in his repentance, David calls blessed those who have obtained forgiveness through the washing of regeneration. The psalm is entitled "of understanding" because people need this above all, since, having sunk deep into the passions, they have been likened to horses and mules. Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Iniquities are forgiven through baptism; sins are covered through bitter repentance. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not reckon sin, and in whose mouth there is no guile. For he is truly blessed who comes to holy baptism with his whole heart. [For whoever is baptized with guile not only fails to obtain forgiveness but will also incur judgment.] By the same author: "because" must be joined to "grew old," so that it reads: Because my bones grew old from my crying out all day long. "I kept silent," being no longer able to utter a sound. And what did he cry out, if not to ask pardon for his sin? Because day and night your hand was heavy upon me. "Being good," he says, "you chastened me severely, turning me back to salvation through chastisement." I was turned to misery while a thorn was fixed in me. He calls sin a thorn. The meaning is this: "Since sin was fixed in my soul," he says, "I was in misery." I made my iniquity known. He indicates the manner of confession. I said: I will declare my iniquity against myself. A righteous man is his own accuser when he first speaks. And, "You tell your sins," he says…

For this every holy one will pray to you. "For the sin forgiven me," he says, "each of your holy ones will pray to you." By this he signifies one of two things: either "I will be an example of repentance to all," or, more prophetically, that all the nations in every age would confess their sin in the very words of David. Yet in a flood of many waters they will not come near him. "A multitude of temptations," he says, "will not overwhelm the one who repents."

You are my refuge. Having said those things about sin, he pleads to be set free from the evils brought upon him because of it. And indeed he receives an answer, for the Lord, lover of humankind, says to him: I will give you understanding and instruct you in this way. To one who has prayed for deliverance from his enemies God replies, promising to guide him in a straight way. Do not be like horse and mule, which have no understanding. He counsels sinners not to give themselves over to irrational passions. With bit and bridle you will constrain their jaws. The words are addressed to the Lord. What he means is something like this: "Those who do not wish to repent, turn back to yourself as if with a bridle." A PSALM of David; without title among the Hebrews. 32.

In this psalm he teaches those who have already believed in Christ to praise their Master, teaching them at the same time the supremacy of his power: that he is the deliverer of all, he is Lord, he sets the wicked at nothing and scatters their counsels, but saves those who hope in him. Rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord … with a ten-stringed harp sing to him. By the ten-stringed harp he means the body, since it has five senses and five operations of the soul, each operation taking place through each sense. Sing to him a new song. He says plainly that the law given through Moses has come to an end. For the word of the Lord is upright. The word of the Gospel, evidently. And all his works are done in faithfulness. "We must believe," he says, "in what he accomplishes in a manner befitting God." The Lord loves mercy and judgment. "These," he says, "he requires of those who believe in him." The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord. He begins to show that he is also the maker of all creation, and first of all of the earth, which he says he has filled with mercy, and which could not otherwise hold together unless it were full of it. Indeed, the heavens too would never have held together unless they were sustained by his word, and likewise their powers, that is, the divine and rational ones. [So he loves mercy toward those who repent, and judgment toward the unyielding. Isaiah too says something like this to God: "For your mercy is by weight"; for he too presents mercy joined with judgment, measured out by balance and number according to each one's desert.] By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm. Here too the Holy Trinity is revealed. And by the breath of his mouth all their host. He calls the Holy Spirit the mouth of God, for the prophets, speaking through him, used to say: For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things. Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin. Summoning—

—summoning the water of the sea, he says, he holds it together in the clouds [?] as in a kind of wineskin; as he also says elsewhere: He who summons the water of the sea and pours it out over the face of all the earth; and again [?]: Bringing up clouds from the end of the earth. Laying up the deeps in storehouses. "The deeps too," he says, "he seals up as in storehouses, so that they may not burst forth and flood the dry land." Let all the earth fear the Lord. "No longer," he says, "let the earth offer its worship to demons." And let all who inhabit the world be shaken by him. "Hearing him," he says, "let the people who inhabit the world be shaken," that is, out of the former position they held as idolaters, and obey their own Creator. For he spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created. "Coming to be" indicates the essential existence of rational beings, while "creation" signifies the change from worse to better. For if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The Lord scatters the counsels of nations. Of the spiritual ones, evidently. And he sets aside the thoughts of peoples, and sets aside the counsels of rulers. For he made all the plots of the Jews come to nothing by rising on the third day. For this was what he wills, and it endures forever. The thoughts of his heart are from generation to generation. "The decrees," he says, "which he has resolved, both for the present age and for the age to come." The thoughts of God are his fitting ordering of things; his heart is what is hidden in his essence. Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord. In these words he calls those who believe in Christ blessed. [The Lord looked down from heaven. He said "looked down" so that no one might suppose him ignorant of what people dare to do.] [From his prepared dwelling place. That is, made ready and set in order. For heaven has been allotted as a kind of house of God.] He who fashioned their hearts one by one. "God alone," he says, "knows the hearts of human beings." That is why the Savior said to the Jews: Why do you think evil things in your hearts? Behold, the eyes of the Lord are on those who fear him. The eyes of the Lord are his all-seeing power; or often the Son and the Spirit, since the Father of lights is as it were between two lights. And to keep them alive in famine. "In a time of persecution," he says, "when spiritual food is not to be had, the Lord himself will nourish them through the Holy Spirit." But our soul waits for the Lord. As people who have already shown their trust in him, they put it forward as a plea. A PSALM of David, when he changed his countenance before Abimelech, who sent him away, and he departed. 33.

…being asked by him the reason for his coming, he denied that he was fleeing and said he had been sent by Saul, so that he even asked for Goliath's sword. Since, then, he said one thing and thought another, it is recorded that he changed his countenance. He sings the psalm for the new people, introducing teaching about spiritual and evangelical worship. I will bless the Lord at all times. In the Lord my soul shall be praised. "Even if I happen to be worthy of praise, because some good is found in my deeds, this must be credited not to me but to God: he himself has made me illustrious and will make me admired." Let the meek hear and be glad. "Let every righteous man who hears of the salvation granted me by the Lord be glad." Since he indeed saves those who hope in him, David does not consent to weave the hymn alone, but makes those who share his meekness sharers in his hymn-singing as well. Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together. As though he were not equal to proclaiming the mighty works of God, he asks the others to join him in this very task and work with him. Come to him and be enlightened. Confident from what he had received, he [urges] the others also to this…

This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him. "Learn," he says, "from my own case to take courage in the God of all. For though I was lowly and a shepherd, he counted me worthy of his providence and made me stronger than those who fought against me." The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him and will deliver them. This agrees with the words of the Apostle too, for he says of the angels: Are they not all ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation? So too the blessed Jacob says in prayer: The angel who delivers me from all my evils. So too the patriarch Abraham said to his admirable servant: The Lord God will send his angel before you, and you shall take a wife for my son Isaac from there. So too the blessed Zechariah says: The angel who spoke with me. Taste and see that the Lord is good. "Taste," he says, "the true bread that came down from heaven." Blessed is the man who hopes in him, for he will have the life to come. The rich have become poor and gone hungry. That is, the people of the Jews. But those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good thing. He means the other people, that of the nations. Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord … and your lips from speaking deceit. He sets out the teaching for the nations, the first part of which, he says, is the fear of God; the second,

not to slander a brother; the third, to keep the lips from all deceit; the fourth, to abstain from all evil and practice good in everything. And on top of all these, to pursue peace and hold fast to it. And peace is Christ. He says that the practice of these things is life and good days. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it. "Turn away from evil" is taught by fear; "do good" by love. Therefore the one who loves is greater than the one who fears. The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer. He has assigned a great reward to the practice of virtue: having God watch over us. The Lord guards all their bones. By bones he means the powers of the soul. These are righteousness, endurance, piety, and, so to speak, every virtue. The death of sinners is evil. He means the death of the soul, which will be followed by eternal fire, outer darkness, the sleepless worm, weeping and [?] wailing of teeth. For Gehenna and darkness [await] them…

The present words are spoken in the person of one who trusts in God and is warred against by the invisible powers, or else by the choir of the apostles. The person of Christ is also introduced, recounting what was done to him by the Jews at his passion, to encourage patience and endurance in those who are warred against for God's sake. Judge, O Lord, those who wrong me; fight against those who fight against me. The opening will suit the person of the apostles. He means the Jews, who, having no peace within themselves, wage wars and fight against Christ, who [?] … Take hold of weapon and shield, and rise up to help me. By weapon and shield and sword he alludes to the punishing powers sent forth by the Lord to aid the righteous. Say to my soul: I am your salvation. "This I ask of you," he says: "to tell my soul that you will be its helper." Let them be turned back. Those who are traveling from virtue to vice are done a kindness if they are turned back. Let the snare he does not know come upon him, and let the net he hid catch him, and he will fall into the snare [?] itself. For the snare was turned back upon the heads of the wicked. Having hunted, they were caught in turn unto death and are handed over to death. But my soul will rejoice in the Lord. So those who set the snare and contrived the plot to destroy Christ, the Savior of us all, will be made to pay the penalty for their drunken outrage against him,

in the ways we have just described; "but my soul," he says, "will be continually beyond every danger," that is, having a joy in God that cannot be taken away, and rejoicing greatly in his salvation. Unjust witnesses rose up against me; they questioned me about things I did not know. From here the person of Christ is introduced, falsely accused at the trial before the high priests. They repaid me evil for good, and childlessness to my soul. He says this because they were shown to be unworthy of being called children of God, which he himself made known most clearly, as in "How often I wanted to gather your children." But as for me, when they troubled me, I put on sackcloth. For he mourned their destruction, so that he grieved and was distressed and wept and prayed for their sin. And I humbled my soul with fasting. Confirming the incarnation, he did not refrain from fasting either. And my prayer will return into my bosom. This would signify that they remained in their sin. "For they gained nothing," he says, "because of the excess of their ignorance, having made the prayer, as it were, come back." As to a neighbor, as to our brother, so I sought to please them. "As a brother," he says, "and a friend, so I was eager to do them good, wishing to heal them; that is why I mourned for them." And they rejoiced against me and gathered together. "This," he says, "is how they repaid me [?] for my anguish on their behalf." Scourges were gathered against me, and I did not know. "Scourging me," he says, "they did not know or find any charge against me." They were split apart and were not pierced to the heart. For the crowd was divided, as the evangelist says, some saying he was good, others that he was evil. "And though these things were happening," he says, "they were not pierced to the heart, nor did they understand against whom their deeds were directed." He said this not as an accusation but out of longing for help: "When," he says, "will you appear and come to the defense of one who is wronged?" Restore my soul from their evildoing. All that he suffers or says, he does for our salvation, because he, namely Christ, came down and took flesh from us. From the lions, my only one. By lions he means either the wicked and hostile powers, which all but roared against Christ, or perhaps the leaders of the Jews themselves. For Jeremiah too makes mention of them, saying: My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; therefore I have hated it. He calls his own soul "only one," using "only-begotten" in place of "beloved." For somehow an only child is always the most loved among children.

Those who hate me without cause and wink with their eyes. That is, contriving deceits. For to me they spoke peaceably, but in their anger they devised deceits. That is, "Good teacher," and "We know that you teach the truth and do not regard anyone's person." And they opened their mouth wide against me. He means the blasphemies uttered at the cross. They said: Aha, aha, our eyes have seen it. As though things had turned out as they had prayed: his being hung on the tree. This is also what those do who exult over the affliction of the righteous. You have seen, O Lord; do not keep silent; O Lord, do not depart from me. The only-begotten Word of God, having become man without casting off his being God, asks the Father to become judge of the wrong done to us by the demons; he asks him to scatter the insolence of the proud. "For in this way," he says, "some will be turned back in shame, while others may rejoice, offering up thanksgiving for their salvation." For the end; for the servant of the Lord, David.

The present psalm contains an indictment of the arrogance of the Jewish people and a rebuke of their wickedness; and also a hymn in praise of the just judgments by which he made the world under heaven; and besides these, thanksgiving to the Father for the benefits he bestowed through Jesus; and on top of all these, a prayer for protection against falling into arrogance. The transgressor says within himself that he will sin. "The one brought up in wickedness," he says, "supposes that no one sees the hidden plans of his soul." For he has put "says" in place of "thinks" or "supposes." The cause of such insensibility is not fearing the Master who oversees all things. There is no fear of God before his eyes. "Having once resolved to transgress," he says, "he puts the fear of God out of his sight." For by the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil. For he has dealt deceitfully before him. He holds this ignorance willingly, not wishing to reckon up what he has done and to hate what has been done wrongly. So that his iniquity may be found out and hated. "He does not reckon with this," he says: "that God finds out his sin, and having found it, hates both it and…"

The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit. Iniquity, because of the insults they heaped on Christ; deceit, because, wishing to ensnare him, they approached him with kindly words. He did not wish to understand so as to do good. "Willingly," he says, "he shut himself out from doing well." He devised iniquity on his bed; he set himself on every way that is not good. Their sleeplessness [?]: their sleeplessness in plotting

against Christ is what this signifies. He did not abhor wickedness. That is, he did not hate wickedness. O Lord, your mercy is in heaven. He shows that by his mercy the heavenly beings too, that is, the rational powers, hold together. And your truth reaches to the clouds. Your righteousness is like the mountains of God. "You have shown," he says, "that the promises made through the prophets are true and sure," for the prophets are clouds. "And you showed them to be true by bestowing such an abundance of righteousness that it can be compared to the mountains of God." Your judgments are a great deep. "Though you have such truth and righteousness, I do not know why you are patient; for your judgments imitate the unsearchableness of the abyss. For just as its depth cannot be seen by human beings, so the understanding of your judgments is beyond reach." Human beings and beasts you will save, O Lord. The Apostle, having spoken of the two peoples—God has shut up all in disobedience, so that he might save all—added: How unsearchable are his judgments! Here too it is similar. For since he was about to recount the salvation of the two peoples, who are signified by human beings and beasts—human beings meaning those from Israel, as instructed by the law and able to discern what matters; beasts meaning those from the nations, as more irrational; for those from the Jews, though taught the mystery through the law and the prophets, fell away, while those from the nations, who had never heard, were received—for this reason he said beforehand: Your judgments are a great deep. Again, by human beings he means those who preserve their rational dignity; by beasts, those who bend down toward the earth and feed on earthly thoughts. So he called not only the righteous but also sinners to salvation. But the children of men will hope in the shelter of your wings. "That is," he says, "they will have you as their shelter and helper through the word of the Gospel." They will be drunk with the richness of your house, and you will give them to drink from the torrent of your delight. The torrent of delight is Christ, according to the saying: I turn toward them like a torrent overflowing with the glory of the nations. He is also the fountain of life and the light…

Let not the foot of arrogance come upon me. He asks to be free of that passion. And let not the hand of the sinner shake me. "Nor let any wicked deed," he says, "move me from my standing with you." A PSALM of David. 36. Argument. The psalm contains teaching, introducing to the new people abstinence from evil and the practice of good, persuading them from both sides: from the hope prepared for the good, and from the punishment laid up for the wicked. Do not be jealous of evildoers, nor envy…

…those who work lawlessness.” He urges us to flee wickedness, and he describes its end as the loss of every good. “And dwell in the land, and you will be pastured on its wealth.” By “land” he means the divinely inspired Scripture, in which lies the wealth of the saints, that is, the promises. He urges us to hold to the divine oracles at all times, out of love for what is laid up in them for the saints.

“Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him, and he will act.” You will be walking openly, he says, on the way that pleases him. “And he will bring forth your righteousness like light.” For it is clear that in the age to come, as the Lord himself has said, the righteous will shine out like the sun. The light of righteousness is knowledge, since righteousness is also the rule of the virtues. “And your judgment like noonday.” That is: he will judge you worthy of light. “And he will act.” When you hope in him, he says, then he will act. He shows what he will do by adding: “He will bring forth your righteousness like light, and your judgment like noonday.” “He will bring forth,” he says, meaning he will make it manifest and display it as if for all to see, not letting the beauty of your good life go unnoticed. For your righteousness will be plain to everyone, shining out like light, the light of noonday. Noon is the name given to the very middle of the day. He not only justifies the one who confesses, he says, and passes on him a judgment of kindness, but he also brings his righteousness into the light; that is, he makes known to all that he has justified him. Such was the thief, whose judgment Jesus brought forth at noon, while he was being crucified in the middle of the day; and he brought his righteousness into the light, that is, into the knowledge of all. For the words spoken to him, “Truly, truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise,” became manifest to the world, or rather became a light to the world, an encouragement to all who are repenting. The brightness of righteousness, he says, will not be hidden as it is now, but will be as conspicuous as the sun at noon, as the Lord says: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.” “Submit to the Lord and implore him.” He will show you worthy of light in the age to come; but you, submit here. “Do not envy the one who prospers in his way.” Do not imitate, he says, a prosperity built up from lawlessness. [Do not marvel at a lawless man who prospers, nor imitate a prosperity built up from lawlessness, nor be provoked into doing the like. Even if everything goes his way, do not be stung or vexed that the wicked do not pay the penalty but live in plenty, as though no one exacted retribution. “Better is a little to the righteous”: that is, greater

is a little mercy from the Lord than all the wealth of the world.] “Cease from anger, and forsake wrath.” Do not look at their prosperity, but wait for the end, and you will see their ruin. Anger is a desire for retribution, and retribution is the repaying of evil. “Do not envy, so as to do evil.” Know well that those who have hung themselves on divine hope and chosen the gentle life continue in quietness and peace, having the purity of their conscience as a lasting delight; but those who trust in passing prosperity will meet a swift reversal and will be given over to utter oblivion. “And you will seek his place, and will not find it.” This is like the saying: “But the ungodly will perish root and all.” “And they will delight in abundance of peace.” The delight of the righteous is abundance of peace; and this is the soul’s freedom from passion, together with true knowledge of the things that are. “The sinner will watch the righteous.” This may also fittingly be taken of the devil, and with these words he offers consolation to those who are wronged. For he shows the lawless man grieving and raging against those who embrace a quiet life, and the righteous Judge laughing at his attempt, since he foresees his swift end. “But the Lord will laugh at him.” He laughs to scorn, he says, the sinner’s plots against the righteous, knowing that he has set a day on which he will give eternal life to the one and eternal punishment to the other. “The sinners have drawn the sword, they have bent their bow … may their sword enter into their own heart.” The wicked demons, he says, have suffered what they plotted to do to the saints. “The Lord knows the ways of the blameless.” That is, he accepts and honors them. “And their inheritance will be forever.” For the rewards of the saints are incorruptible and eternal. “They will not be put to shame in an evil time.” In times of persecution, he says, when teachers are lacking, the Lord himself will feed those who believe in him with his own Spirit. [“They will not be put to shame in an evil time.” The evil time is the time of wrath against the ungodly, in which some will experience God’s righteous judgment, while others will receive glory and honor and incorruption and eternal life.] “The sinner borrows and will not repay.” The sinner, he says, [does not?] give back thanks for the benefits he receives from God. “But the righteous has compassion and gives.” He gives back compassion, he says, imitating his own Master.

“For those who bless him will inherit the land.” This is like what was said to Abraham: “I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse those who curse you.” “A man’s steps are directed by the Lord.” He accepts, he says, the practical course a man follows in his life. “When he falls, he will not be dashed down.” Even if the righteous man happens to slip a little, he says, he will come to no harm, since he has God to hold him up. “Nor his offspring seeking bread.” He means spiritual bread, which is the divine words. “And dwell forever and ever.” And you will inherit, he says, the eternal tents. “But the righteous will inherit the land.” In many places he has mentioned the land given to the meek, urging us to desire it. “The mouth of the righteous will meditate on wisdom.” It is fitting, he says, to carry the divine oracles about both on the tongue and in the mind, and to meditate on them continually. For in this way the lover of virtue learns what he must do, and will stay steady and unshaken, prevailing over those who try to throw him down. He said this in the first psalm as well: “But his will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he will meditate day and night,” and so on. “And his tongue will speak judgment.” He means righteous judgment, not the judgment of a law court but the judgment that comes from an unerring and sound faculty of discernment. “The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps will not be tripped up.” “The sinner watches the righteous …” “But the Lord …” He says the same things in different ways, making the memory more lasting through more meditation. What he says is this: the Master will not overlook the righteous man when the wicked plot against him, nor will he side with those who dare such things, but he will enable him to leap over their nets. Abraham enjoyed this providence when Sarah was twice taken from him; so did Isaac, who suffered the very same thing; so did Jacob, envied by his brother and his father-in-law; so did Joseph, assailed by envy and slander. But why list them all? It is easy for those who love learning both to gather the ancient examples and to observe the new ones. “Nor will he condemn him when he is judged.” That is, when he is being judged. “You will see when sinners are destroyed.” You will see the sinners, he says, being cut down. “I saw the ungodly exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon.” As it is said: “Our life is a shadow.” “And I passed by, and behold, he was not.” When I saw wicked men prospering, he says, I wondered how they had come by it. Then, as I pondered such things and thought them over again, I could not see them; [?] I could not even make out the place where they had seemed to stand.

“… a remnant for the peaceful man.” Let the punishment of the wicked, he says, and the remnant, that is, the inheritance of good things, lead you to practise simplicity. A Psalm of David, for remembrance, concerning the Sabbath. Psalm 37.

He sings this psalm to remind himself of the misery that gripped him, which he endured because of his sin. And through himself he asks God to grant him sabbaths, that is, rest from his calamities. “Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor discipline me in your anger.” [The demons who serve in carrying out punishments, and the punishing powers, are called God’s wrath and anger. So he begs not to be rebuked through wicked powers, nor disciplined by the sending of grim angels, but through saving words.] The Lord disciplines us to bring us to remember virtue. The saint does not refuse rebuke or discipline, but only the kind that comes with wrath and

“For your arrows have stuck fast in me.” By arrows he means the punishing powers. “And you have pressed your hand upon me.” Your hand, he says, has laid hold of me, disciplining me for my sin. “There is no healing in my flesh because of your wrath.” My flesh has been ruined, because wrath was brought upon me. “There is no peace in my bones because of my sins.” The strength of my soul, he says, has failed, and the cause of the weakness is sin. “For my iniquities have gone over my head.” The heavy burden of sin, he says, has bent me down. And the stench of those festering wounds distresses me, wounds I took on when I cast off prudence and served folly. Because of this I am robbed of all joy; I am continually vexed and distraught, and I find no relief from my gloom. “Like a heavy burden they have weighed me down.” He speaks emphatically of the weight of a conscience driving toward despair. “My wounds have stunk and festered because of my folly.” For every sin is foul and stinking; unless the soul fell into folly, it would not put up with sin. From this we learn the nature of sin. What kind of thing is it, except that sins befall us out of folly? “All day long I went about gloomy.” This should be said to those who laugh a great deal and take delight

[“I was miserable and bowed down,” and so on. The weight of conscience, as driving toward despair. “For my loins are filled with mockeries.” For from then on, he says, I saw my enemies mocking me; he means the spiritual enemies. “I was afflicted and humbled exceedingly.” From that desire, he says, I reaped this harvest: to be bowed down

to the ground and to lament continually because of the bitter pains of my heart. For this reason I changed the working of desire and made it a servant of the divine will. For he added: “I roared from the groaning of my heart.” Scourging my conscience, [I made?] my heart send forth groans

“And my groaning was not hidden from you.” Let the longing for repentance, he says, stand before you, the desire I have in wishing to be saved. And what is the desire of Christ? To accomplish on our behalf

“My heart is troubled, my strength has forsaken me.” By “heart” he means the reasoning faculty. “And the light of my eyes, even that is not with me.” The light of the eyes is the Spirit that shines on the eyes of his mind. “My friends and my neighbors drew near against me and stood.” When I had been struck, he says, they stood against me. He says this because of Absalom and Ahithophel. “And my nearest stood far off.” For the angels who served alongside him forsook him because of his sin. Perhaps the holy powers too withdraw in the time of temptation, to test the one being tempted, or to

“And those who sought my life used violence.” Naturally, once the angels had abandoned him, the demons attacked more fiercely. “And those who sought evil for me spoke vanities.” They spoke among themselves, he says, devising a plot against me. “But I, like a deaf man, did not hear,” and so on.
