While they were saying these things, he says, I dared neither to listen nor to speak, since sin had taken away my freedom of speech. “For in you, Lord, I have hoped … for I said: Let my enemies never rejoice over me.” Amid all the evils that have befallen me, he says, I have one hope of salvation: the help that will come to me from you. “And when my feet were shaken, they boasted against me.” Sin, he says, by shaking my feet, has given them grounds for arrogance against me. “For I am ready for scourges, and my pain is continually before me.” He says he gladly accepts the discipline that turns him back. “For I will declare my iniquity, and I will be anxious over my sin.” For this reason I become my own accuser, and I will take every care for my recovery. “But my enemies live, and have grown stronger than I.” And yet, he says, though I am not insensible of my sin but constantly anxious about it, I see my enemies growing strong. These enemies, who have suffered no wrong from me, slander my sin and make it a pretext for

war against me; they persecuted me, claiming to act justly. And so I have become to them like a loathsome corpse. That is why I pray to you, the Lord, not to depart from me, but rather to hasten to our help. Psalm 38. For the end, a song for Jeduthun.

Jeduthun, a sacred psalmist crowned with prophetic grace, strikes up a song in which he gives voice to David himself confessing his sin. “I said: I will guard my ways.” A clear proof of a steadfast heart. “I set a guard on my mouth when the sinner stood against me.” For the spiritual enemies stood by him and reproached him with his sin. “I was struck dumb and humbled, and kept silent from good things.” When I was reviled, he says, I did not revile in return, for I recognized that I had fallen from good things. “And my grief was renewed.” Instead of speaking to those who reviled me, I reminded myself of my sin. And the memory of sin became like a fire about my heart. “And in my meditation a fire will be kindled.” When I remembered my sin, he says, I burned as with fire. “I spoke with my tongue: Lord, make known to me my end.” “With my tongue” means quietly, as it were, in a whisper, not uttering the word before many. And the word was a question about his remaining days. He asked because he wanted to learn whether the time left of his days would be enough for him to repent. “Behold, you have made my days handbreadths, and my existence is as nothing before you.” Even if my life stretches to great length, he says, it will be reckoned as nothing before you. For if a thousand years in your eyes are as one day, what would the lifetime of one man be? Symmachus in turn translated this as follows: “Behold, you have given my days as spans, and my life is as nothing in your presence.” For you are without beginning and without end, while our life is measured out, as it were, in spans and handbreadths. By this he indicated the brevity of human

“But all things are vanity, every man living. Surely man walks about in an image; yet he is troubled in vain.” If man walks in an image, he says, and not in truth, it is fitting that he first spoke of vanity; for we do not live the true life but one in a kind of image, nor do we devote our efforts to the things that are truly good, and that is why we are troubled in vain. The life of those on earth, he says, since it revolves around worldly cares, may be judged vanity. Or thus:

All the years of our life are a vapor before you; for in place of “vanity” Symmachus rendered “vapor.” “He stores up treasure, and does not know for whom he will gather it.” Since we do not now live the true life but one as in an image, and do not devote our efforts to the things that are truly good, we are troubled in vain, revolving around worldly desires and gathering treasures without knowing who will inherit them. “And now what is my patient hope? Is it not the Lord?” Fittingly he says that he has his hope in the Lord, since he has condemned the distractions of life. “And my existence is with you.” The expectation, that is, the

“You have made me a reproach to the fool.” Do not hand me over to reproach, he says, for it is you who are reviled in me. “I was struck dumb, and did not open my mouth, for you have done it.” When reviled, he says, I kept silent, knowing well about this that it is you who, for punishment or rather for discipline, appointed me to be reproached in this very way. “Remove your scourges from me.” He means the punishments inflicted on him by the demons, with God not permitting them. (Reg. 1 reads thus:) He means the punishments inflicted on him by the demons as coming from God, since God permitted him to suffer because of his sin. “For I have fainted under the strength of your hand.” We have often noted already that the punishing power is called the hand of God. When he scourges them hard, the one being punished faints, insofar as he is what he is: weak, that is, and unable to hold out long against scourges. [“Yet they are troubled in vain.” The one who lives in lawlessness, so as to need such discipline.] “With rebukes for lawlessness you have disciplined man.” By rebuking me for my sin, he says, you have disciplined me. “Give ear to my prayer.” That is: hear me, and forgive my sin before my death. [For this is what “For I am a sojourner” means.] “Relent toward me, that I may be refreshed.” Before my death, he says, grant me forgiveness of sins, that I may go to Hades with confidence. “And I shall be no more.” I shall not be such as I might become through the relief granted me by you. God’s relief is the soul’s freedom from passion, together with true knowledge of the things that are. For the end. A Psalm of David. Psalm 39.

The song is spoken in the person of the new people, who have been brought up out of the pit of misery. Then, in the middle, the person of Christ is introduced, teaching those who give thanks the manner of the dispensation. Then comes again the person of those from Israel who have believed, asking to be rescued from the sin incurred through disobedience, and at the same time recounting the evils that befell them through unbelief. “I waited patiently for the Lord, and he attended to me.” This is like: “By your endurance you will gain your souls.”

“And he brought me up out of the pit of misery.” [And what did he grant you? Having been heard, he said: he brought me up from the depth of sin and from the soft living of the muddy body, or from the gates of death and the corruption there, or from the distractions of the world.] “And from the miry clay.” From the depth of sins, which like mire cover over those caught in them. For the pit of misery is vice and ignorance. “And he set my feet upon a rock, and directed my steps.” The apostle Paul says: “The rock was Christ.” For I learned to walk the way that pleases God, that is, through the practical life and right doctrines. “And he put a new song into my mouth, a hymn to our God.” He means the law of the gospel; for after we have attained freedom from passion we sing a new song, our house having been renewed. “Many will see and fear, and will hope in the Lord.” For the preaching has spread through the whole world. “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not looked to vanities and false frenzies.” He calls blessed only the one who has set down his hope in God, not the one distracted by the cares of life, which are both frenzy and falsehood

[“… his hope.” Then he adds another point by way of exhortation. Truly blessed, he says, is the one who has had God alone as his hope, and has not looked to the pursuits of the present life, which are vanities and false frenzies and cares spent on nothing. But there is a sober frenzy: [?] the condition of the present life, because of which the prophets seemed to most people to be out of their minds, and in which the righteous man too takes pride when he says: “I said in my ecstasy.”] “Many are the wonders you have done, O Lord my God.” What you have done in the time of the dispensation, he says, is many and wonderful; and so I have proclaimed it to others as well. The proclamation, he says, has run through the whole earth under heaven, so that those who believed have become beyond number. “Sacrifice and offering you did not want, but a body you prepared for me.” Here the person of Christ is introduced, speaking to the Father. Since, he says, you did not want sacrifice and offering, nor [?] were you pleased with the burnt offerings prescribed by the law, I have come, taking a body which you yourself prepared for me. For the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High overshadowed [?] the holy Virgin. And I have come to do your will. For what the Father’s will was, the Lord himself explained when he said: “This is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.” As for the words “in the scroll of the book,” [?] interpretation. The Hebrews call a volume a “scroll.” And Isaiah [?] the mystery of the incarnation of the

…being taught by the Only-begotten, he heard: “Take a new scroll, and write in it with a man’s pen.” This signifies that the decrees of the new law will be written not on tablets of stone but on tablets of flesh, as he says through Jeremiah the prophet: “I will put my laws into their mind, and I will write them on their hearts.” This shows that the Church would receive the new law in the innermost, spiritual chambers of the heart, and would greatly desire the commandments. “I have proclaimed righteousness in the great congregation.” The great congregation, the great Church, is the soul in every nation that has believed in the Savior. It has also been justified, since it has him who justifies the ungodly. “I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart.” By righteousness he means the righteousness proclaimed through him, which is above the law and the shadow. “You knew” stands for “you made it your own.” “I have spoken your truth and your salvation.” I have not kept silent, he says, nor held your truth back within myself. By truth he means the preaching of the gospel. Nor have I hidden your salvation, that is, the way of the salvation given by you, namely the grace that comes through faith. By “a great congregation” he means the Church gathered from Israel and from the nations. For Christ reveals to rational nature the words about mercy and truth, and those about salvation. The words about truth it will find in contemplation, and those about salvation in the practical life. “But you, Lord, do not remove your compassions far from me.” After Christ has taught the mystery of the dispensation, the person of Israel, which remained in disobedience, is introduced. As one who disobeyed God’s mercy, and was therefore passed over and fell into every evil, he comes back to his senses and to repentance, begging to be pitied. This signifies their calling, which will take place at the last time. “May your mercy and your truth always uphold me.” We confess, he says, that he alone is the one who saved and upheld us of old. Even after obtaining salvation, the Church of God again needs God’s providence because of the manifold assaults of men and demons, which he mentions in what follows. “For evils without number have surrounded me.” He recounts the evils that befell them after their unbelief toward Christ. “They have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head, and my heart has forsaken me.” It is as if he said: I have become like those who have no mind or heart; for they became a foolish people and not wise. “Let those who wish me evil be turned back and put to shame.” They cry out either against the spiritual enemies, or against the scribes and Pharisees who plotted against the salvation of his soul, who said of Christ at one time, “He casts out demons only by Beelzebul,” and at another, “You have a demon; who is seeking to kill you?”

“But I am poor and needy; the Lord will take care of me.” Israel, once so bold, has come to repentance and calls himself poor and needy. And indeed he declares [?] that he has the Lord himself as his hope.

“You are my helper and my protector; my God, do not delay.” To these ends, he says, the Church will advance. Before, she was poor and passed through great poverty in the world, but she has been enriched by power from you and glorified by help from you. She asks that this help not delay, and because she asks, it will not delay, as it is said: “He who is coming will come and will not delay.” For the end. A Psalm of David. 40. The present psalm calls blessed those who have believed in Christ himself, and indeed gives them his help as the reward of their faith. The person of the Savior himself is also introduced, denouncing the rulers of the Jewish people and above all the traitor himself. “Blessed is he who considers the poor and needy.” He calls Christ poor and needy, in keeping with the saying: “Though he was rich, he became poor for our sakes.” Here he has set [?] moral teaching ahead of the prophecy, wishing the psalm to profit us in both ways. And whom does he call blessed? The one who considers the poor and needy, that is, the one who understands that Christ, though rich, became poor for this reason: that we too might show mercy to the poor as brothers of our Creator and Judge. And what is the gain of loving the poor? “On the evil day the Lord will deliver him.” He means the day of judgment, which brings pains and toils upon sinners. The Lord, he says, will deliver those who love the poor. For he owes them kindness, since he himself has borrowed alms from them. He said through Solomon, “He who has mercy on the poor lends to God,” and with his own tongue, “Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me.” “On the evil day the Lord will deliver him.” By the evil day he means the onset of temptations and the persecutions of enemies. I think he also hints at the day of judgment, which is fearful and brings harm to the lawless. He promises that a sincere understanding of that poverty will free a person from the evils of the fearful day. [Blessed is that man who considers what is fitting [?] concerning the poor; that is: the one who is able to understand the poverty that Christ took on for our sake.] “May the Lord protect him and keep him alive, and make him blessed on the earth, and not hand him over into the hands of his enemies.” His spiritual enemies, clearly. “You have turned all his bed in his sick-

(Commentary on Psalm 40.) -ness.” He will be changed for the better, he says, and will turn to good health. For divine Scripture customarily uses “turning” for “change,” as in: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me.” “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul.” David also prays for his own sin, since he knows that he himself is one of those who consider the poor and needy. Again, he who suffers for men speaks of men’s sins as his own, and seeks for himself the mercy toward us that those sins call for. He undoes the contempt of those who did not know him, revealing the glory: in his own case according to his own power, and in ours according to the grace of Christ. “My enemies spoke evil against me.” From this point the person of Christ is introduced, recounting what was done to him by the Jews. Up to the present verse we must suppose that the prophet has spoken about the whole catholic Church, so that his words fit each of the earnest faithful rather than the Lord’s humanity. For he does not say these things, as some have supposed, about him alone. He did not say with the article, “Blessed is he who considers the poor and needy one.” Said without the article, it signifies someone indefinite, a particular person. After this he passes from the other members of the Church to the Lord himself, namely Christ, who says, “My enemies,” and so on. “When will he die and his name perish?” For “he is grievous to us even to behold.” “And if he came in to see, he spoke vain words.” He says this about Judas. What he means is this: He had access to me, because he was ranked among the disciples, yet he was double-tongued and a busybody. He spoke vainly, that is, he was not truthful. “His heart gathered iniquity for itself.” He had decided, he says, to hand me over to those who envied me. “He went outside and spoke to the same purpose”: that is, “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” “All my enemies whispered against me.” He means the Jews’ taunts against him, their plots against him and their hidden schemes, speaking of the chief priests who came to an agreement with Judas. They whispered as they made their arrangements about Jesus with Judas. They whispered, for they did not dare to make these arrangements openly, being afraid of the crowd. “They laid down a lawless word against me.” That is: “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!” That this was lawless is clear from the saying: “You shall not kill the innocent and righteous.” “Will not he who sleeps rise again?” He laughs at the schemes of the Jews, who thought they could crush him through death as if he were one of us. But he says: How do you think you can enclose life in death? Suffering is but sleep

to me. He says that resurrection must follow sleep. Sleep is death; so resurrection will necessarily follow death. “For even the man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my bread, has lifted up his heel against me.” That is, mockery, plotting, deceit. He calls Judas a man of peace because he seemed to be ranked among those well disposed to him and among his friends, since he had come to be a disciple. “But you, Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up, and I will repay them.” Because of the self-emptying, he speaks to his Father rather in a human way, although he himself is God’s mercy and physician, and the resurrection and the life. “By this I knew that you delighted in me.” Again he speaks as a man, in order to commit himself to God the Father. “That my enemy will not rejoice over me.” If Christ says this in the person of humanity, the enemy would be understood as the one who contrived death for us; but if he says it as Christ himself, he means the rulers of the Jews. That they were grieved is clear from their slandering his resurrection.

“But you upheld me because of my innocence.” He who upholds all says that he received support. He did not need it insofar as he is understood as God; but having become man, he speaks on behalf of men. “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, from everlasting.” Here again he seals the present song with thanksgiving. From the present age, he says, to the age to come. So our blessing of God begins in the present age but is perfected in the age to come. For we know in part and prophesy in part, and so we also bless in part. “But when the perfect comes,” says Paul, “the partial will be done away.” For as we advance toward the greater, the partial ceases. That is why the Psalmist added, “So be it, so be it,” doubling the prayer. Blessed are those who begin here to bless God through faith and through the accomplishment of other good works, and so crown that blessing in the age to come. For the ungodly and unbelieving are not permitted to bless God there. It should be known that some divide this prophecy of the Psalms into five books and consider the first to end with this psalm, since at its close it has the blessing of God as a kind of crown. On this basis they also divide the four [?] remaining books. For the end, for understanding, for the sons of Korah.

Psalm 41. The sons of Korah were sacred singers. They sing the song after receiving it from its composer, that is, David, and it signifies what will happen at the last times. They introduce the person of the very

“As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God.” These rational deer, because the spiritual spring had left them on account of their iniquities, wept night and day over their own ruin. “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” The face of God is the Word. This signifies that they greatly long to reach the time when their own calling will also take place, so that they too may appear before the face of God the Father. And this face is the same as that of the Son. “With the voice of rejoicing and confession, the sound of one keeping festival.” He announces beforehand that in due time he will obtain salvation and life through Christ, and will dwell in the divine courts together with the other saints. “Why are you so sorrowful, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” He rebukes his griefs, fortifying himself with hope in Christ. If a time has been kept in store, he says, O soul, when our calling through faith will bring us into the tabernacle with those who keep festival, why are you so sorrowful and worn down by grief? “Therefore I will remember you from the land of the Jordan and of Hermonim, from a little mountain.” Since my soul was troubled, he says, I will console myself by recalling your wonders, both those you showed us at the Jordan and those at Mount Hermon. Or this way: Having been in the Jordan, he says, that is, having been counted worthy of holy baptism, I will then remember you through the word of confession. And I will also remember Hermonim. Hermonim is interpreted “way of a lamp,” since holy baptism opens to them a way of illumination. “Deep calls upon deep at the sound of your cataracts.” Again they remind themselves of other wonders. When foreigners marched against them, and Samuel offered sacrifice for them, so much hail came down on their enemies that nearly all of them fell, though no man fought against them. So he calls the onrush of the hail deep running upon deep. “Calls upon” stands for “summons.” The sounds of the cataracts may be understood as the onrushing hail. Elsewhere, however, the cataracts are the prophets of God. “All your billows and your waves have passed over me.” Again he reminds himself of another wonder. For they passed through the sea

[?] variant reading. Thus: The face of God is the Word. It signifies [?] that they desire [?] to arrive at the time [?] … when their calling will also take place, so that they too may appear before the face of the Father. Paris. [?] Gen. 27.

through its midst, fleeing the wickedness of Pharaoh. The billows of the waves, that is, their heights, seemed to bear down on them, but they did them no harm, for the waters stood firm like a wall. [“Deep calls upon deep.” The Father is a deep; the Son is a deep. The deep of sins calls upon the deep of God’s compassion to dash down sin, its causes, and corruption. It is as if to say: It is your custom to bend down to sinners who entreat you. Why then do you overlook us as we fall down before you?] “By day the Lord will command his mercy, and by night his song.” Again he recalls another wonder. Rabshakeh surrounded Jerusalem and threatened that not even God could deliver them from the hand of the Assyrians. But God gave a promise, saying, “I will shield this city.” Then, fulfilling the promise, in a single night he slew one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians. This is what “By day the Lord will command his mercy” means. “A prayer to the God of my life.” As one who has already believed, he offers the words fitting for believers, ascribing to him his own

“I will say to God, You are my helper.” The repentant people repeats its supplication, appealing all the more to God for mercy. A Psalm of David, without a title among the Hebrews. 42. “Judge me, O God, and vindicate me.” The present psalm has the same subject as the one before it. Again those of Israel come forward asking for salvation through Christ. That is why he says, “Send out your light and your truth.” For he was going to lead them into the holy mountain, that is, into heaven and the dwellings above, which he also calls tabernacles, and to the spiritual altar. And he was going to gladden their youth. By youth he means the gladness that also renews their soul. That is why they also promise to offer him confession on the lyre. We have often taught that the lyre should be understood as the body. For the end, for the sons of Korah, for understanding.

…to us, but you also turned us back, so that we became plunder for those who hate us. The prophetic choir says these things, making the people’s [sufferings] its own. “And those who hate us plundered for themselves.” [?] us into dishonor, he says. “And there was no multitude in our shouts of triumph [in our exchanges].” A shout of triumph is a victory song. The sense is this: You have cast us off so completely, he says, that we were defeated even by a few, and those who shouted in triumph over us were only a handful. “You have made us a reproach to our neighbors.” Everything they did to Christ has been paid back to them. They reproached, and they were reproached; they mocked, and they were mocked in turn; they shook their heads at him, and others shook their heads at them. “All day long my shame is before me.” Long and unceasing, he says, has been the disgrace upon us. “All these things have come upon us, and yet we have not forgotten you.” We have already said that it is the prophets who offer the supplication in the person of the people, making their own what befell the people because of its sins.

“And you have turned our paths aside from your way.” They say this because, having acted impiously toward Christ, they were also barred from performing the sacrifice prescribed by the law. “For you have humbled us in a place of affliction.” He says this because they can no longer take any pride in themselves. “And you have convicted us as sinners in the world.” “And the shadow of death has covered us.” He refers to the darkness that came into the hearts of those who did not believe. “If we have forgotten the name of our God.” They say this because after their final fall they no longer worshiped idols; or, again, they speak in the person of the prophets. “For your sake we are being put to death all day long.” This is like the saying, “They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they died by the sword.” Just as they make the people’s sins their own, so too they ascribe their own good deeds to the people, as it were, as though the whole were a single body. Or this way: Because of the unbelief we showed toward you, he says, we have come to such misery that we are like men under sentence of death, and indeed [?] like men led to the slaughter. “Awake! Why do you sleep, O Lord?” They liken to sleep the great forbearance God showed because of their sins. “Arise, and do not cast us off forever.” He says “Arise,” not that God should change his posture, for the divine has no form, but that he should set his power in motion to help us. “And do not cast us off forever,” neither those who do wrong nor those who suffer it, so that the sufferers do not stumble, as if wholly handed over to their trials, and the

wrongdoers do not grow bold through the judge’s patience and advance further in lawlessness. They pray that the appearing of Christ in the last times may be granted to them, so that they may not be deprived of his

David dedicates the present song to the Beloved, that is, to Christ, who came in the last days and brought about the change, that is, the conversion from idolatry to the worship of God. He also mentions the sons of Korah, referring the person to the apostles. We must understand all these things, which is why it is also entitled “for understanding.” “My heart has poured forth a good word.” The Father says this about the Son, for he has been begotten God from God. “I speak my works to the king.” Although as God he is king, he is said to come into the beginning of a kingdom because he became flesh. In the same way, the things he knows by nature as God he is in turn said to hear, by reason of his humanity, in accordance with the dispensation. “My tongue is the pen of a swift scribe.” The Word that he spoke he also calls his tongue. It is called the pen of a swift scribe because he says something and it happens at once, as in: “I will it; be clean,” and at once he was cleansed; and, “Young man, I say to you, arise,” and at once he rose. And there is also this: “The Lord will make a word cut short in the whole world.” “You are fairer in beauty than the sons of men.” One can see the comparison of the good [?] Spirit from what John says: “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” Moses too was a fine pen, for he wrote for us a law to be our tutor; but he was not like him who also wrote our names in heaven. “Grace has been poured out on your lips.” For our Lord speaks sweetly when he says, “I came that they may have life, and have it more abundantly,” and, “I am the bread that came down from heaven,” and gives life to the world. “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one.” He rouses the Only-begotten to battle on our behalf. Then, since he has given him a soldier’s appearance by saying “sword,” he adds “thigh” as well. For the sword is his own as God, and does not come from outside; for he is mighty, that is, of the powers

…Lord, and this is his by nature. He is also comely to those who have recognized his appearing and are able to perceive his beauty, which is above the world. He fitted the sword to his thigh as a threat to the unbelieving and against the battle lines of the adversaries. Concerning the disobedient, at any rate, the psalm says: “If you do not turn, he will burnish his sword.” “In your comeliness and your beauty.” The comeliness and beauty of the one who has gone to war is his divinity and his preeminence over all things. “And bend your bow, and prosper, and reign.” “Bend your bows,” he says, and prosper those who have been justified by you, over whom you reign, he says, having set them free from the tyrant. He shows that the victory is spiritual: having mentioned weapons, he also mentions meekness. It belongs to the meek to forgive those who wrong him what has been done against himself. “And your right hand will guide you wonderfully.” Since he had mentioned a sword, it followed that he should also mention a right hand. His right hand is his right counsels, and using these he admitted nothing of sin.

“Your arrows are sharpened, O Mighty One.” By arrows he means the holy apostles, who struck mortal blows in the heart to the enemies of the King of those who reign. These arrows, having struck the spiritual enemies in the heart, had the power to bring the whole world under heaven beneath the feet of Christ and to place it under the yoke of his kingdom. The verses are in hyperbaton, so that they should run thus: “Your arrows are sharpened, O Mighty One, in the hearts of the king’s enemies.” “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.” Those who have been called through the apostles, confessing the divinity of the Only-begotten, say: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.” “A rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom.” In divine Scripture uprightness signifies righteousness. He is saying, then, that those over whom Christ reigns will learn to walk the road of righteousness. “You loved righteousness and hated lawlessness.” Since human nature, having undergone the change, forsook righteousness and loved lawlessness, for this very reason the Only-begotten became man, restoring in himself, for human nature, the loving of righteousness and the hating of lawlessness; and this is the reason for the incarnation. That is why he says: “Therefore God has anointed you.” Therefore—for what purpose? Surely so that those who have come to share in you may also rejoice, inasmuch as they have received mercy, because through you the loving of righteousness and the hating of lawlessness has been accomplished in them. “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you.” “For this God, your God, has [?] you,” he says; for “anointed” is interpreted as “smeared with oil.” The explanation of this is connected with the earlier words, “You loved righteousness.” “Myrrh and stacte and cassia from your garments.” The garments of the Only-begotten might be understood as his

powers, majesty and glory, according to the verse: “The Lord has become king; he has clothed himself with majesty; the Lord has clothed himself with power and girded himself.” This glory and majesty of his, then, has become fragrant to us, ranking as every kind of incense, according to what is said elsewhere: “Your name is ointment poured out,” and: “We will run after the fragrance of your ointment.” Stacte is a very fine kind of myrrh: when the aromatic substance is pressed, the part of it that flows is set apart as stacte, while the thicker part that remains is called myrrh. Cassia is a very fine and fragrant bark that is wrapped around woody twigs. “From ivory palaces, from which they have gladdened you.” The palaces are the costly and choice houses, that is, temples. He calls them ivory as being polished, as it were, and exceedingly beautiful. He names the holy apostles kings, since they also reign with Christ. Their daughters are the souls reborn through them into the knowledge of God, who make their own hearts into most beautiful temples to the honor of God, and so gladden him. It is as if he were saying: “You will be gladdened, O Master, by the ivory palaces which the daughters of the kings have built in your honor.” “The queen stood at your right hand in a robe of gold.” The queen is the Church, as having become the bride of the great King; standing at the right hand signifies the honor she will enjoy in the age to come; her many-colored clothing is faith, hope and love; and she also has another, more splendid garment, Christ himself. For “as many of you as were baptized into Christ,” he says, “have put on Christ.” “Hear, O daughter, and see.” This word too, again, is addressed to the Church. “And forget your people and your father’s house.” For no one would come in purity to faith in Christ without having completely forgotten former things. The Church’s people of old were the idolaters. Her father’s house is the wise of this age, in whom Satan dwells as in houses. “And the daughter of Tyre with gifts.” From one nation, that of the Tyrians, he signifies the calling of the Gentiles. He named the Tyrians because they above all were enemies of the godly commonwealth. “The rich of the people will entreat your face.” Similar is the verse: “We shall be caught up in the clouds” [?]

…of the virgin signifies the Church: “For I betrothed you, to present you as a pure virgin to God.” “Those who are near her will be brought to you.” For near to virginity is self-control. As many souls, then, as practice self-control—from evil deeds, that is—they too will be led away along with her. And it comes about that those who are led find gladness and everlasting exultation. “They will be led into the temple of the king.” The heavenly…

“In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you.” Since he had said to her, “Forget your father,” he says: in place of your former fathers, that is, in place of the teachers, you will have sons. By sons he means the holy apostles, according to what the Lord said: “By whom do your sons cast them out?” Or else those who lead the churches, who became sons of the Church but were appointed rulers over all the earth by the Lord Jesus, according to the saying: “Go and make disciples of all the nations.” “You will appoint them rulers over all the earth. They will remember your name in every generation and generation.” Clearly through the divine writings: the name of God is remembered in their sacred syllables. “Therefore peoples will praise you forever.” Because of the preaching; and the word is addressed to Christ. Because they recall, through the Scriptures, the wonders of God which he worked from ancient generations, and teach them to the generations to come. “For the end; for the sons of Korah; concerning the hidden things.”

The present psalm signifies the calling of the Gentiles, the expulsion of the spiritual enemies, and their imprisonment in the abyss. Since these things are said as if in parables, the psalm is fittingly entitled “concerning the hidden things.” Those who have believed in Christ sing it, and above all his apostles. “God is our refuge and strength.” He says this because of the persecutions raised against them by enemies both spiritual and visible. “Therefore we will not fear when the earth is troubled.” Because we have you as our helper, he says, we will despise every disturbance that rises against us. For the whole earth was in turmoil when the preaching began, as those who remained in unbelief rose up against those who believed the preaching. “And the mountains are moved into the hearts of the seas.” By the hearts of the seas he means the abysses, and by the mountains the opposing powers. Since the demons were about to be cast into the abyss, they stirred up war against them. “But we will not fear such as these,” they say. [“A helper in afflictions.” Because we have you as our helper, he says, we will despise every disturbance that rises against us.

Or by mountains he means the demons, who were once lofty and conspicuous and for this reason are likened to mountains.] “Their waters roared and were troubled.” Waters here, he says, are the multitudes, which the strangeness of the preaching threw into turmoil. “The mountains were troubled by his might.” The strength of the one who was preached, he says, shook the unclean demons, who were once lofty and conspicuous and for this reason are likened to mountains. “The rushing streams of the river gladden the city of God.” By the river he means the Gospel word, which also gladdens the Church. “The Most High has sanctified his dwelling.” For he is holy, resting among the holy, dwelling among the holy; which is the…

“God is in her midst, and she will not be shaken”—the Church, that is. “God will help her toward morning.” [?] early, about daybreak. For in “will help her” here too, the person of the Church may be understood as the holy apostles and those who lead her in succession, whom he also vigorously strengthens so that they are able to take hold of the preaching. “Nations were troubled, kingdoms bowed down.” The nations, he says, made war against the Church; yet their kings bowed down, that is, they were defeated and fled; but afterward they too bent their necks to Christ. For he says that you will quickly be built up by those by whom you were torn down. For they exalted the Church, nobly offering gifts. “The Most High uttered his voice, and the earth was shaken.” Christ on the cross. By his voice he means the Gospel word. For if a rational soul hears the voice of the Lord, it is shaken, passing from vice to virtue and from ignorance to the knowledge of God. “The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our helper.” He ascribes to the Lord himself the victory won against the spiritual enemies. Jacob is fittingly mentioned because of the wrestling that took place with him. “Come and see the works of God, the wonders he has set upon the earth.” He signifies the peace brought about through the preaching by saying that all war has ceased from the earth. By wonders he means the destructions, that is, the abolitions; for he abolished all war. “He will break the bow and shatter the weapon, and burn the shields with fire.” Here the bow, the weapon and the shield signify a most evil condition and wicked thoughts. “Be still, and know that I am God.” For unless a person is free of every worldly care, he cannot know God; for stillness is needed in order to know God. “I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth.” He promises them the triumph of the preaching over the nations. “The Lord of hosts is with us; our helper…”
The psalm is sung in the person of the holy apostles, exhorting the nations to leap for joy, through good deeds, over the victory won against the accursed ones.

“All you nations, clap your hands.” That is: practice good deeds. “Shout to God with a voice of exultation.” The psalm is a victory song. Since the opposing powers have fallen, then, he urges the nations to sing. “For the Lord Most High is fearsome.” Most High because he has become so for the Church, and fearsome against the [?]. “A great King over all the earth.” No longer, he says, do the wicked rule over those on earth. For he has given them power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and he has subjected the very nations of the wicked demons beneath their feet. “He has subjected peoples to us, and nations under our feet.” They rejoice over what has been given them by the Lord. “He has chosen his inheritance for us, for himself.” And what would the Lord’s inheritance be, if not the one of which the Father said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance”? “The beauty of Jacob, which he loved.” By the beauty of Jacob he means the prophecy concerning the nations, of which he said: “And he will be the expectation of the nations.” And this is beloved. And by whom is it beloved, if not by the one who laid down his [?] for it? This beloved one, then, he says, he has chosen. “God has gone up with a shout.” By these words the Lord’s ascent into heaven is signified. “The Lord with the sound of a trumpet.” He called the praises of those who ascended with him the sound of a trumpet. “Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises.” Since the angels, he says, hymn him as he ascends, you too, O nations, keeping up the same service, sing praises to God who has become king of the earth; for singing praise belongs to those who are cheerful in a godly way. “Is anyone among you cheerful?” he says. “Let him sing praise.” [“Sing praises with understanding.” Not with harps, as those of former times did; for this is what “with understanding” means.] “God has become king over the nations.” For they accepted faith in him. “God sits upon his holy throne.” This signifies his future coming, at which he will sit to judge the world. “The rulers of the peoples have gathered with the God of Abraham.” Similar is the verse: “You will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” “For the mighty ones of God of the earth have been greatly exalted.” In the land of the meek, he says, which will be given to the saints, the mighty ones of God have been exalted on high and glorified exceedingly, as we have been taught by the word that said: “You will sit on twelve thrones.”

This psalm too is sung in the person of the holy apostles, recounting the persecutions brought on by the preaching and the victories won over them. “Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, in the city of our God, on his holy mountain.” No longer, he says, over Judea alone, but also over the sanctified mountain. By mountain here he means the Church, because of the loftiness of its doctrines about God. “Well-rooted, to the exultation of the whole earth.” He extended the exultation, he says, over the whole earth; for he spread the exultation of his divine manifestation, and his grace, into all the earth. “The mountains of Zion, the sides of the north.” Jerusalem lies in the south, while the nations are in the north. Since the Jews prided themselves on being the only ones who dwelt in Zion, the word shows that Zion is the nations that received the Gospel word. For the foundation of Zion is the region of the north, and this region of the north is indicated by “the sides”: instead of saying “the region of the north,” he has said “the sides.” Formerly Paul was the “sides of the north,” from which all evils were kindled upon the earth; but now he has become the mountains of Zion, having in himself Christ who speaks, who came from Zion and turned away ungodliness from Jacob. “The city of the great King.” These sides of the north, he says, that is, the nations, may be called the city, in which God is known as helping them and saving them from temptations. “God is known in her palaces, when he helps her.” The palaces would be the great and choice ones of the city of God, those who excel in it. “For behold, the kings of the earth were gathered together.” The war waged against the apostles because of the preaching, by the visible kings of the nations and indeed by the invisible demons who formerly reigned, was dissolved and vanished. “They themselves, seeing it, marveled.” They were astounded, he says, and amazed, as they beheld the help given by God to the saints. “They were troubled, they were shaken, trembling seized them.” For the surpassing greatness of the strength of the Savior [brought] wonder and astonishment upon them…

…Church, which is the city of God? “God has founded her forever.” Similar to what was said by the Lord: “On the rock I will build my Church.” “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple.” Instead of “we have beheld,” “we expected,” he says, that the name of God would be glorified throughout the whole earth, inferring from your mercy that you would not overlook the people outside Israel; though we were settled in one place and one temple, we hoped for the mercy that embraces the whole world, knowing that your name is universal and over all. “As is your name, O God, so also is your praise.” He says this because he has given grace to all, simply and without partiality, according to the saying: “In Christ Jesus there is neither slave nor free.” “Let Mount Zion be glad.” Mount Zion is clearly the Church. “And let the daughters of Judea exult.” He says that the daughters of Judea are the souls of the holy apostles, for they were of the Jews. “Because of your judgments, O Lord.” Having judged the cause of the nations, you drove away the war of the demons against them. “Encircle Zion and embrace her.” The Holy Spirit gives this command to the apostles, that they become as it were a wall for Zion, that is, for the godly commonwealth. “Tell of it in her towers.” And who would the towers of the Church be, if not those who lead her in each age, and the righteous, to whom the… also recount the mighty works of God…

[To the divine powers and holy angels who guard the Church and the godly commonwealth the Holy Spirit calls out, saying: “Encircle the towers.” For the strongest parts of the city, as being more vital to its defense, are assigned by number to the guards.] “Set your hearts on her strength.” Again, the strength of the Church is the words that support her, which he commands the holy apostles to instill with their whole heart. “And divide up her palaces.” Let each one, he says, rule over a part of the nations. For the Twelve, he says, divided up the world among themselves. “That you may tell it to another generation.” For the apostles tell it also to the generations after them, through the writings about Christ that they have left behind. “For this is our God forever.” He states the reason for the division. For this reason teach and divide, so that it may be heard by the generations that will come later as well, that this one who shepherded the people justly (he means the Lord), this is the one who also, into the ages to come that have no end, will…

Through the present psalm the things concerning the divine tribunal are proclaimed to all people, and that day on which God will bring every work into judgment. The sons of Korah would represent the apostles, who initiated into the mysteries the [world] under…

“Hear these things, all you nations; give ear, all who inhabit the world.” Just as the word summons every race of humankind to salvation, so in the same way it calls all together to be taught about the divine judgment. “Both earthborn and sons of men.” By the earthborn he means the coarser sort of people, the barbarians, who live in wildernesses and do not live under laws; by sons of men, those who follow a more civilized way of life and are governed by laws. “My mouth will speak wisdom.” Just as he divided his hearers into many ranks, so he also distinguishes his teaching into different modes. It is the apostolic choir that utters these words, bearing on its lips Christ, who is the Wisdom of the Father. Since, then, they bore Christ on their lips and constantly meditated on him in their minds, they had understanding. And their minds were so sharpened for understanding that they understood even the Savior’s parables recorded in the Gospels. That is why, when Christ said to them, “Have you understood all these things?” they said to him, “Yes.” “I will incline my ear to a parable.” I, he says, having sharpened my own mind for the understanding of the saving parables, have been able to follow the meaning they carry; and for those who cannot do this because of their immaturity, I will open what is closed and make plain the riddles and parables. And I will do this by means of my own psaltery—that is, the body, which resounds like an instrument—through which the soul is turned to hymnody, moving skillfully through each sense, limb and part. “Why should I fear in the evil day?” Here he begins, having first set out the opening matters of his teaching as in a preface. He begins with a question, so that it may also receive an answer. The question is this: “Why should I fear?” One must punctuate after “fear,” so that the sense is this: If anyone asks, he says, “Why should I fear?”—wanting to learn from me the cause of the anguish that grips me—let him hear plainly that there is an evil day, which I shudder at and fear. And I shudder because on that day the iniquity of my heel will surround me, that is, the turning aside from the divine way that I have committed in my life, having transgressed the divine law through distraction and deceit. This ungodliness, then, will surround me, he says; that is, the evil deeds I have done will stand around me…

[en]circling me on every side and besieging me, and not letting me escape punishment. He calls the day of judgment evil because it is evil for those who are punished. The Apostle also called it the day of wrath, saying: "You are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath." "Those who trust in their power." The words "Hear these things" apply to both: "Hear these things, you who are confident in wealth and power." And what is it that they ought to hear, if not that wealth will be of no use to them on that day? For nothing will redeem them from the wrath that their sin will bring upon them. Just as not even a brother, say, who is beloved of God, nor any other human being, can redeem anyone on that day, so, if a brother cannot, even one beloved of God, much less will wealth be able to. "A brother does not redeem": he means a brother beloved of God and [?] honoured. "And the price of the redemption of his soul." Having taught that wealth is of no use on the day of judgment, he also teaches what is of use. And what is this, if not to take up a toilsome and laborious life? For such people will also be counted worthy of the life promised in the age to come. "He who toils through the practical life will live to the end through knowledge." "And he will cease forever, and will live unto victory." "And he toiled forever, and will live to the end. He will not see corruption when he sees the wise dying." For they will be so far removed from the ungodly that they will not even come near their destruction. And who are the wise who die, if not those of whom it is said, "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise and the understanding of the prudent"? (Mattiaco [?].) For throughout, the present Scripture teaches that on the day of judgment neither the rich man nor the man reputed wise will rescue himself. Only the one who has worn himself down in the present life will attain eternal life. "The fool and the senseless will perish together." The wise and the foolish alike, he says, will be handed over to destruction, for they did not differ from one another at all, since they were alike idolaters. "And they will leave their wealth to strangers." For they did not want to make it their own by doing good to those in need. "And their graves are their homes forever." By the graves he signifies the deadness with which they clothed their souls, since they thought nothing right or upright about God. "Their dwellings from generation to generation." The tents in which they lived while alive, he says, will pass from some to others through the generations. He said this above too: that they will leave their wealth to strangers. "They called their names upon their lands." They ought, he says, to have arranged through faith and a splendid way of life for their names to be written in heaven; but they called them upon the earth, founding places named after themselves.

"And man, being in honour, did not understand." He says that the cause of their falling into arrogance is their [?] desires. That is, they did not understand their honour, namely that they were made in the image of God. "Like the senseless beasts," they exchanged the heavenly tents for dwelling on earth, and the life that comes from God for graves. "This way of theirs is a stumbling block to them." Divine Scripture is accustomed to call each person's life, and the span of each person's life, a way. This way, then, he says, they made rough and hostile for themselves, since they thought nothing right. But while they were stumbling in it, they did not notice the stumbling blocks. "And afterward they will be pleased with their mouth" [?], that is: they will confess, having repented, that they walked such a path, when they will no longer have [?] for repentance.

"Like sheep they are laid in Hades." Since they did not want to be under the good shepherd, but thrust away their own honour, their bodies were corrupted like those of beasts. For this reason they have become the flock of Hades, so that from now on he shepherds them and will lead them off to his pastures: some into the eternal fire, some to where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth, and some into the outer darkness. "And the upright will rule over them in the morning." They no longer rise up against the godly as they did in the present life; on the contrary, those counted worthy of the time of morning and of the new light will rule over the ungodly. "And their help will grow old in Hades." All their help, he says, that is, the strength they had from their glory, will be dissolved by death. For "will grow old" is put for "will be dissolved." "But God will redeem my soul from the hand of Hades, when he receives me." God, he says, will redeem the soul of me who say these things, so that it is not led away with them and left desolate along with the sheep of Hades. "Do not be afraid when a man becomes rich." Having learned, he says, what the end of the ungodly will be, do not count those who are rich in this life blessed. Do not be afraid, as though you were shut out from all hope, and do not lose heart, as though you were deprived of great goods in the present. Know well that redemption from death and eternal life await you; but the man whom the many count happy for his wealth and glory and for his falsely so-called wisdom will have nothing more, for he will be led away stripped of everything in this life. "For when he dies he will not take everything with him." This alone, he says, is what the godless seemed to gain

in this mortal and temporary life, while those people praised them and called them happy for the goods they seemed to have. "Nor will his glory go down with him," since all things are temporary, he says. Such a man will give thanks to you, the Creator, only when you multiply his possessions. "He will go in to the generation of his fathers." He will imitate the zeal of his fathers, he says, and since he comes from wicked men he will inherit their wickedness. "He will not see light forever." For those who think such things have become blind in their souls: they were not enlightened by the light of knowledge in this mortal life, nor will they be counted worthy of the eternal light in the life to come. A PSALM of Asaph. 49. Argument. Asaph sings the psalm, bringing in the person of the Lawgiver, overturning the ancient sacrifices and introducing those of the New Covenant, the offerings of praise. [The leading men among the Jews, neglecting virtue, thought (sic) that it consisted in reciting the laws by heart, proclaiming them, and offering sacrifices. But reading the Law and offering sacrifices are the fruit of virtue already present within; to do these things without it is like oiling oneself for wrestling but neglecting the bouts themselves, which are what win the crown. Against those so disposed, then, blessed David makes his rebuke, bringing in God reproaching them and showing that when virtue is absent he turns away from their sacrifices. He also said this through Isaiah: "The lawless man who sacrifices a calf to me is like one who strikes down a man," and so on. So he gives the Word a form in an image, and brings in God coming from heaven, sitting in judgement and judging the rulers of the Jews. "The God of gods has spoken."] "The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and called the earth." The gods are the saints in God's sight: "I have made you a god to Pharaoh," and, "I said, You are gods." And when are they called by God, if not when, having become man, he spoke and called together the whole earth? And what did he speak, if not "Go and make disciples of all nations," and "This gospel must be preached in the whole world"? "Out of Zion is the splendour of his beauty." For from the Zion above, and the second coming [?]

"Out of Zion is the splendour of his beauty. God will come openly." "Out of Zion," he says, signifies the first coming, and "openly" the second. At his first coming and glorious divine manifestation, he kept silent while he was judged by men and did not openly display his own divinity. But when he comes the second time, he will come openly and will not keep silent; he will convict the world of its sin. For if God will come openly, and Christ

is God, then "openly" indicates the flesh. "God will come openly." For not secretly, as at the first coming, but, as he himself says, like lightning filling everything from east to west. "Our God, and he will not keep silent." He will not then, he says, keep silent toward the ungodly as he did before. "A fire will burn before him." Fire, to hand over those who deserve it because of their ungodliness. Similar is the verse: "A river of fire flowed before him." Blessed Daniel saw these things very clearly. For "A river of fire," he says, "flowed before him; his throne was a flame of fire, its wheels burning fire." (So Corderius.) The fire signifies either the light that comes from him, for the spiritual light that comes through faith leads the way to the knowledge of Christ (its type was the pillar of fire that led Israel by night); or else that the Saviour rekindled us, who had grown cold in every kind of sin, to eagerness for every good thing, casting in, as a spiritual fire, participation in the Holy Spirit. He said, indeed, "I came to cast fire on the earth"; for all of us who have been granted such grace have come to live by the Spirit. That is why fire is also mentioned together with the grace of the Holy Spirit; for, according to the word of John, we are baptized in Christ with the Holy Spirit and fire. One of the prophets also said, "He goes out like a refiner's fire and like fullers' soap; and he will sit down refining and purifying like silver and gold." For the power of the Holy Spirit melts away all filth in us. But it did the synagogue of the Jews no good, because they did not accept the grace. Concerning them God says in Jeremiah: "The bellows have failed from the fire, the lead has failed. In vain the silversmith works the silver; their wickedness has not been melted away." "He will summon the heaven above." ([?].) Formerly those on earth were portions for foxes, as he says somewhere in the Psalms, serving unclean spirits and in each place regarding whatever they pleased as god. But the Saviour appeared and made the light of the true knowledge of God shine upon us. He turned back what had strayed and bound up what was sick, like a good shepherd; he drove the wild beasts away from the sheepfold; he sanctified it by the Spirit, secured it with angelic powers, and appointed holy teachers of the mysteries throughout the whole earth. He will summon, then, he says, the angels in heaven and those chosen on earth for the apostolic mission, in order to judge between his people. For the apostles brought to God those who were persuaded, but handed the unbelievers over to Satan, all but saying, "Walk, then, in the light of your fire and in the flame you have kindled." To the unbelieving Jews, at any rate, they say: "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you thrust it away and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles." That angels work together with the teachers of the mysteries and their

disciples Paul shows when he says, "Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?" The ladder that Jacob saw also showed this: it reached from earth to heaven, the Lord stood firmly upon it, and angels ran up and down it. Such too is the verse: "The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and will deliver them." Through them, then, they work together, and they themselves judge between the people. "He will summon the heaven above." The righteous, he says, who practise a heavenly way of life, he will gather into the dwelling places above. "And the earth, to judge his people." He says that sinners and all those on earth will be gathered, so that the righteous may be separated from those who are not. "Gather to him his holy ones." The words are addressed to the angels, according to what the Lord said: "And he will send his angels, and they will gather the righteous from the four winds of the earth." "Those who make his covenant upon sacrifices." Spiritual sacrifices.

"And the heavens will declare his righteousness." The heavens, he says, will glorify God, because he counted even human beings worthy of the heavenly abodes. (Corderius.) He wants the holy ones of the former people to stop, before the coming judgement, the sacrifice made by slaughtering irrational animals, and to take up the sacrifice that accords with understanding and knowledge. At this the heavenly powers sing the praises of the Judge, because he began with the holy ones, and the heavens proclaim his righteousness, rejoicing with them in their salvation. But the earthly dwelling will be left to the order that was not counted worthy of the heavenly calling (a). "For God is judge." Here he plainly calls Christ God; for the Father has given all judgement to the [Son]. And if the Father has given all judgement to the Son, and God is judge, then Christ is God. "Hear, my people, and I will speak to you." Since he is introducing a new legislation, he puts first the words "God, your God, am I," so that no one might suppose the word to be human or from some angelic power. The sense is this: "Do not think that I am someone else because I am laying down different laws today. I am that very one who laid down the laws about sacrifices through Moses. I testify to you that you will not be charged with transgressing the laws given through Moses. For I am the one who there too gave commands for the benefit of my child, and now I testify this: there is no need for you to keep the ordinances about sacrifices. Even if you do not offer them, it is as though they had been offered. For your whole burnt offerings are before me continually, even if they are not offered. But if you are determined at all costs to bring these as something precious and necessary, hear me say plainly that I will accept none of them from you. For they are all superfluous

to me, since the animals grazing in the fields, cattle and beasts, the birds of the sky and the beauty of the field, are all mine, and I lack nothing. And if I ever needed food, I am not so needy as to ask such things of you, for the world is mine. What acceptable sacrifices will you offer me? Praise, hymns, and speaking of God. When you have fulfilled these, then, as one who has fulfilled a divine law, you will receive in return that when you call you will be heard." And to show which people he is addressing, he added: "Israel, and I will testify to you." Then he shows his own lordship: "God, your God, am I," who freed you from slavery in Egypt, who gave you the sea as a road, who fed you in the desert, who gave you that law. "Do not think me a different lawgiver when you see the differ[ence] of the laws

["God, your God" [?]. That is, he who has displayed great wonders to your race from the beginning until now.] "I will not reprove you for your sacrifices." I do not charge you, he says, with neglecting sacrifices, for you offer them continually; but I urge you not to make them the measure of righteousness. "But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my ordinances?" Here he calls the teacher of the law of the divine Scriptures a sinner. It is like the saying, "Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner." For if he transgresses all the commandments, practises every kind of wickedness and lends his tongue to deceit, why does he even carry the divine [words] on his lips

"You wickedly supposed that I would be like you." Formerly, he says, I was patient, but now I will not do so. I will set your sins before you to convict you. You supposed that they no longer existed and would never come to anyone's mind; but I, as God, will bring them to light, and they will be set before you. I do not hide them as you do, nor make myself like you. I will bring them out so that by making them known I may pour shame upon you. "I will reprove you and set your sins before your face." "Understand these things, you who forget God." Because he loves humankind, after the reproof he adds an exhortation, leaving room for repentance. Understand that I am patient, not because I take pleasure in what you have done, but to give you time for repentance. Otherwise the lawless one, that is, lawlessness, seizes us, and there is no one to rescue us. For I rescue those who recognize the evils they are in, who stop, and who say, "We have transgressed, we have done wrong, we have acted ungodly." For one who is still doing evil cannot confess. "Lest he snatch you away, and there be no one to deliver you." Repent, he says, before death takes your soul away; for there is no one to deliver those who are held fast in Hades by their sins.

"A sacrifice of praise will glorify me." He takes up again what was said, urging them to offer spiritual worship. After his long accusation he has shown the remedy for sin, namely, partaking of the mysteries. For that is truly the sacrifice of praise that glorifies God, since then we stand praising him together with the angels and with all creation. "And there is the way by which I will show him my salvation." In the sacrifice of praise, he says, lies the way of salvation from God. For the end. A PSALM of David. 50. When Nathan the prophet came to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba.

He sings this psalm, which contains the confession of two crimes: the murder of Uriah and adultery with Bathsheba. [He also shows all people that repentance is the way of salvation, a kind of art of winning continual victory over the enemy. For whoever always practises it and succeeds in it becomes a constant victor over the one who is always wrestling against him. He also brings in the redemption that comes through baptism when he says, "You will sprinkle me." Indeed, he also teaches that the gift of prophecy had been preserved for him. For he does not ask for it as one who had been deprived of it, but begs that it not be taken away, saying, "Do not take away."] He also brings in the prophecy of the universal redemption from sins that would come through holy baptism, and teaching about worship in the spirit. Throughout you will find him seeking atonement for the two transgressions. "Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy." Since the sin is great, he asks to obtain God's great mercy. "And according to the multitude of your compassions blot out my iniquity." For only God's compassions can wash hands stained by murder. [Making his meaning clearer, he says, "Wash me thoroughly." Here too he asked for abundant cleansing, to show that the offence was great in every respect. Or else, since he had heard of his forgiveness from Nathan, and his many and varied misfortunes had cut away much of the sin, he now says: "I need soaps and washings, so that what clings to me may be scraped off completely."

"Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity": that is, he says, the iniquity of the murder. "And cleanse me from my sin": that of the adultery. "For I know my iniquity." This too he said of the murder. "And my sin is ever before me." He turns over and over the memory of the sin of adultery, which does not let him go or depart from him, but is constantly with him and choking him.

["Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin." By sin he means the adultery. One should know that sin is a falling away from the good, while iniquity is an offence against the divine law; and each of these has its own origin. But they also coincide. For the one who sins has missed the mark that is according to nature and within nature; for the mark set for human nature is to live according to reason, far removed from irrationality. Likewise the one who acts lawlessly offends against the law given in nature, living without self-control. So John, the apostle and disciple of Christ, rightly brought both together when he said, "Everyone who commits sin also commits lawlessness." Or else: sin corresponds to lawlessness. For everyone who acts lawlessly sins, though not everyone who sins acts lawlessly. It can also be taken as said in parallel, because of "Everyone who commits sin also commits lawlessness."] "Against you only have I sinned, and done what is evil in your sight." That is: "In my transgression I hid from the eyes of everyone, yet yours alone I did not escape." That is why he says, "And done what is evil in your sight. For although I had enjoyed many good things from you, I repaid you with the opposite." He does not say this as though he had not wronged Uriah (how could that be?), but because the greatest transgression had been dared against God himself, who chose him and made him king when he was a shepherd. Or because, though he hid from the eyes of all, he did not escape God's, but was convicted through the prophet. Or because, as king, he was not subject to human law, but, as a God-fearing man, he was subject to God alone. Or because no human being reproved him, but God alone corrected him. "Against you only," he says, "have I sinned." "So that you may be justified in your words." You convicted me through the prophet, he says, of having transgressed; and you are righteous, always rescuing me from my enemies and honouring me with kingship and prophecy, while I am profane and a murderer. "And prevail when you are judged." A demonstration, or confession, of his sins. "For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother craved me." For God's original purpose was that we should not come into being through marriage and corruption; but the transgression of the commandment brought in marriage, because Adam acted lawlessly, that is, set aside the law given him by God. All who are born of Adam, therefore, are conceived in iniquities, since they fall under the condemnation of our forefather. The words "And in sins my mother craved me" mean that Eve, the mother of us all, was the first to crave sin, as though lusting after pleasure. That is why we too, falling under our mother's condemnation, are said to be craved in sins. He shows that from the beginning human nature fell under sin through the transgression in Eve, and that birth came under a curse. He weaves his discourse from the very beginning because he wants to show the greatness of God's gift.

"For behold, you have loved truth; you have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom." The sense is this: You, Lord, he says, who are truth and love truth and want us to live in truth, will cleanse us of the ancient sin. And so you will cleanse us with hyssop, so that we are made whiter even than snow. He likens the working of the Holy Spirit to hyssop, because it is warm and scours away all the filth in us. [The cleansing will come about through hyssop, that is, through the Holy Spirit, for hyssop is a cleansing herb.] The words "You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom" show that all the things to come, whatever God laid down in his own wisdom, [were made known] to him through the Holy Spirit [?]

"You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed." Having said, "You have given divine laws and ordinances," he says the greater thing: "In the law you granted certain purifications, among them sprinkling with hyssop. In keeping with this purpose, then, grant us something similar now as well, since you are the same God." Or he seems to hint at a mystery. Moses in Egypt commanded that the blood of the lamb be sprinkled on the doorposts with hyssop, and we too have been bought with blood, but with more precious blood. That blood became a safeguard, so that those living in the house should suffer nothing from the destroyer. So David, recalling that blood in a hidden way, fittingly says, "You will sprinkle me with hyssop," and what follows. He is hinting at the cleansing that would come to all through the blood of Christ, the true Lamb, and longing, as it were, to obtain it, for it alone can wash a person thoroughly and make him whiter than snow. "You will make me hear joy and gladness." You will grant, he says, that through the Spirit I may hear again the joy and gladness that will come in the last times. And what would this be but the knowledge concerning the resurrection, which he taught when he said, "The bones that have been humbled will rejoice"? When will our rotted bones rejoice, if not at the time of the resurrection, when, as another prophet says, "Our bones will [?] like grass"? "The bones that have been humbled will rejoice." The strength of my soul will rejoice, which before was weakened by sin. "Turn your face away from my sins." Again he returns to confession. "Create a clean heart in me, O God." Renew, he says, my soul, which has grown old and decayed through sin. "And renew a right spirit within me." "Right" here means "steadfast." It is as if he said: Secure my mind, so that it no longer falls easily into sin. "And do not take your Holy Spirit from me." He prays again that the prophetic spirit may come to him, for it had left him because of the [?]

"Restore to me the joy of your salvation." This refers to the whole human race. By "the joy of salvation" he means the coming of the Lord, as Simeon said: "For my eyes have seen your salvation." And he himself prays to share in it. "And establish me with a guiding spirit." What he called above a "right spirit," here he calls "guiding." "I will teach transgressors your ways." Once you have rescued me from sin, he says, and given me your Holy Spirit again, then I will teach those who transgress to walk in your ways once more. "Deliver me from bloodshed, O God, God of my salvation." Again he makes supplication over the murder of Uriah, that he may be delivered from the defilement that came from it. Or rather, "from blood" means from sacrifices made with blood, as the following verses of the psalm show, where he says, "For if you had desired sacrifice, I would have given it," and so on. "My tongue will rejoice in your righteousness." Symmachus translated this as: "My tongue will proclaim your mercy." For having received forgiveness I will not keep silent, but will go on hymning you and recounting your favors. Since, he says, you rejected the sacrifices of the law, because they cannot forgive sins, I have therefore offered you the one you loved. And this is the sacrifice of repentance and a broken heart. "Do good, Lord, to Zion in your good pleasure." Here he calls the Church Zion. For when God the Father was pleased to sum up all things in his Son, then he also gave his good promises to his Church. "And let the walls of Jerusalem be built." By the walls of Jerusalem he means the holy priests who fence his Church about. "Then you will be pleased with a sacrifice of righteousness." When, he says, you do good to Zion and the walls of Jerusalem are built, then indeed sacrifices will be offered: not those of blood, but those of righteousness, that is, of praise. "Offering and whole burnt offerings" also refers to the offerings of righteousness and of the bloodless sacrifice. "Then they will offer calves upon your altar." These too are calves of righteousness, so that everything belongs to righteousness: sacrifices of righteousness, offerings of righteousness, whole burnt offerings of righteousness, calves of righteousness. "To the end. Of understanding, for David, when Doeg the Idumean came and told Saul, saying to him: David has come to the house of Abimelech." Psalm 51.

When David fled from Saul and in his flight came down to the house of Abimelech, he ate the priests' bread and received the sword of Goliath. Someone went and reported this to [?] … can forgive sins. Which sentence below [?]

stirred Saul's soul to war, so that he sent men to destroy the whole city of the priests, sparing not even their livestock. When David heard this, he spoke the words before us, addressing them to the person of the Syrian. The psalm also refers to the person of the Jewish people and of Judas. It also contains a promise of good things to come, and of the establishment of his saints in the house of God, when it says: "But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God." That is why the psalm is titled both "of understanding" and "to the end." For much understanding is needed to recognize the [?] of the dispensation of David according to the flesh [?]

"Why do you boast in wickedness, you mighty man?" He addresses his words to the Syrian himself, or to the devil who was at work in him. "Like a sharpened razor you have worked deceit." He says this because Doeg, as it were, shaved off and cut down the entire city of the priests. "You have loved evil more than goodness." For he did wrong by telling lies against the priest and all those with him, and by saying things against him that had never been done. To say that he had inquired of God on David's behalf was a lie and not the truth. "You have loved all words of drowning, a deceitful tongue." Everything he did aimed at plotting, envy and the death of the priest and of all those put to death with him. That is why the words of Doeg's lies are called words of drowning: with his words he sank the entire city of the priests at a stroke, as if into the deep. These things could rightly be said also of the rulers of the Jews, and of Judas himself. "May he pluck you out and remove you from your dwelling." For they were removed from their holy tabernacle and became captives because of the cross they brought upon the Lord. "And your root from the land of the living." This is like "Let them be blotted out of the book of the living." ["Therefore may God destroy you to the end." These things could rightly be said also of the rulers of the Jews and of Judas himself, because they loved what is harmful. "To the end" means "utterly."
