Therefore he who brings down the proud will tear you down, as something badly built, and, as something badly planted, will pluck you out, remove or uproot you, and from your dwelling, that is, from living together with [?]

"The righteous will see and fear." For when the ungodly are destroyed, the righteous are struck with fear. You, he says, suffer these things, but the righteous, that is, your peoples, will be seized with fear when they see your destruction. For the punishment that falls on you is enough to frighten them too. And yet it is because of your [?] against them

that you are going to suffer such things. "Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but hoped in the abundance of his riches." For the traitor loved to take gold more than to have Jesus as his helper. "And he grew strong in his vanity." That is: he prevailed in fulfilling the desires of his vain heart; he did not repent and cease from his impiety. ["But he hoped in the abundance of his riches." He rightly called wealth and power vanity, judging from the facts themselves. For they did not help [?], nor the Assyrians, when he killed them by the coming of a single angel, and unburied [?]] "But I am like a fruitful olive tree." For the glory of those who believe in Christ is evergreen. ["But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace," and so on. Since the saint had this fruit in himself, he said, "But I am like a fruitful olive tree." He likens himself to a fruitful olive tree because mercy prevailed in him, and the other virtues followed in consequence. So too we call Job brave, Joseph chaste, and the others by the virtue that prevails in them [?].] "I have hoped in the mercy of God forever." The divine Scriptures call the Lord the mercy of God, because through him mercy came to us. For he summed up all things in himself and restored them to their first elements. "And I will wait for your name, for it is good before your holy ones." May I have confidence in your name, he says, and I will proclaim it before all your saints, for this will be good and kindly for me. "To the end. Concerning Maeleth. Of understanding, for David." Psalm 52.

He sings this psalm on behalf of the choir of the apostles and of those who believed in Christ, who also rejoiced and were glad. "Maeleth" is interpreted as "chorus" or "choral dance." He necessarily speaks of the time before the coming of the Lord, to show how great the benefit of that coming is. It should be noted that the thirteenth psalm contains the same meaning throughout and almost all the same words, so that those seeking the interpretation can find it plainly there. "The fool said in his heart, There is no God..." "God looked down from heaven upon the sons of men." Since they did not reckon that God watches over human affairs, judges with just judgment and restrains all lawlessness, God for this reason looked down from heaven. For this clearly signifies the Lord's coming among men. "All have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there is none who does good, there is not even one." This is not said as an exaggeration. Nothing in Scripture is said by way of exaggeration; everything is said with truth. All

the Jews, then, turned aside from the way that says, "I am the way." So they became worthless, because they did not want to receive it, and none of them did good. For they were all ignorant of him, hardened by the letter of the law. "To the end. Among hymns. Of understanding, for David. When the Ziphites came and said to Saul: Is not David hidden among us?" Psalm 53.

Fleeing from Saul, David stayed in the wilderness of [?]. Then the Ziphites went to Saul and told him the place where David was hiding as a fugitive, and urged him to come and seize him. But David took his lyre in hand and sang the words before us, since he knew by the prophetic spirit that he would suffer no harm from Saul. And indeed, when Saul had set out to capture him, he received news of the Philistines and hurried back with his men. These words could also refer to the person of the apostolic choir: recounting the uprisings of the Jewish nation and the fury of the kings of the Gentiles, it asks God to be saved from them all through his name. And it declares prophetically that God turns the evils back on the heads of the enemies, while he himself will offer sacrifices of victory. That is why the psalm is titled "of understanding," referring us to the meaning just stated. "O God, save me by your name." He asks to be saved by nothing else than by his name. [Since I call upon your name, he says, grant me my salvation in that very name. "And in your might," that is, in your Son, "you will judge me"; that is: let me be handed over for examination not to other judges, but to your power.] "And in your power you will judge me." For having judged their case, he handed some over to destruction and saved others from their enemies. "O God, hear my prayer." Receive my supplications with kindness. "Give ear to the words of my mouth." This is like "And now, Lord, look upon their threats." "To the end. Among hymns. Of understanding, for David." Psalm 54. Argument. The Prophet saw by the Spirit what would be done against Christ by the Jewish people and by Judas himself. Filled with grief and perplexity, which in this psalm he also calls "musing," he remains troubled and at a loss over the outrages committed. He calls on God first to give ear to his prayer and grant him this; then, second, to take note of the petition sent up in the prayer; and third, to look upon the condition of the one who sends up the prayer; and so to deem him worthy of being heard. That is why he adds: "Attend to me and hear me." "Give ear, O God, to my prayer." He offers various

supplications, begging that they be received. Do not overlook me, he says, as I implore you, but attend to me kindly and stretch out your help. "I was grieved in my musing, and I was troubled." For he was filled with perplexity at seeing the lawlessness committed against the Savior, which he goes on to describe, saying: "At the voice of the enemy and at the affliction of the sinner." The whole sense is this: Attend to how I was grieved, how I was troubled, how I am filled with musing; and accepting these things, hear [?]

"For they turned lawlessness upon me." He refers everything that befell the Savior to his own person. [They did these things to me out of rancor born of irrational anger. Rancor is lasting anger. For this reason I became terrified and troubled, as though death were already upon me. Such anguish and fear came over me that the sunlight no longer seemed to shine but to have gone dark. I reckoned flight better than anything else, and I prayed that wings might be given me so that I could depart and find rest elsewhere.] "My heart was troubled within me, and the fear of death fell upon me." Behold, he says, my heart has wrung my insides; and the fear of death too has fallen upon me. He is speaking either of the saving death, at which the Prophet was filled with fear, moved by human reasoning, or of the death of souls, those who would perish because of such outrages. Fear and trembling fell upon the Prophet as he saw the beloved of God suffering such things at the hands of the ungodly, and darkness covered him, since what was done against the Savior truly deserved darkness. Then, as though left behind in the midst of those doing these things, with no way of escape at all and nowhere to turn aside and get clear of the evils, he prays to be lifted up on high and, becoming winged, through the air [?]

"I waited for God, who saves me from faintness of spirit and from the tempest." He calls the grief that came upon him through the passion a tempest. "For I have seen lawlessness and strife in the city." He gives the reason why he also made the prayer [?]

"For if an enemy had reproached me, I would have borne it." These words can rightly be referred to the person of the traitor. "But you, a man of one soul with me, my leader and my acquaintance." That is: you were appointed a leader by me; he means Judas. "Who shared sweet food with me." It is as if he said: who was often granted a place at the same table. "In the house of God we walked in harmony." He says this because Judas had often gone with him into the temple. "Let death come upon them, and let them go down alive into Hades." Since they were unwilling to receive you, the Life, death will therefore take its place in them. And "Let them go down alive into Hades," because

they knew he was the heir and said, "Come, let us kill him." For he had used "alive" to stand for knowledge. "I cried to God, and the Lord heard me." "I cried to God." And what did he cry? That his soul be redeemed from those seeking to destroy it. That is why he was heard. "Evening and morning and noon I will tell of it." That is: I will not stop recounting how you heard me and redeemed my soul. "For they were with me in great numbers." For the many came together against me, wanting [to take] my soul

"For they have no exchange." They will be humbled, he says, since they have no exchange for their soul. For once they had rejected the precious blood of Christ, which was accepted as the exchange for the life of the world, they no longer have any ransom to hand. "He stretched out his hand in repaying." He stretched out his hand, the one that bestows good things, so that they might share in the blessing. But they not only did not receive it; they also profaned the covenant, namely the covenant of the gospel. "They were divided by the anger of his face." Since they acted wickedly toward their benefactor, he therefore scattered them to every wind. "And their hearts drew near." Again he directs his words at Judas: In his heart, he says, he consented to betray Christ. He offered words that were soft and smooth, but they were full of malice. And what words were these, if not "Hail, Rabbi," spoken to betray him? "Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will sustain you." This is like "Do not worry about what you will eat, or what you will drink, or what you will wear." "He will never let the righteous be shaken." That is: at every time he will snatch the righteous from every uprising of their enemies. "But you, O God, will bring them down into the pit of corruption." He means those who rose up against him and handed him over to the cross. By the pit of corruption he means Hades. "Men of blood and deceit will not live out half their days." By men of blood he means those who killed the Author of life, who did not complete the span of their own lives, since they were handed over to the sword of the Romans. "To the end. For the people far removed from the holy ones. For David, for an inscription on a pillar, when the Philistines seized him in Gath." Psalm 55.

Fleeing from Saul, David had six hundred men following him. Then he passed over to Gath and was honored by the Philistines, for they assigned him Ziklag as a place to live. The psalm could also refer [Note: perhaps "came together" should be read, and shortly after, "to take away." Ed.]

to the person of the Church. Long ago it was far removed from the saints, at the time when it worshiped idols and served demons. But it was rescued from its spiritual enemies by the one who came from the seed of David according to the flesh, who fought on our behalf and, as it were, inscribed our victory on a pillar. For then the foreigners also counted him worthy of honor, that is, those from the Gentiles who believe in him. "Have mercy on me, O God, for man has trampled me." David says this either about Saul, or else every saint says it, because of the afflictions they have in the world. Often each one of us too undergoes this hard war, attacked all day long by Satan and trampled by him. For even though the psalm mentions a man, it still hints at Satan himself, who is often called by that name in divine Scripture, or at one of those who serve as soldiers under him there. Yet it is also fitting for the people of the Gentiles to sing these words, since they were deceived by Satan for a long time and endured his war through the plotting of the demons, at whom he hints more clearly in what follows. "My enemies trampled me all day long." He knew that Saul plotted against him at the prompting of the invisible demons. Or it also points to the saying, "Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places." "For many are those who war against me from on high." Even though they rise up, he says, I will defeat them all, hoping in you. For this hope gave me such strength that I do not fear those who have long warred against me. "In God I will praise my words." When I am attacked by my enemies, he says, I arm myself so as to suffer no harm, making all my words hymns and dedicating them to God, and placing my hope in him. That is why I also cast out all fear of flesh. "All day long they abhorred my words." All day long, he says, I dedicated my words to God, but they did not stop all day long from combining their efforts against me for evil. "They will sojourn and hide; they will watch my heel." "They will sojourn" stands for "they will gather together." The sense is this: In this way, he says, they spent every day stirring up words against me, and all their thinking was directed against me. They were eager to gather together and make secret preparations against me. Nor did they stop there, but they also pried into my heel, that is, the course of my life, to see whether they might somehow trip me and throw me down. And they watched my footsteps, what kind [?]

…where I walked, so that they might seize me. These things they did against me, persecuting me in vain. But you, Lord, my hope, would rescue me from their unjust scheme, and pursuing them with your wrath would cast them down. “O God, I have declared my life to you.” Speaking with boldness, he says, and not ashamed of my own life, I have declared all of it to you. And you accepted it and did not reject my tears, but set them before your eyes, confirming your promise which says: “While you are still speaking I will say, Behold, I am here.” So it came about that, when I was heard, my enemies retreated backward. Hence I say: “On whatever day I call upon you, my enemies will turn back.” I have learned this from the facts, he says, and I know for certain that my hope is not in vain, but that I have gained God as my helper. “In me, O God, are vows of your praise, which I will render.” Since you have counted us worthy of your dispensation, he says, and have saved us, what shall we render to you but sacrifices of praise? “For you have rescued my soul from death.” From spiritual death, he says, that is, from ignorance of God. “And my feet from slipping.” He means sin, for it was sin that brought us down to death. “That I may be pleasing before the Lord in the light of the living.” For whoever has been rescued from sin and made pure will be pleasing to the Lord in the age to come, in the land of the living. The coming of the Lord has secured for us our rescue from death, our freedom from sin, and a share in the land of the living as well. That is why the psalm is also inscribed “for a stele inscription” for David. “For the end. Do not destroy. Of David, for a stele inscription, when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave. Psalm 56 [?].”

Fleeing from Saul, who was pursuing him, David came into a cave with four hundred men; it was then that he cut off the edge of Saul's cloak. And it was then that he sang this psalm. It also refers to what Christ did on our behalf when, in the last days, he appeared on earth in the flesh and drove away our corruption. “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me.” He offered the hymn to him in the person of humanity. “For my soul has trusted in you, and in the shadow of your wings I will hope.” It is the custom of divine Scripture to call God's protecting power “wings,” as in the saying: “How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings.” So it is on your help, he says, that I set my hope. “Until iniquity passes away.” That is, until Satan is removed from the midst, along with the wicked powers that are with him…

“I will cry out to God Most High, to God who has been my benefactor.” I will give thanks, he says, and offer my gratitude to you, my benefactor. “He sent from heaven and saved me.” He clearly proclaims the descent of the Lord. “He gave over to reproach those who trampled me.” Clearly the spiritual and hostile powers. [Grant me, then, this benefaction, so that I may say with boldness that you looked down from heaven upon our affairs, and set ours right, but brought those of our enemies to reproach. Or else he means the deliverance by which he was saved in the cave, when instead he had his enemy in his power, and yet [?] spared him. This was indeed a reproach to the one who had been saved, since he had plotted in vain against his savior.] “God sent forth his mercy and his truth.” The Son is the mercy and truth of the Father. “And he rescued my soul from the midst of the lions' whelps.” [Left in the midst of the whelps of the [?] foreigners. As far as it depended on me, I fell asleep troubled, even by human impiety [?]. But the Most High sent his Word and rescued my soul, so that it suffered no harm from the turmoil of the whelps. And what are these beasts? They are the sons of men. Their teeth are weapons, and their counsels [?]: that is, they are harmful in every way. Just as a sword, once sharpened, easily kills, so also the tongue, once sharpened, kills with slanders.] Clearly the spiritual whelps. “I slept troubled.” Since I have been rescued, he says, from the spiritual whelps, I will therefore rest, although formerly I was troubled by them. “Sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows.” He says this to point to what was dared [?] against the Savior at the time of the passion, when the Jews cried out to Pilate against Christ, “Away, away, crucify him,” and, “If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you.” “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth.” Even though you lowered yourself, he says, into a voluntary self-emptying for our salvation, and became obedient unto death, yet ascend again into the heavens, for by ascending you will fill all the earth with your glory. “They prepared a snare for my feet.” Those who tried to bring me down with snares, he says, you caused to fall into the very pit they dug. Therefore, having accomplished this, be exalted above the heavens. “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready.” He asks to receive the Holy Spirit, which [?]… (Note: “ei de”; perhaps read “ou kai.” Ed.)

“I will give thanks to you among the peoples, Lord; I will sing to you among the nations.” By his thanksgiving he proclaims the good news of the conversion of all the nations, since all the nations sing his hymns. “For your mercy has been magnified up to the heavens.” This is like the saying: “For creation itself will be set free from corruption into the freedom of the children of God.” “And your truth up to the clouds.” You have proved true by events, he says, the voices of the clouds, that is, of the prophets. [“Your truth up to the clouds.” The voices of the clouds, he says, that is, of the prophets, were proved true by events. “Up to the heavens” is like the saying: “For creation itself will be set free from corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.”] “For the end. Do not destroy. Of David, for a stele inscription. Psalm 57.”

The present psalm has the same subject as the preceding one; or rather, it explains clearly what end came upon those who rose up against the Savior. “If you truly speak righteousness…” Since they gathered against the Savior as though they were avenging the law, the prophetic Spirit fittingly commands them, if they really care about justice, to judge uprightly, that is, justly. But they did not judge justly, for they wanted to kill the innocent and righteous one. “For in your heart you work iniquities on the [earth].” Even if their words are fair, he says, as they pretend to defend the law, their heart is full of bitterness, and their deeds are likewise full of lawlessness. “Sinners have been estranged from the womb.” He shows that they had no ground whatever for salvation. [For through the prophet Isaiah God said to the Jews: “I knew that you would surely deal treacherously, and that you are lawless, and you will be called so from the womb”; by “womb” he means holy baptism.] “Their anger is after the likeness of the serpent.” By “anger” he means the soul, which he also says is like the serpent in paradise, who brought in death while feigning words of friendship. Since these men likewise said “Rabbi” and “Teacher” and “We know that you have come from God,” and uttered other such words, while plotting to hand him over to the cross, they are for this reason compared to the serpent. “Like a deaf asp that stops its ears.” They could be likened not only to the serpent, he says, but also to an asp that carries its venom in its teeth and refuses to listen to the charms that would make it cease from its anger. He says this because they too, in the words of Isaiah, made their ears heavy so as not to hear the words of the Lord. “God will break their teeth in their mouth.” By “teeth” here he means the slanders they devised against the Lord, especially those about the resurrection. Or by “teeth” he means power,

since the power of lions lies in their teeth. “They will be brought to nothing like water that runs away.” They will be easily despised, he says, like water spilled out and utterly useless. “He will bend his bow until they grow weak.” By “bow” here he means the sentence that will be pronounced at the divine judgment seat. “Until” stands for “and,” so that it reads, “and they will grow weak.” “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun.” Cast into the eternal fire, he says, they did not behold the sun of righteousness. This is like the saying: “Let the ungodly be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the Lord.” “Before your thorns perceive the bramble.” A bramble is a thorny plant, and he means the crown of thorns. Before your thorns grow, he says, that is, your sins, and become a bramble—that is, before they blossom and bear fruit—the divine wrath will overtake you. “The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance.” The righteous, he says, seeing the wicked demons removed from the midst at the time of righteous judgment, will rejoice at the just judgment of God, since they themselves have been found innocent and free of the punishment unto death. For “he will wash” is to be understood of the innocent, as in: “I will wash my hands among the innocent.” “Surely there is a God who judges them on the earth.” “Surely” stands for “truly.” “Surely there is a God who judges them.” They confess, he says, that the judgment pronounced against them is truly just, the judgment of…
“For the end. Do not destroy. Of David, for a stele inscription, when Saul sent and watched his house in order to put him to death.”

Saul, envious of David, though David had been his benefactor, sought to kill him, at one time hurling his spear at him, at another besieging him in his house. The psalm refers to the person of the Savior, who was the benefactor of ungrateful Israel—whose person Saul also represented—and yet was plotted against by it. It also proclaims the good news of the calling of all the nations, while Israel is clearly cast out of the godly way of life because of its impiety. “Deliver me from my enemies, O God.” He prays to be freed from enemies both visible and spiritual. For these, doing lawless things, were envious of him. “Not for my iniquity, nor for my sin, Lord.” This is like the saying: “For he committed no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth.” “Give heed to visit all the nations.” He prays that the idolaters may be converted to faith in Christ, and that Israel may be cast off because of their iniquity. “Do not have mercy on any who work iniquity.” “They will return at evening.” He gives the reason why he prayed that no mercy be shown

to them. The reason is that they would conspire against the Savior at the time when, in the last days, he came to dwell in the world in the flesh. “And they will hunger like a dog.” They will hunger because they did not receive the life-giving bread; and he calls them dogs because of the shamelessness of their soul. And “They will go around the city,” because, having been driven from their homeland and barred from it by imperial laws, they wander around it from outside, barely glimpsing it from somewhere far off. “Behold, they will speak out with their mouth.” That is, they will blaspheme. “And a sword is on their lips.” That is: “Away, away, crucify him.” “And you, Lord, will laugh them to scorn.” They blasphemed, he says, and even plotted as far as the cross, saying that God would not see their words and deeds. But even if they intended these things, you, Lord, he says, will make them a laughingstock. They dare such things, but you hear and see, and laugh at their vain madness. “You will bring all the nations to nothing.” Clearly the spiritual nations, which also stirred these men up to war against the Lord. Above he said, “Give heed to visit all the nations”; here, “You will bring all the nations to nothing.” Throughout, including the verses in between, he has arranged his words in careful order. To show that he is not simply asking for punishment against them, he first asked God to look on and examine what was happening; then he described the sort of things they do, as though they thought there was no one exercising providence; and only then did he add the punishment, saying in effect: “For these things you will punish them as they deserve, and by your punishment you will show them to be nothing.” “My strength I will guard toward you.” They, he says, have committed such impiety against you; but I, the prophet who speaks these things in the Spirit, will have my strength and my kingdom kept safe through you. For you have also helped me, and even before my prayers you surrounded me with your mercy, so that I have seen the fall of my enemies. “Do not kill them, lest they forget your law.” He prays that the race of those who rose up against the Lord may not be wholly wiped out from among men, but rather asks that they be scattered and live in captivity because of the sin of their mouth and because of their arrogance. “And for cursing and lying they will be talked of at the consummation.” May their end become widely known, he says, because of the curses with which they curse you, lying against your glory. By “consummation” he does not mean the total destruction of the nation, but the overthrow of their glory. Their glory was the worship prescribed by the law, the divine temple, the prophets, the high priests, the teachers of the law, and the appearing of angels—all of which came to an end together after the murder of the Lord. [?] (Patrol. Gr. XXV.)

“And they will know that God rules over Jacob and over the ends of the earth.” Stripped of all their glory, he says, they will know by experience that you are the Master of Jacob and have extended your Church to the ends of the earth. “They will return at evening.” He repeats what he said before, making the prophecy against them more certain. [Since he had said, “In the wrath of consummation, and they shall be no more,” he fittingly used the repetition “They will return,” so that no one would think the prophet was contradicting his earlier words, “Scatter them by your power.” Taken literally, the verses are obscure. For he means to use the example of dogs, which, when gathered around some food, devour one another before touching the food; and so they are scattered and fail to get any food.

“They will be scattered to eat; and if they are not satisfied, they will grumble.” Let them go about seeking the word of the Lord, and they will not find it. And if ever they partake of some phrase of divine Scripture and think they have enjoyed it to the full, even so they will grumble, since they are forever grumblers who speak against God. “But I will sing of your power.” So much for them, he says; but I—clearly the people from the nations—having come to know your power, will rejoice in your mercy, which has come about in the light and on your day of resurrection. For through it you helped us and became our refuge in affliction. Therefore I send up psalms to you, the God who has had mercy on me. “For you are my helper and my refuge.” For I have always enjoyed your aid, and through your providence I have escaped the misfortunes that befell me. That is why I know you alone as God, and call you the fount of mercy and of love for humankind. Blessed David, seeing these things from afar with prophetic eyes, foretold the misfortunes of the Jews and promised that he himself would always hymn the Master; and he fulfills his promises by offering that hymnody through the godly. “For the end. For those who will be changed. Further, for a stele inscription, of David, for instruction, when he set fire to Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Sobal, and Joab returned and struck the Valley of Salt, twelve [?] thousand.”

Psalm 59. Since the history is clear [?], having been recorded accurately in the second book of Kingdoms, we will speak of what is useful in it: the person of David refers to the person of the Lord, who brought about the change and renewal of things at the end of the ages, and struck the foreign nations, that is, the spiritual ones. For Scripture teaches us this when it says “for instruction.” We are taught, then, that at the time when the one descended from David according to the flesh struck the enemies, and the nations were made his own, the Jewish people, coming to a sense of the

punishment it suffered on account of Christ, makes a kind of turning back, asking that it too may be counted worthy of the grace that comes through Christ. But first it laments the ruin that befell it because of its impiety toward Christ, and so it says: “O God, you have cast us off and torn us down; you were angry, and you had compassion on us.” You punished us, he says, for the impiety committed against you. But you also had compassion on us: “you had compassion” stands for “have compassion.” Or else “you had compassion” means that you made us pitiable and wretched, so that our misfortunes have now made it time for us to be pitied. “You have shaken the land and thrown it into turmoil.” He means Jerusalem, because it was besieged and the temple in it was overthrown. Or he also means their spiritual land, which was shaken by the rejection that came upon them. “Heal its breaches, for it has been shaken.” Again he recounts what took place. “You have shown your people hard things.” By the multitude of our misfortunes, he says, you have dazed us as if with wine, and filled our souls with grief. “You have given us the wine of compunction to drink.” Aquila also translated it this way: “You have given us the wine of stupor to drink.” By the wine of compunction he means the punishments in the divine Scriptures that were proclaimed to them beforehand on account of their impiety toward Christ. For when they read them and learn by experience what was foretold, they are pierced in conscience. “You have given to those who fear you a sign, so that they may flee from the face of the bow.” The sign is the illumination by which one can discern spirits, both good and evil. For when this knowledge is present, we flee from what is worse and keep far from evil deeds and from the wicked spirit. By the same author. We, he says, have been punished for the impiety we committed; but those who fear you have received a sign (clearly the one with which we have been sealed [?]), so that they may be beyond the reach of every punishing assault. A type of this sign was the blood of the sheep smeared on the doorposts in Egypt. “God has spoken in his holy one.” This is like the saying: “In these last days he has spoken to us in a Son.” For he is the Holy One of God the Father. But what did he speak, and to whom? Since in the preceding psalm he prayed, saying, “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth,” God answers that he will divide Shechem, that is, the kingdom of Israel, for that was in Shechem. For he has given it to the foreign nations that believed in him. “And I will measure out the valley of tents.” Divine Scripture calls the dwelling place of all humankind a valley. This whole valley, then, he says, I will measure out into tents for myself; that is, I will make it full of churches. “Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine.” By Gilead and Manasseh he signifies that at his appearing he proclaims grace first to the Jews.

But Ephraim too, he says, and Judah, the two kingdoms of Israel, will likewise receive grace. "The strength of my head" stands for "the might of my rule." For of the rule he exercised, that is, over Israel, Ephraim was the strength, since the kingdom of Israel came from him. "Moab is the cauldron of my hope." A cauldron is a vessel. He means that even the Moabites, that is, the formerly godless nation, receive hope in me. "Over Idumea I will stretch out my sandal." In Idumea too, he says, I will walk about. Idumea, again, was a nation of foreigners. Through these words it is made plain to us that the nations too will accept faith in him. That is why he says, "Foreigners have been made subject to me." "Who will lead me into a fortified city?" The prophet, having heard through the Spirit that the nations receive grace, says: "Who will lead me into a fortified city?" By the fortified city he means the Church, fenced about by the power of God. The prophet says this as if speaking for the people of the Jews who repent and long to receive faith in Christ. "Or who will guide me as far as Idumea?" He shows what the fortified city is. What then is it, if not Idumea? By Idumea he signifies all the nations that have received grace. "Is it not you, O God, who cast us off?" Who else, he says, could lead us into the fortified city but you yourself, who for our iniquities also cast us out of your household? "Give us help out of afflictions, for vain is the salvation of man." It is not through human alliance, he says, that we hope to be set free from the afflictions that will come upon us, but only through your aid. "And vain is the salvation of man." For everyone who hopes in salvation from man has set his hope on something vain. Symmachus rendered it more clearly by adding the conjunction and saying: "Give us help out of affliction, for vain is the salvation of man."

"In God we shall act with power." Come to the aid, he says, of those in distress. You alone are able to put an end to calamities, and human aid is vain without your assent. So we will call upon his providence and take courage in his power. For it alone is enough to resolve our hardships and to break the dominion of those who make war on us. It is as though they were urging one another to place their hopes of salvation in God alone from now on. That is why he says: when we hope to be made strong in God, then we shall find that our enemies are nothing. For the end; among hymns; of David. Psalm 60.

He offers thanksgiving to God both for himself and for the people saved through faith. He also promises that, once he has come into the eternal dwellings, he will send up praise without ceasing. "Hear, O God, my supplication." Since I am filled with despondency as I look upon the oppression and tyranny of the demons, for this reason

I beseech you to appear and deliver us from the hand of those who do us violence. "From the ends of the earth" signifies that he makes his entreaties on behalf of the whole world. "From the ends of the earth I cried to you." For since Babylon lies many stages' journey from Palestine, the captives supposed that they were living at the extremities of the world, having been assigned to dwell in that land. "You lifted me up on a rock." He shows that he was heard at once, in keeping with the saying: "While you are still speaking, I will say: Here I am." And he plainly proclaims through whom salvation comes, for he says he was lifted up on a rock. For through Christ, who is called a rock by the blessed Paul, we have become stronger than and superior to the demons who abuse us. "You guided me, for you became my hope." For if he is the way and he is the door, it is clear that he will teach us to walk the good path, having prepared us to hope in him. "A tower of strength against the face of the enemy." It is as if he said: You have become a wall and a safeguard, so that we suffer nothing when our enemies abuse us. "I will sojourn in your tabernacle forever." From the good things he has already received, he hopes for those to come as well: that once he has come into the tabernacles above, he will be under God's shelter forever. "You have given an inheritance to those who fear your name." And what is the inheritance but the kingdom of heaven? For he says: "Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world," and so on. So they inherit the kingdom of God, and on earth are called Christians. "You will add days upon days of the king." The verse means that eternal life too is part of the inheritance. For this is what it is to add days of days to the years of the king, since by days he signifies certain periods and ages. "He will remain forever before God; who will seek out his mercy and truth?" The sentence is inverted, so that it runs as follows: if anyone seeks out his mercy and his truth, he remains before God through the endless ages. "So will I sing to your name forever." So: how? Is it not by remaining before you in the age to come? For then, when I have been deemed worthy of that blessed station, I will send up unceasing hymns. Thus and in no other way does a person give glory, and he will not cease forever to pay his vows to the Lord. For the faithful do not cease, day after day, to celebrate the divine mysteries. For the end. By Jeduthun. A Psalm of David. 61.

Jeduthun was one of the choir leaders in the divine temple. When he had fallen into sin, he received from David this psalm, which prepared the way for his recall to virtue. In it he also prophesies the

redemption that would come to the whole human race through the Saviour's dispensation, and the overthrow of the spiritual enemies. He also brings in an exhortation to human beings that turns them away from wickedness, setting before them what concerns God's judgment. "Shall not my soul be subject to God?" Even if you have been shaken, O soul, he says, and have fallen from your standing in virtue, still submit to the Lord. For he will both help you and save you from being shaken any further. "For he is my God." For he will provide salvation to the one you have wronged, and will surely rid him of your wickedness. "How long will you assail a man?" He cries out against the opposing powers, because they assail human nature when it has inclined toward evil, when through its natural weakness it is somehow like a leaning wall about to fall and a fence knocked down. "But they plotted to thrust away my honor." For they all but robbed us of reason itself, compelling us to worship wood and stones, so that it was even said of us: "Man, being in honor, did not understand." "They ran in thirst." This is the race, he says, that the opposing powers were running, thirsting to rob me of my honor. "With their mouth they blessed, and in their heart they cursed." He says this because, while suggesting pleasant things to us, they make us children of cursing through those very things. "But submit to God, O my soul." Again he speaks to his soul, strengthening its submission to [?]. He shows the magnitude of the temptations, and speaks the Apostle's words: "that he will not let you be tempted beyond what you are able to bear." "In God is my salvation and my glory." In him I have my hope of salvation and of glory. That is, he will both keep me safe and make me glorious, having made me victorious over these. ["But submit to God, O my soul." For they all but robbed us of reason itself, compelling us to worship wood and stones, so that it was even said of us: "Man, being in honor, did not understand." But they, O soul, are such as these; as for you, submit to his service. Then he adds that [?] this is what I hope for from him: to obtain salvation, since he helps me and does not allow me to become an exile and a fugitive from him, or to exchange him for another master. For from that source I expect both to be saved and to be helped, through hoping in him.] "Hope in him, all you assembly of peoples." Having first prepared the course toward repentance in himself, he urges the others toward it as well, and at the same time, more prophetically, he foretells the calling of all the nations. "Pour out your hearts before him." It is as if he said: Do not approach him with a divided heart, but as it is written: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your mind."

"But the sons of men are vain." Knowing that all will receive the call through the Gospel, he laments over those who do not believe, and especially over the leaders of the Jews, who were also false, inasmuch as they thrust the truth away. Not only did they practise injustice with balance and weights, but they also gathered together for vanity. For truly vain was their plot against the Saviour. "Do not put your hope in injustice, and do not long for plunder." He says this to them because they plotted against him out of greed, hoping to receive from the people the produce owed under the law. "Once God has spoken; these two things I have heard: that power belongs to God." God, he says, has pronounced a word about the judgment, through which I have heard these two things: first, that to those who deserve wrath because of the excess of their sins he will render wrath; and second, that to those who have done what is worthy of mercy he will allot mercy. For "power" signifies wrath and the severity that falls on those who deserve it. Of David, when he was in the wilderness of Judea. Psalm 62 [?]. Argument. He sings this psalm while fleeing from the face of Saul, and calling on God for help on the strength of the virtue of his life. It also applies to the soul that was formerly a desert, empty of every good, and was then turned back by the grace of Christ. "O God, my God, I rise early to you." By these words he signifies the earnestness of his devotion. To you, he says, I rise at dawn, to send up to you both hymns and prayers. "My soul has thirsted for you." Not only, he says, is the soul filled with divine love, but even more so the flesh. For we must not only practise piety but also please God through the body, for instance by fasting, by continual prayer, by sleeping on the ground, and by working with our hands so as to provide for those in need. "In a desert and trackless land." I suffered no harm from the desert, he says; rather, as though standing beside your holy tabernacle itself, I offer my hymns. For by "in the sanctuary" he means the tabernacle, since the divine temple had not yet been built. "So I appeared before you in the sanctuary." So: how? Is it not by thirsting and longing for union with you, the Holy One? And who would the Holy One be but the Only-begotten? "For your mercy is better than lives." Those who have come to the mercy of God, that is, to Christ, count the life of this present existence as nothing, and so they utter this cry, saying that the mercy given them through the Only-begotten surpasses an abundance of life, meaning the present life. "So I will bless you in my life." This I will go on doing all my life, praising with my tongue, stretching out my hands, and asking for your loving-kindness. "In your name I will lift up my hands." No longer, he says, as before, will I stretch out my hands to a foreign god,

but to you alone, calling upon your name in my prayers. "May my soul be filled as with fat and richness." He shows how great is the gain of those who have chosen to place their hopes in him alone. "And with lips of exultation my mouth will praise." Whenever, he says, I call your name to mind, then indeed my lips are filled with joy. "If I remembered you upon my bed." "If I remembered" is put for "remembering," so that the meaning is: remembering you, he says, I lay sleepless over your praises and over the gifts of light that you give to those who call upon you. "For you became my helper, and in the shelter of your wings I will exult." Since you help me by the protection your help affords, I receive gladness. For he calls the protection that comes from his help the shelter of wings. Sheltered by you, he says, I will rejoice with joy. "My soul has clung close behind you." Not even for a little while, he says, can I withdraw my thoughts from remembering you; but kindled by warm love, I am bound to my longing for you by memory, as if by a kind of glue. Then he shows the fruit of that longing. "Your right hand upheld me." And who would the Father's right hand be but his only-begotten Son? "But they sought my soul in vain." Next he cries out against the opposing powers, protesting the violence he endured, and prays that they be handed over to eternal punishments. "But the king will rejoice in God." Having described the end of those who acted impiously against Christ, and shown that the lowest parts of the earth will be their portion and lot, he turns his discourse to the other company. This was the company of those who believed in Christ, who, having been counted worthy of the kingdom of heaven, are fittingly also called kings, according to the Apostle's words: "And would that you did reign!" This was the reigning people, which rejoices with the spiritual gladness that God himself has graciously given it. I, he says, who received the kingdom from you, rejoice in your aid, not in their death. "Everyone who swears by him will be praised." So too, he says, Christ will be the boast of those who reign, so that those who make him the one by whom they swear are rightly praised. For they will swear by the true God, according to what is written: "For the mouth of those who speak unjust things has been stopped." And who are these but those who dared to say, "Away with such a fellow from the earth, for he ought not to live"? Their mouth was stopped when the Lord trampled down death and rose on the third day. And the mouth of the opposing powers themselves was stopped too, once sin had been abolished through grace, according to what is said elsewhere: "And all iniquity will stop its mouth." For it is God who justifies; who is he that condemns?

He sings this psalm in the person of the holy apostles, who pray to be delivered from the enemies of the Gospel preaching and recount plainly the schemes devised against them by the rulers of the Jewish people, and what they themselves endured. It is clear that this came from the rulers already mentioned, because of their impiety toward Christ. "Hear, O God, my voice when I make my petition." Receive my supplication, he says, O Master, and strengthen my mind, so that I do not fear their assaults. "From fear of the enemy rescue my soul." This is like: "And now, Lord, look upon their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your word with boldness." "Who sharpened their tongues like a sword." He says this because, blaspheming Jesus, they said to the apostles: "We strictly charged you not to speak in this name." "They bent their bow, a bitter thing." He compares the deadly words of their tongue to arrows shot from a bow. For how could words not be deadly that try to persuade people not to believe that the [?] is God

"Suddenly they will shoot him down, and they will not fear." Lying in ambush, he says, they attack suddenly, not fearing the God who watches over all. "They made an evil word strong for themselves": the insistence that "The Lord did not rise from the dead." "They talked of hiding a snare." Back and forth, he says, they plotted to kill the heralds of the Gospel teachings in secret. "Who, they said, will see them?" They did these things, he says, thinking that God would not call them to account for such impiety

"A man will draw near, and a deep heart." The lawless, he says, did not cease plotting evil against the Lord, for this is what "They searched out iniquity" means. But the man of God, who takes wise counsel (for this is what the deep heart signifies), having understood the mystery precisely, will exalt God with fitting hymns, according to what is said elsewhere: "I will exalt you, O Lord my God, my King." "Their blows became the arrows of infants." Having spoken of their arrogance against the holy heralds, he goes on to describe their downfall as well. "And every man was afraid." For who would not be afraid, seeing God's judgment coming upon the impious? "The righteous will rejoice in the Lord and will hope in him." Above all, those who are diligent in the divine laws, filled with delight, will make their hope in God firm. "And all the upright in heart will be praised." Those who keep a straight course toward God and will not bear to walk off the straight road will also reap good repute among men.

In this psalm he introduces the person of the nations who believed in Christ, who cry out against the wise of this age and ask forgiveness for their former impiety. He also sends up a prayer on behalf of those who were once fruitless but became fruitful through faith in Christ. "A hymn befits you, O God, in Zion." No longer, he says, will we send up hymns to those we took for gods, since we know that it is not fitting to sing their praises, for they are wood and stones and demons; but to you alone such a debt is most fitting. "And to you a vow will be paid in Jerusalem." He means either the one on earth, which is the Church, or the heavenly one, where we shall arrive and send up our praises. "Hear my prayer; to you all flesh will come." With these words he announces the good news of the calling of all the nations, according to what is said by Joel: "I will pour out of my Spirit upon all

"Words of the lawless have overpowered us." By the words of the lawless he means the wisdom of the wise of this age, through which they too grew weak, having fallen away from true knowledge. "And you will be merciful to our impieties." They pray to be freed from the impiety that befell them in their error. "Blessed is he whom you have chosen and taken to yourself." They call blessed those who have been made perfect in virtue and have attained the prize of the upward call. "We shall be filled with the good things of your house." By the good things of the house he means the various gifts of the Spirit. For he says: "To one is given through the Spirit wisdom, to another a word of knowledge," and the rest of the gifts. "Holy is your temple": either the heavenly or the earthly one, according to the saying: "For the temple of God is holy, and that temple you are." [Full of sanctification; and through your oracles it instructs in your righteousness those who draw near.] "Hear us, O God our Saviour, the hope of all the ends of the earth." So hear us, and grant these things. In you, he says, the ends of the world put their hope, and those far from the

When the nations are troubled, he says, that is, the hosts of the demons, then indeed the people at the ends of the world will also fear you, having seen the great signs. By signs he means those that took place at his coming. "You will make the outgoings of morning and evening a delight." For when the people who inhabit the world have seen the great signs and fear with the good fear, then indeed at the outgoings of morning and of evening, that is, at every time, they will have delight, as they exult over what your coming has accomplished. "You visited the earth and made it drunk." He shows what the delight of all the nations consists in. And what is it in, but in his counting the earth worthy of his visitation and making it drunk, with his gifts, that is? "The river of God is filled with waters." Here he calls the Gospel word a river, and says it has been filled with waters. And which waters, he says, but the divine promises that he made to those worthy of the kingdom of heaven? These promises would be "Blessed are the poor in spirit" and the rest of the Beatitudes. "You prepared their food." By food he means spiritual food. He says it has been prepared because the mystery concerning Christ was determined before the foundation of the world; and Christ is the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world. "Make its furrows drunk; multiply its produce." By furrows he means the depths of hearts, and by produce, pious thoughts. "In its drops it will rejoice as it springs up." Even the small portions, he says, of the divine gifts given to it make it rejoice and cause it to spring up, that is, with spiritual fruit. You will understand its drops from what is said about Christ: "He will come down like rain upon the grain, and like a drop dripping upon the earth." "You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness." By the year he means the time of the age to come, and he calls it a crown of goodness because in it the saints are crowned with great goodness. "And your plains will be filled with richness." By plains, again, he means the souls of those who have believed in him. "The beautiful places of the desert will be made rich." By mountains he means the holy apostles and evangelists, who have been well nourished by spiritual gifts; and by the desert he means the Church of the Gentiles, which was formerly a desert, empty of the knowledge of God. "And the hills will gird themselves with exultation." By hills he means the presiding bishops of the Churches. "The rams of the flock have clothed themselves." By the rams of the flock he means the rulers of the peoples. And with what will they clothe themselves but the garment of incorruption and the tunic of gladness? He also calls the holy apostles rams of the flock, since they stood out in front and were able to butt the enemies with their horns, just as the Lord said: "Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves."

…and the valleys will abound with grain. The souls of the nations, he says, which were once utterly destitute and barren, will be full of spiritual fruits. They will cry aloud, for indeed they will sing hymns. The valleys, he says, changed for the better and made abundant in spiritual fruits, will fervently send up hymns to you. For the end: a song of a psalm of resurrection. Psalm 65.

Through the present psalm he points to the calling of the nations and announces the good news of the resurrection of their souls that is to come, according to the saying: "He who raises the poor from the earth." He also brings in the person of the apostles, who teach how much they suffered for the preaching of the gospel and how their many afflictions led them out into everlasting joys. The rejection of the Jewish people is also indicated. Shout to God, all the earth; sing praise, then, to his name. Shouting is a victory hymn, sung over fallen enemies. So, since the rulers of this age have been destroyed, plainly through the coming of Christ, all the nations are urged to send up victory hymns. Say to God: How awesome are your works! And what works does he mean, if not the divine signs and the routing of the hordes of unclean demons? In the greatness of your power your enemies will lie to you. Here he accuses the Jews of stupor, since not even the overwhelming wonders moved them to believe. Let all the earth worship you and sing to you. Since the Jews, he says, though they saw extraordinary signs being performed, lied to you, in their place the whole multitude of the nations will worship you. Come and see the works of God. Here the person of the apostles is introduced, teaching the nations that the very one who worked the divine signs during his coming in the flesh is the same who long ago dried up the Red Sea and also cut off the streams of the river Jordan, so that the sons of Israel crossed over on foot. He turns the sea into dry land. And the proof of this is what has already happened, how he changed the sea into dry land. Symmachus puts it this way: "He changed the sea into dry land; they crossed the river on foot." For this is the God, he says, who grants us too our return and our salvation, who long ago parted both sea and river and bade our forefathers cross without danger. There we shall rejoice in him. "There" indicates a time. He says, then, that at the time when he reigns over the new age, there we shall reign with him and rejoice with joy unspeakable. His eyes look upon the nations. He attends to all and examines everything that is done. Those

who provoke him, let them not exalt themselves. And who might those who provoke him be, if not those of whom it was said, "Son of man, go to the house that provokes me"? And indeed, "They provoked him in the wilderness"; and again, "Do not harden your hearts as in the provocation." Bless God, you nations. All of you, having come together, praise him and marvel at him all the more. [Who has set my soul in life. I will rejoice in such wonders and in him who did them, who, as Master overseeing all things, makes distinctions among those on earth and surrounds the unworthy with punishments. By "eyes" he means the apostles.] For you have tested us, O God; you have refined us by fire. The prophetic Spirit foretells the afflictions that would come upon the apostles because of the preaching, listing them in their person; and it points to the snares, that is, the prisons, and to the trials through fire and water. I will enter your house with whole burnt offerings. The heavenly house, clearly; for they dedicated themselves wholly to God as whole burnt offerings. [With spiritual burnt offerings. Your doings, Master, he says, are such as these; ours are, as it were, to enter the temple and sacrifice thank offerings to you. He means the same thing by "distinguished and spoke" [?]. And this is what he means by "which I vowed."] I will pay you my vows. What I vowed, he says, when I was afflicted, I will pay you. And I vowed, as of the afflic- [?] … praises. I will offer you burnt offerings full of marrow. Whatever you commanded to be offered to you, I will sacrifice eagerly. He has called "full of marrow" those that are well fed and fat; for the law too commanded that offerings be unblemished and whole. And the prophet Malachi curses those who have such animals but offer maimed ones. This was also the beginning of those evils for Cain. We too are taught to honor God with the more precious of what we have. I will offer you oxen with goats. But all of these are spiritual, as I said: the burnt offerings, the oxen and the goats that he promises to render. Come and hear, and I will tell. And what else does he tell, if not what he has already set out: "You have tested us," and the rest? If I had regarded iniquity in my heart, let the Lord not hear me. I knew that if I had dealings with iniquity, God would not consent to hear my prayer. Aquila: "If I had seen what is useless in my heart, the Lord will not hear." He means that, in bringing my requests to God, I took care for what was fitting, knowing that my request would be of no benefit to me unless I did what I ought. And something else of these [?]. Ezek. [?], 6.

Here again the person of the apostles is introduced, teaching the nations and praying to be delivered from those who oppose their teaching. [This psalm also follows on from the one before it, for it has the character of the priestly blessing, and nearly the whole prayer is found in Judges. So, since this too was going to happen after the return, it was foretold; and it proclaims the divine incarnation and appearing, and the salvation of the nations. It is entitled "in hymns," since to be hymned belongs to God, while to be extolled with praises belongs to human beings.] May God have pity on us and bless us. We beg for your compassion, Master, he says, and for the shining of your face, so that we may be able to preach the way of your holy Gospel openly to all the nations. For he calls his coming saving everywhere. Let the peoples give thanks to you, O God. He prophesies that all the nations will confess Christ. Let the nations be glad and rejoice. The prophetic Spirit, delighting in the salvation of the world, utters the same words often, enjoying its gladness in the constant retelling. Let the peoples give thanks to you, O God; let all the peoples give thanks to you. He has not set down the repetition idly, but to make his hearers more eager. The earth has yielded its fruit. The spiritual earth, clearly; and its fruit is progress in godliness. [Let the peoples give thanks to you, O God. Just as he twice roused the nations to sing hymns, so he twice sought blessing for them, since they, clearly, have also enjoyed the blessing itself. Or because those who come from it do not fail to know the God who is over all, but offer him the sweetest fruit of godliness; and if we offer you this, that is, the practice of virtue, we are blessed by you.] [May God bless us. It should be understood that when people bless God, they bring him words only and cannot benefit him by deed. But when God blesses, he confirms his words with deeds and supplies those he blesses with an abundance of every kind of good thing. Then he teaches how.] For the end: of David, a psalm of a song. Psalm 67.
In this psalm he points to the coming of the Lord, the overthrow of the spiritual enemies, and release from spiritual captivity. Moreover,

he teaches that he is the same one who long ago led the sons of Israel out of Egypt. Besides this, he promises the gift of the Holy Spirit to those who receive the preaching. He also brings consolation to the apostles, promising to rescue them from every affliction, namely the affliction that came upon them because of the preaching. Further, he promises to turn back many of those who provoke him, and also of those who have fallen into the sea of pleasures. No less does he proclaim the appointing of the apostles, who they were and where they came from. And he announces the good news of the faith of all the nations in the Lord. On top of all this, he plainly teaches the Lord's ascent into heaven. One may see all these things in detail by attending to the verses. Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered. The text indicates God's setting out to judge the unclean demons. For by his coming, of the tyranny over human beings [?]…

Make a way for him who rides upon the west. Make yourselves fit, he says, to walk in the ways of him who, at the end of the times, was seen in the flesh by those on earth. Or, "him who rides upon the west" means the one who made his descent as far as Hades. Let them be troubled before his face. The nations of the demons, clearly. Of the father of orphans and judge of widows. By orphans he means those without a protector; by widows, the souls that do not have the Word as their bridegroom. For he is the protector of the weak and of those without human help, such as we are. And who is this, and of what kind? God in his holy place. Since he said that he rode upon the west, that is, down to the depths of Hades, he teaches in turn that, having ascended into heaven, he came to be in his own places, although in the nature of his godhead he had never in any way left them. God makes the single-minded dwell in a house. By the single-minded he means those who have devoted their own life to him alone and have estranged it from all double-mindedness and worldly desire. These, then, he promises to settle in his house, the heavenly city. Leading out the prisoners with strength. This is like the saying: "To those in bonds, Come out; and to those in darkness, Show yourselves." By bonds and darkness he means the worship of demons. Likewise those who provoke him, who dwell in tombs. He means that when he went even to Hades he preached to the spirits there, who had once disobeyed. For "who provoke" stands for "who provoked."

O God, when you went forth before your people, when you marched through the wilderness. He shows that the one who descended as far as Hades is the same who long ago, through Moses, led Israel out of Egypt. He says, then, that when you went before your people who had come out of Egypt, the earth shook, that

is, his exodus became known throughout the whole earth. The earth shook, for the heavens poured down. The heavens poured down spiritual food, clearly; he also means the manna. Before the face of the God of Sinai. That is, of him who laid down the law on Mount Sinai. Before the face of the God of Israel. Israel means "a mind that sees God." A willing rain, O God, you will set apart for your inheritance. By rain he means the word of the gospel, according to: "He will come down like rain upon a fleece." "Willing" is in contrast to the worship of the law. For those things were not willingly accepted by him, according to the saying: "Who required these from your hands?" and: "Your burnt offerings are not acceptable, and your sacrifices are not pleasing [?] to me." And it was weak, but you restored it. It was weak long ago, when it worshipped idols; but you restored it by calling it through the preaching of the gospel. Your living creatures dwell in it. By living creatures here he means those who have partaken of life-giving food. "In it": in what, if not in his inheritance? In your goodness, O God, you have prepared for the poor. And what has he prepared, if not what eye has not seen and ear has not heard? And who are the poor, if not those of whom he said: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven"? The Lord will give a word to those who preach the good news with great power. He himself, he says, will give a word to his holy apostles so that they may be able to preach the Gospel. Similar is: "Do not worry about what you will say or what you will speak, for what you are to say will be given you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of my Father speaking in you." "With great power" goes with "The Lord will give a word," not with "to those who preach the good news," as some have supposed. For he means that God with great strength will give a word to those who preach the good news; that is, to those who wish to proclaim our blessings he himself supplies the word, he who also [gives] the occasion of the good news [?]…

The king of the hosts of the beloved. It is the Lord himself who gives a word to those who initiate others into the mysteries; for he is the king of the beloved people, and again he is himself its power. For the beauty of the house, to divide the spoils. The house is those who have believed in Christ; the beauty of the house is his holy disciples and apostles. He says, then, that to the beauty of the house, that is, to the evangelists, he himself will give a word so that they may divide the spoils, that is, draw the nations to the faith and despoil Satan. If you lie down among the lots. The words are addressed to the holy apostles. If, he says, the lots receive you. By lots he meant those who believed from the two peoples. If, then, he says, you rest among them, they will be given the wings of a dove whose back is overlaid with gold. He means that those who received the holy apostles will be counted worthy of the Holy Spirit. 1 Cor. 2:9. Matt. 5:[?]. Matt. [?].

received the apostles. And he says that the dove's back is gilded because it makes the minds of those who receive it precious, that is, wise. When the heavenly one appoints kings over it. By kings he means the apostles who ruled over his inheritance. "They will be made white as snow" means "they will be cleansed." And "in Salmon" is interpreted "in recompense." He says, then, that those who received the holy apostles will receive from the heavenly king recompense, that is, a reward, for their hospitality: the cleansing of their sins. The mountain of God is a rich mountain. He calls the Church a mountain, and rich because it makes the souls of those within it well nourished and sleek. A curdled mountain, a rich mountain; why do you suppose there are curdled mountains? It is indeed curdled, that is, full of milk, the milk, clearly, of the simpler word, according to: "I gave you milk to drink, not solid food." So he rebukes those who suppose the churches of the heretics to be curdled. For there is nothing in them that can nourish one to a spiritual state. Why then, you people, do you suppose that there are other curdled mountains outside the Church, and not rather this mountain alone, in which God was pleased to dwell? That he dwells in the Church is clear from what he himself said: "Here I will dwell, for I have chosen it." The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands of those who flourish. By the chariot of God he means the heavenly and spiritual powers on which God rides. It is like the saying: "A thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him." These also flourish, since they are freed from sin. The one who rides on this chariot of myriads is the Lord himself, who also gave the law on Sinai, the holy mountain. And again he is the one who ascended on high (he means the height of the cross) and led captivity captive, that is, took captive in turn the souls taken captive by the devil. For he himself promised this, saying: "When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all to myself." You received gifts among men. And from whom did he receive men as gifts, if not from the Father, who said: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance"? For even the disobedient, that you might dwell among them. These people, he says, whom you received as gifts, were formerly disobedient. Yet among them too, he says, you made your dwelling. The sense is expressed by a transposition: You received gifts among men so as to dwell among them, that is, among those given. And these very people, he says, whom you received, were formerly disobedient. Plainly this was when they worshipped the creation rather than the Creator. Blessed be the Lord God; blessed be the Lord day by day. For a great achievement he sends up a hymn to God: the chorus of the apostles, clearly. God will prosper the way for us, the God of our salvation.

You, Master, he says, will open a door for the word, so that the way of preaching may prosper for us. Our God is the God who saves, and to the Lord, the Lord, belong the ways out of death. He is clearly confident that he will nobly bring out even those who have come as far as death because of the preaching. For he says that the ways out of death are his. But God will crush the heads of his enemies, "his" meaning the enemies of the apostolic chorus. For in delivering them he will deliver them, clearly by crushing the heads of their enemies. The expression is taken from the likeness of snakes, which, when they rear up against someone, are then struck on the head and perish. The words also refer to the rulers of the Jewish people. The hairy crown of those who go about in their offenses. By the hairy crown, again, he means the head. He says that he will crush the heads of these, who sin without repenting. The Lord said: I will bring back from Bashan. Bashan is interpreted "bitterness" or "provocation." He says, then: from the house that provokes me, that is, Israel, I will bring them back to myself. I will bring them back in the depths of the sea. And those who have been dragged down, he says, into the depth of pleasures I will bring back to

That your foot may be dipped in blood. He teaches how they are brought back. And how are they brought back, if not when the evil powers have been destroyed? For they brought their blood down to the earth, according to the word of Isaiah, so that his foot too was dipped in blood. The text writes such things in a more historical manner. The tongue of your dogs, from the enemies, by him. By dogs he means the guardians of the spiritual flock, the holy preachers, whose tongue all but tastes the blood of the spiritual enemies. He says, then, that the voice of the apostles will all but cause the death of the evil demons. Your goings, O God, have been seen. By God's goings he means the acts performed in the dispensation: the birth from the Virgin, the working of signs, the ascent onto the cross, the death undergone for the sake of the dispensation, the return to life from the dead, and the ascent into heaven. He says that these goings have become manifest. The goings of my God, my king, who is in the sanctuary. See how plainly he says that the one who made these goings is both God and his own king. And he proclaims that he is the one in the holy place, that is, on Mount Sinai, according to what was said above: "The Lord is among them, in Sinai, in the holy place." Rulers went ahead, next to those who sing. By rulers he means the holy apostles, of whom it is said: "You will make them rulers over all the earth"; and by those who sing, those who send up spiritual sacrifices of praise. He says, then, that the rulers went ahead, that is, were the first to begin the [?]…

[?] that is. In the midst of maidens playing timbrels. By "maidens" he means the souls of believers, made strong through the Holy Spirit, who make the whole world under heaven resound with the proclamation of the Gospel. In the midst of these the holy apostles came to be, that is, of the worship

In the churches bless God the Lord from the fountains of Israel. The fountains of Israel would be the blessed prophets, and before them the Law. So he is saying that it is not fitting for us to sing God's praises drawing from any source other than these. He says this because of the heterodox writings of the heretics. For the Lord is blessed out of the Scriptures of the Law and the Prophets by those who are able to draw water from them with gladness, since they are springs of salvation. Of this water the Savior said: "Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will have in himself a spring of water welling up to eternal life." Those who divide the Old and the New Scripture must be refuted: they cannot bless God in the churches, since they do not have the fountains of Israel, nor the Lord of those fountains, for they dare to divide even the Godhead. There is Benjamin the youngest, in ecstasy. "There": where? Surely in the midst of those who are singing? And who is Benjamin but the blessed apostle Paul, who was of the tribe of Benjamin? "The youngest," because the Lord appeared to him after the other apostles. He says "in ecstasy" because of the surpassing greatness of his revelations, in keeping with what Paul himself said: "If we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you." It is fitting that he mentioned him first, before the others, since he labored more than all the others. The princes of Judah, their leaders. The princes of Judah, he says, were appointed leaders and princes of those who sing, from the tribe of Judah, from that of Zebulun, and from that of Naphtali. From Zebulun and Naphtali came Peter and Andrew and James and John, as the Gospel shows; from Judah came Levi, that is, Matthew, and the others of the

Command, O God, your power. He calls the Son the power of the Father, according to the saying "Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God." So the apostolic choir asks the Father to strengthen for them what he has wrought for them. And what has he wrought for them but the body? They ask him, then, to free it from corruption and clothe it with incorruption. This the Lord will do when he comes down from heaven and the dead are raised

Because of your temple at Jerusalem kings shall bring gifts to you. By his temple he means the Church, and by kings he means those who have believed in Christ, according to what was said to them: "But you are a royal priesthood." So he is saying that those who have been called through faith will bring him gifts from the earthly temple, that is, the Church, into the Jerusalem above. These are clearly spiritual gifts.

Rebuke the beasts of the reed. Many are hostile to the godly way of life of the saints, above all the unclean demons. That is why he prays that they be rebuked, since they are beasts of the reed. Now Reed is a place in Palestine through which those going up to Jerusalem used to travel. This Reed is full of lions that lurk in dens by the marsh, and they used to lie in wait for those going up to Jerusalem. Just as the lions lay in wait for those going up to Jerusalem, so the spiritual lions lie in wait for those going up to the spiritual Jerusalem. The gathering of bulls among the heifers of the peoples. He is speaking of other opponents of the proclamation. And who are these but the rulers of the Jewish populace, who were also called bulls? That they were called bulls is clear from the verse "Many calves surrounded me; fat bulls closed in around me." They also stirred up the crowd to make war on the heralds. That those who have been tested with silver may be shut out. The silver is the divine oracles. He is saying: Rebuke the spiritual and the visible enemies, so that the heralds of the Gospel may not be shut in and kept from preaching any longer. Or else thus: Rebuke both the one group and the other, he says, so that the heralds may not be shut out from preaching. Scatter the nations that want wars. He clearly means the spiritual nations, and by wars he means those waged against the saints. Ambassadors shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall hasten to stretch out her hand to God. Once the spiritual enemies have been scattered and bound, Egyptians and Ethiopians will run to the proclamation. By the Egyptians he signifies those who are utterly given to idolatry and opposed to the way of life of Israel, and by the Ethiopians the ends of the earth. How Ethiopia ran to the proclamation can be seen from the Ethiopian eunuch. Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God. He shows that all the other nations too, together with their own kings, will believe in Christ. Sing psalms to the Lord who has mounted upon the heaven of heaven. Earlier he proclaimed the passion of Christ and his descent as far as Hades, so now he also proclaims his ascent into heaven. The phrase "toward the east" is figurative. For just as the sun rises up from west to east, so too the Lord rose, as it were, from the depths of Hades and mounted upon the heaven of heaven. Behold, he will give to his voice a voice of power. By "a voice of power" he means the voice that raises all the dead, since they will rise at his command. Give glory to God. So too Paul: "Glorify God," he says, "in your body and in your spirit, which are his." For it is right to glorify our benefactor through all things. Over

Israel is his magnificence, and his power is in the clouds. God is wonderful in his saints; the God of Israel himself will give power and strength to his people. Blessed be God. The text has made mention of his second coming, when he will raise all the dead, and so it also teaches us about the honors that will be rendered in different measure to the saints, and about the different ranks of the saints. The ranks it indicates by Israel, the clouds, the saints and the people; the honors it displays through the magnificence, the power, the wonder and the strength. And over all these it says that God is blessed.
