For it is clear that when the saints have come into those dwellings, the heavenly ones, they will bless God without ceasing, imitating the order of the spirits above. For the end; for those who shall be changed; of David. Psalm 68.

The psalm contains a prayer of the Savior, offered in the person of humanity, and the reasons why they brought upon him death on the cross. It also narrates the passion itself clearly, and the calamities that would befall the Jews after the passion. Besides these it contains the introduction of the gospel way of life and the teaching about worship in spirit and truth, with which it brings the psalm to a close. That every prayer the Savior prayed, he prayed in the person of human nature, he points out at the end of the psalm, where he says: "For the Lord has heard the poor, and has not despised his prisoners." Save me, O God, for the waters have come in even to my soul. Since he took up our sins, he grieves on our behalf; and so he fittingly prays to be rescued from the trials that have surrounded his soul like a torrent. I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no foothold. For human nature had suffered these things, brought down by sin to death, and into the very region of Hades, which in this passage he calls "the mire of the deep" and "the depth of the sea." I am weary with crying out; my throat has become hoarse. What he cried out, and why, he taught clearly in what follows, saying: "Let me be rescued from those who hate me, and from the depth of the waters," and "Let not the storm of water drown me," and the rest. For, as I said, he was praying for human nature, that the power of death might be abolished and that Hades might not shut its mouth upon it. That is why he also says: "Nor let the pit shut its mouth upon me." Those who hate me without cause are more than the hairs of my head. For many are the demons who plot against human nature; they have suffered no wrong from us, and yet they are eager to destroy us.

My enemies who persecute me unjustly have grown strong. He shows that the sentence against him was passed unjustly. O God, you know my foolishness. By "foolishness" he means what people took to be folly, I mean the folly of the passion. For, as the holy Apostle says, the cross of the Lord became a stumbling block to the Jews and folly to the Gentiles. So he is saying: You, Father, know the dispensation of the cross. He says this because he became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. And my offenses are not hidden from you. This is like the verse "Him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf." That is the meaning of "They are not hidden from you." Let not those who wait for you be put to shame on my account, O Lord, Lord of hosts. "On my account" means "because of me," that is, because of my passion on their behalf; and "let them not be put to shame" means "let them no longer be put to shame," since they had long been put to shame by the corruption they had endured. The sense is this: Since I have consented to taste death for them, let the shame that came upon them long ago through death be taken away. For death reigning over man, who was created in the image of God, was a shame. He signifies, then, that through his resurrection death will be done away with. The next verse, which is similar to this one, belongs to the same interpretation: Nor let those who seek you be confounded on my account. He rightly said "on my account" both above and here. For since he was the one who had urged them on, had he been defeated he would have brought shame on those who had been persuaded by him, as though they had chosen the danger out of being deceived and too easily convinced. For for your sake I have borne reproach. I ask, he says, that death be removed, since it was in obedience to you that I have taken it [?] upon myself. I have become estranged to my brothers. He says this because of the desertion he suffered from everyone at the time of the passion. For zeal for your house has consumed me. They denied me, he says, because I exposed their impiety concerning your house. John clearly tells the story of when he drove them out of the temple with a whip. And the reproaches of those who reproached you have fallen upon me. Not only did I become a stranger and estranged, he says, but I was also reproached by those who reproach you with their wicked deeds. And I suffered such things for no other reason than zeal for your house. And I covered my soul with fasting. Grieving, he says, over the destruction of their souls that was to come, I did this and that. But those for whom I did these things talked of me at every time and in every place, reproaching me for the hardships I endured for their sake. But as for me, with my prayer to you, O Lord. Even if they repaid me evil for good, he says, I still do not cease making

prayers for them. This is clear from the way the evangelist presented him, praying even at the cross for those who were crucifying him. A time of favor. "When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law." He who came for this purpose [?] A time of favor,

Save me from the mire, that I may not stick fast. These were the things he cried out as he prayed for humanity, so that he even said, "My throat has become hoarse." "Has become hoarse" signifies how intense the prayer was. Let not the storm of water drown me, nor the deep swallow me up. A boundary and a dreadful curse have been laid down: even if an angel should preach to us anything contrary to what Paul taught, let him be accursed. Who, then, is able to overrule Paul, or rather Christ who speaks in him? Paul refers such a prayer to Christ himself, and bears witness to it in the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that in the days of his flesh, that is, as he was going to the cross, he offered up prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears to the one who was able to save him from death, that is, to the Father, and was heard because of his reverence; although he was a Son, he learned obedience from what he suffered. Here Paul, or rather Christ who speaks in him, has taught us even what the evangelists passed over in silence and left out, saying that the prayer "Father, let this cup pass from me" was made with loud cries and tears. It was not made in pretense, nor to lure Satan, nor by taking on the will of the world as his own; rather, Christ, in his own person, according to the dispensation, prays willingly with a cry, with tears, with sweat and clots of blood, with an angel strengthening him and, as it were, encouraging and consoling him, although he is truly the Son of God. Moreover, he prayed in agony, as the evangelist says, and more earnestly, and he brings the prayer to the Father twice and even three times. Since, then, Paul, or rather, I say again, Christ who speaks in Paul, refers such a prayer to Christ himself, who can falsify what Christ himself has testified about himself? Turn not your face away from your servant. Since God the Father had turned away from human nature because of the transgression in Adam, he asks him to turn his face toward it again. Attend to my soul and redeem it from what held it fast, that is, from death. Rescue me because of my enemies. From the injustice we have suffered at the hands of our spiritual enemies, he rouses the Father to have mercy on us. For you know my reproach. This is like what was said before: "For for your sake I have borne

reproach." My soul has expected reproach. From here on he narrates the passion to us, which the evangelists also narrated clearly. Let their table before them become a snare. From here on he indicates what would befall the Jews after the passion. It is as if he were saying: May they suffer the same things they made me experience. For woe to the wicked, for evil will befall him according to the works of his hands. Let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see. How could they not be darkened, when they did not receive the Sun of righteousness? And bend their back continually. For their captivity was not temporary, as it was under the Babylonians. Let their homestead be made desolate. He says this because of the sack that befell Jerusalem. And let there be no one to dwell in their tents. That is, no one from among them; for none of the Jews dwells any longer in the tents in Jerusalem. For they persecuted him whom you struck. This states the reason why they will suffer such things. It is like the verse "I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered." This one, then, he says, who by your good pleasure was struck in the passion, they did not receive, but drove him away, outside their own salvation. And they added to the pain of my wounds. He says this because he humbled himself, and they went further and put him to death. Add iniquity to their iniquity. He says this too because after the cross and the resurrection they slandered him. And let them not enter into your righteousness. They will be far, he says, from the delight that will be granted to the righteous. Let them be blotted out of the book of the living. Even if they were enrolled in it, he says, inasmuch as the promises were theirs, yet since they did this and that, they will fittingly be blotted out. I am poor and in pain; your salvation, O God, has helped me, and so on. From here on the gospel way of life is proclaimed, which the one who is poor in God's sight began, to whom it was also said: "Blessed are the poor in spirit." This choir of the poor comes in giving thanks for the salvation it has received from the Only-begotten, for he is the face of the Father. It promises no longer to offer sacrifices of blood, but rather sacrifices of praise and of spiritual

Let the poor see and be glad, and so on. When they know these things, he says, the poor in spirit will rejoice. The apostles say these things on account of those who have believed in Christ through them. For the Lord has heard the poor. And what prayer did he hear, but the one the Only-begotten prayed for them? And what did he pray for, but that they be rescued from the bonds of death? Therefore [?] And his prisoners

he has not despised. For he burst the bonds of all, saying to those in bonds, "Come out," and to those in darkness, "Show yourselves." And he has not despised his prisoners. He did not spurn us when we were in misfortune; and he rightly called them prisoners because of what they were suffering. Let the heavens and the earth praise him. If there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, how much more will they rejoice when the whole earth has been set free! And if heaven rejoices at the salvation of human beings and praises God for it, how much more will those on earth who have been saved praise the one who saved them! That is why he added: The sea and all that creep in them. He says this because the islands too were going to receive the salvation of God. "In them" means both on the earth and in the sea. For God will save Zion, and the cities of Judea will be built. What does he say Zion is, if not the holy Church, whose cities have also been built, namely the souls of human beings that have been raised up? For they had fallen when they did not know God. These are the souls raised up through confession, for "Judea" is interpreted as "confession." And they will dwell there and inherit it. Those who are now captives, he says, once they have obtained their return, will build their own cities and dwell in them. And not they alone, but their children and descendants as well; for this is what he added: The seed of his servants will possess it, and those who love your name will dwell in it. His servants are the holy apostles, as Paul calls himself "a servant of Jesus Christ"; and their seed are those who have believed in Christ through them. For the end. A psalm of David, 69. For a remembrance, that the Lord may save me.

He sings this psalm in the person of humanity, which begs God to rise up and help it. For in this way it would come about that the hostile demons who oppose it would be put to shame, and that all who rejoice at its salvation would be made glad. O God, attend to my help, and so on. Let them be ashamed and confounded. May those who desire my slaughter fail, he says, and reap the shame that comes of it. Let them be turned back, and so on. Here again, in these verses, he calls down curses on those who plot against him and wish him to suffer harm, and he says to them: May those who gloat over my misfortunes be put to flight in shame when they see my change of fortune. Let them be turned back at once in shame. That is, those who long ago gloated over the fall that befell me through the curse of death.

"But I am poor and needy." That is: I am deprived of the righteousness of those just mentioned, and since I live in poverty I do not have the wealth of righteousness; so I beg to receive your help. "You are my helper and my [deliverer?], O Lord; do not delay." For I have received your providential care. Hear me as quickly as you can, and do not put off my request.

Of David. A Psalm, for the end; of the sons of Jonadab, and of the first who were taken captive. Without a title among the Hebrews. Psalm 70.

The sons of Jonadab were devout and righteous men, strict keepers of their father's commandments, and so God-fearing and upright in character that God himself, speaking with the prophet Jeremiah, bore witness to their virtue. It was in their time, too, that the first captivity of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans took place. They may stand for the apostolic choir, which kept the commandments of the heavenly Father with the greatest care and received praise through the beatitudes addressed to them. In the same way, in the time of these apostles, I mean, the first captivity of Jerusalem by the Romans took place. So in the present psalm these friends of God, that is, the apostolic choir, are presented as offering prayer and thanksgiving to God for themselves. They give thanks that he rescued them when they were afflicted, both by those who persecuted them for preaching the gospel and by the spiritual enemies who plot against their souls, the demons. They also promise to offer only sacrifices of praise, since they have plainly been set free from worship according to the law. "In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me never be put to shame." He holds out his hope in God as a great ground for confidence. "In your righteousness deliver me." The Son is the righteousness of the Father, and through him we were delivered from the sin that held us fast for corruption. "Be a protecting God for me." The apostolic choir knows that he has promised to be a wall of fire all around those who believe in him, and so it asks that this promise be fulfilled for it in deed. "For you are my strength and my refuge." For he is the rock on which we who have been built upon it have our foundation, and he is the wall that holds us together, so that we suffer nothing from the onslaught of evils. Rescue me, he says, from these men who hold power and lead me into slavery as if by the hand, men full of sin, lawless and unjust. "O my God, deliver me from the hand of the sinner, and from the hand of the lawbreaker and the unjust." By "the sinner" he means the Jews, for it was they who were both lawless and unjust: lawless, because they condemned the innocent; unjust, because they had no reasonable pretext against them.

"For you are my patience, O Lord; Lord, my hope from my youth." Deliver me, he says, from this lawless people, because I endure such things for your sake and for the sake of my hope in you. I received this hope from my first birth, my very beginning, which came through you, as it is said: "As many as received him, to them he gave power to become children of God." "On you I have leaned from the womb." He shows that Christ, for whose sake they endured such things, is the very one who by his creative providence brought them out into the light while they were still being carried in the womb. "From my mother's womb you are my protector." Since you yourself, the Lord, he says, sheltered me by your divine power even while I was still in my mother's womb, and delivered me from the lawless people, I too, having felt such constant kindness, never cease to send up hymns to you. "My hymn is of you always." I continue to hymn and glorify you, and through your providence I have become renowned. "I became like a wonder to many." By "wonder" he means something extraordinary and great. What he says amounts to this: Even if I have been lifted on high, he says, and have come to be [regarded?] as someone great and outstanding among the many nations, I did not gain this good by my own power. For it was you yourself who made me strong and noble with your help. "Let my mouth be filled with praise, that I may hymn your glory." Since I am only human and cannot make a fitting return for the great benefits given to me, I ask that my mouth be filled with praise from your wisdom; only in this way will I be able, if barely, to hymn your glory. "[All] the day long your magnificence." When my mouth has been filled with praise, he says, and I begin to hymn your glory, I will also hymn your magnificence all day long. By "glory" he means the dispensation that he carried out on earth, through which he filled the earth with his glory. By "magnificence" he means the Godhead, through which all those things [?]

["Let my mouth be filled with praise." It is possible to praise God always, to bless always, and to be self-controlled always. But how is it possible to hope always? For whoever hopes always never obtains the thing he hopes to obtain. One person will say that "always" refers not to the breadth of the ages but to this life of the senses. Another will take "always" to refer to the breadth of the ages as well, so that the goal of hope is the knowledge of the Holy Trinity.] "Do not cast me off in the time of old age." Here he calls weakness "old age." So he says: May there never come a time, O Master, when I am shown to be weak. He prays, then, never to fall away from hope in Christ. For he himself is the strength [?]

"When my strength fails, do not forsake me." Even if it should happen, he says, that as a human being I sin at some time, do not forsake me because of the sin, Lord, but call me back again, since you love humankind. "For my enemies spoke against me." "For they spoke" means: lest my enemies should say, "Let us attack him, for he will be our plunder, since God is not helping him." "O my God, do not be far from me." Since they say these things, then, do not put off your help for very long. "O my God, [attend] to my help."

"Let those who slander my soul be put to shame and fail." When they attack me, he says, because I seem to have been forsaken by you, if you yourself help me, they will be turned back in shame, since the slanders they made against my soul will be shown to be empty. And what are these slanders? Those that say, "God has forsaken him." "But I will hope in you always." For they never cease to confess their hope in Christ in their own writings. "And I will add to all your praise." Through the hymnody of those [?] through them

"My mouth will proclaim your righteousness." I never cease, he says, O Master, to keep your righteousness always on my lips. For the righteousness of the Father is his Only-begotten; for he became righteousness for us from God, as the holy Apostle says. "[All] the day your salvation." I will always remember, he says, the dispensation through which you granted us salvation. "For I have not known learning." By "learning" he means either the vain and tangled distractions of life, or the many kinds of sacrifices that the law commanded to be offered. Since I have cast all these aside, he says, I will enter the dwelling places above, for the Lord gives me the power to do so. This is like the saying: "Look, we have left everything and followed you; what then will we have?" when they received the promise of the kingdom of heaven for this very reason. "I will enter in the power of the Lord." By your power and help I will gain entry into the land of the promise. "Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone." Leaving aside everything mentioned, he says, I will remember only the righteousness through which you set us free from sin. "O my God, the things you taught me from my youth." For from the very first day, so to speak, on which he chose them, he handed down to them the things concerning the kingdom of heaven. "And until now I will declare your wonders." I have not forgotten, he says, what I was taught; the very things I learned, I have also declared to others. "And to old age and advanced years." Since Christ himself, after his return to life from the dead, made a promise, saying to them, "Look, I am with you all the days

until the end of the age," he asks for this reason that this promise be fulfilled for him. "O my God, do not forsake me until I declare your arm." If you do not forsake me, he says, as you promised, O Master, then it will be possible to declare your arm to the faithful generation that is to come from the nations. And he goes on to say what the arm is: "Your might and your righteousness." He says "might" because he bound the strong man and plundered his goods; "righteousness," because he has redeemed us who were unjustly held captive. "O God, up to the highest heavens." I will declare, he says, that by your own blood you redeemed not only the things on earth but also the things in heaven. This is like the saying: "For the creation itself will also be set free from its slavery to corruption." "O God, who is like you?" He gives thanks because, although long ago he had been justly condemned to death on account of sin, he did not remain in death, but through God's love for humankind has been set free from corruption through Christ. "How many great afflictions you have shown me!" What kinds of evils, and how many, you made me experience! "And you turned and gave me life, and brought me up again from the depths of the earth. You increased your greatness upon me, and you turned and comforted me." The repetition seems to signify that repentance for sins committed after baptism is acceptable to him who, as has been said, has increased his goodness and righteousness toward us. So the first phrase, "you gave me life," is said as of regeneration, and the second, "you comforted me," as of someone worn down by despondency over his sins. It is also possible to take the first phrases as referring to the redemption from Egypt, and to understand the second ones of the coming of the Lord, when complete comfort was given to us. For those who came out of Egypt, even if they were delivered from temporal death, still fell under eternal death, since the resurrection had not yet been granted. "For I too will confess your truth to you with vessels of psalmody, O God." In this way, he says, through confession I will prepare myself to become fit to be called a vessel of hymnody. And if the phrase "a vessel of election" has been used, then plainly there can also be "a vessel of hymnody." "I will sing psalms to you on the lyre." He means the harmony of the soul. For when the soul does or suffers nothing at odds with itself, either in its way of life or in its doctrines, then it might rightly be called a spiritual lyre. "My lips will rejoice when I sing psalms to you." This is said in contrast to the law: those commands were burdensome because they were hard to carry out, but these are kind and light, so that they fill with pleasure those who are counted worthy of them. "And my soul, which you redeemed": from sin, from corruption, from slavery to Satan, from death itself.

"And my tongue too will meditate on your righteousness all day long, when those who seek evil for me are put to shame and confounded." When my spiritual enemies have been removed, he says, and those who dwell in the abyss are clothed with shame, then, since nothing hinders me any longer, I will praise you, O Master, with unending hymns.

For the end. A Psalm of David, for Solomon.

[The] coming of Christ is signified by these words, and the calling of the nations. The psalm is entitled "For Solomon." For he is the true Solomon, the peaceful one, since he made both one and broke down the dividing wall of the fence [?]. "O God, give your judgment to the king." It has been decided by you, he says, O Father, that your only-begotten Son should shine upon those on earth. So let this, he says, which was decided long ago, be brought to fulfilment. "And your righteousness to the king's son." Although he is himself the righteousness of the Father, he is said to have received righteousness because of his humanity. He is Christ, who is both the king and the king's son. "To judge your people in righteousness." This is the reason for the incarnation: to judge Satan's greed against us. That is why, when he was about to be crucified, he said: "Now is the judgment of this world; the ruler of this world will be cast out." "Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness." By mountains and hills he here means the angelic powers. In former times, because of the impiety that had spread everywhere, they did not visit the earth, but now they are bidden to take up peace toward all people. "He will judge the poor of the people." By "the poor" he means those born of idolatrous fathers, who were impoverished of every good, and in general the whole human race. For "all have turned aside," in the words of the psalm. "And he will humble the false accuser." He means the devil. "And he will endure as long as the sun." His kingdom, he says, will extend to the ages. "And before the moon, for generations of generations." He who reigned over those on earth at his coming, he says, is the same one who was the creator of all things before the ages. "He will come down like rain on a fleece." Without a sound, he means; he said this because of the hidden manner of his coming. "In his days righteousness will rise." For at the time of his coming all war among the nations was done away [another reading: "had been done away"]. "And abundance of peace until the moon is taken away." So great, he says, will be the abundance of peace that comes about at his coming that it will extend even into the times to come, when the sun will be darkened and the moon will not give its light [?]. "And he will have dominion from sea to sea." He says this because all the nations accepted faith in him. In other words: he will rule over all the

ends of the inhabited world. For beyond the land lie the great and boundless seas, which some call Atlantic, the Ocean, both western and eastern. So he fittingly expressed dominion over the inhabited world by means of the seas that encircle it from outside, and the verse that follows makes this clearer. "And his enemies will lick the dust." His foes will be so completely subdued that no battle against him will be seen. The image comes from those who fall to the ground as a sign of their submission. "For he delivered the poor from the mighty." From the farthest ends of the world to the farthest, he says, the nations and kings will worship him, giving thanks that he redeemed them from the tyranny of Satan. "From usury and injustice he will redeem their souls." He blots out the bond written against them and forgives both the one who owed five hundred and the one who owed fifty. "And his name will be honoured." He will be revered and glorious, he says, among all. "And he will live, and he will be given of the gold of Arabia." He says this because of Herod, who sent men to kill the infants. So he says that he will not be caught up with the children who were slain. And "He will be given Arabian gold" plainly refers to the gifts the Magi offered. "And they will pray for him continually." They will name him in their prayers and ask the Father to grant them good things through him. "There will be a support in the land": of the Church, he says, and of the inhabited world. "On the tops of the mountains": that is, of the apostles and prophets. "His fruit will be exalted above Lebanon." Lebanon is Jerusalem, and its fruit is the word of the gospel. So he says that the preaching of the gospel will be above worship according to the law. "And they will blossom out of the city like the grass of the earth." By "city" he means the Church, of which it is written: "Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God." "His name endures before the sun." He shows that the one who was not killed with the infants is the one who exists before the foundation of the world with the

"Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone does wonders." Having gone through everything that he will accomplish in his dispensation for those on earth, he sends up a hymn to him, saying that he is the God of Israel, the only one able to do these wonders. And what wonders are these, if not abolishing the power of Satan and rescuing those who are plotted against from the tyranny of the demons? Notice that nothing said in the psalm will fit Solomon, the son of Uriah's wife: neither "His name is before the sun," nor "All the nations will serve him," nor "Before the moon, for generations of generations." From all this, then, it is clear that it was spoken of our Lord Jesus Christ.

"And blessed be the name of his glory." Therefore it is fitting that he be hymned by all. For even if we do not know his nature, since it is beyond our reach, we have nevertheless been taught his saving name. "The hymns of David son of Jesse are ended."

A Psalm of Asaph. Psalm 72.

In this psalm he sets out the inconsistency that people perceive in God's judgments. For those judgments are deep and unsearchable and full of great incomprehensibility, and those who do not know the reasons for the dispensation at work in each case fall into helpless reasoning. So he first sets these thoughts before us, namely the ones that arise because of the prosperity of the impious ("For look," he says, "sinners, and prospering"). After this he teaches what kind of end the impious themselves will have, so that, knowing these things clearly, we may not be at a loss amid the inconsistencies of affairs in this life. "How good is God to Israel, to the upright in heart!" He is about to describe the prosperity that comes to people who live in impiety and the bitter punishment stored up for them afterward. So he first states that God is good to the upright, so that those who choose the side of piety may know that God will be good only to the upright in heart, and no longer to those who sin most wickedly. So even if they seem to prosper, he says, let no one be troubled, but let him bear in mind the punishment that awaits them a little later. ["But as for me, my feet almost slipped." He relates that the pious meet such a death that no one would refuse if someone asked him whether he would like to meet such a death.] "For I was envious of the lawless, seeing the peace of sinners," and so on. He recounts the things that caused the turmoil in his soul. They are these: first, that they go on in deep peace; next, that they prosper throughout their lives, so that their prosperity lasts all the way to death, and that the impious meet such a death that no one would refuse if someone asked him whether he would like to meet such a death; in addition, that even if a scourge came upon them for their sin to turn them back, it was not harsh but light and easy to bear; and on top of all this, that they do not share in human labours and do not need daily work to provide the food they need. For this labour of the hands has been given to human beings as a kind of substitute for scourges

"Therefore pride has taken hold of them completely." Since they enjoy every good thing and no evil, they cultivated pride to excess. This pride made them unjust and impious, and to such a degree that even their impieties are fat and, as it were, well fed.

They have passed into the disposition of the heart. Their lawless prosperity, he says, produced an evil habit in their soul. And how is this clear, if not from their thinking and speaking wickedness? They spoke injustice on high. This signifies the intensifying of their wickedness, so that they now even direct their blasphemy against God himself. They set their mouth against heaven. They uttered blasphemous words against God, he says, and that though they were lowly and had their tongue upon the earth. Therefore my people will turn back here. This, then, is why they were cast down after being lifted up. The sense is this: some benefit, he says, and conversion will come to my people from the punishment of these men. For having seen what kind of end awaits the ungodly, they would never come to this, since they clearly know that God watches over human affairs. And full days will be found in them. When, he says, they have acquired such a mind, then indeed they will fill up the time of their life well, according to what was said: He fell asleep full of days; that is, their days have become full of every good. And they said, How did God know? My people, he says, will benefit from the ungodly being cast down. But the impious and godless men mentioned before were so ungodly that their life became a stumbling block to those who saw it, so that these were at a loss and said: Does God then watch over human affairs? For 'How did he know?' is said in place of 'How does he know and govern our affairs, and how does he have knowledge of what concerns us?' Behold, these are sinners, and prospering forever they have held on to wealth. He sets out the cause of the stumbling of those who see the ungodly prospering: namely, that they go on in prosperity throughout the present life. And I said: Was it then in vain that I justified my heart? And I, he says, seeing these things, was troubled in my thoughts, considering within myself whether perhaps my labour for virtue would prove vain for me. Now the labour was this: to practise righteousness, to keep clean of unjust action, to scourge oneself for former sins through confession, and to rise up for this as from a bed, so as to afflict oneself for one's sins. If I said, I will speak thus, behold, I would have broken covenant with the generation of your sons. These things, he says, I considered within myself: that if I declared to others these thoughts that had stolen in upon me (and they were: Was it then in vain that I justified my heart?), I would become the cause of every stumbling for them. And in doing this I would transgress the covenants of your sons, that is, of righteous men. And these were the covenants of the saints: not to become a cause of stumbling to one another. And I undertook to know this; it is a toil before me. Having set out, he says, to know such deep judgments, I cast myself into toil, since they are

deep and unsearchable. Yet I have provided for myself the proper time for knowing them; and this was the time of the divine tribunal, when you will repay each according to his works. But because of their deceits you have appointed evils for them, and so on. I, he says, set the coming time before myself as the one suited to exact knowledge of these things; so that, knowing by the prophetic spirit what is to be, I declare that the deceitfulness of their character will become the cause of bitter punishments for them. For their exaltation will turn to their fall. And this present wealth of theirs will be judged like the phantoms of dreamers, without substance and weaker than any shadow. And in your city you will bring their image to nothing. The city of the Lord is the Jerusalem above, and their image is that of the man of dust. What he says is this: since, he says, they have borne the image of the man of dust and not that of the heavenly man, for this very reason they will be brought to nothing; for at that time they will hear, I do not know you, since they do not bear the image of the heavenly one himself. For my heart was inflamed and my reins were changed, and I was brought to nothing and did not know, and so on. Since I have been very zealous for the Lord, so that my heart and reins were filled with the zeal of fire, for this reason I was counted worthy to be enlightened and to know what has been done concerning your city and concerning the image of the ungodly. But before this I went on like a brute beast, unable to grasp the reasons of Providence. Yet I did not forsake you, my God, nor did I fall away from my hope in you; but I was with you continually. And this I did not by my own power but by your grace. For you yourself, in your love for humankind, took hold of my right hand and held me together and held me fast, so that my steps would not be shaken nor my feet moved from their standing before you. For what have I in heaven, and besides you what have I desired on earth, and so on. Since, he says, I have nothing in heaven but you alone, of necessity I wished to receive nothing of the things on earth, since all of them are perishable and temporary. I prayed to obtain one thing only, and wore myself out on earth with longing for it: namely, that you should become my portion, and you alone. Behold, those who remove themselves far from you will perish, and so on. I clung, O Master, to union with you, he says; and I call this good, knowing that the end of those who are outside you will be destruction. But those who are with you will have a good portion. For it will be granted them, once they are in the heavenly Jerusalem, to inherit the good portion; and this is to delight forever. Of understanding, for Asaph. 73.
In these words the prophet sings a supplication, foreseeing the final captivity of Israel, that he might not cut them off completely from their close relationship with him,

He also describes the capture that befell both the city itself and the divine temple. Why, O God, have you rejected us to the end? This is like: Wrath has already come upon them to the end. For they will no longer have any respite from their evils. Remember your congregation, which you acquired from the beginning. Through Abraham and Isaac and Jacob. You redeemed with the rod your inheritance. 'Remember' is to be supplied from what precedes: Remember your inheritance, which you redeemed with the rod; that is, an inheritance made ready for a kingdom, according to what was said to them: You shall be to me, out of all the nations, a chosen race, a royal priesthood. This Mount Zion, in which you dwelt. Because of the appearing in the divine temple of the

Lift up your hands against their arrogance to the end. That is, of those who made war on the divine temple. And those who hate you boasted in the midst of your feast. Since it was at the feast of Passover that they raised war against the Lord, for this reason they were handed over to their enemies at that very season. For when all the Jews had gathered for Passover according to the law, the siege took place, justly, at the very season in which they had also nailed the Saviour to the cross. They set up their signs as signs. He means the emblems of war; he is speaking of what armies call 'signa', which they set up on the road of the city. And they did not stop there, but went further, he says; that is, they even burst into the divine temple itself, not knowing that it was God who was handing the city over to them because of the impiety of its inhabitants. Being ignorant of this, they marvelled at their own power and condemned as weak the God worshipped in the divine temple. That is why further on he says: How long, O Lord, will the enemy reproach? The repetition in naming the signs would be that of someone marvelling at how the divine temple was handed over into the hands of the enemy. As in a thicket of trees, with axes they cut down its doors, and so on. In these verses he describes the overthrow of both the city and the divine temple. Using woodcutters' and carpenters' tools, they demolished the surrounding walls and hacked the doors to pieces, destroying what had been well and beautifully wrought as though it were a thicket. They burned your sanctuary with fire, and so on. Coming upon us with great calamity, they had one aim: to abolish the law given by you. For by 'the feasts' he indicated the worship prescribed by the law. And they dared these things, he says, neither seeing the wonders performed in the days of our forefathers nor being rebuked by prophetic grace. For they had suddenly been left bereft of all these. For in former times, even after the return, they had prophets: Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. And the prophets older than these

foretold to the people and to the kings what was to come, and exposed the plots of their enemies. And this is easy to learn from history. We have not seen our signs. They urged one another on to put an end to the Lord's feasts while they were still being celebrated, and indeed added deeds to their words; but we, while these things were being done, did not witness those signs of which we had often been eyewitnesses in earlier wars. And these signs were help against the terrors that pressed upon us. Therefore, as people who have not witnessed them, we say: Why, O God, have you rejected us to the end? There is no longer a prophet, and he will no longer know us. And this above all makes us despair of salvation: that we no longer see in the nation a prophet able to entreat God on our behalf. How long, O God, will the enemy reproach? Having completed his description of the capture from the side of the enemies, he calls on God for mercy, and [?] how everything that happened was an outrage against God, by saying 'In the midst of your feast', and 'your sanctuary', and 'the dwelling place of your name', and 'the feasts of the Lord', and 'your name'

Why do you turn away your hand, and so on? Why, he says, do you cut off the giving of the good things which you once supplied us as from your bosom? But God is our King before the ages. Now, he says, you cut off the flow of good things to us; but long ago, deigning to be called both our God and our King, you wrought such salvation for us that it escaped the notice of no one on earth. He has worked salvation in the midst of the earth. Taking this as their starting point, some have declared Jerusalem to be the eye

You made the sea strong by your power; you crushed the heads of the dragons upon the water. He describes in words the way in which he wrought their salvation of old. First, the waters of the sea were congealed like a wall when they went out of Egypt; and this is 'You made the sea strong'. Second, the head of the Egyptians was crushed upon the waters; he also names them dragons because of the wickedness of their tongue; and then, together with them, the king who led them was crushed as well, whom he likewise calls a dragon. [You made the sea strong by your power. Having crushed Pharaoh with his captains and chariots like dragons' heads, because of the wickedness of their intent, upon the water, you gave the Egyptians, who were neighbours of the Ethiopians, to them as food; you defeated them and their king before the face of the Ethiopians.] You gave him as food to the peoples, the Ethiopians. That is, Pharaoh himself, together with his army, of course. By 'peoples' he here means the flocks of birds among the Indians, which devoured the bodies of the Egyptians cast up from the sea onto the land.

You broke open springs and torrents. He means what happened in the wilderness, when he gave the people drink from the rock. You dried up the rivers of Etham. Etham is interpreted 'south'; for the Jordan lies to the south of the land of the Jews. Yours is the day, and yours the night. Not only, he says, were you our provider at the Red Sea and in the wilderness; you have also been the source of good things for the whole human race, creating day and night, sun and moon, summer and spring, and fixing boundaries upon the earth. And he says these things now as he calls on him for help in the present as well. Therefore he says: Remember this creation of yours. If you made creation for the sake of human beings, he says, grant help to those for whose sake creation came into being. Remember this: the enemy has reproached you, O Lord. Having called on God to pity the people by appealing to creation, he again calls him to pity in another way. And this way is the arrogance of the enemy. And a foolish people has provoked your name. See again another way of moving him to pity: that the enemies have provoked his name. Do not hand over to the beasts a soul that confesses to you. He heightened his appeal for pity by calling the enemies beasts, implying that those who had sinned had some claim to pardon through their confession. And he prays that Israel may not perish in the same way; and this is what happened. For many tens of thousands even of those who crucified him believed and were saved. Look upon your covenant. Again another way of moving him to pity: for they draw down mercy from the very things in which he showed himself good toward them by making a covenant with them. For the darkened places of the earth have been filled with houses of iniquities. What he says is this: even if many houses have become full of darkness because of the iniquities they committed against you, O Lord, still let not the whole people be turned away or handed over to shame. For some had within themselves a hope of salvation; they were saved through the apostles, and especially through Peter in his first public speeches, so that they came to number three thousand, then five thousand, then tens of thousands. [The poor and needy will praise your name. When those worthy of salvation have been saved, he says, the poor in spirit, that is, the company of the apostles, according to 'Blessed are the poor in spirit', send up to you the praises that befit you.] Arise, O God, judge your cause. Pleading for the punishment of those who deceived the people, he rouses God. Remember your reproach. Again he calls on God to pity by appealing to the reproach he suffers. To the end; do not destroy,

exhorting people to cease from ungodliness by setting before them that fearful and divine tribunal. We will confess to you, O God... I will recount all your wonders. The company of the apostles, delivered from its persecutors, promises to recount God's wonders. I will judge uprightly. The Saviour says this, hearkening to their promise. The earth melted, and all who dwell in it. Judging justly, he says, you melted the earth, that is, Jerusalem, and all who dwell in it. This can be understood in two ways: in a good sense, with 'melted' meaning 'gave way and yielded up its wickedness'; and in a bad sense, to indicate the punishment that came upon them. I have made firm its pillars. The pillars of Jerusalem are the holy apostles, according to what is said, 'The pillar and foundation of the truth', says the Apostle; and, 'And when James and Cephas and John, who were reputed to be pillars, recognized the grace given to me.'] I said to the lawless: Do not act lawlessly. From here on the apostles speak in their own person, exhorting people to cease from ungodliness. [He humbles the Jewish people because of its arrogance, and exalts the people from the nations because of its humility.] Do not lift up your horn on high. For horned animals take great pride in their horns. The word charges them not to increase their lawlessness by boasting, nor to move their tongue against God. For neither from the outgoings, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains. By these he indicates the whole order of the inhabited world: by 'outgoing' the east, whence the sun goes out; by 'west' the evening; and by 'desert mountains' the northern and southern regions, for these are uninhabitable because of excessive cold and heat. Do not act lawlessly, then, he says, because no one anywhere in the inhabited world could escape God's notice when saying something blasphemous against him. This one he humbles, and that one he exalts. Being a good judge, he says, he humbles the ungodly and exalts the humble of heart. These words must also be understood of the two peoples, I mean the Jews and the people from the nations; for the one has been humbled because of its boasting, and the other is exalted because of its humility. 1 Tim. 3:15. Gal. 2:9.
evils; just as, indeed, the saints will drink the cup of life in the kingdom of heaven with the Lord Jesus, according to the word of the Lord himself: Until I drink it in the kingdom of heaven.

And I will break all the horns of sinners. If, when sinners are humbled, the horn is lifted on high, then clearly, when the saints are exalted, the horns of sinners will be shattered. And who would the sinners be, if not the evil demons who oppose the people of God? And the horn of the righteous will be exalted. By 'horn' he means kingship, or dominion. When, then, he says, the righteous receive strength, the evil powers having of course been destroyed, then indeed the wonders of God will also be shown. That is why, at the beginning of the psalm, he said: I will recount your wonders, when I receive the appointed time. To the end, among hymns, a psalm for Asaph, an ode concerning the Assyrian. 75.

This psalm too keeps to the same subject as the one before it; for it too recounts what concerns the divine tribunal. God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel. By Judea and Israel he here means the soul that has come to know God; for this is the true Judea and the true Israel. His place has come to be in peace. For if it is written of the Judea above that there pain, sorrow and sighing have fled away, clearly it will be a place of peace. And his dwelling place in Zion. He means the spiritual Zion, that is, the one above, the soul of the saints. [His place has come to be in peace. In the soul of the saints. The Hebrew has 'Salem', and the other translators rendered it so, which means 'peace'. In this, then, whether the soul or the Church, the fiery darts that the evil one sends are shattered; or else in the Jerusalem above.] There he shattered the might of the bows. By these words he signifies the opposing powers, which are shattered when the saints are allotted to dwell in the mansions there. You give light wondrously from the everlasting mountains. By 'everlasting mountains' he means the heavens. God enlightens us from above, sending the Spirit down to us from heaven. 'You are a surpassingly great illumination from the mountains of capture.' 'You give light wondrously from the mountains of the hunt.' 'You are wondrously fearful from the fruitful mountains.' [You give light wondrously from the everlasting mountains. From there he sends down the Holy Spirit, from the everlasting mountains. He means Zion, from which they thought God set out to do these things, and where a temple had been built for him.]

All the foolish of heart were troubled. Those who have not received the illumination that comes through the Spirit will be in turmoil and agitation when the divine tribunal appears. They slept their sleep and found nothing. Having given over their life to negligence and idleness, he says, those who were once rich in this mortal life found, at the time of the divine judgment, that they held nothing in their hands. For how could they find what they had not worked for? All the men of wealth, in their hands. Symmachus renders it thus: All the strong men, their hands. The strength of their hands, he says, by which they expected to seize the wealth of all, profited them nothing. And teaching why they gained nothing from it, he added: At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, those mounted on horses slumbered. When the just verdict against them was pronounced, he says, they were given over as it were to sleep and stupor; that is, they could not lift up their heads. And who are these who are mounted on horses? Divine Scripture customarily calls 'horses' those who have turned uncontrollably toward pleasures, according to: They became horses mad after females; each neighed after his neighbour's wife. You are fearful, and who will stand against you? For if he shuts against a man, who will open? as Isaiah says. From heaven you made judgment heard. They will have no defence when they are punished, he says, for he proclaimed to them beforehand what concerns the divine tribunal. The earth feared and was still. Here by 'earth' he means the whole of human nature, which will also be afraid at that time. For there will be no one then who does not fear, when that day arrives. [For being the God of heaven, he says, you judged, and made the judgment manifest by punishing the enemies of Jerusalem.] When God arose to judgment, to save all the meek of the earth. The divine tribunal, he says, will grant salvation to the meek, just as, indeed, it metes out punishments to sinners. For the thought of man will confess to you. We will stand before that fearful judgment seat, called to account not only for what we have done but also for what we have planned. And the remnant of thought will keep festival to you. The remnant of thought is the purified reasoning, according to the saying, 'a remnant chosen by grace'. When, then, he says, the reasoning is found pure at that time, then indeed may it share in your feast. [For the thought of man will confess to you. For every tongue and every reasoning and thought will confess to the Lord at the time of judgment, when even hidden things are exposed.] Vow, and pay your vows to the Lord your God. The discourse turns to exhortation. Since what has been said

[?] will be, he says, at the divine tribunal. For this reason, while you are in the present life, vow to the Lord to be diligent in good works, and do not be slow to pay what you have vowed. They will bring the gifts, terrified by the miracles that have taken place. "To the one who is fearsome and takes away the spirits of rulers." Promise, he says, to do good, knowing that when you come to that place you must bring your own deeds to God as gifts. And God is so fearsome that the spirit will be taken away even from those who ruled of old and became wicked. For at that divine and fearsome judgment seat, what was given through baptism is taken away from each of those who have sinned. And this is what the Lord said: "The master of that wicked servant will come and cut him in two, and will assign him his portion with the unbelievers." For the end, for Jeduthun, a Psalm of [?]

Jeduthun had heard what was said about the people of the Hebrews, namely: "O God, why have you rejected us forever?" He was grieved beyond measure and troubled, and lamented their complete rejection. So Asaph composes a psalm for him, teaching him that in such matters one must take refuge in God alone and find consolation from him. That is why he begins: "With my voice I cried to the Lord, with my voice to God, and he gave heed to me." At the beginning of the psalm he teaches Jeduthun that the Lord is near to those who call upon him. "In the day of my affliction I sought God, with my hands by night before him, and I was not deceived." Such affliction, he says, flooded my soul that I not only made supplication by day but also spent the very hours of the night in prayer. But in doing this I did not run in vain or labour in vain; and this is what "I was not deceived" means. "My soul refused to be comforted; I remembered God and was gladdened." I would not accept, he says, a single consolation from men; the remembrance of God alone became the gladness of my heart. "I mused, and my spirit grew faint." When I relied on human reasonings, he says (for this is what "I mused" means), then indeed I sank into dejection. "My eyes anticipated the watches; I was troubled and did not speak." For this, he says, is what causes trouble: when the enemies have seized in advance the posts of our watches, that is, the battlements of the walls. "I considered the days of old." I was pondering these things within myself, he says, and was troubled at how God once helped the people but now has rejected them. And

this is what stirred my despondency: the fear that their rejection might become permanent. I kept recalling those ancient days. "This is the change of the right hand of the Most High." As I turned over my thoughts about the rejection of the nation, he says, I understood at long last that this change, which brought the nation from good to evil, came about for no other reason than because of the right hand of the Most High. It is as if he were saying more plainly: because of what was done against Christ the Saviour, who is the right hand of the Father. "For I will remember your wonders from the beginning." I considered, he says, how many good things he showed them, and what evils they paid him back in return. "And I will meditate on all your works." Even if they acted so, he says, yet may I go through, from beginning to end, the benefits you began to bestow on us; that is, may none of the good things done among us be forgotten.

"O God, your way is in the holy." By "holy" he means either the sanctified company of the apostles, with whom he performed the extraordinary divine signs, or that no one can come to the Father except through Christ, who is truly holy, as God. "Who is a great God like our God?" You surpass all, Master; for you alone work whatever wonders you will. "With your arm you redeemed your people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph." For he preached the gospel of the kingdom of heaven to them first. The arm of the Lord, that is, Christ. "The waters saw you, O God, and they were afraid." And when did the waters see him and fear, if not when he rebuked the sea and [?]? "The clouds gave forth a voice; for your arrows pass through." By clouds here he means the holy apostles, who minister the heavenly word of the gospel; and by arrows, the workings of the Holy Spirit. It is as if he said: the workings in your holy disciples have been heard of throughout the whole world. One should know that he himself is called a chosen arrow by the prophet Isaiah. "The voice of your thunder in the wheel." By thunder he means the word of the gospel, which resounded through all that is under heaven. That is why he also called the evangelist a son [?]

[?] as one can also learn from Ezekiel. It is as if he said: your word, the gospel, has been spread to the whole human race. "Your lightnings shone on the world." And who could the lightnings be but those who flash spiritual light upon us, the holy apostles and evangelists, to whom the Saviour said, "You are the light of the world"? "The earth was shaken and trembled." Meaning: the saving proclamation was heard by those throughout the whole earth, and through it a pure fear seized everyone, according to the words, "Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with [?]"

"Your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters." By the sea he means the world, and by many waters the various races of men in it. Christ commanded the apostles, saying, "Go and make disciples of all nations," and, "Behold, I am with you all the days"; and they ran through the whole world under heaven and preached to all the nations, the Lord plainly being present with them invisibly, according to his unfailing promises. For this reason he added, "And your footsteps will not be known," because the Lord's journeying with them was invisible. Yet he alone, as God, also walked on the visible sea, as the evangelist says. "You led your people like sheep." Just as sheep do not know where they are going from or where they are going to, so you led us, using Moses and Aaron and those with them as your servants for this purpose. All of this, from "I remembered the works of the Lord" onward, he connected with "I remembered God and was gladdened." For in recalling these things, he says, I was comforted in mind and gladdened. When I considered how many and how great were the things we had through your help, I was convinced that you, who had done so much for our salvation and for our deliverance from those who held us then, would never now endure to overlook us entirely while we are in slavery, captivity and misfortune. "By the hand of Moses and Aaron." You yourself, he says, O Master, who are present with the holy apostles, long ago led your people out of Egypt through Moses, with Moses and Aaron as their commanders. For understanding, for Asaph, Psalm 77. Argument. Asaph sings this psalm exhorting the new people to attend to the law of the gospel, and accusing that old populace of the Jews, who received many benefits yet remembered none of them, but instead turned their thanksgiving into its opposite and repaid their benefactor with ingratitude. "Attend, my people, to my law." And what people do you exhort, if not the one from the nations? And what law does he urge them to attend to, if not the gospel? That the nations are his people the prophet Zechariah declares: "And many nations will flee to the Lord, and they will be a people to him." "Incline your ear to the words of my mouth." Listen eagerly, he says, to what I say. "I will open my mouth in parables." The evangelist plainly interpreted this as fulfilled when the Lord spoke his many parables in the Gospels. "And our fathers recounted to us." All that we learned by hearing from our fathers, he says, we have come to know through his works and his coming. "It was not hidden from their children for another generation." Not for another generation, he says, but for the children

of theirs were all the Saviour's mighty works done; that is why they did not cease announcing to them beforehand the praises of the Lord and his mighty acts. "And he set a law in Israel." He gave a law, he says, to their fathers, and the tabernacle of witness, tutoring them through the law to know the Saviour who in due time would come to dwell among the human race. "Sons who would be born." By these he means the Saviour's holy disciples, who declare to their sons, that is, to those who came to the faith through them, the wonders that Christ accomplished. "And not forget the works of God." They will recount these things to them, through which they will be able to set their hope on God alone. "That they may not become like their fathers." The apostles, he says, will declare the praises of God to those tutored through them, so that they may seek out God's commandments and not imitate the wretchedness of their fathers. For that generation, he says, did not have a heart upright toward God, nor was its spirit faithful with God. "A generation that did not set its heart aright." For they did not acquire a firm faith in God; they would not walk the straight road but held to a mind opposed to the divine ordinances. "The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting with bows." By the one tribe of Ephraim he indicated the whole people of Israel that broke away from Judah. For these set up the heifers and departed from the worship prescribed by the law. Having touched on the wickedness of the fathers, he next recounts all their evil: the abundance of good things God gave them, their unbelief toward God, and the destruction that overtook them as a result, so that, taught by these things, people might flee their evil example. He says that the sons of Ephraim, that is, all Israel, who had been taught to fight against the evil demons and had been fashioned for this like a bow, changed sides at the very moment of battle, denying their Master and God and turning instead to Barabbas, that is, to Satan. "They did not keep the covenant of God." He means the new tradition of the Gospel, and the words, "Behold, a day is coming, and I will make a new covenant with them." This gives the reason: because they did not keep it, though it is God's new law, they turned back in the day of battle. For they did not believe him when he said, "I came forth from the Father and have come." They ought to have shot at and fought those who fight against God; but instead they took up war against God. "And they forgot his benefits." Although they had received many benefits, he says, they swept them all from their memory. And the proof of this is that they handed him over to Pilate. They forgot how he went about doing good to

them all and healing those oppressed by the devil. "The wonders he did before their fathers." So, he says, they forgot the benefits and wonders of Christ, just as their fathers, of course, forgot what had happened in Egypt when God was setting them free. For "before their fathers" seems to hint at something like this, as if he said more plainly: they have become like their fathers in their evil zeal; and as those forgot God, so did these. "He split the sea and brought them through." And not only this, he says, but he also divided the sea and brought them all across. From here he begins to narrate the wonders of the former redemption. For when the Red Sea had been split into many divisions, and the waters were separated and raised up on each side and lifted to a height, he enclosed them by a divine power as in a wineskin, so that they would not pour out and flood the [?]

"Therefore the Lord heard and delayed." Meaning: he put off for a little while and, as it were, held back his beneficent hand. "And he gave them bread of heaven." Not only, he says, did he nourish their bodies with the manna, but he also fed their souls with a certain rational and heavenly power, just as indeed he feeds the angels too. This can be seen from the conjunction, since "And he gave them bread of heaven" is said as by way of addition. But it can be learned no less from the Apostle, who said of them that they ate spiritual food. This was what is here called the bread of angels. "And winged birds like the sand of the seas." Here he means the quail. "While the food was still in their mouth." For their food turned into a bout of cholera for them, since they had given themselves over entirely to gorging on meat. "And he remembered that they are flesh, a spirit that goes and does not return." He pitied them, he says, although he saw that they had turned aside wholly to the flesh, that is, to minding the things of the flesh, and that they had a spirit always going after the desire of the flesh and not returning to repentance and to seeking God with their whole soul. So he pitied and saved them for no other reason than his own love for humankind alone. That is why he said beforehand, "For he is compassionate and merciful." "They did not remember his hand, the day when he redeemed them from the hand of the oppressor." Having listed the good things given to them at the sea and in the desert, he lists another kind of benefaction. These are the terrors that beset their enemies: the turning of the river into blood, the dog-fly, the frog, the blight, the locust, the hail, the frost, the fire, the sending of evil angels, and the rest, up to the destruction of the firstborn.

"He made a path for his wrath." Having given the mystery of the lamb, he says, he gave his wrath a way out, so that it would pass over his people and not [?] those who performed his mystery. But having guarded these by giving his wrath a way out, he did not spare from death the souls of the others, that is, of the Egyptians; for he handed them over to the destroyer. "And he brought them to the mountain of his sanctuary." He means Jerusalem and the temple later built in it. "The mountain which his right hand acquired." For Christ himself is the right hand of the Father, who also of old went before the people and gave them the land of promise as their inheritance. "And he drove out nations before them." The Amorite and the Hittite and those named after them. "And he allotted them their inheritance by measuring line." That is, the inheritance of the seven nations that had been driven out and destroyed. For they inherited the cities and houses of those who had been expelled. "And they tempted and provoked God the Most High." He refers to the idolatry that took place under the judges and under the kings. "And they did not keep his testimonies. And they turned away and broke faith, just like their fathers." Just as their fathers, he says, made the calf in the desert, denying their redeemer, so these too in turn set up the heifers and sacrificed to them, forsaking God. "And they provoked him to anger on their hills." For on every mountaintop they sacrificed to unclean demons, as the prophet Hosea says. "God heard and disregarded them, and utterly despised Israel." For they were handed over to various captivities. "And he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh." For the tabernacle was formerly in Shiloh, when Eli and Samuel served as priests. "The tent where he dwelt among men." By the tent he means the ark, which was taken from those men by the five satrapies that captured it. "And he gave their strength into captivity, and their beauty." Their strength, and indeed their beauty, was the ark, which was handed over into the hands of the people of Azotus. "And he shut up his people to the sword."

[?] because Shiloh was in the portion of Joseph, and Ephraim was a son of Joseph. "And he chose the tribe of Judah." For from it he raised up the kings, the first of whom was David. One should know that he chose tribe for tribe, Judah in place of Joseph, and place for place, Mount Zion in place of Shiloh. "And he built his sanctuary like that of a unicorn." By sanctuary he means the divine temple built in Jerusalem. The unicorn is an invincible beast, because it bears a sharp horn on its forehead and kills all the other beasts with it. He says, then, that the divine temple was so built that all the nations seemed inferior to the strength within it. "From following the ewes in lamb he took him." That is, the ewes giving birth and bearing young. From his skill as a shepherd, he says, and from his knowing how to watch over the lambing sheep, he rightly took him up and made him shepherd of rational flocks as well. "To shepherd Jacob his servant." That is, he became for them a teacher of good ways, by which he showed that he had trained them. "And by the skill of his hands he guided them." By the skill of hands he means every action performed in a fitting way. A Psalm of Asaph. 78.

He sings this psalm on behalf of those who were cruelly slain in the times of Antiochus, asking by his supplication for vengeance on the bloodshed committed against the nation, the calamities being turned, of course, upon those who brought them [?]

"O God, the nations have come into your inheritance." For Antiochus brought in many, entered Jerusalem, and burned the divine temple. "They have defiled your holy temple." See, he says, others have seized what is yours, and your possessions are held by foreigners. "They have made Jerusalem a watchman's hut in an orchard." A [?] place where the one who [?] the fruit has his hut

"They have given the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of the sky." For in the excess of their inhumanity the enemy did not even allow the relatives to bury their dead. "The flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth." For how could those not be holy who shed their blood for keeping the law, among whom were the Maccabees? "Your zeal will burn like fire." Be zealous, he says, for your name, which is blasphemed by the enemies. "Do not remember our ancient iniquities." By ancient sins he means those in Egypt. "Lest the nations say: Where is their God?" Even if the multitude of our sins, he says, stands in the way of our salvation, yet for the sake of your name act on our behalf, because of the reproach they bring

[?] because of the blood of your servants that has been shed, because of the groaning of the prisoners. "According to the greatness of your arm, preserve the sons of those put to death." By the power of your arm, he says, save those who are left from among the slain. For the end, for those who will be changed. A testimony of Asaph, a Psalm concerning the Assyrians. 79.

According to the plain sense of the words, he asks that those enslaved by the Assyrian be shown mercy; but according to the higher meaning, he prays for those who, after the cross of the Lord, endured the spiritual captivity at the hands of the spiritual Assyrians and of their ruler himself, I mean Satan. So he puts forward a supplication, asking for the appearing of our Saviour and the liberation of the whole race of Israel. "You who shepherd Israel, give heed." You, Master, who care for the people like a shepherd, I entreat to receive my supplication. "You who sit upon the cherubim, appear [?] before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh." On the march of the tabernacle three tribes went first: [?], Issachar and Zebulun. Three others followed toward the south: Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh. The glory of God rested on the golden cherubim above the ark, for it went before them on the march. You, then, who sit upon the cherubim and go before the ark, so as to be in front of Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh (for "before" means "in front of"), [?] salvation through your own power
"A vine out of Egypt you [?]." He means Israel. "You drove out nations and planted it." For going before them, you drove out from before them

"Its shadow covered the mountains." By the shadow of the vine he means the worship according to the law, since the law has a shadow of the good things to come; and by the mountains he means the one at Shiloh and the one at Zion, for the tabernacle was set up in these two places. So it signifies nothing other than that the things of the law, which were a shadow of the good things to come, were performed on these two mountains. "And its climbing branches covered the cedars of God." The cedars are the heavenly powers; the climbing branches of the vine are the prophets from among the people, raised on high and resting upon the rational powers above. "It stretched out its shoots to the sea." By the shoots and offshoots of the vine he means the whole multitude of the people, which held the land from the river Euphrates to the Indian Sea. "Why have you torn down its hedge?" Its hedge was the guard of angels, which God withdrew from them. "And all who pass along the road pluck its grapes." For it has been given as pasture

…to the unclean demons, who also feed on their souls and strip them of spiritual fruitfulness. "O God of hosts, turn." I beseech you, then, mighty Master, to look down from above on the ravaging of the vine and to grant healing to its affliction. For it was your providence that gave it its former good fortune. "And restore what your right hand planted." Since you planted it, he says, and then it was burned with fire and dug up and perished when you rebuked it, restore it and make it ready for salvation. And make it ready through the son of man. For "upon the son of man" means "through the son of man." And who is the son of man but our Lord himself, as he says of himself in the Gospels? "Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand." Let this work of the people's salvation, he says, which is signified by the hand, be upon the man of your right hand, that is, through the man [?] of your right hand. And who is this but the Son of Man, who is the right hand of the Father, even though he became man? When this happens, he says, and your right hand saves us, the one who was called man and Son of Man, we will never turn away from you, since we have shared in your life and have been called by your name, that is, Christians. "O Lord God of hosts, turn us." He keeps putting forward his supplication, urging that the appearing of the Only-begotten come quickly, for through him they will be saved. For the end, concerning the winepresses. PSALM

In interpreting the eighth psalm we have already explained that the winepresses are the churches. So from this psalm too one can see how he calls the nations to faith in the Lord. He teaches them never to fall away from him by telling how the former people was rejected for its wickedness. "Rejoice in God our helper; shout aloud to the God of Jacob." A shout is a victory hymn. He urges the nations, then, to sing victory songs to God, who helped them and delivered them from the tyranny of the demons. "Take up a psalm, and bring the drum." By "psalm" here he means the divine teaching. A drum is an instrument made of skins. So he says: Now that you have become obedient to the divine oracles, present your bodies as a living sacrifice, acceptable to God. "A pleasant psaltery with the lyre." Again, by the psaltery he means the body, because of the concord and harmony the soul has with it. So God's people are to become complete, dedicating their souls to God and the body too, not to the world but to the Lord. "Blow the trumpet at the new moon." Just as once

Israel took material trumpets and blew them at the new moon, because God had given this command and as a testimony that they had been freed from slavery in Egypt, so too the new people, using the trumpet of the gospel, whose sound has gone out into all the earth, is commanded to blow the trumpet at the new moons, that is, at the renewal of its mind. In doing so it confesses and testifies that he freed it from the spiritual Egypt, that is, from the power of darkness. "He heard a language he did not know." The people, he says, on coming out of Egypt, heard a language it had not known before. And what was this but the voice of God that came to the people on the mountain? "He removed his back from burdens." That is, "from the burdens." He means that he freed them from the loads they carried while building cities for Pharaoh. "His hands served in the basket." He says this because they carried the clay and the straw to the work in baskets. "In affliction you called on me, and I delivered you." This is like: "For I have heard their groaning, and I have heard their voice, and I have come down to deliver them." "I heard you in the secret place of the storm." That is: I delivered you from great and overwhelming affliction. "I tested you at the water of contradiction." When the people were thirsty and said to Moses, "Give us water to drink," he said, "Why do you quarrel with me, and why do you test the Lord?" "Hear, my people." He gives the people an exhortation, telling them to make themselves ready to obey him. For if it does this, it will not serve another god, and the Lord himself will not become a new god to it. For he is the one who long ago redeemed them from Egypt. "Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it." He promises those who obey him both bodily and spiritual food. "But my people did not hear my voice." Since I promised these things but they stopped their ears, I rejected them for this reason, giving them the punishment their practices deserved. "The enemies of the Lord lied to him, and their time will be forever." As if he said more plainly: Because the people lied to the Lord, a time of punishment will come upon it, and this is the time of the age to come. "And he fed them with the fat of wheat." They lied to him, he says, but he, being good, filled them with spiritual food. This food is the Lord himself, the living bread who came down from heaven and gives life to the world. "And with honey from the rock he satisfied them." The rock is the Lord himself, and the honey is his divine oracles. So he says that he filled them with his holy oracles. PSALM of Asaph. [?]

Here he sets out more clearly the reasons why God rejected them. "God stood in the assembly of gods." He called the rulers of the Jews gods, since they had been called sons of God. So God stood in their midst when he made his saving coming, in order to judge them by exposing what they had done. "How long will you judge unjustly?"
