He brings into the open the injustice they committed against the people. "Let all the foundations of the earth be shaken." By the foundations of the earth he means the rulers of this age. These paid the penalty even before the people of the Jews: they were cast out of their tyranny over us through the saying spoken to us, "Now the ruler of this world will be cast out." For they were shaken from the position they once held. So, since they were the first to be brought to nothing through his cross, and Israel was then cast off after the gospel had been proclaimed to all the nations, he added: "I said, You are gods. But you die like men, and fall like one of the rulers." And which rulers, if not those he indicated a little earlier by the shaken foundations of the earth? A SONG OF A PSALM of Asaph. 82.

Here he raises a prayer to God, asking him to punish the nations of the Assyrians for their arrogance, since they joined together in the war against Jerusalem. These were the ones indicated next in the psalm…

"O God, who will be likened to you? Do not keep silent, and do not be still, O God." No one, he says, will be like you, who bear no grudge and are patient toward wrongs. But I pray that you will not keep silent at the injustices our enemies have committed against us…

"For behold, your enemies have made an uproar." The injustice they have done to us, he says, has become loud enough for all to hear. "They became a help to the sons of Lot." Those named before, he says, came to the aid of the sons of Lot and fought alongside them in the war against us. The sons of Lot are the Moabites and the Ammonites. From this we learn that the demons call on one another to destroy the soul, to bring utter ruin upon us and to consign the renowned Israel to oblivion. Then he lists the neighboring peoples, who summoned the others as well…

"Do to them as to Midian and to Sisera." Once Midian and Sisera, and Jabin too, rose up against Israel and were utterly destroyed, some at the torrent of Kishon and others at Endor. In the same way, may those who attacked us together with Assur meet a like punishment. Sisera was the commander of the army, and Jabin the king of Canaan. In Judges they are routed at the torrent of Kishon by the hand of Barak and of Deborah, a woman of Israel.

"They were utterly destroyed at Endor." That is, in a shameful place, for Endor means unseemliness. "They became like dung for the earth." For they were left unburied and decomposed, and mingled with the earth like dung. "Make their rulers like Oreb." See to it that the Edomites, Ishmaelites, Moabites, Hagarenes and the allies mentioned suffer the same as Oreb and the others. Wicked as these men were, they perished wickedly. "My God, make them like a wheel." That is: Let them not stay in the same position, but let them be rolled backward. "Like stubble before the wind." That is, they will be easily blown away, just like the stubble of the ear of grain. "Like fire that will burn up a forest." Let them reap the fire they themselves kindled, he says, and let that very fire devour them, just as material fire devours a forest. This is like: "Behold, all of you kindle a fire; walk in the light of your fire and in the flame you have kindled." "Like a flame to burn up mountains." The saying is a comparison. Just as a fire that falls on mountains burns them, he says, so they will be burned up by the punishment you will bring upon them. He also compared this punishment to a storm because of its violence and intensity. "Fill their faces with dishonor." For when they fail to get what they want and are filled with shame, they will recognize your power. "And they will seek your name, O Lord." He means that the punishments will be of benefit to them. "They will seek" instead of…

In this psalm too he speaks again about the churches, as is clear from its being inscribed "concerning the winepresses." "How beloved are your dwellings, O Lord of hosts!" By dwellings he means the holy churches of God established in each place, to which every God-loving soul hastens. "My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God." As if he were saying: In both body and soul I have presented myself to serve the living and true God. "The living God" is said to set him apart from the idols, since they are dead and made of soulless matter. "For the sparrow has found itself a house, and the turtledove a nest for herself where she will lay her young: your altars, O Lord." By the sparrow he alludes to the human soul hunted by the spiritual hunter, as it is said: "Our soul was rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters." By the turtledove he means the soul that lives in purity and self-control. He says, then, that every soul will find this refuge, the refuge at the altars…

"Blessed are those who dwell in your house," that is, the heavenly one. "Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has set ascents in his heart." Having taken you as his helper, he says, he builds up good thoughts in himself day by day. Here he calls these thoughts ascents, because through them there is, as it were, an ascent from earthly things to heavenly ones. "Into the valley of weeping." By the valley of weeping he means mortal life. So he says: In this mortal life you will fill them with good thoughts, building them up day by day. They have gained perception through your help. "For the lawgiver will give blessings; they will go from strength to strength." The lawgiver, he says, will give them rewards for their good thoughts, that is, the one who gave them the law of the New Covenant. And what could these blessings be but going from strength to strength? He means going from the godly way of life here to the Jerusalem above, where, once they have departed, they will see God as he is. "Look upon the face of your Christ." By Christ here he means the people called to be a royal priesthood. "For one day in your courts is better than thousands." By one day in the courts of God, that is, in the churches, he alludes to the Savior's day of resurrection. By thousands, or rather a thousand, as it is found in the Hebrew Scripture, he means the worship under the law. This held sway for a thousand years, from the time of Solomon, when the divine temple was founded, until the coming of the Savior. So he shows how much greater the worship of the gospel is than the worship of the law. "I have chosen to be cast aside in the house of my God." As if he were saying: I would rather be someone small and insignificant in the Church than someone great among the sinful people. These words suited those in Babylon and are fitting for us too. For the grace of the Spirit taught them not to overlook the desolation of the divine house, and we are taught always to long for and love the sanctuaries dedicated to God. "The Lord will not withhold good things from those who walk in innocence." For those who have this disposition enjoy all these good things. Mercy springs up from the divine sanctuaries, and from them flows a great and abundant supply of truth. There we receive the teaching of sound doctrine and draw divine grace from the springs of the all-holy Spirit. There, too, we become admired and greatly renowned. In short, there we receive the enjoyment of every good thing, as we are freed from vice and wickedness and choose to live in simplicity and truth. For the end, for the sons of Korah. PSALM 84. Summary. In this psalm he shows the calling of the nations

and the forgiveness they received by turning to God. After the calling of the nations he also brings in the people of the Jews, confessing the sins they committed and asking that they too may obtain mercy through Christ. "You have been pleased, O Lord, with your land." For truly God the Father was pleased to sum up all things in Christ. "You turned back the captivity of Jacob." For he preached first to the Jews themselves and redeemed many of them from the spiritual captivity that had seized them. The Savior made this plain after reading the prophecy of Isaiah that said: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind." He said: "Today this prophecy has been fulfilled [?] in your hearing." For he is the one who put an end to our serving the error of many gods and the demons, and who loosed the chains of our sins. Both things are prophesied here: the return of the sons of Israel from Babylon and the salvation of the world. So the whole psalm is interpreted in two ways. As for the spiritual sense: The Lord is pleased with the good and earnest heart, which is his land because it receives the seed he sows and bears fruit a hundredfold. "You forgave the iniquities of your people." He means the people that became his through faith, the people drawn from the nations, as the prophet Zechariah said: "In that day many nations will flee to the Lord, and they will be to him for…"

"Turn us, O God of our salvation." From here on he sends up a supplication in the person of the Jewish people, who ask that they too may obtain grace. "Show us, O Lord, your mercy." When Cyrus reigned over the Persians and, as Isaiah had prophesied, gave them permission to return, they were eager to reach their homeland. That is why they beseech God to grant them speedy salvation in his love for humankind. Show us your goodness quickly, O Master, he says, so that we may obtain your salvation and be delivered from this place. After offering the supplication on their behalf in this way, the prophet receives God's answer and says: "I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me." Having ceased his supplication, the prophet waits in silence for the Spirit's answer. "Surely his salvation is near those who fear him." While the prophet awaited the answer, the one "I shall hear from God about my race," he came to know this: God is ready to come near to all, if only they embrace the fear of him, and those who embrace it will come to dwell in glory. "That glory may dwell in our land."

By these words he signifies the incarnate dispensation of the Only-begotten. For from God the Father he has become righteousness and peace and mercy and truth for us. Having had mercy on us, he taught us the truth. He also declared us righteous, making peace among all things in himself, both those in heaven and those on… "Mercy and truth have met." He clearly proclaims the truth that dawned upon the world through the Theotokos and Ever-Virgin. For he himself is the truth, even though he was born of a woman. "For righteousness and truth have kissed," clearly referring to the … that dawned upon the world from the Ever-Virgin Theotokos…

"And righteousness looked down from heaven." This is like what was said to the Virgin: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you," and the rest. "For the Lord will give goodness." When the Lord shines upon those on earth with surpassing goodness, he says, then we too, being spiritual earth, will yield the spiritual fruits of righteousness. "Righteousness will go before him." Having said that the spiritual earth will yield its fruit, he teaches how it will do so. And how will it, but when the righteousness of the one who does good goes ahead on the road that leads upward and directs the steps [?] of the one who walks it? A prayer of David. PSALM 85.

Blessed David had foreseen [?] through the Spirit what concerned the coming of the Only-begotten and the forgiveness of sins that would come to everyone who flees to him. So he fittingly sends up a prayer, asking that he too may be found among those saved by grace. "Incline your ear, O Lord, and hear me." For humility is truly a great help toward having one's prayer heard. "For I am poor and needy." The prayer opens with humility. For though both David and Hezekiah possessed the wealth of righteousness, they did not look to this. Instead they looked to the poverty of their nature and implored God to have pity on it, since it was yoked to poverty. He wrote "Incline your ear, O Lord" as a metaphor drawn from a sick man who is too weak to speak loudly and so makes the physician bend his ear to his mouth. "Preserve my soul, for I am holy." He asks to be heard on the strength of the good deeds he has accomplished. "Save your servant, O my God, who hopes in you." Since he had declared himself holy, he brings his words back down to humility, enrolling himself as God's servant and professing that his hope of salvation rests on him alone.

"Have mercy on me, O Lord, for to you I will cry." The passage teaches us that whoever wishes to receive some good from God must be unceasing in prayer. "For you, O Lord, are kind and gentle." He teaches those who come to God not to grow weary, even if God delays the gift for a little while. For he will surely hear them, since he is kind and exceedingly rich in mercy. "There is none like you among the gods, O Lord." By gods he means the holy prophets, to whom the word of God came. He means that none of the prophets was able to deliver human beings from sin, but only the Lord himself, as it is said elsewhere: "Not an elder, not an angel, but the Lord himself saved us." "Let my heart rejoice to fear your name." Whoever has reverence toward God embraces the way of life the law prescribes, and such a life is the mother of gladness. Fittingly, then, the prophet expected that his own heart would rejoice through fear. So he says elsewhere too: "Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice"; and again: "I remembered God and was glad." "I will give thanks to you, O Lord my God, with my whole heart." He at once turns his prayer into thanksgiving for having been rescued from Hades, and declares the cause of his sin. He speaks of the plotting of many mighty ones, alluding to the invisible powers that did not set God before their eyes. But you, Lord, he says, granted what they did not expect, rescuing my soul from the lowest Hades in your love for humankind. Christ says these things when the kings of the earth stood up and the rulers gathered together against him. "For your mercy toward me is great." As though their prayer had already been fulfilled, he says that he will praise God's great mercy forever, because God freed their souls too from the hand of Hades. "O God, transgressors have risen up against me." By this he shows how he fell into that sin. And how did he fall, if not because a gathering of evil spirits rose up against him and tripped him on the course of virtue? "And you, O Lord my God, are compassionate and merciful." Even if the evil spirits rose up against me, he says, and I was brought down into sin, and through it into the lowest Hades just mentioned, yet you yourself, O Lord, spread your own compassion over me too and rescued my soul. Therefore I ask once more to receive mercy. And this mercy will come to me when you look upon me. "Work a sign with me for good." Just as long ago in Egypt God gave the sons of Israel a sign so that they would not be harmed by the…
…of the destroyer, so he also asks that a sign be given to him, so that he may be kept safe through it, and may put to shame those…

The divine sons of Korah again sing this psalm to the Church. Through it they proclaim the calling of the Gentiles, and the light that shone on the Church from the Only-begotten through his dispensation in the flesh. "His foundations are on the holy mountains." "His" means the foundations of the people called through faith. He is saying that a people from the Gentiles was built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets. "The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob." By the gates of Zion he means the introductory and elementary teaching of the Church, and by the dwellings of Jacob the worship according to the law. So he is saying that God has judged the gospel way of life more desirable than the worship according to the law. "Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God." The city is the Church. What glorious things were spoken of it, if not that the Only-begotten would dwell in it, as it is said: "Here I will dwell, for I have chosen it"? "I will remember Rahab and Babylon." I will remember for good those who turn to me, he says, even those who had strayed outrageously into the love of pleasure, and those who were utterly given to idolatry. This is what he signified to us by Rahab and Babylon. "And behold, foreigners, and Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians." The word teaches us clearly that the Church is made up of all the nations. "'Mother Zion,' a man will say, and a man was born in her." He says "mother." Clearly we who have believed will inscribe Zion, that is, the Church, as our mother, in which is the man [?], namely the very one who founded her. This is the one who became man for our sake, and who promised to found the Church upon the rock. "The Lord will recount in the register of peoples and of rulers." The Lord will recount the register, he says, of the peoples and the rulers who have come to be in the Church itself. And what else could this be, he says, but the enrollment made in the heavens, which he himself will recount to them, saying: "Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven"? "As of all who rejoice is the dwelling in you." When, he says, all who are in the Church come to dwell in you, then they will also be… of gladness

…having preached to the spirits in Hades, he might grant them the resurrection. He also weeps for Jerusalem, since it was going to fall away from its hope in him. This Jerusalem, that is, the people, was once like a kind of chorus, in that it was called his portion and inheritance. That is why the psalm also has the title "For Maeleth," that is, "of dancing," or "of a chorus." But the mystery of Christ is deep, and a very subtle spiritual understanding is needed to grasp it, and for this reason the title also says "Of understanding." The psalm is said to be by Heman, and to have been composed in Egypt before Moses. This Heman was a descendant of Israel, since he came from Zerah, who was a son of Judah, the son of Israel. "O Lord, God of my salvation, by day I have cried out." Since he is good, and knows [?] of the people and the perdition of the disciple, he sends up prayers to the Father on their behalf, so that they too, having no part in the wickedness, might obtain the salvation that comes through him. "For my soul is filled with evils." Since he bore our sins and suffers pain for us [?], he fittingly says that he is filled with evils. "And my life has drawn near to Hades." He says this since by the grace of God he tasted death for everyone

"I became like a man without help, free among the dead." Jesus alone died for the iniquities of the people, being led to death, as Isaiah's words say. And though dead, he alone was free, for he had no sin to make him subject to death. That is why he said: "I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again." "Like the wounded who sleep in the grave." I have become like men who are wounded and lie in tombs, he says, who have not obtained your help and so have not obtained resurrection. But I was wounded, he says, for the sins of the people, and I came to be in the tomb, yet I did not remain there, because you remembered me even after the wounding and the laying in the tomb. For I rose, having trampled the

"Your wrath has pressed hard upon me." By the wrath of God he means the curse of death brought upon the human race. Since he became a curse for us, he says for this reason that the wrath of God pressed upon him. "And all your billows you have brought upon me." By "billows" he means the punishment brought down with severity upon the human race for the transgression. Again it signifies death. "You have removed my acquaintances far from me." He says this because all of them abandoned him at the time of the passion. "They have made me an abomination [?]

…loathe the name. "I was handed over, and I could not go out." He says this because he was shut up in the house of the ruler of the synagogue. "My eyes have grown weak from poverty." I wept for the people, he says, seeing that they were about to fall away from the riches that are according to God, and had been brought down to the utmost poverty. "I have cried to you, O Lord, all day long." Grant, then, a single way of release from these terrible things: your providence, O Master. For I stretch out my hands to you continually and entreat you. This posture shows the bitter pain of the soul. A person compelled by need entreats more earnestly the one who can give

"Will you work wonders for the dead? Will physicians raise them up?" He teaches us the reasons for his descent into death, all but saying this: It is not possible to work wonders for the dead, nor for physicians to raise them up so that they may confess you, nor could those in perdition know your truth. For this reason, O Father, I too have been counted among those in Hades, so that those in the land of forgetfulness might rise up and experience your wonders, and those who were long in darkness might recount your truth. "Will anyone recount your mercy in the grave?" Is it not possible, he says, for the dead, who have been dissolved into dust, who dwell in the gloom of death and have been given over to oblivion, to share in your love for humankind and be made spectators of your wonders? "Will your wonders be known in the darkness?" Just as there is no truth among those who have perished, so there are no wonders among those who are in darkness. The land of forgetfulness is a rational soul deprived of the fruits of the Holy Spirit. "Why, O Lord, do you reject my soul, and turn your face away from me?" He prayed for the people, but they showed themselves unworthy of salvation through the excess of their wickedness, and so, as it were, made his prayer for them ineffective. "I am poor, and in labors from my youth." He was poor because he took the form of a servant, and in labors from his youth because from his very swaddling clothes he was plotted against by Herod and those like him. "Having been exalted, I was humbled and brought to despair." By "exaltation" he means the ascent onto the cross, as he himself said: "When you lift up the Son of Man." And he says "I was humbled" because of his descent down to Hades [?]. "Your wrath has passed over me." You have stirred up all your wrath against me, he says, and have thrown me into turmoil with the most fearful punishments, and with these, as with waters, you have plunged me under. "You have removed far from me friend and neighbor, and

my acquaintances, because of my misery." By "misery" he signifies the time of the passion. So he is saying that at the passion both his friends and his acquaintances abandoned him. He became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross, and on the cross he was abandoned by the disciples; for this reason he says that his Father removed his friends and acquaintances far from him. A PSALM of understanding, of Ethan the Israelite.

In this psalm he prophesies the birth of Christ from the seed of David, and his kingdom, and also the saving passion that he endured for us. The title says "of understanding" because a spiritual mind is especially needed to grasp the depth of its mysteries. As for Heman, the fact that he too was a prophet has been clearly set out in what came before. "Your mercies, O Lord, I will sing forever." And what are the mercies of the Lord that he has done for us, which we also ought to sing, if not that he overthrew the principalities and powers, and the very might of the devil, and set us free from sin and death? "To generation after generation I will proclaim your truth with my mouth." The truth of the Father is the Son, whom the saints bear [?] on their lips from generation to generation. For the word is spoken as though from the apostolic

"For you said: Mercy will be built up forever." You, O Master, he says, deigned to promise that great and wonderful mercy would be built up forever, without ceasing, that is, it would be established, or rather raised up. For what is built is in a sense raised up and made to stand. This is the salvation and grace that come through Christ. The mercy of God builds up human beings, while the truth prepares the holy powers. "Your truth will be prepared." Just as the salvation that comes through Christ is mercy and grace, so again it is also called truth, since it has been raised up even to the heavens, he says, through the blood, whether on earth or in

"I have made a covenant with my chosen ones." He means Abraham and Jacob, for to them God gave the promises concerning Christ, as it is said: "And in your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed." "I have sworn to David my servant." And where did he swear it, if not when he said to him: "And it shall be, when your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, that another shall arise from your seed, who shall come from your womb. And I will prepare his kingdom forever. He will build a house for my name. And I will establish his kingdom forever. I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me." "The heavens will confess your wonders." He says this on account of the birth of Christ, and because to shepherds

the angels brought the good news, saying: "For today Christ the Lord is born to us in the city of David." And a multitude of another, heavenly host appeared, saying: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth [?]" "For who in the clouds will be equal to the Lord?" Even though the Only-begotten became man, he says, and lowered himself into a voluntary self-emptying, and took the form of a servant, even so he is beyond comparison with all, even with the heavenly powers. They hold the rank of servants, but he is Master and Lord of all. Nor indeed is anyone among the sons of God like him. They themselves bear witness to this when they say: "From his fullness we have all received." So he gives as God, and they are enriched by what comes from him. "God, who is glorified in the council of the saints, great and fearful." The foolish are scandalized when they see him in the form of a servant, yet hear him say, "I am the truth," and "Before Abraham came to be, I am." The saints, on the contrary, glorify him and call him great and fearful. This is clear from the fact that Peter, as if from the mouth of all, cried out: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God"; and again, all of them said, "Truly you are the Son of God," when he rebuked the sea and the winds. "Mighty are you, O Lord, and your truth is all around you; you rule the might of the sea." The word shows that the one who is in the form of a servant is the very one who in the beginning brought forth the watery substance. He is the one who set the sand as a boundary for the sea and said to it: "This far you shall come, and you shall not pass beyond." He showed that this was true by rebuking both the sea and the winds when he was sailing with the disciples. "And you calm the surging of its waves." "You have humbled the proud like one who is wounded." For he is the one who bound the strong one and the proud one, and who gave his own the power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon all the power of the enemy. "Yours are the heavens, and yours is the earth." Just as he is Master of the sea, so he is also maker of the heavens and of the whole earth. "The world and its fullness you have founded. The north and the sea you have created, Tabor and Hermon." By these he signifies the four parts of the world: by the north the northern regions, by the sea those of the west (for Scripture calls the west "sea"), by Mount Hermon the south, and by Mount Tabor the east. "Yours is the arm, with power." May your arm, O Master, he says, be displayed to all with power. For although he became man and appeared as one of us, yet there became manifest the surpassing

greatness of his majesty. And this is what is meant by: "Let your hand be strengthened; let your right hand be exalted [?]." "Blessed is the people that knows the shout of triumph." Having proclaimed the incarnation of the Only-begotten, he fittingly calls blessed those who have thoroughly learned his mystery. This means singing victory songs to him. For the shout of triumph is the song raised over fallen enemies. He went into battle for us and has conquered the opposing powers. "O Lord, they will walk in the light of your face, and in your name they will exult." He calls his holy apostles blessed, since they performed all the wonders they performed by his name and his power. "And in your good pleasure our horn will be exalted." By "horn" he means glory. So he says, as if to the Father: Since you were pleased to send the Only-begotten, for this reason our glory has been raised up. For we have been glorified, having been raised together with Christ and reigning together with him. "Then you spoke in a vision to your sons." "Then" means "of old." He is saying: you spoke through prophetic visions to your sons, meaning those called to the dignity of adoption. And what did you speak, if not this: "I have laid help upon one who is mighty"? It is as if he said: I have given help to the weak and to those overreached by Satan, so that they may take refuge in one who is mighty. And the mighty one whom the Father has given us for help is surely Christ, for he is the Lord of powers. "I have exalted one chosen from my people; I have found David my servant." Understand this of Christ, from the seed of David, who is called chosen; that is why God also highly exalted him. He calls him David again because he was of the seed of David, and also "servant," because he appeared in the form of a servant. "With my holy oil I have anointed him." When the Word, who was God, was born according to the flesh from a woman and came forth as man while remaining God as he was, then, having received the anointing for your sake, he was named Christ. For the Word, being God and existing as king before the ages, made what is ours his own, so that we too might be enriched with what is his. "For my hand will support him." The Saviour said: "The works that the Father has given me to do, these very works bear witness about me, that he has sent me"; and again: "I speak nothing on my own; but the Father who abides in me does the works himself." And this is what the Father now says about him: "For my hand will support him, and my arm will strengthen him. The enemy will gain no advantage over him." Although they said, "Come, let us kill him, and let us have his inheritance," yet the scheme brought no profit to Satan and the Jews, and their attempt turned out fruitless. For the Saviour came back to life on the third day, having trampled death and despoiled Hades. He ascended to the Father and God in heaven, and he is at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty

on high, ruling over all together with the one who begot him. So what was said is true: "The enemy will gain no advantage over him." "And I will cut down his enemies before his face." For they were handed over to the Roman army and perished utterly. "And my truth and my mercy will be with him." By "truth" he means the worship in spirit and truth that Christ introduced to us, as he said to the woman in Samaria: "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth." And God has shown mercy to us through no one else than through his only-begotten Son. For through him alone we learned worship in spirit and truth, and received mercy, when death was abolished and corruption was removed from our midst. "And in my name his horn will be exalted." For the Son himself is also glorified with the names that most befit the Father. For example: the Father is true God, and the Son is this too, for he is the truth. And the Father both is and is called life by nature, and the Son again is this too, for he says: "I am the resurrection and the life." He said this to his own Father: "All that is mine is yours, and

"And I will set his hand on the sea." By "sea," as we said before, he means the western region, and by "rivers" he means the land between the rivers, that is, the east. So he is saying that his work will extend over the whole world. "And his right hand on the rivers." Christ's hand is set on the sea, and his right hand on the rivers. And if he wills, the sea becomes a river; and again, the river, if it keeps the river that flows from its belly, becomes a sea of living water. "He will call upon me: You are my Father, my God." Here again, in keeping with the dispensation, the incarnate one calls the Father his God, saying: "I am going to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God." For the prophet, speaking of him and prophesying a child to be born, called him mighty God, Father of the age to come. "I will keep my mercy for him forever, and my covenant." "For him" means for the people who have believed through him. By "mercy" he means the forgiveness that comes through faith. By "covenant" he means the new covenant, which he also calls faithful, that is, secure, firm and enduring. For the first covenant has come to an end because of its weakness and uselessness, since the law made nothing perfect. "And I will establish his seed forever and ever." For the name of Christians will not cease, nor the power of the worship of the gospel; rather, it will be perpetual and unending.

"Once I have sworn by my holiness that I will not lie to David." This is like what is said elsewhere: "The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not set it aside." "His seed remains forever." By the seed of David he means Christ, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, and who also remains forever. For it is not possible that one who is God, and truly the Son of God, should not be altogether and above all eternal [?].

"And his throne is like the sun before me." Understand the throne of Christ to be the Church, for he rests upon it. So, he says, the Church of Christ will shine like lightning and give light to everything under heaven, and will endure perpetually, like the sun and the moon. For this text reads in full: "And his throne is like the sun before me, and like the moon established forever, and the witness in heaven is faithful." "But you have rejected and scorned, you have put off your Christ." The blessed prophets are speaking of what happened at the precious cross. So they say, as if to the Father and God: You promised that the seed of David remains forever, and his throne like the sun and the moon; but you have rejected and scorned, you have put off your Christ. "You have rejected and scorned" stands for "you have permitted him to be rejected and scorned." For the Father did not reject and scorn his own Son; rather, the Jews did this, though by the permission of God the Father. And this is what is said: "He who did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all." "You have overturned the covenant of your servant." You have postponed fulfilling the promises concerning him, he says, for in the meantime he suffered. He states how God postponed them by saying: "You have overturned the covenant of your servant." For you promised, he says, that he remains forever, and this was your covenant concerning him. But the Jews crucified him, and he was counted among the dead. He suffered, he says, and was crucified; therefore you have overturned the covenant of your servant. "You have profaned his sanctuary to the ground." You have dashed his glory to the ground, he says, for when he came to suffer, the lawless Jews thought him a mere man. But he did not remain dead, he who was free among the dead, as the prophet's words say. Nor did the passion bring any dishonor upon him; rather, he was glorified by destroying the one who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and by setting the human race free. Still, the prophets are speaking of what happened. "You have torn down all his hedges." By his hedges and strongholds he means the holy apostles, who all abandoned him and fled in fear. That is why he says: "You have made his strongholds a terror." "They plundered him [?] . . . . . You have gladdened all the

…his enemies. For they rejoiced and shook their heads at him when they saw him hanging on the tree. "You have turned back the help of his sword." Those who crucified the only-begotten Son of God the Father deserved to pay the ultimate penalty, yet they were not punished at once. In his great love for humankind he granted a time for repentance through baptism to them as well. For this reason he is said to have turned back the help of his sword. "You turned back" stands for "you held back." "You have brought him down from his cleansing." "You brought down" here stands for "you cast down." So you cast him down, he says; that is, you arranged things with regard to people believing that he is pure. For he was thought to be wicked, was condemned as a sinner, and was counted among the lawless. "You have dashed his throne to the ground." He suffered in the flesh and became free among the dead. Those who crucified him thought that, having suffered, he had been brought low and had ceased altogether to exist or even to be named. So the psalm explains what the crucifiers supposed, saying: "You have dashed his throne to the ground." "How long, Lord, will you turn away forever? Will your wrath burn like fire?" That is: how long will the reckless deeds of the Jews prevail, who pressed for the crucifixion of the Only-begotten, our Savior? Symmachus has: "Until when, Lord, will you hide yourself forever? Will your anger blaze like fire?" Until when, he says, Master, will you refuse to look on our pains? Will you not appear and put an end to our misfortunes, instead of kindling your wrath like fire at the memory of our sins? "Remember what my substance is." You made man for incorruption, he says, and fashioned him in your own image; but through deceit he has come under corruption, he says. So grant incorruption, that they may be saved, just as the creature was fashioned for it. "Who is the man who will live and not see death?" No one, he says, will prove stronger than death, or rescue his own soul from the hand of Hades, unless you, O Master, he says, [grant?] the resurrection…

"Where are your mercies of old, Lord?" God's ancient mercies, he says, are the refashioning into incorruption that was determined before the foundation of the world. "Remember, Lord, the reproach of your servants." Your enemies, Lord, reproached me, claiming that the promises given to the nations concerning me were false. Those promises were that the nations would be saved and set free from death and sin. They reproached me because they looked at my death, and they declared the promises empty. For this reason I ask you to remember. "For they reproached the exchange of your Christ," he says. His exchange would be his death and his blood, the ransom given…

…for the salvation of the world. This they reproached, supposing that he had been overcome by death. But he who was free among the dead did not remain there; rather, he rose on the third day. That is why the psalm also sets its seal with: "Blessed be the Lord forever. So be it, so be it." It speaks as of one who has already risen, ascended into heaven, and is blessed, that is, praised forever with his own Father. A Prayer of Moses, the Man of God. Psalm 89. Summary. This prayer, it is said, Moses wrote down in secret and handed on. His purpose was that those of later times might know how they ought to make confession when they fell into the misfortunes that came upon them at the end of the times, after their disobedience and bloodguilt against the Lord. And so that time would not consign it to oblivion, it was placed among the Psalms. It fittingly comes after the 88th, which also points to the Lord's passion. "Lord, you have been our refuge from generation to generation." Since he is about to call on God for mercy, he fittingly opens with the benefits God has already conferred many times. One can see how God did good from generation to generation by looking at what happened under Pharaoh, under Joshua, and under Babylon. "Before the mountains came into being and the earth was formed." Looking at the Lord's flesh, they thought him a mere man and said, "You are not yet thirty years old, and you have seen Abraham?" This ignorance of his divinity, above all, was the cause of their fall. So now, in their confession, they say plainly that he is the one who was with the Father before all creation. "Do not turn man back to humiliation." Here the confession begins. He asks that, since God called all the nations to the knowledge of the truth, he too may be brought back. "You said, O Master," he says, "'Return, you returning sons, and I will heal your fractures.' Since, then, we have returned, do not turn us back to humiliation." "For a thousand years in your eyes, Lord." He means the time of worship under the Law, when it flourished most, after the divine temple was completed. From Solomon, who built the house, to the siege that took place after the precious cross, this comes to a thousand years. But these thousand years, he says, may be reckoned as one day before you, or rather as a small part of a day. And he fittingly likens the time before the Savior's coming to night. Then all people were in an untimely hour and in confusion, because the Sun of righteousness had not yet risen for them.

"Their contempt shall be years; in the morning…" It is as if he said more plainly: their years, the years of those who denied you, will be spent in great contempt. For they have become something trampled underfoot by men and demons, since they denied the one who redeems and saves them. "In the morning may it flower and pass away." By "morning" they mean the time when Christ appeared to them on Mount Sinai. The "grass" means the worship of the Law, since it was soon to wither. "In the evening may it fall, harden and wither." By "evening" he means the time at the end of the age, when the Only-begotten also appeared. At that time the flowering of worship under the Law passed away, hardened by the deceit of disobedience. "For we have failed in your wrath." They declare plainly the misfortunes brought upon them for their own sins. These words suit both the Jews and all people. For human nature, paying the penalty for transgression, has been subjected to misfortunes and is swamped by every kind of great wave. And the Jews fell from freedom because of the wickedness of their disposition. "You have set our iniquities before you." You did not pass over our iniquities, he says, since we called them down on our own heads by saying, "His blood be on us and on our children." "Our age in the light of your face." It is as if he said: our life and the deeds in it appear wicked before your face. For you were ignorant of nothing that was done among us from beginning to end. "For all our days have failed, and in your wrath we have failed." Sin, he says, stirred up your wrath against us. Wrath brought punishment, and punishment brought pains. For we have spent our short life in pains. "Our years were spinning like a spider." Human nature, he says, has nothing secure or stable; it is easily torn apart like a spider's web. "The days of our years: in them, seventy years." This is like what the patriarch Jacob said: "My days are few and evil; they have not reached the days of my fathers." There are indeed some who live longer than the time stated, but that happens to few. Here he teaches what is common and holds true in most cases. Just as he made no mention of those who meet an untimely end, so he passed over the very old with their long lives. Yet even this short time, he says, is full of pain and toil. "For gentleness came upon us, and we shall be disciplined." Our life is something dead and worthless, and we do not know what will come to us from your power after this. For this reason, he says, discipline us gently. For "came" stands for "may it come…"

…he says. They ask to share in the discipline that comes through Christ, who is the right hand of the Father. So he says: "So make known to me your right hand." "Make known" applies to both clauses, so that it reads: "Make known to us your right hand," that is, Christ; "and make known to us those who have wisdom in their heart." These would be the holy apostles and evangelists, through whom we also learned the ways of returning. "We were filled in the morning with your mercy." They say such things as though they had already seen their prayer fulfilled. For the Sun of righteousness will rise for them too at the end of this age. "And look upon your servants and upon your works." "Look" again stands for "you looked," that is, you visited us as your servants and as the works of your hands. Having seen the brightness and light of our God through your visitation, and having turned back, may we be guided in the things by which we carry out the work of returning. "And let the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us." The light of the knowledge of God has made us too bright and conspicuous [?]; and after the return the Jews were again held in admiration. "And direct the works of our hands." The works are those of the Law; the work is what is accomplished in the New Testament. For in the Old there were various sacrifices, but in the New the Son alone is sacrificed. "And direct the work of our hands." The works of the hands are our daily actions; the work of the hands is the knowledge that results from them. A Praise of a Song, of David; it has no title among the Hebrews. Psalm 90 [?].

Having shown the turning away of the Jewish people in the eighty-ninth psalm, he follows it naturally in this psalm by bringing in the voice of those who are made perfect through Christ. Through him they conquer their spiritual enemies: the principalities and powers, the world-rulers of this darkness, the spiritual forces of wickedness, and the accursed Satan himself. These enemies are signified in many ways in the passage before us: the terror by night and the arrow that flies by day, the thing that moves about in darkness, the mishap and the noonday demon, the thousands and ten thousands, the asp, the basilisk, the lion and the dragon. Over all these he proclaims victory for the man of God. "He who dwells in the help of the Most High." The prophetic Spirit calls blessed the man who has made Christ his help and support, for Christ is indeed the Most High. How could he not be blessed who has been counted worthy to have the God of heaven as his protector? "He will lodge in the shelter of the God of heaven." Whoever remains in this help is sheltered and guarded. "He will say to the Lord, 'You are my helper.'" And who is it that says this to the Lord, if not the man who trusts in him and leans on his salvation?

"For he will rescue you from the snare." He has already taught that the opposing powers are signified by these things. "He will overshadow you with his shoulders." The man of God has said that God himself will rescue him from the hunters' snare and from troubling words. The prophetic Spirit answers, encouraging him and spurring him on to spiritual courage: "He will overshadow you with his shoulders." It is as if he said more plainly: he will cover you under the shadow of his wings, and he will also shelter you with a shield. When this has happened, none of the opposing powers will harm you. "From the arrow that flies by day." Here he calls some unclean power an arrow. "From mishap and the noonday demon." [?] a demonic encounter [?] at noon. For he says that the noonday demon is the demon of listlessness. "A thousand shall fall at your side." "Side" fittingly means the left part. He says that the thousands plot against this side, while the ten thousands plot against the right. For our right-hand qualities, our virtues, are strong and more wonderful, and so the multitude of evil powers tries to undermine them. "Only with your eyes you will observe." You will be harmed by none of those who plot against you, he says; instead it will be your lot to see your enemies fallen. "You have made the Most High your refuge." The prophetic Spirit answers the words of the man of God, showing how great is the gain of hope in God. "Evils shall not come near you." For evil by its nature comes from outside, while virtue has its source within. God made man upright; but man sought out evil reasonings and drew evil upon himself from outside. "And no scourge shall come near your dwelling." He urges them to take courage and expect to suffer nothing unpleasant, because they believe that an angel is sent down to help those who believe in God. "For he will give his angels charge over you." He said this in the 33rd psalm as well: "The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him and will rescue them." Let us also hear the patriarch Jacob saying: "The angel who rescues me from all my evils." And the great Abraham, encouraging his servant, said: "God will send his angel before you, and from there you shall take a wife for my son Isaac." From every side, then, we learn that the God of all guards those who trust in him through angels as well. "To guard you in all your ways." The one who stumbles in nothing is the one who is guarded in all his ways.
"Lest you strike your foot against a stone." The foot signifies the soul, and the stone the…

"You will tread upon the asp and the basilisk." Not only will you suffer nothing terrible, O man of God, he says; you will also see the very hosts of spirits brought under your feet, so that you will tread on their heads without fear. "Because he hoped in me, I will rescue him." He brings in the voice of God, promising salvation as the reward of faith. The God of all, then, said these things to teach what the fruit of hope is. For I will rescue him, he says, from the visible and invisible plotters already mentioned, since he has fortified himself with hope in me. Therefore I will guard him, hear him when he calls, and receive his petition. "I will shelter him, because he has known my name." Not only will I rescue my own from those who plot against them, he says, but I will also grant them unending life, and indeed of the salvation…
The Sabbath rest, that is, the Sabbath, would be the inheritance to come, because rest will follow the toils of this life, when we receive our rewards. So he praises that which is to come…

"It is good to give thanks to the Lord." He puts forward praise, he says, and promises to recount it unceasingly, day and night, for what the Only-begotten has done. And what has he done, if not prepare the resurrection for us? "To proclaim your mercy in the morning." That is, to proclaim your mercy at dawn and your faithfulness by night. "On a ten-stringed psaltery, with a song on the lyre." He calls the body a ten-stringed psaltery, since it has five senses and five activities of the soul, each activity taking place through one of the senses. "For you have gladdened me, Lord, by your work." For when I see your works of creation and your ineffable dispensations, I exult and rejoice, and in the soul's delight I move my tongue to sing hymns. "How great are your works, Lord!" As for me, he says, as I sing of your works, I am also amazed at the depth of your thoughts, which you carried out in the dispensation. But the foolish do not understand the depth of the mystery. "A foolish man will not know." He said these things in different ways, because the one who is sick in mind and lacking in understanding…

"When sinners sprang up like grass." Those who do not understand the mystery, he says, will be like grass, having no depth, and they will quickly fall and wither. "And my horn will be exalted like that of a unicorn." When the enemies perish and are scattered, he says, then indeed my horn, that is, the kingdom that has been prepared, will be plain for all to see. And we who know you, having seen your enemies destroyed, will exult in you and hold our heads high, since we have been set free from the error of many gods and worship you, the God who truly is. He brings in the unicorn here again so that the one horn may point to the one God. For just as that animal received one horn from nature, so those nurtured in true religion will worship one Godhead. "And my old age in rich oil." After the toils I endure, he says, I will be anointed as with oil for a royal priesthood, and this will be my reward for my long toils. "And my eye has looked upon my enemies." Along with my other blessings I will have this: I will see those who plot against me fall.

…he says, those who are likened to these cedars have God as their planter and the divine temple as their paradise. "They will flourish in the courts of our God." That is, in the dwelling places above, which he also calls the courts of the Lord. "They will yet be multiplied in rich old age, and will be well off." "Well off" stands for "faring well." For they will be given what eye has not seen and ear has not heard. "That the Lord our God is upright." When they have come into the dwelling places above and enjoy the good things prepared for them, then indeed they will also proclaim that the Lord is just and upright. He made the lawless and ungodly wither like grass, but planted the just and godly like cedars and palms in the tents above. There is no injustice with God, because he cannot admit any evil. For the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was settled: a praise of a song, of David. [Psalm 92?]

In the previous psalm, "for the Sabbath," the Lord's second coming is signified, when he will reign over the new age with his saints. So "before the Sabbath" would clearly be his first coming, when the earth was also settled. That is, it was when the Church was founded throughout the whole world, after the holy apostles and evangelists had proclaimed to the earth the word about Christ. [?]

"The Lord has become king; he has clothed himself with majesty." The human race had revolted from God's kingdom and come under the tyranny of Satan. For this reason the Only-begotten came to dwell among us, to bring it once again under his own scepter, and this is what happened [?]. By "majesty" he means the salvation of the race itself. For if he had not become flesh, taking our nature without sin, salvation would clearly not have come to us. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. "The Lord has clothed himself with power and girded himself." By these words he points us to the overthrow of the opposing powers, which he accomplished as though he had put on a soldier's dress. "For he has established the world, which shall not be shaken." Having first destroyed those opposing demons, he set the Church on the rock, against which not even the gates of Hades will prevail. "Your throne has been prepared from of old." He says this because the salvation of the human race, to come about through his own saving work, was predetermined from the foundation of the world. For by "throne" he means the resurrection of the Only-begotten for the judgment of the demons who wronged us. You yourself, then, O Master, he says, who now sit on it as on a judgment seat to judge and avenge us, are the God who is before the ages. "The rivers have lifted up, Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voices." Here he calls the holy apostles and evangelists rivers, for they gladdened God's Church with spiritual streams. For it was said to them: "Rivers of living water will flow from his belly." "Wonderful are the surges of the sea." The many teachings in the mysteries, he says, and the thoughts of the apostles and evangelists, like streams, have made the surges of the sea wonderful. By "sea" he means the multitudes of the nations who believed. Their surges, that is, the raising of their minds, have become wonderful. For they no longer think small and lowly thoughts about God, but great and wonderful ones. "Your testimonies have been made very sure." By "testimonies" he means the promises God made to the nations through the holy prophets. At the end of days he showed them to be trustworthy, fulfilling them in deed by his own coming. "Holiness befits your house, Lord." His house is the Church, and it is fitting for her to be holy, since she has the only Holy One dwelling in her. When this comes about, she will also share in and enjoy unending holiness. A Psalm of David, for the fourth day of the week. [Psalm 93?]

In this psalm he takes up the subject of providence. He teaches us not to be distressed or troubled even if, for a time, sinners prosper and the godly are persecuted. For none of these things remains the same…

[?]…eternal enjoyment of good things, but for those who [?] after what only seemed to be good things, punishment for endless ages. The psalm is entitled “On the fourth day of the week” because in the fourth month (he has put the day in place of the month) the calamities began in the city of God, when the Babylonians marched against it, as Jeremiah relates. “The Lord is a God of vengeance; the God of vengeance has spoken out boldly.” Just as he is a compassionate God and a God of consolations, so he is also a God of vengeance. And again, by saying this at the outset he brings great comfort to those who have grown dejected under their afflictions. The words “has spoken out boldly” point to the sentence that will later be pronounced against the ungodly at the divine tribunal, in which he says: “Depart from me, you accursed.” “Render recompense to the proud.” He sends up a prayer for the afflicted, asking help for them from God, who alone has power. “How long shall sinners boast?” With these words he indicates God’s intense and surpassing forbearance. “They have humbled your people, O Lord.” He rouses God to zeal against the enemies, saying that the people being mistreated by [?]… are his own people and inheritance.

“They have killed the widow and the orphan.” The interpretation of these words was given in the verse above, but it will be stated again all the same. Whoever interprets the divine Scriptures wrongly kills a widowed soul and a proselyte mind. An orphan is a mind deprived of its heavenly Father. “The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain.” For how can those notions not be full of vanity that try to banish from reason the benefit of providence? “Blessed is the man whom you discipline, O Lord.” Those people, he says, are wretched and lowly who do not accept your discipline, but blessed are those who are disciplined by you and taught from your law. For these, being made gentle even in afflictions, will be relieved of their griefs, knowing that afflictions will turn out to end in good. By “evil days” he means the days of judgment. “Until a pit is dug for the sinner.” Those who have been disciplined, he says, will endure their afflictions with confidence until a pit is dug for the sinner, that is, until the sinner goes to the place of punishment prepared for him. By “the sinner” he means Satan, or every opposing power. “For the Lord will not cast off his people.” This would be the answer to what was said above: “They have humbled your people, O Lord, and afflicted your inheritance.” “And he will not forsake his inheritance.” This depends on the verse above…

…“For the Lord will not cast off his people.” It is as if he were saying: He will guard his people, he says, through the whole time of affliction, and he will steer and guide them until the divine tribunal sits. But when Righteousness, that is, Christ, takes its seat there, all the upright in heart will draw near to it, as it is said: “For they shall see God.” For this is what the [?]… indicate.

“Until righteousness returns to judgment.” Until Christ judges the world. For he became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption; and the Father has given all judgment to him. “Who will rise up for me against the evildoers?” This is the voice of the afflicted. He says: Who will become my ally against those who do evil to me? Then, having quickly become aware of his helper, he says that his soul would long ago have been brought down to Hades had it not received help from God. “When I said, ‘My foot has slipped.’” When I was afflicted, he says, and saw myself slipping, I said: “My foot has slipped,” that is, “I am about to fall from my steadfastness before God”; and at once I felt your help and your mercy coming to my aid. “Your consolations have gladdened my soul.” You did not leave me without comfort, he says; as many afflictions as I had, so many consolations I received from you. And so I turned my griefs into gladness. “Let not the throne of lawlessness be joined with you, which fashions trouble by decree.” For this reason, he says, you comforted my heart in its afflictions: because no throne of lawlessness will be joined to you, that is, because as God you are a just judge, and there will be no lawlessness in your judgments (for the throne signifies judgment), as there is with the one who fashions trouble by decree. This would be the opposing demon, who makes God’s commandments heavy even though they are light, and causes people toil over them. He called the devil a throne of lawlessness, since Christ, who opposes the devil, is also a throne of righteousness. “And they will condemn innocent blood.” These evil and opposing demons, he says, will seek by every means to hunt down the soul of the righteous. But for this, he says, they will be condemned. For this is what “And they will condemn innocent blood” means. He is saying that in return for the blood innocently shed by them they will be handed over to judgment and punishment. “And the Lord has become my refuge.” But I have enjoyed the providence of the Master, and I have him as a strong wall around me.

From this point the choir of the saints urges even the disobedient of Israel to come to the salvation that is through Christ, showing that he will hear them if they fall down before him, since he is their maker and loves his own work. After the exhortation of the saints, the person of the Holy Spirit himself is brought in, bidding the disobedient themselves not to imitate the unbelief of their fathers. “Come, let us rejoice in the Lord.” They bid the disobedient come as if to a feast, calling them to exultation, so as to win them over by this. “Let us shout aloud to God our Savior.” He rightly says “let us shout aloud,” that is, having come, let us sing the hymns of victory. For a shout of triumph is a hymn sung over fallen enemies. By these words he signifies that Christ fought the opposing powers on our behalf and removed them out of the way. “Let us come before his face with confession.” As if he were saying: Before he sits in judgment, let us come before his face, that is, the Son, with confession, and make him favorable toward them. For in this way it will come about that you end in good things; for confession has a good end. And this is what the phrase in the Psalms shows: “Let us shout aloud to him.” “And a great King over all the gods.” That is, over those who have believed and have received as their reward the name of being called gods, as it is said: “I have made you a god to Pharaoh.” If we offer confession, he says, we shall not fail; for he will have compassion on us as his own people. “For the sea is his.” He shows that, since he is the creator of all creation visible and invisible, he would not overlook his own handiwork when it falls down before him in confession. “Come, let us worship and fall down before him.” They say that they themselves are among those who worship and weep, so as to make their hearers more eager for confession. “Today, if you hear his voice.” From this point they are exhorted by the Lord himself to be obedient, and not to be like their fathers proved to be in the wilderness. “As on the day of testing in the wilderness, where your fathers tested me.” For they put God to the test, going now one way and now another, and not on the straight way of the Lord. “As I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter into my rest.” The word signifies three rests to us: one is the fleshly rest of the Sabbath; another is the entry into the land of promise, when Joshua gave them rest; and the third is the heavenly rest, which the word now signifies to us. He would not have mentioned another rest here if that one were truly rest.

It is shown, then, that the true rest is the one that comes after departure from this world: the dwelling in the mansions above. PSALM 95. A song of David, when the house was built after the captivity.

In the preceding psalm he foretold the rejection of the Jews if they persisted in unbelief; in this one he introduces the calling of the Gentiles, which came about after their release from their spiritual captivity, when the Church was also founded throughout the whole world. “Sing to the Lord a new song.” The Spirit bids the apostles expound the new song, that is, the New Testament, to the nations throughout the whole world. “Sing to the Lord, all the earth . . . . Proclaim the good news of his salvation day after day.” For they will not cease, until the end of the world, speaking to us the mysteries of the New Testament. “For the Lord is great and greatly to be praised.” Teach the nations, he says; for once they have obeyed they will come to know the divinity and greatness of the one who is preached, and knowing it they will praise him. “He is to be feared above all gods.” This above all urges the nations to the fear of the Lord, since they have seen the burning of those whom they formerly called their gods. For they came to know that all those were not gods but demons, and that the Lord alone is the maker of the heavenly things. “For all the gods of the nations are demons.” For the so-called gods were shown to be evil demons, but our Lord made the heavens. “Holiness and majesty are in his sanctuary.” His sanctuary is the Church, which is both holy and majestic. For lofty is the adornment of the…

“Bring to the Lord, you families of the nations.” By “families” he means the leaders of the churches, I mean priests and bishops. And it is fitting for them to glorify God by good works, and indeed to honor him from their just labors, and moreover to offer him spiritual sacrifices, offering them in his divine courts, that is, in the churches. “Let all the earth be shaken before his face.” For the preaching was about to be heard throughout the whole world and, as it were, to shake the earth from its former state. “For he has set the world aright, and it shall not be shaken.” For he founded the Church on the rock, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it. “He will judge the peoples in uprightness.” For he came and judged our case, and cast out the wicked tyrants, meaning the unclean demons. “Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth exult.” For at the setting aright of the world the heavenly powers rejoiced and said: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace.” “Let the sea be shaken, and all that fills it.” By the sea here

he signifies the multitude of the nations, which has indeed been shaken, that is, moved to receive the preaching. “The plains shall rejoice and all that is in them; then all the trees of the forest shall exult.” By the plains and also by the trees he signifies holy souls, who exulted at the salvation of the world. PSALM. Of David, when the [?]…
Here too, once again, he signifies the salvation of the world, and the [?] of all the nations toward him…

“The Lord has become king; let the earth exult, let the many islands be glad.” He calls the churches islands, since they are buffeted by every wind and are also surrounded by the briny waters of hardship. “Cloud and darkness are around him.” This signifies his hidden descent among humans, when he appeared in the form of a servant. “Righteousness and judgment are the foundation of his throne.” This, he says, became the cause of our forgiveness: that he judged justly our case, that is, the case we have against the evil and opposing powers. “Fire shall go before him.” For by his divine power he burned up every evil and opposing activity. “His lightnings shone upon the world.” He says that his lightnings are the holy apostles and evangelists, who like light shone upon the [world] under…

“The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord.” By mountains he means the opposing powers, which melted like wax, plainly from the fire mentioned before. What the north wind freezes, the south wind melts; and so the bride rightly says in the Song of Songs: “Awake, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let my spices flow.” “Let all who worship carved images be put to shame,” namely when they see those whom they once thought gods melted like wax by the Lord. “Worship him, all his angels.” Give thanks, he says, for what he has set aright under heaven. “Zion heard and was glad.” Zion is the Church. And what did it hear, if not the gospel preaching, which became the cause of its gladness? “And the daughters of Judea exulted.” By the daughters of Judea he means holy souls, joined to God through confession, who exulted at God’s judgments, seeing, that is, the tyrants cast out and those held in slavery brought into freedom. “You who love the Lord, hate evil.” An exhortation is brought in for those who have been redeemed into freedom, teaching them to turn away from every form of evil. “The Lord guards the souls of his holy ones.”

If, having turned away from the evil one, you have become holy, then it will come about that you also receive the Lord’s protection from the evil one; for he is properly “the sinner.” “Light has dawned for the righteous.” The light of the gospel, that is. And “for the righteous” means for this people made righteous through faith. “And gladness for the upright in heart.” One must put a stop after “for the upright,” so that gladness may dawn for those who become upright in heart; and “will dawn” must be supplied from the preceding clause. PSALM. Of David. 97.

This psalm too signifies the first coming of the Lord, and the faith in him of all the nations, which he brought about according to the promises made to the fathers. For this reason the word urges all the nations to shout aloud the victory song for the victory he has won on their behalf. “Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvelous things.” For it is truly marvelous that death has been abolished and the human race has come back to life. “His right hand has saved for him.” For Christ, who is the right hand of the Father, has brought the world under heaven to his own Father. For he had no need of human help. “The Lord has made known his salvation.” He signifies his coming in the flesh, which is salvation, as Simeon said: “For my eyes have seen your salvation.” “Before the nations you have revealed his righteousness.” By casting out the ruler of this age, and by justifying us who had long been under tyranny. “He has remembered his mercy.” His mercy to Jacob; for he promised that in his seed all the nations would be blessed. “All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.” For no place is without a share in the kingdom of Christ. “Sing praises to our God with the lyre.” By the lyre he means the harmony of the body with the soul. “With beaten trumpets and the sound of the horn trumpet.” By the beaten trumpets he signifies the fiery and far-reaching character of the gospel preaching; by the horn trumpets, its royal character, since kings were anointed from a horn. And not only that, but they also proclaimed the kingship with a horn trumpet. “Let the sea be shaken, and all that fills it.” By the sea he signifies the present life, because of the bitterness of its cares. It has been moved, then, from its former state, that is, from idolatry. “The rivers shall clap their hands together.” He says that the rivers are the holy teachers of the mysteries, and by their clapping together he signifies the zeal of their preaching. “The mountains shall exult, for he comes to judge the earth.” The angelic powers, that is. For there is joy over one sinner who repents.

This psalm too signifies the kingdom of Christ and the arrogance of the high priests. “The Lord has become king; let the peoples be angry.” It is Christ whose kingdom the Jews, in their anger, do not accept. “He who sits upon the cherubim; let the earth be shaken.” For this very one, who is to reign in the last times over those on earth, is the one who rides upon the cherubim, by whom the earth was also shaken. So he says: You who are upon the cherubim are the one who, having become one of us, moved the earth from its evil standing. By “standing” he means the standing of idolatry. “The Lord is great in Zion.” Zion is the Church, in which Christ is glorified and exalted, as it is said: “I will exalt you, my God, my King.”

“Let them confess your great name.” His name “Jesus” is great, since it is interpreted “salvation of the people.” Great, again, is the name that is above every name, at which every knee is to bend and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. “For it is fearful and holy.” Fearful to the angry peoples who do not accept his kingdom, but holy to those who believe in him. “And the honor of the king loves judgment.” Since the honor, or glory, of the king loves righteousness, which is expressed by the word “judgment,” for this reason his command is fearful to those who have disobeyed, but holy to those who obey. “You have prepared uprightness.” For he is going to judge the world in righteousness. “Exalt the Lord our God.” He who is exalted as God and has all creation under his feet became man without change. Him therefore, he says, who became man without change, exalt, worshiping him with a single worship together with his own flesh. “Moses and Aaron among his priests.” This one, he says, who now, inasmuch as he became man, has become king over those on earth, is the one on whom Moses and Aaron and Samuel called long ago. So, having said, “Worship at the footstool,” and having proclaimed the incarnation and the divine plan of salvation, he again makes us secure by signifying his divinity through the term he has indicated. For he remained God, even though he took the form of a servant for our salvation. “O Lord our God, you answered them.” Even if they seemed to sin in some way, being human, you did not overlook it, he says. Thus Aaron was reproved for sinning over the calf, and Moses at the water of contradiction. “And worship at his holy mountain.” He means either the earthly or the heavenly Jerusalem; or else the mountain is to be understood as the Only-begotten himself, according to the words: “A stone was cut from a mountain without hands.”

In this psalm he brings an exhortation to those who have already come to the faith, that they should offer thanksgiving for what has already been done. For “confession” here signifies thanksgiving joined with praise. “Shout aloud to God, all the earth.” He bids them, as people who have been redeemed, to sing the victory song. And those redeemed were the whole human race. By “the earth” he means those who inhabit the earth. “Serve the Lord with gladness.” Service to men produces a destructive fear, but service to the Lord produces a pure fear, from which gladness arises in the soul. “Come before him with exultation.” Whoever has already received into his mind the gladness of the shout stands, as it were, before Christ and rejoices with joy, and this is exultation. “Know that the Lord, he is our God.” This Lord, he says, who ransomed the whole earth with his own blood, is also the creator who made us. For we did not come together by chance; we are the work of his hands. That is why we are his people and his sheep: the people being the more rational, and the sheep those who hold the less rational rank and are not [?] experienced in the divine oracles, as it is said: “I went astray like a lost sheep.” “But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture.” Some are his people, the better ones; others are the sheep of his pasture, the lesser ones. Nevertheless, since he is God and maker of all, he calls all and makes them his own. For God saves both men and beasts: the former as his people, the latter as the sheep of his pasture. “Enter his gates with confession.” By the gates of the Lord he means the Church on earth, in which we must make confession, first declaring our sins and then recounting the benefits done to us. Of David. PSALM 100.

In this psalm he describes for us the perfect man, the one who lives according to God, teaching us what way of life those who desire to attain the kingdom of heaven must pursue. “Of mercy and judgment I will sing to you, O Lord.” These things, he says, I always carry on my lips, which I know to have been accomplished for us [?]; judgment will be given, that is, just judgment. For he [?] vindicated our case against our enemies. “I will sing and understand in a blameless way.” By “I will sing” he means a hymn; as if he were saying more clearly: I will not cease singing hymns and making my way blameless, as I await your coming, O Master. For we must be ready for the Lord’s arrival. For this admirable man acquired such purity that with boldness…

to cry out to God, “When will you come to me?” That is: I have made the palace fit for you; I long for your presence, O Master, I yearn for your appearing; grant me what I long for. “I walked in the innocence of my heart in the midst of my house.” I had, he says, no unjust thought living with me, but I conducted myself in complete purity. “I hated those who commit transgressions.” For we must not only keep away from evil things but also turn away from those who do them. “A crooked heart did not cleave to me.” The devil's counsels, since they have nothing straight in them, are crooked and perverse, and I have never let them into my heart. “When the wicked man turned away from me, I did not know it.” I counted the wicked as so utterly unimportant, he says, that I was unaware both of their presence and of their absence. So I did not notice when they left, and so I did not notice them when they were there either, if they were there at all. And it is proof of a mind devoted to God that it takes no account of things below because its attention is on what is above. “Whoever secretly slandered his neighbour, him I drove out.” I did not accept accusations made in secret; I drove out those who tried to make them. “With the man of proud eye and insatiable heart, with him I did not eat.” Nor did I make those who practise arrogance and greed…

“My eyes are on the faithful of the land, that they may sit with me.” Those adorned with faith, who set great store by divine things, shared in my councils and deliberations. But those not so disposed, whose minds were set the opposite way (I mean on arrogance, injustice and contempt), I cast far from me, so that I would not see them. “In the mornings I slew all the sinners of the land.” By sinners he means evil thoughts, which he punished with morning prayers and constant attendance on God. “To destroy from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity.” By the city of the Lord he means the holy soul, as it is said, “Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God.” A prayer of the poor man, when he is weary and pours out his supplication before the Lord. Psalm 101.

The man who is poor in God's sight, that is, the choir of the prophets, is filled with grief at the overthrow of the first people. He comes to the Lord on its behalf (on behalf of the people, that is), sending up supplications with fasting and tears, so that the people too may be shown pity.
