He also proclaims the calling of the nations, which came about at the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ. “Lord, hear my prayer.” The prophetic choir takes as its own what happened to the people…

“For my days have vanished like smoke, and my bones have been parched like kindling.” These words were interpreted above, but they will be discussed again. For all their strength, which upheld the worship prescribed by the law, was destroyed and lost. This consisted of the high priesthood, the temple, the sacrifices of animals, the self-government of the…

“I became like a night raven in a ruined house.” He says this because of the darkness that had seized the people, for they did not know God. What is peculiar to the night raven except crying out through the night, which is how it got its name? Since he spent whole nights in prayer, then, he naturally compares himself to the night raven. “I kept watch and became like a sparrow alone on a housetop.” I, he says, who was not caught up in the time of sin, have been left so alone that I am like a single sparrow. Out of so many tens of thousands, even if more than one were saved, they would count as one compared with the tens of thousands. “All day long my enemies reproached me.” I became a laughingstock to my foes, and those who once envied me swear by my calamities, praying not to suffer the same. The phrase “with ashes” is like the seventy-ninth psalm: “You will feed us with the bread of tears.” If even mealtime was full of pain, no other time could have been free from suffering. “And those who praised me swore against me.” Even my friends, he says, who once admired me, made my calamities into an oath, saying, “May I not suffer what Israel suffered!” “For I ate ashes like bread.” This refers either to the calamities of the captivity, or to the hardship they took on themselves so that the […] might be pitied.

“For you lifted me up and dashed me down.” For of all the nations, Israel alone was exalted, since it alone had knowledge of the true God. “My days have declined like a shadow.” By his days he means those of the worship under the law, which is also called a shadow of the good things to come. “And I have withered like grass.” “I” stands for “the people”. For, as I said, he takes everything that belongs to the people as his own. “For your servants took pleasure in her stones, and they will pity her dust.” By stones he means those who believed in Christ after the resurrection and became holy stones, as Zechariah says. By servants he means the holy apostles, through whom those who believed in Christ were saved. By dust he means the peoples who still live a more earthly life and still do not believe, and he says that they too are worthy of pity. For the remnant is being kept for the last day, and they too will be saved through Elijah the prophet.

“And the nations will fear the name of the Lord.” Fittingly, in the midst of the good pleasure taken in the stones of the former people, he adds the calling of the nations. “And all the kings of the earth your glory.” “Kings” stands for “kingdoms”. For there is no kingdom or nation that does not worship the glory of the Lord. “For the Lord will build up Zion.” That is, the Church. “He has looked upon the prayer of the lowly.” For the prophets, humbling themselves in prayer, used to say, “And you, Lord God of Israel, take heed to visit all the nations.” “Let this be written for another generation.” The prayer in the psalm, and the promise prophesied about the nations, were given to the Jews engraved as if on a pillar, to be kept for the new Israel and the generation that belongs to Christ. “And the people that is being created will praise the Lord. For he has looked down from his holy height.” He sets before us the reason for the calling of the nations. This is the appearing of our Saviour Christ, which he brought about by bowing the heavens. “To hear the groaning of those in fetters.” And who are those in fetters, if not those whom the demon who hates the good has bound with the chains of sin? “To set free the sons of those put to death.” The sons of those put to death would be those from the nations, since their fathers died in their own sins, still worshipping idols. “To declare his name in Zion.” He says that this too is a reason for his coming down: so that the Church might learn to sing hymns to his name. For this is the…

“When peoples are gathered together.” The prophets, who had seen through the Spirit the gathering of the nations to the Lord, prayed that they too might be found worthy of this blessed sight and of seeing how things would turn out. “He answered him in the way of his strength.” The one answering, or rather questioning God, is the prophetic choir. By the way of his strength he means his coming on earth. For he came to bind the strong man. “Tell me the fewness of my days.” Tell me, he says, what our life is like. For he prayed to see whether his life would last until the days when the Only-begotten was to become man and appear on earth. “Do not take me away in the half of my days.” By the half of his days he means the part of his life before he came to behold the appearing. So he prayed that his whole time might be completed, and if possible that his life might be prolonged, so that he might be found worthy of seeing how things actually turned out. For that is how his whole life would be fulfilled. “Your years are through generation upon generation.” The prophetic choir, knowing through the Spirit that it would not live to see the end of these events, says: I shall fall asleep, since I am mortal; but you alone, O Master, even into those

generations you remain, since you yourself are God, who also made the heavens in the beginning. “They will perish, but you remain.” You alone, O Master, he says, possess eternity, since you are God. The heavens, though they are a great and exceptional creation, will nevertheless also be subjected to corruption. But this corruption will lead to their renewal, for they will be rolled up and changed into a better form. “The sons of your servants will dwell.” For when the heavens are rolled up and a new creation comes into being, then indeed the sons of your servants will be in the eternal dwellings. These would be those who have believed through his holy apostles. “And their seed will be directed forever.” The seed of the holy apostles is the saving proclamation of the gospel, which remains forever. A Psalm of David. 102.

In this psalm the new people from the nations is taught to sing hymns to God, who has done it great good. These benefits are the removal of sin and the glory of the resurrection. “Bless the Lord, O my soul.” He rouses himself to the hymn, holding up the blessing of God as a good remedy for his salvation. In the things by which God was going to show mercy to the people, he is glorified for his righteousness as judge, freeing them from corruption and granting them the kingdom of heaven, so that the present hymn suits everyone. “And all that is within me, his holy name.” By “all that is within” he shows that God is to be called upon with the whole heart, with all one's strength and with the whole mind. “Bless the Lord, O my soul.” He lingers over urging himself to the hymn, knowing that he owes this in return for God's great benefits. For anyone who remembers the divine benefits will never stop singing hymns. “And do not forget all his recompenses.” For in return for the great sins we committed, he repaid us with kindness, mercy and compassion. These we must not forget. “Who is gracious to all your iniquities.” These are God's recompenses to us: first, he made atonement for our sins; second, he healed our infirmities; third, he redeemed our life from corruption by doing away with sin; fourth, in his own love for humankind, his mercy and his compassion, he crowned us with the gift of adoption as sons; fifth, he filled us with spiritual good things, giving himself to us, he who is the bread of life. “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle's.” God renews our youth like the eagle's through rebirth. He is pointing us to the gift of the resurrection. He likened those who are renewed to the eagle, because it flies highest and is the most kingly of all birds, and alone can gaze steadily at the brilliance of the sun.

“The Lord performs acts of mercy and judgement for all who are wronged.” This Lord, he says, who in his mercy has granted us what was mentioned above, is the same who long ago judged with just judgement, redeemed the sons of Israel from Egypt, and gave Moses and all the people knowledge of his commandments. “The Lord is compassionate and merciful.” For these were the cause of such great benefits both long ago and now, as Moses too says: “The Lord is long-suffering and abounding in mercy and true, showing mercy to thousands.” These, then, are the powers of his that he made known to Moses, which are called “ways”, and the virtues by which he governs all things. “He will not be angry to the end.” Even though he was angry, he says, because of the transgression in Adam, and condemned the race to death, he does not prolong his anger to the end. For in the last times he shone forth to abolish corruption. “For he knew how we were formed.” For he pitied us as his own creation and the work of his hands. “But the mercy of the Lord is from everlasting.” This is like the saying: “And showing mercy to thousands of those who fear…”

“And his righteousness is upon sons of sons, for those who keep his covenant.” For since he is holy, he rests among holy ones, that is, among the angelic powers. “The Lord has prepared his throne in heaven.” He rests, he says, upon the spirits above; yet the things on earth have not been withdrawn from his kingdom either. For as God he is the one who has authority over all things. “And his kingdom rules over all.” It says that he is master over all, not that he reigns as king over all, since not everyone is worthy of his kingdom. That is why the Saviour promised the kingdom of heaven to those who succeed in living the life of the gospel. But the Lord also holds sway over the [un]worthy [?]. “Bless the Lord, all you his angels.” He teaches the people who are coming to faith that whoever devotes himself to the hymn will have the same dignity as the angels. For if their ministry is to praise and glorify God, and the soul is commanded to do this very thing, speaking and glorifying God always, then it clearly attains the same dignity. For those whose occupation is the same have the same dignity. “Bless the Lord, all his powers.” Not only angels are called to praise, but any other heavenly order there may be, whether thrones, principalities, authorities or dominions. He has indicated all these orders to us by the word “powers”. Of David, on the creation of the world. Without title among the Hebrews. 103.

…the people [coming] to faith to offer hymns to God, he teaches in these verses, and he shows how great a thing his providence over all things is. For he exercises providence not only over heavenly and airborne things but also over earthly things and the smallest of them, so that he does not neglect even the humblest animals but provides for them too. “Bless the Lord, O my soul.” He teaches us to bless God with our soul for his great providence as well, just as in the preceding psalm we did for release from our sins. “O Lord my God, you have been greatly magnified.” Looking at your providence, O Master, we magnify it, amazed at its greatness. For this is how he wraps himself in our confession and majesty, that is, in praise with doxology, as in a robe. “Wrapping himself in light as in a garment.” He begins to weave his hymn to him from the light perceived by the mind. And just as elsewhere he is said to dwell in unapproachable light, here this very light is said to be what he wraps himself in. “Stretching out the heaven like a skin.” He puts this down as the second work of providence: that the heaven is stretched out like a hide in a craftsman's hands. He has shown at once both its shape and the ease with which the Creator made it. For just as it is easy for a man to stretch out a skin, so it is easy for God to make the heaven that did not exist. At the same time he also hinted at another lofty thought: that we are journeying toward another life, that present things are a shadow of things to come, and that we have not yet reached the inner sanctuary but are still living in a tent in this present life. For a tent belongs to things that are taken down. And a little further on: So too, when the heaven is changed, there will be another way of life and a better lot than the present one. For there will be a new heaven and a new earth. But let us hear what the prophets say about heaven, so that we may stop the mouths of those who pride themselves on their beards, who say whatever comes into their heads and claim that heaven is also beneath the earth. Standing against them, the prophet said, “Stretching out the heaven like a skin.” A skin is not a sphere, as their nonsense has it; rather it resembles a sort of circle or hemisphere. Another prophet made this plain when he said, “Who set up the heaven like a vault, and stretched it out like a tent to dwell in over the earth.” And again, that it does not revolve but stands fixed. So the prophet says, “Who fixed the heaven.” And to show how extremely fine it is, he said, “The heaven was made firm like smoke.” “Who roofs his upper chambers with waters.” He shows that the masses of water are not carried about in the air at random. He himself directs this by his own providence, so that the regions around the heavens seem to be roofed by the orderly arrangement of the clouds.
…of the winds. He shows that not even the movement of the winds happens at random. He himself is like their charioteer, by mounting upon their…
“Who makes his angels spirits.” Making the angels light and lofty, he says. “And his ministers a flaming fire [?].” So Moses saw the angel in a flame of fire, speaking…

“Who founded the earth on its firm base.” After showing the Creator's providence in heaven, he goes on to his providence over things on earth. This is the very point: that the earth, though solid and heavy, was established on a liquid substance. “The abyss is his covering like a garment.” By “his” he means the element of earth itself. He says that he clothed the earth with the abyss as with a garment, surrounding it entirely on the outside with water. “Waters will stand upon the mountains,” and so on. The waters of the abyss rise up like mountains, he says, lifted high, as if threatening to flood the earth. But at your nod and by your power, which is signified by the thunder, they retreat, he says. Or perhaps he says that the thunders were made for this purpose, so that the waters of the abyss might be struck with fear by what happens. And if those things experience this, how much more must we…

“Mountains rise up and plains sink down.” When the waters are lifted up, he says, they may be compared to mountains; but when they spread out again out of fear of you, they become like a plain, level ground. For you established for them a place they cannot overstep. That is what is meant by “You set a boundary that they will not pass.” This is why they cannot flood the earth. Similar is what was said to the sea through the prophet: “Thus far you shall stand and not go beyond, but your waves shall be broken within you.” “Waters will pass between the mountains.” He goes through providence point by point, glorifying it, and marvels at God's goodness joined with wisdom, since God has taken care for the survival of the irrational animals. For having made them, he both feeds them and gives them drink. That is why he cut through the mountains and made a passage for the waters. “They will give drink to all the beasts of the field.” So he provides even for irrational animals, reptiles and wild beasts, supplying them too with what is needed for life. “Wild asses will wait for them in their thirst.” This too is a work of your providence: that waters are given not only in the seasons of torrents, in the ravines and warm places, but also between the mountains, so that the tame animals may escape from the wild ones and rest in due season. “Watering the mountains from his upper chambers.” For he waters mountains and plains not from springs in the ravines or rivers flowing over the ground, but from above, supplying sufficient rain. “From the fruit

of your works the earth will be satisfied.” Just as he provided the supply of waters, so he arranged for nourishment to come from the earth. “Who makes grass spring up for the cattle, and green plants for the service of men.” By the service of men he means the tame animals, such as the ox, the ass and the like. “To bring forth bread from the earth.” This is why, he says, you took care of the cattle: so that by their work on the land we might find what we need for life. For he does good to all those creatures for our sake. “The trees of the plain will be satisfied.” He shows that the trees growing in the forest too, such as cedars and the rest, will grow at his bidding. They were made for a great many other purposes, which we know from experience, and also for the sparrows' nests. “The heron's house leads them.” He says that the heron's nest leads the sparrows themselves, because the heron takes the highest trees to nest in, generally firs, the tallest of all trees. “The high mountains for the deer.” To the deer too, he says, he gave the mountains as a refuge, to escape the wilder animals. “The rock is a refuge for the hares.” Just as he gave the mountains to the deer for safety, so he gave the hollows of the rocks to the hares. And so they too, being kept safe by these, said in the earlier verse, “From among the rocks they will utter their voices,” praising, clearly, the…

“He made the moon for the seasons.” He goes back again to the providence shown in the heavens. He says the moon was made for no other purpose than for counting and distinguishing months and days. “The sun knew its setting.” It too, by divine command [?].

“You appointed darkness, and it became night.” He says this so that we will not think that there is one creator of the day and another of the night. “Man will go out to his work.” People were prevented from going out on journeys and to work the land. But now they go out by night seeking food from God, since the earth did not make grass or green plants spring up for them too. “How magnified are your works, O Lord!” Having gone through his account of providence, he turned his discourse to a hymn to the Creator, giving the ears a rest, as it were, by this [?]. Then he comes again to another part of providence, telling us about travel on the waters, which could never have happened if God's providence were not steering in it. “You made all things in wisdom.” It is marvellous indeed that the Lord made all things in wisdom; for Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. “This dragon, which you formed to make sport of it.” He inserted a mention of the dragon into his account of the sea, saying that it was brought into being for no other purpose than to be made sport of. And it is fitting that he mentioned it in his account of the sea…

[?]… since our whole life is something briny, buffeted from every side and tossed by wild waves. All things look to you. For whether human beings, or herds of wild beasts, or cattle, or creeping things, none of them could be fed in any other way unless he supplied what sustains their life. You will take away their spirit, and they will fail. By these words he shows that he is the master of both death and life. The Lord will rejoice in his works. And what kind of work is this [?]? The one he wrought in renewing our nature. For by these words he signifies the knowledge of God that human beings were to have, when God will rejoice, not at being worshiped, but at seeing them saved. He who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble. He adds the universal judgment, which will bring fear to everyone on earth. For there is no one who does not dread that terrible and divine tribunal. He who touches the mountains, and they smoke. By mountains he means the hostile powers, which he will also burn up at the time of the judgment, of which a symbol is also the

May my meditation be pleasing to him. "Meditation" here means "my choice." He means what he chose: to want only to sing hymns to God, which will also please the one to whom the hymns are sung. May sinners vanish from the earth. At that time, clearly. For they will hear: "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels." And the lawless, so that they are no more. Clearly, they will be absent from the portion of those who bless God. Bless the Lord, O my soul. For he will both remove you from the lot of the wicked and make you worthy of the lot of the saints. Alleluia. Psalm 104.

"Alleluia" is praise to the Invisible One. It is said that the angels praise God with this cry, as the cherubim do with "Holy, holy, holy." The holy fathers have handed this down, having heard it with their own ears, as Isaiah heard the seraphim. "Alleluia" is divided as follows: al, "God"; el, "strong"; ouia, "mighty." Give thanks to the Lord, and call upon his name; proclaim his works among the nations. In this psalm the Holy Spirit commands the holy apostles to make known to the people from the nations all the miracles that the Lord performed at his coming. Be praised in his holy name. For praise and glory belong to those who recount God's excellence. Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice. How great is the benefit that comes from giving thanks

[?] he teaches. For if you seek him, he says, you will gain both gladness of mind and the strengthening and glorifying of our head. Remember the wonders he has done. He means the divine signs he performed at his coming, whether those in the New Testament, or those in the Old through Moses and the saints before him. For they too worked many miracles through the Son of God. These he commands their heralds to hand on to the nations, since they do not know them, in addition to what the Savior did in the New, and all that his mouth has decreed through both the Old and the New. Command them to keep these as royal laws. His portents and the judgments of his mouth. Portents are the miracles that took place, such as walking on the sea, raising the dead, and the rest; the judgments of his mouth are the words he spoke when driving the unclean demons out of people, or else the commandments of the New Testament. Seed of Abraham, his servants, sons of Jacob, his chosen one. The word is still addressed as if to the apostles, so that the sense is [?]: "Since you are the seed of Abraham and his servants, and sons of Jacob and his chosen ones (for he chose them), proclaim among the nations that he is the Lord [?]"

And they passed from nation to nation. From the nation of the Babylonians to that of the Palestinians. And he rebuked kings on their account. Abimelech, for his outrage against Sarah. Do not touch my anointed ones. Abraham and his household are also "anointed," because they were counted worthy of the appearance of God the Word in visions. And he called a famine upon the land. He caused the famine by his providential plan, so that, going down into Egypt because of it and multiplying there, they might receive the land of the promise. He broke every staff [?] of bread. This is what usually happens in famines through God's wrath: people are not sustained
Until his word came. He means the fulfillment of the dreams. So he says that he suffered hardship until then, weeping in the struggle for his life, until the time came for the dreams to be fulfilled
To instruct his princes as himself. This resembles: "Do not interpretations belong to God?" For he would not have interpreted the dreams for Pharaoh had God not granted him the power to understand

And Israel entered Egypt, and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham. The sons of Noah were Shem, Ham, and Japheth; and Ham's son was Canaan. His son Mestraim is interpreted "Egypt," and the country takes its name from him. So when Jacob entered Egypt, it is likely that Ham, being the grandfather of Mestraim, had settled in Egypt, while Canaan lived in Palestine. By

Israel and Jacob, who entered Egypt, his sons too are meant. For Scripture said that Israel went down into Egypt with seventy souls. And Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham. Ham begot Canaan, and Canaan begot Mestraim, which is interpreted "Egypt." That is why he calls Egypt the land of Ham, as belonging to Ham's descendant. And he increased his people greatly. So that the [?] who did not know Joseph said: "Behold, now the nation is very numerous and stronger than we are." But they would not have grown strong as they increased had they not enjoyed Joseph's protection and Pharaoh's welcome. And he turned his heart to hate his people. Since, because they were honored by the Egyptians, they had lapsed into an idolatry like theirs, he therefore brought it about that the Egyptians hated them and laid heavy labors on them, so that, once afflicted, they would flee to God, and the promise to Abraham would find room to be fulfilled. He sent Moses his servant, and so on. For to Moses and Aaron alone he revealed by word the turning "into blood" and the other signs. He sent darkness, and it grew dark. Since the Egyptians abandoned the Creator and served the creation, he punished them through the creation itself — I mean through air, and fire, and earth,
He turned their waters into blood. For he changed not only the color of the waters but also their very taste, so that every kind of fish perished. Alleluia. Psalm 105.

In this psalm he lists the sins of the former people, teaching how their rejection came about. They are these: first, they provoked him while crossing the Red Sea, saying, "Because there were no graves in Egypt, he brought us out here to destroy us"; second, they tempted God in the desert; third, they angered Moses in the camp; fourth, they made a calf at Horeb; fifth, they despised the desirable land; sixth, they were initiated into the rites of Baal of Peor; seventh, they angered him at the water of contradiction; eighth, they failed to destroy the nations, as the Lord had told them, but even worshiped their idols, so far as to offer their own children to them in sacrifice. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good... Blessed are those who keep judgment, and so on. For these alone are worthy to speak of the mighty deeds of the Lord: those who do what God has decreed in the Scriptures, who carry out everything with judgment and reason, and who always keep God's judgment before their eyes.

For these, consequently, are also doers of righteousness, accomplishing what is just in deed. Remember us, Lord, in the favor you show your people. Here the persona of the Jews is introduced, praying to share in the salvation given to the nations. The water covered those who afflicted them. That is, only the afflicters; for the mixed multitude that came out with them were not among the afflicters but among those who believed. And they believed his word and sang his praise. For when, through God's goodness, the waves of the sea had also been [?], they believed at once and sang him the song recorded in Exodus; then they consigned everything to oblivion. And they sang his praise. When the women came out dancing with Miriam, saying: "Let us sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously." And they tempted God in the waterless desert. As for "And they tempted God in the waterless desert": they provoked him immediately after the Red Sea. And they exchanged his glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass. God was their glory, and they abandoned him and worshiped the calf. Had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach. When he said: "If you will forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me too out of this book of yours that you have written." And they despised the desirable land. This is the fifth charge, after the Red Sea, the desert, the outrage against Moses, and the calf at Horeb. For the spies, returning and speaking ill of the land, turned the others away as well, except Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh. And they grumbled in their tents. When the spies came and perverted the mind of the

And they were initiated into the rites of Baal of Peor. This is an idol of the Ammonites, called Kronos by the Greeks. And Phinehas stood up and made atonement. When he killed the Midianite woman together with the man who had committed fornication with her. The passage teaches us how much the piety of a single man can avail for

And they went whoring in their practices. The books of Judges and of Kingdoms teach this: how they were handed over at different times to different peoples — Moabites, Ammonites, Amalekites, Midianites, Philistines — and were disciplined by being handed over. And those who hated them ruled over them. Babylonians and Assyrians prevailed over the Israelites because of their transgressions. Many times he rescued them. But they embittered him by their counsel. He was sweet to them out of his love for humankind, but they compelled him to show himself bitter to them. And again he saved them, as the Savior he is; but they perished, having entangled themselves in works of destruction; and after doing this many times [?], they perished in the end. "Many times" resembles "How often

would I have gathered your children together"; and "And they were brought low in their iniquities" resembles "You were not willing." For while bringing discipline upon them, he again granted them his love for humankind; but they repaid him with hostility. And he gave them over to compassion in the sight of all who had taken them captive. He says this because of Cyrus, who released them from captivity, and Darius and Artaxerxes, who even gave money for building the temple. Alleluia. Psalm 106. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good. After the rejection of the Jewish people, he fittingly indicates the calling of the nations, which took place through the apostles. That is why he commands us to praise God and give him thanks for his great mercy. From east and west, and north and sea. And who are these gathered from the four regions of the world, if not all the nations, which had long been destitute of true religion and had not received even a drop of divine moisture, but were in great thirst? They found no way to a city to dwell in. For they had no good way of life, but were in great error. Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them. For they had neither the bread that strengthens the human heart nor the living water of which it was said: "Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst." And he led them on a straight way. Faith in himself, clearly. For he himself said: "I am the way." To go to a city to dwell in. He means the Church, or the heavenly

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies... for he satisfied the empty soul. And what soul is that, if not the soul of those of whom it was said: "Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them"? And he filled the hungry soul with good things. With the spiritual bread, clearly. Those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death. You would not be wrong to call idolatry and deeds done in godlessness the shadow of death; for these are what separate us from true life. And we were formerly in them, because we embittered God and provoked the counsel of the Most High. For though we ought to have contemplated the Maker of all things from the greatness and beauty of his creatures, and to have perceived his eternal power and divinity from the creation of the world, we, like blind men, living in darkness and the shadow of death, with the rational powers of the soul fettered and crippled, exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds and four-footed beasts. Bound in poverty and iron. Each is held fast by the cords of his own sins, impoverished of everything good and noble.

Because they embittered the words of God. By refusing to accept the divine law at all, and devoting themselves to the wise of this age. And they provoked the counsel of the Most High. And what was the counsel of the Most High, if not that he wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth

They grew weak, and there was no one to help. For no one had the power to destroy sin. And he saved them from their distresses. For what greater distress is there than to be enslaved to evil spirits in ignorance of God, in poverty of soul and the destitution of wickedness? And he burst their bonds. "Burst" shows the sudden and complete overthrow of sin. Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies. He has said the same thing a second time, in thanks for his benefits. For he shattered the gates of bronze. This signifies the Savior's descent even into Hades; by making it he flung open the gates of Hades, long closed to all with unbreakable bonds. For there was no way back for those who wished to return; but he himself said to those in bonds, "Come out," and to those in darkness, "Show yourselves." Their soul loathed all food. For there was no word able to nourish them. And the gates of death are the sins that lead to death. And let them offer him a sacrifice of praise. He turns the word to the holy apostles; for they are the ones who handed down to us the mysteries of the New Testament. He turned rivers into desert. He means the once well-watered, now reprobate race of the Jews. For those who had long wasted away with famine and lacked spiritual food he settled by those rivers. Fruitful land into a salt marsh. He means the synagogue of the Jews. For demons were the inhabitants of that earthly commonwealth, and ungodliness made it bear fruit. But the apostles dried it up with the salt of their teaching, of whom he says: "You are the salt
He turned the desert into pools of water. He means the people from the nations; for the prophecy is mixed, bringing in the persona of the two peoples: of the one, the rejection [?]

Contempt was poured out upon their rulers. He means the scribes and Pharisees. And he made them wander in a trackless place, where there is no road. For they wander, he says, not knowing him who said, "I am the way." And he helped the needy one out of poverty. And who is the needy one, if not the one of whom it was said, "Blessed are the poor in spirit"? And he made families like flocks of sheep. He counted as his own, he says, the flocks gathered from all the families. The upright will see it and rejoice. And who are the upright, if not those of whom it was said, "But blessed are your eyes, for they see"? And all iniquity will stop its mouth. "It is God who justifies; who is to condemn?" A Song. A Psalm of David. Psalm 107.

In this psalm too the Lord's coming to the nations is proclaimed. Since all the verses of the present psalm have already been interpreted in earlier psalms, it would be superfluous to use the same material again to interpret the passage before us. My heart is ready, O God. In this psalm too the Lord's coming to the nations is proclaimed. We have already given the interpretation of these verses at Psalm 52. Awake, my glory. His glory is the contemplative and practical disposition by which he is inclined toward moral virtue and the virtue of service. For your mercy is great above the heavens. So great is your mercy that it surpasses the height of heaven, and the rays of your truth flash everywhere, as prophets, apostles, and teachers water the earth with its drops. Be exalted above the heavens, O God. From the beginning up to this phrase, it is the same as in the fifty-sixth psalm, and from here to the end the same as in the fifty-ninth. And what was fitting has been said there.

I will be exalted, and I will divide Shechem. He promised with joy to divide the choice and select possessions of the Jews among the nations and to measure them out as an inheritance. For like a good father he rejoices in receiving and acquiring many sons. But he says these things symbolically and in riddles. For this place, called Shechem and also Sikima, lay at the valley of the nations. There Jacob, coming up from Mesopotamia with his children, settled, and there Hamor, the son of Shechem, fell in love with Dinah, Jacob's daughter, carried her off, and violated her. For Jacob's sons confronted him and slaughtered him along with all his people. Thus Sikima, the valley of the tents, became the property of the patriarch. So, in dividing this place among his sons, Jacob gave Joseph a choice portion, since, being young, he had taken no part in his brothers' deed. And for this reason measure

The present psalm points to the sufferings of Christ and to the punishments that were to come upon both Judas and the Jewish people itself. Whatever is said in the psalm in the form of a wish, one must understand that it is all said prophetically. For example, when it says, "Let the devil stand at his right hand," it means "will stand." For he does not pray for this to happen; he foretells what is going to happen because of that man's wickedness; and likewise in the other cases. "May these too," he says, "have accusers, and may these never leave them. And if they are judged, may they be condemned before them. But even if they call upon you," he says, "in the time of need, may it be counted to them as sin, as their sins are remembered. Cut short their days, so that, while they are still alive and watching, another may seize the office that they never truly bought. Then destroy them as well, so that the calamity passes on to their offspring: so that their sons are left orphans and their wife is given over to widowhood, and the sons, forced out and dragged away, pay the penalty for their fathers' transgressions." O God, do not pass over my praise in silence. As long as the churches of Christ, springing up everywhere, endure, God praises the Son in them. So Christ says to the Father: "Even if Judas, by betraying me, seems to hinder my praise, praise me nonetheless, bearing witness to my divinity, in which Judas did not believe, and so betrayed me." For the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful has been opened against me. The sinner is the devil, for he is a sinner in truth; the deceitful one is Judas; for both spoke against Christ. In return for loving me they [?] me... and they repaid me evil for good, and so on. Some words come from love, others from hatred, and others from neither. For he flattered him as his teacher, while by guile, as he thought, he worked toward betraying the teacher. Set a sinner over him. The sinner is Satan himself, the inventor of sin; and "set" stands for "is about to be set." And over whom, if not the traitor Judas? And let the devil stand at his right hand. In Zechariah too it says: "And the Lord showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and the devil was standing at his right hand to oppose him." But the devil does not oppose Judas. When he is judged, may he go out condemned. At the judgment to come, he says, he will have no word of defense. And let his prayer become sin. There are some whose very prayer becomes sin, as when gentiles approach idols or the creation, and Jews not through Jesus Chri-
[?] of those who pray to God; and of heretics who pray to a God who does not exist; and of those who pray in anger and amid wandering thoughts, or with a divided mind: the prayer becomes [?]

Let his days be few. For immediately after the betrayal he did away with himself by hanging, departed, and was seen no more. And let another take his office. He says this about Matthias, for he was reckoned as righteous and counted in the lot of the apostles. Let his sons become orphans. His sons are his thoughts, for they were orphaned of the grace of Christ. His wife is his soul, for it too was widowed, having fallen away from Christ through lawlessness. Let his sons be tossed about and wander and beg. For his thoughts, which we said are his sons, having wandered away from Christ, stretched out their hand toward love of money, toward silver, like the needy and beggars. Let the sin of his fathers be remembered before the Lord. "His" means "of the people": for he joins the lawless people to the betrayer. By the iniquity of the fathers he means the killing of the prophets, according to what the Lord said: that all the righteous blood shed from Abel to Zechariah the prophet will be avenged on this generation. And let the sin of his mother not be blotted out. By the mother of the impious people you will understand that wicked synagogue, which so often provoked the

Let them be before the Lord continually, and let their memory be utterly destroyed from the earth. God, he says, who always beholds all that they dared to do, will not grant him any mercy; and he speaks as if of all who have refused to believe. And since he is not speaking of Judas alone, he said "their memory" in the plural. You might also say, in another sense, that the fathers of Judas are those who begot him into betrayal. These would be the ones who urged him on with the silver: first Satan, who put it into his heart, and the rulers who have the wisdom of this age, of whom Paul says: For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. And let his memory be utterly destroyed from the earth. By "his memory" he means that of Judas; or, in another sense, that of those rulers who rose up against Christ. For not even their seed remained as a memorial [?]

Because he did not remember to show mercy. He did not want, he says, to receive the mercy which the Father gave to humankind, and above all to the lost sheep of Israel themselves. For he has put "to show" in place of "to receive." And he persecuted a man who was poor and needy. He means the Lord himself, who though he was rich became poor, so that we through his poverty might become rich. And one broken in heart, to put him to death. Instead [?]

And he loved cursing [?] and he clothed himself with cursing as with a garment. Since, he says, they have given up blessing me and curse me every day [?], as the children of the Jews do to this day, for this reason all the things foretold will happen to them. And it entered like water into his inward parts. For the evils surround them and flood over them not only from outside but also from within. And like oil into his bones. For oil keeps its moisture permanently. He speaks of an onslaught of evils: the water shows their violence, and the oil their permanence. By these, he says, let him be covered as with a garment and bound tight as with a belt. This is the work of those who slander me and speak evil against my soul. These are the fruits that will be harvested by those who took up hatred against me, and by the betrayer who served them. For since they called him an enemy of God and a lawbreaker, he fittingly said: of those who slander me before the Lord. And you, Lord, Lord, deal with me for your name's sake. These things too the Master, Christ, said in his humanity. For he fulfilled everything human except sin. He was born according to the law of nature: from a woman, as belongs to human nature, but, beyond that nature, from a Virgin. He received swaddling clothes and circumcision and nourishment from milk; he offered sacrifices, fasted, hungered, thirsted and grew weary; and so too he is recorded in the holy Gospels as praying continually. Here too, in his humanity, he calls on divine help. Deliver me, for I am poor and needy. This too we find said by him in the sacred Gospels. For when he was about to go to his passion he said: Now my soul is troubled. And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But [?] it was for this that I came to this hour. Like a shadow when it declines I was taken away. Like a declining shadow I came to the end of my life; and like locusts tossed about by the winds I lived, having no city, no village, no house, but moving now here, now there, even into the mountains, and sometimes running off into the desert. They saw me and shook their heads. He says this because when he was on the cross they shook their heads and said: You who destroy the temple, save yourself. And let them know that this is your hand. Here by "hand" he means the deed he accomplished by raising himself from the dead. They will curse, but you will bless; let those who rise up against me be put to shame. And indeed they were all put to shame, for they have no priest, nor

sacrifice, nor priesthood, nor oracle, according to the word of the prophet. But your servant will rejoice. Not even this word will force us to refer the passage to another subject; for Paul says: But he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; and Isaiah: Thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb to be his servant; and he himself says in the Gospels: The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve. Let those who slander me be clothed with shame. For what shame do the Jews not bear? They see their own holy places razed to the foundations; the tomb of the one they dishonoured and crucified worshipped; and his churches everywhere growing so greatly both in number and

I will give thanks to the Lord greatly with my mouth. "Giving thanks" here means the thanksgiving which the Son offers through the nations. And in the midst of many I will praise him. For through the Church [?]

PSALM 109. The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand. In these words he points to the Lord's birth according to the flesh, to his gospel word which has won lordship over all the nations, and to his ascension into heaven, with which the psalm begins, saying: The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand. Until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet. Who these enemies are, the Apostle shows when he cries out: When he abolishes the rulers and the authorities and the world-rulers, the last enemy, death, is abolished. The Lord will send out for you a rod of power from Zion. He means the gospel word that was sent out, which also overcame all the enemies. With you is the rule in the day of your power. By this he signifies either the time of judgment, when by divine power he will judge all, coming with his holy angels; or the time of his birth, which is also called a day of power. For the rule will be with you, since he holds authority over all things, even though he became man. In the splendours of your saints. "In the splendours of your saints" points to nothing other than those choirs of holy angels who, on the night Christ was born, cried out: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace. From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you. See how the Father claims as his own the birth of the Only-Begotten according to the flesh. For the Father says to the Son: before the birth of this visible world and of the radiant light, I have begotten you. Not that God has a womb; but because what is genuine, and not illegitimate, is by nature [?] from the womb. The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind. The

oath of God is his word, assuring those who hear it and giving each of them confidence that what he has promised and speaks will certainly come to pass. For God does not swear as a human being does; rather, his word serves us in place of an oath to confirm the truth, since everything he will not change his mind about will come to pass, the promise having the force of an oath. You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. Because Melchizedek was not anointed to the priesthood with oil, as Aaron was; and because he did not offer blood sacrifices; and because he was high priest of the nations; and because he blessed Abraham with bread and wine. The Lord at your right hand has shattered kings in the day of his wrath. By the day of wrath he means the time of judgment, when he will shatter the men who once ruled through the deceit of demons, shutting them up in the abyss. He will judge among the nations; he will fill them with the fallen. The nations of the unclean demons, he says, he will punish at the time of judgment and show to be full of the fallen, that is, of punishment in the lower parts of the earth. He will shatter the heads of many on the earth. This is like what he said through Isaiah: And I brought down their blood [?] to the earth. He will drink from the brook on the way. Scripture calls temptation a brook. "The way" signifies his journey on earth, during which he endured the passion, which is also referred to by the brook. Therefore he will lift up his head. "Therefore": for what reason, if not that he suffered in the flesh? Similar is the saying: He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death. I will give thanks to you, Lord, with my whole heart. The present psalm is spoken in the person of the apostles, who recount how many and how great were the works of the Saviour's dispensation. They teach these things to the new people too, while giving thanks for their own salvation; and for this reason it is also entitled [?]. In the council of the upright and in the congregation. By "the council of the upright" he means the people of the new congregation, to distinguish it from the old. For that one was not upright, since it always went astray in heart. Great are the works of the Lord, sought out in all his wishes. In the congregation of the upright all the wishes of God are sought out. For there is no commandment given by him that the congregation of the upright does not seek out and carry out, always striving eagerly to do his will. Thanksgiving and majesty are his work. By "works" he means what he accomplished in the dispensation. Let them be praised in hymns, since they are majestic. And his righteousness endures forever. He calls the gospel word righteousness, because it offered salvation equally to all people. The Lord is merciful and compassionate. Long ago he promised through his prophets in the [?] of the dispensation

he chose to fulfil. And what were the things he had promised, if not: Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the rest of the signs? And not only these, but also the calling of all the nations, which he accomplished in both word and deed. He gave food to those who fear him. He means the spiritual bread that came down from heaven. He will remember his covenant forever. The covenant with Abraham: that in you all the nations shall be blessed. The power of his works. The apostolic choir, he says, proclaimed to the people called to faith the power of Christ's works; that is, [?] the works which he is always working in his own

His seed will be mighty on the earth. By "seed" he means good deeds, which will have spiritual power to bring them into that land of the meek, so that they may receive the rewards of what they have done. Glory and riches are in his house. Do not count this glory and these riches among passing things; for nothing like them is found [?] among the saints. Light has dawned in darkness for the upright. Through knowledge and teaching. And who [did this], if not the apostolic choir, which [?] the ignorance of the nations through the preaching of the gospel? He will order his words with judgment. For one must not set the word of the mysteries before everyone simply and without discernment. And this is what the Lord said to them: Do not give what is holy to the dogs. He will not fear an evil report. For the fear of those who are punished does not touch the saints. He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor. Here too you will understand the poor to be those in need of the divine word, namely the nations, who, like farmers, sowed the spiritual word. For nothing prevents us from taking it in its historical sense as well. His righteousness endures forever, and so on. That is, the righteousness of the one who distributed the gospel
The sinner will see it and be angry. By "the sinner" he means the devil, who will also be indignant when the nations are saved, since he thirsted for the destruction of all. PSALM 112. Alleluia.

In this psalm the new people is taught to offer an unceasing hymn to the one who redeemed them; and at the same time it points to the calling of all the nations. Praise the Lord, you servants; praise the name of the Lord. The new people is taught that, even though

our Lord was taken up and is at the right hand of the Father, nevertheless the whole earth is full of him and enjoys his care. Who raises the poor from the earth. That is, the people of the nations. Who settles the barren woman in a house. The barren woman is the multitude of the nations, which has also become a spiritual house, since it has the Lord dwelling within it. And she has also become the joyful mother of many children. For she and her children were saved through faith in Christ. This also implies a certain contrast with the synagogue, which did not rejoice over its children, since they had been handed over to destruction. PSALM 113. Alleluia.

In this psalm too the calling of the nations is signified. And there is teaching here for those being saved, so that they may also know that the Old Testament is God's, and that the earlier salvation of the people of the circumcision came about through the Lord. [Judea became] his sanctuary [?]. When, he says, it was set free from slavery to the Egyptians, then Judea became his sanctuary. Yet he did not rule over Israel alone; now, he says, grace is given to all the nations. The mountains skipped like rams. As God showed himself among them, they leapt, as it were, at the salvation of Israel. What ails you, O sea, that you fled, and you, Jordan, that you turned back? Since these were without reason and without life, he himself makes [?] on their behalf

At the presence of the Lord the earth was shaken. Each of these things, he says, happened because of the Lord who appeared. He was the cause of the earth's quaking and of the parting of the sea. For it was he who flooded with an outpouring of water even the barren rock, which was deprived of all moisture and was so hard that it could not even be cut, commanding abundant springs of water to gush from it. So there is nothing surprising, he says, in what happened: the Maker commanded, and the sea was divided, the sheer rock gushed, heaven supplied manna, and the winds gathered the quail; and all the other things were done by him

Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory. He seems to be hinting at the falling away of the people of the circumcision, and to be giving them a prayer of confession, since they no longer have the divine power watching over them. So he teaches them to say: we are unworthy of the grace that every nation has been granted; but act for the sake of your name, which from the beginning was called upon us. Not as granting rewards for righteousness, but because you are the true God, unlike [?] the idols; and so he went on:

The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. In some copies this is the beginning of another psalm, so that it becomes the hundred and fourteenth. But we, following the Hebrew division, take these verses to belong to the hundred and thirteenth. For those being taught are the servants to whom he said, Praise the Lord, you servants, that is, the new people. Which Lord is it fitting to praise? Him, of course, who worked so many wonders for those who came out of Egypt; and with this they also learn what sort of gods the people of old had. For the idols not only had nothing in common with the God who works wonders, but did not even match the lowest of living creatures, which at least have perception. Those creatures are the works of God, but idols are products of human craft. And they are taught to say: May they become like them. They are not cursing human beings; rather, we learn what end awaits idolatry. For those who senselessly cling to idols will not differ from them at all in mind, so great is the harm done to them by the demonic power lurking within. May those who make them become like them. They will perish in this way, just like money and those who hoard it. The house of Israel hoped in the Lord. The nations say this: that just as he once saved Israel when it believed, so now too he will save the nations. For those who fear the Lord would be the nations. Once the house of Israel, that is, the whole multitude, and the house of Aaron and the house of Levi are set apart, who else can those who fear the Lord be but the people from the nations? May the Lord add to us, to us and to our children. For he is the one whose laws we keep. So that no one would think the law given through Moses belonged to some other god, before giving the law he handed down the account of the world's creation, through which he teaches that there is one God and that everything else is created. The dead will not praise you, Lord. He calls the dead those who serve demons, who do not have life in themselves, that is, the knowledge of the only God. Alleluia. PSALM 114.

In this psalm he signifies the struggle of those who follow the gospel way of life, their godly victory, and the crown that awaits them for their labours. I loved, because the Lord will hear the voice of my supplication. And whom did he love? The Lord God, with all his heart, with all his mind and with all his strength; and as the reward of his love he received the

And in my days I will call upon him. Which days, if not the days of struggle, when his soul was in danger? The pangs of death surrounded me. He points to the overwhelming afflictions that came upon him because of

his piety, which he also calls the pangs of death, the dangers of Hades, affliction and pain. But by calling upon God, he says, he rose above them. That is why at the beginning he said: I loved, because the Lord will hear the voice of my supplication. O Lord, deliver my soul. Above, he spoke in the singular: And I called upon him in my days. Now he teaches what the invocation was. And what is it, if not "O Lord, deliver my soul"? He said this knowing that, being merciful, he will hear him. And our God has mercy. Mercy is a feeling toward those brought low beyond what they deserve, arising in those disposed to compassion. Since we too have gone from glory to disgrace, having fallen from our life in paradise, God has mercy on us when he sees what we have become in place of what we were. For it was the voice of mercy that called to Adam: Where are you? Clearly meaning: from where have you fallen? The Lord guards the little ones. By "little ones" he means those reborn in Christ through the Holy Spirit, who are little ones according to Jesus' commandment, by turning and becoming like children. These the Lord guards, not allowing the enemies to attack them, because it is not yet their time for struggle. For by "little ones" he means those reborn through the Holy Spirit in Christ Jesus. In the plain sense, too, he himself guards babies in the womb: in so small a space and in so much moisture [?], where they can neither move nor breathe, he keeps them from suffocating, gives them movement and nourishment, and keeps them from dying of the cold when they come out of the warmth of the womb into [?] surroundings. Or it may be taken thus: Since I humbled myself like a little one and received the kingdom of heaven like a child, the Lord who guards the little ones saved me. And another way: Those who strive, according to Jesus' commandment, to turn and become like children, the Lord guards, keeping them untested, because it is not yet their time for struggle. But me, since I have grown beyond childhood, he humbled through great struggles, yet kept me undefeated. Return, my soul, to your rest. By his rest he means the dwellings above, which he will receive as the reward for his struggles. Again, the soul's rest is abstaining from sins. For he has delivered my soul from death. He means the death of sin. Fearing that he might somehow be brought down into it, he did not cease weeping and asking to escape it. For this reason his feet too, that is, the steps of his soul, stood firm in a godly stance, beyond the reach of any slip. By the land of the living he means the heavenly Jerusalem, where those who have struggled in God's service will hear, as the finest of victors: Well done, good and

PSALM 115. Alleluia. I believed, therefore I spoke. Having said, "I believed, therefore I spoke," he speaks as one who has pleased the Lord and has arrived in the dwellings above. He would not have put forward this statement unless he had been confident in God's promises, and these were full of mercy: "Blessed are those who weep now, for they shall rejoice." And if their eyes were full of tears, clearly they will receive their exultation in those dwellings. Paul quotes this phrase to the Corinthians, saying: "Having the same spirit of faith, according to what is written, 'I believed, therefore I spoke.'" For "with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth one confesses unto salvation"; "we too believe, and therefore we speak." By "spirit of faith" he means either the disposition that faith produces, or the Spirit supplied by God to the one who has faith. In harmony with "I believed, therefore I spoke" is also this: "Unless you believe, neither will you understand." First one believes, then understands, and after that speaks. "But when," he says, "having believed, I spoke great things, then, seeing myself as nothing, I was greatly humbled." Such is John's saying about Jesus: "He must increase, but I must decrease." For he decreased, not by losing any of the greatness he had, but by comparison with the surpassing teaching and way of life of Christ. So here too he said "I was humbled," not because his height was taken away, but because of a contemplation greater than himself. But I said in my ecstasy, Every man is a liar. Having come to be above man, he says, I disparaged everything human; for "ecstasy" signifies a change of state. Having said, he says, "I will be well-pleasing to the Lord," and then knowing that every man is a liar, for the reasoning of men is deceitful, I therefore humbled myself and disciplined myself harshly with hardships, lest I fall from such a standing. Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones. There will be no other repayment from us, he says, for what we have received from God, than to endure death for his sake, and in this way to imitate our own Master. And this death will indeed be among the most precious things

O Lord, I am your servant, and the son of your handmaid. Confidently he says that he is a servant, as the apostle does; and by "son of the handmaid" he refers to the earlier introduction through the law. You have burst my bonds. And what are the bonds but those of sin, as it is said: "For each one is bound fast by the cords of his own sins"? To you I will offer a sacrifice of praise. As one who has made progress, he declines the sacrifices made with blood, and promises to offer those of praise. I will pay my vows to the Lord. [?] By vows he means promises. And what did he promise, but, having taken the cup of the Lord, to call upon his name? [?]

Alleluia. PSALM 116. Praise the Lord, all you nations ... for his mercy has prevailed over us. The nations, he says, would not have obtained such a change, unless God's mercy had proved stronger than our sins. And the truth of the Lord endures for ever; for he has given the salvation that he promised through the holy prophets. This is what the blessed Paul says too, when he begins his letter to the Romans: "Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures"; and again: "I say that Christ Jesus became a servant of the circumcision for the sake of God's truth, to confirm the promises made to the fathers, and that the nations might glorify God for his mercy." Since, then, the God of all has fulfilled his promises, has given the salvation he promised, and has opened the springs of mercy to all, you who have come over from the Jews and you who have believed from the nations, blend together a harmonious hymn and repay your Benefactor. Alleluia. PSALM 117.

The new people, made up of Jews and of the nations, is taught that one must call upon one helper only, the incarnate Word of God himself, and seek from him in time of persecution every aid, the help sent down from heaven; that one must offer to him thanks for the victory, ask for the ways that lead through the virtues, and, besides all this, give thanks to the Lord who is called the stone, rejected by the builders but become the head of the corner. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever. Let the house of Israel now say. He bids them be the first to begin the thanksgiving, since they were the first to be called through the preaching of the gospel. Out of affliction I called upon the Lord, and he heard me and brought me into a broad place. The present verse teaches two things: first, that those who come to the faith must expect affliction, as in "If you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation"; and second, that when afflicted one should call upon no other helper than the Lord himself, who leads our affliction out into great spaciousness. For in return for small labors we shall receive great rewards. All the nations surrounded me ... They surrounded me like bees around a honeycomb, and in the name of the Lord I fended them off. For the people of God called on God alone, and by speaking his name fended off enemies both visible and invisible; but the men who plot against

them trust only in human rulers and powers. The phrase "all the nations" is hyperbole, for all the nations surrounded the whole of Judea. Or it resembles "In the mornings I destroyed all the sinners of the land," that is, the passionate thoughts brought in by demons, and the sophistical arguments they might launch. For these are [?] the nations. Sometimes one also destroys them by calling upon God, cutting off the impulses of passion and overturning sophistical arguments. Drones resemble bees, so that they escape the notice of those who do not know them; but they have no sting and make no honey. Having a larger body, they eat up the bees' work, and the bees band together and destroy them. The Church, then, is a bee; and the honey-maker is she who honors the wisdom of God above all, whose labors kings and common people take for their health, even though she is weak, according to the saying: "not having the preaching in the persuasive words of human wisdom." Yet she has her sting "in the demonstration of the Spirit" and of the power of God, possessing the word of faith, so that she destroys the heresies like drones by refuting them, cutting them off [?] from the truth. One is the bee that has honored the wisdom of God; but many have departed from the wisdom of God. They are not bees but drones, like bees, wishing to consume the honey of the one that truly exists; and they blaze up like fire among thorns. For those of the heresies kindle the shameful fire of lusts, as Paul says: "For the things done by them in secret are shameful even to speak of." And the Gospel interpreted the thorns as pleasures. The one who calls upon God overturns their arguments: "For his weapons are not of the flesh, but powerful for God, pulling down every height that is raised up against the knowledge of God." The voice of exultation and salvation is in the tents of the righteous. Since the spiritual enemies who at various times persecuted the people of God have now been destroyed, it is fitting that from now on the voices of exultation are heard, and nowhere else than in the [tents] of the righteous
The right hand of the Lord has wrought power. This is the voice of exultation that arose in the Church: to confess that the power of the Lord alone has saved those who struggled and made them higher

Open to me the gates of righteousness. By "gates of righteousness" understand advances in virtue, along which those travel who have endured the times of affliction. This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter by it. Those who walk by way of the virtues will arrive at that gate which leads to the very contemplation of the Lord. And what is this gate, but purity of heart? "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God."

The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner. You yourself, who for our sake became the rejected stone: the builders rejected you, but after the conversion of the nations you have become the head of another corner. And what is this [?] the two peoples into one new [man]

This is the day which the Lord has made. And what would this be but the day of the Lord's resurrection? And what day is this, but the day of salvation for all the nations, on which the rejected stone became the head of the corner? The word signifies the day of our Savior's resurrection, which has been named after him, namely the Lord's Day. O Lord, save now; O Lord, prosper now. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. The hymn of praise in Jerusalem also taught to whom this refers. As for "We have blessed you from the house of the Lord," the prophets say this to those who believe in Christ: "We will call you blessed," they say, "because you have become a spiritual house; for the Lord dwells in you." Join together in a festival among those that cover thickly. Join together in a festival. He bids those who have come to the faith to gather together and fill the divine tabernacle, so that because of their multitude they reach even to the horns of the altar. By "those that cover thickly" he means the cherubim that overshadow the mercy seat; for this is what "those that cover thickly" means, since "to cover thickly" is "to cover." And the cherubim covered the mercy seat with their wings. You are my God, and I will give thanks to you. They are taught to offer this thanksgiving to Christ the Savior

In this psalm he describes the way of life of the saints: the struggles, the afflictions, the contests, the uprisings of the demons, the countless thoughts they suggest, the snares, the traps; and not only these, but also the means by which they prevail: the law, the oracles, endurance, the alliance from above; and then, after the labors, the prizes, the crowns, the
Blessed are the blameless in the way. He who never sins in any way at all would be blameless; and indeed also

Blessed are those who search out his testimonies; they will seek him with their whole heart. For one must not fulfill the law at one time and become a transgressor at another. What gain is there in merely searching out his testimonies, if one does not seek God with one's whole heart? For those who work lawlessness have not walked in his ways. So the one who sins does not know the divine law; for to know it is to do it.

You have commanded that your commandments be kept diligently. O that my ways were directed to keep your statutes! Knowing that without help from above no one can become a keeper of the law, he achieves this for himself by prayer; "O that" stands for "may it be." I will give thanks to you in uprightness of heart. After the prayer he also sets down the part that belongs to free choice. And the beginning of salvation is confession. Do not utterly forsake me. Again he calls upon the alliance from above. By what shall a young man set his way right? Youth, he says, is full of many stumbling blocks. How then would one get past them, except by keeping God's words continually in memory? For meditation on the divine law is entirely both cleansing and protective. With my whole heart I have sought you. If the remembrance of God, he says, enables one to slip out of Satan's nooses, and I have devoted my whole mind to you, O God, then I am worthy not to remain outside your commandments. [?] Lest, he says, [?] anyone [?] with regard to what we shall say, using desire for the law, [?] has given lack of understanding; which turns the zeal of many to the opposite, so that in the very things in which they think they are doing right they have erred, as Solomon says: "There is a way that seems right to men, but its end comes to the depths of Hades." So whoever seeks God with half a heart, wishing to devote himself now to him and now to the world, he casts out of his own commandments like an unfit soldier. I have hidden your sayings in my heart. For unless one locks up God's commandments in one's heart as in a treasury, the evil one comes and snatches them away. He sins against God who, having been deemed worthy of more secret sayings that deserve to be hidden from the many, does not hide them from those from whom he should. For it is dangerous not only to speak falsehoods, but also to speak truths, whenever one proclaims at all what one should not. For pearls must not be cast before swine, nor holy things given to the

Blessed are you, O Lord; teach me your statutes. Perceiving the progress he has made by seeking God with his whole heart, he blesses him, already giving thanks for what he has been deemed worthy of; and he seeks to learn from him what meaning his statutes have. With my lips I have declared all the judgments of your mouth. What had to be hidden I hid, he says, and what had to be proclaimed I proclaimed: that all must stand before your judgment seat, so that we may receive according to what we have done. In the way of your testimonies I have delighted, as in all riches. He is taught what the riches are that accord with God; therefore he says: Nothing has held me [?] in the present [?] EXPOSITION [?] ON PSALM 118.

[?] not gold, not rank, not power; in place of all these, your testimonies are to me gladness and [?]. I will meditate on your statutes; I will not forget your words. Meditation does not stop at the words, but makes the one who has understood them do them. For it is not the hearers of God's statutes who are righteous before God, but the doers of them. In this way no one would ever forget them. Repay your servant; give me life. And what does he want to be given him in return for what he has contributed, but that his mind be enlightened so as to know the wondrous works of God? Unveil my eyes, and I will perceive wonders out of your law. I have not made the vanity of this life my own, he says; therefore I ask to receive [?] knowledge of the divine commandments. For some are known and some unknown: known, such as "You shall not murder" and the like; unknown, such as why infants are circumcised on the eighth day, or why sacrifices are offered for the newborn. You rebuked the proud. He who opposes the proud also rebukes the proud. The Lord therefore rebukes the proud. The Lord opposes the proud; the Lord also rebukes the proud. Remove from me reproach and contempt. Those who reproach in time of persecution will treat [me] with contempt [?] ... I ask, then, that [?] against me become vain

[?] by words. If, he says, I have come to utter helplessness in this way, being hard pressed, I ask to be saved from the lawbreakers according to your promise. For rulers also sat and spoke against me. For this reason, he says, I asked that the reproach be removed, since they made it their business to speak against me. Yet even when the rulers of injustice do these things, the servant of God does not depart from his statutes, having as his counselors for this the words of God, which he called statutes. Such a person accepts not a single wicked counselor. But the rulers of this age too, as in the case of Christ, gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ. Theirs is the wisdom of this age. My soul has cleaved to the ground. I have come to utter helplessness, he says, being hard pressed by the lawbreakers, and I ask to be saved according to your promise, which says: "And torrents will not engulf you."

[?] the servant of God does not depart from [his] statutes [?] ... his; [having] the words of God, which he called statutes [?] ... [?] ... gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ. Theirs is the wisdom of this age. My soul has cleaved to the ground. I have come to utter helplessness, he says, being hard pressed by the law[breakers] [?] ... your [promise], which says: "And torrents will not engulf you." I declared my ways, and you heard me [?] ... [?] ... so as to travel [this way], I shall be able to speak and discourse about the wonders in them. [?] ... My soul has slumbered from weariness. He teaches [?] ... that the spirit of weariness is not otherwise [?] ...

[?] So one must be sober and keep watch, because of the one who said, "Watch and pray." Remove the way of injustice from me, and with your law have mercy on me. I have chosen the way of truth. The one he asks from God; the other he contributes himself

Turn away my eyes from seeing vanity. Vanity is the mania for spectacles, the gazing at things one ought not to look at, and also improper imagination in the mind, which Paul too makes clear when he says: "in the vanity of their mind, being darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God." Notice that he speaks of "vanity of mind": when someone has a mind and does not use it to contemplate the truth, but hands it over to Satan, who binds it. Praying for this, then, he says: Turn away my eyes from seeing vanities. For this too is the grace of God. By the same author. The things that are beautiful in the body and appear fair to the eyes of the flesh he calls vanity. Establish your word for your servant unto your fear. Since the fear of God is necessary in all the commandments, like a tutor, he therefore prays that God himself set it over him. And "Remove my reproach" comes after setting it over him as a kind of guardian of the divine laws. He also confesses, reproaching himself, the things of which he was already conscious before. Establish your word for your servant. Since, being your servant, I fear you, and I wish to have fear rationally and in accordance with reason, establish your word unto your fear: the fear that is yours, not the fear by which you fear, but that by which I fear you. So that we may have neither fear without reason nor reason without fear. And God establishes his word unto his fear by confirming it through demonstration to the devout. For just as some have zeal, but not according to knowledge, so some have fear of God, but not according to knowledge. Remove my reproach, which I suspected. The prophet, having sinned as a man, makes entreaty, since he sees the reproach that follows at the divine tribunal after the resurrection, and he speaks the present verse. But you would not be saying this if you said, "Remove your reproach." For when I am reproached for Christ's sake, that reproach is not mine but Christ's; but when I am reproached for my own sins and do not repent, I ought not to say, "Remove from me my reproach, which I suspected, for your judgments

Behold, I have longed for your commandments; in your righteousness give me life. As his reward he asks for the righteous and virtuous life, since he has not only kept the commandments but is also lovingly disposed toward them, and fulfills them not for the sake of anything else, but for their own sake. And since the Son is the righteousness of the Father, it is the one who wishes to live in the Son who says this.

And let your mercy come upon me, O Lord. If I obtain your mercy, he says, and this mercy comes to me through your salvation, I will have boldness toward those who reproach me and rise up against me.
