And I will give an answer to those who reproach me, for I have hoped in your words. For I will say that one who holds such doctrines does not deserve to be reproached. The foolish, who are strangers to the faith, laugh at these doctrines, but I will show that they are full of understanding and wisdom. And I will give an answer, since I have hoped in your words. And do not take the word of truth utterly out of my mouth, for I have hoped in your judgments. Until my last breath, he says. If we live in a way unworthy of the good things we say, the [?] will take the word of truth out of our mouth.

And I will keep your law continually. I will be a keeper of your law, he says, not succeeding at one time and failing at another. Rather, I will fulfill it both in the present life, he says, and in the life to come. And I spoke of your testimonies before kings. Paul was such a man, and so was Peter, and so was the company of the apostles and of the martyrs. This will fit the martyr who is led before governors and kings for Christ's sake. It will also fit those who open their mouths before the kingly souls of the saints. For anyone who has not received from God a word for preaching the gospel with great power deserves to be ashamed, since a life lived according to the law produces boldness. And I meditated on your commandments, which I loved exceedingly. And I lifted up my hands to your commandments. Here he says that the hands are our practical activities. For action is the goal of meditating on the commandments. After taking up the word of the commandments, it is good to lift up the hands to do what the commandments require, not grudgingly or under compulsion but willingly, and after that to ponder and speak of them continually. Remember your word to your servant. And what is the word he asks him to remember, if not that he would be with them, according to the promise he had given them? That promise became their comfort in persecutions. This has comforted me in my humiliation. The Seventy: you will bring me back to life. This hope, which arose in me from your word, comforted and consoled me. Whenever hardships or danger overtook me, or the trial of death, or grievous illness, or loss of possessions, or persecution, or anything else that people consider hard, my hope in you was my comfort. For your saying has given me life. Nothing else makes a rational soul live its own life as the saying of God does. To the extent that the saying of God grows [?], as it is understood and received into a person's soul, to that extent the things of life also grow. And these are [?]

to live virtuously here, and after this it also gives eternal life. The proud transgressed exceedingly, but I did not turn aside from your law. For I lived by it and guarded my ruling faculty, so that no hidden, lawless word should arise in my heart. While they transgressed to the utmost, I did not transgress your law even slightly. I remembered your judgments of old, O Lord, and was comforted. For the righteous man remembers what will be rendered to each person from eternity to eternity, and so he is comforted and remains free of grief, saying: The sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us. I remembered the judgments you executed long ago on those who wronged Israel, and I was comforted. I knew that I too will not be forsaken in persecutions, and that everything happens to human beings according to God's judgment. Despondency seized me because of the sinners who forsake your law. Among sinners, some sin without the law, because they have never had any experience of laws at all, while others sin under the law by transgressing it. And a little later: For if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; and if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it. So we too ought to grieve over our brothers who sin, because they are like this, and to be disposed as this saint was. Your statutes were songs to me in the place of my sojourning. By the place of sojourning he means the present life, as in the verse: Knowing that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. There I rejoiced in harmony as I spoke your statutes, partly by contemplating them and partly by doing them. I considered your ways, and turned my feet to your testimonies. Since I devoted my whole mind to your commandments, he says, I walked for this reason in the [way] of the testimonies

I was prepared and was not troubled. He knew the saying: Child, if you come forward to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation. Because he meditated on this continually, he was not troubled when assaults came, since he had trained himself to bear them nobly. The cords of sinners have entangled me. And what were these cords, if not the evil thoughts through which they tried to throw him down from his stand before God? At midnight I rose to give thanks to you. Not only by day, he means, but also by night, in the very middle of the night, when sleep comes over people with the greatest pleasure, I continued to sing hymns to you and to praise your righteous verdicts. The divine Apostle did this too, with Silas. There, with his feet fastened in the stocks, amid abuse and scourging, he

blended hymnody with prayer and gathered the fruit of that good vigil, for he received a gift of God's generosity. I am a companion of all who fear you. The perfect would be a partaker of Christ, as it is said: For we have become partakers of Christ. But the present speaker, as a beginner, says that he is a companion of those who fear the Lord. He does not mean simply those who fear, but those who keep God's commandments because they fear. The keeping of the commandments is the sign of the fear of God. The earth, O Lord, is full of your mercy; teach me your statutes. He speaks prophetically of what will be: the whole earth will be full of those who fear the Lord. And he says that this will come about from no other source than your mercy. For you yourself do this out of mercy, giving yourself to be the teacher of human beings. You have dealt kindly with your servant, O Lord. The one who has been trained in the divine oracles is taught not to be insensible to God's benefits. He would not otherwise have been freed from sin and numbered among the servants of the Lord, unless some divine grace had brought these things about for him. Before I was humbled I went astray. Because of the sins I committed earlier, he says, I was handed over and humbled, and I suffered this by the righteous judgment of God. For this reason, having been handed over to discipline, I ask to be taught, so that I may know that the humbling came upon me out of kindness and for discipline.

You are good, O Lord. In all things, even when what happens is bitter, the righteous man says to God: You are good. The verse I will bless the Lord at all times is like this. And in your goodness teach me your statutes. He asks to be taught by the good God, because God's statutes are good, since they are applied according to each person's desert. Of them it is fitting to say: Your judgments have been justified, O God. The injustice of the proud has been multiplied against me. They carried their pride so far, he says, that the heart within them became — Their heart was curdled like milk. [?] you will be handed over to evil and wicked temptations [?]; by their life and conduct they humble [themselves], and they teach us to discipline the body and bring it into subjection, and not to travel the broad and spacious road of the proud but the narrow and hard one. For the heart of the saints is lean, but the heart of the proud is fat. It is good for me that you humbled me. It is as if he said: I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions and distresses, so that I may be found worthy of your statutes, since I seek what cannot be learned in any other way. The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver pieces. The beginner is taught how great an honor a human being has been granted. Your hands have made me. Another honor is

that he is able to receive and contain his mind. Give me understanding, and I will learn your commandments. Quite fittingly, after the thanksgiving for his creation comes [the request] for the intellectual power that enables one to understand the

Those who fear you will see me and rejoice. He teaches that he will not keep the gift to himself alone; it will reach all who fear the Lord as well. For the righteous man is pleasant only to the pious, when he is seen with the eyes and in his speech and in the thoughts of the wisdom he has. To others he is burdensome even to look at, because his life is unlike that of others and his paths are different. That is why he says: They will rejoice, because I have hoped in your words. I know, O Lord, that your judgments are righteousness. We are taught that God brings everything upon us justly. So we must not make light of his disciplines but rather fall down before him, and through keeping the law beg for his mercy. Let your mercy be for my comfort. The Son is the Mercy of the Father, and he comforted our hearts when they were tyrannized by Satan. Or take it this way: I ask that, according to your word, your mercy may be comfort and consolation to me your servant. For many who obtain comfort are deceived into thinking that they have it from their own good sense. So that I may not be led astray as they are, let your mercy come to me your servant, according to your saying. Let your compassions come to me, and I will live. Do as you promised, he says, and give comfort, having compassion on your servants. Let the proud be put to shame, because they unjustly acted lawlessly against me. If I obtain help from you, he says, then the wicked, that is, the demons and the people who are enemies of the truth, will be put to shame. But when they are put to shame, I will not be puffed up; instead I will meditate on your commandments. Let those who fear you turn to me. May I receive teaching from your servants. And that teaching will be the kind that knows how to turn souls around, because they are rich in the fear of you. Let my heart be blameless. If after all this he already had a blameless heart, he would not say, Let my heart be blameless. Similar to this is: Create a clean heart in me, O God. For only when I keep God's commandments blamelessly will I not be put to shame. My soul faints for your salvation, and I have hoped in your word. The prophet teaches us to long for the word and to be passionately in love with God's salvation. And what else could this salvation be but the coming of the Lord? I have hoped in your word. Take this to mean the promise. The divinely inspired Scripture is also called an oracle. So it is not only the one who awaits the divine promise who faints,

and who looks for release from the evils pressing on him, but also the one who reads the divine oracles and longs to understand their meaning exactly, and receives comfort and delight of soul [from] the

My eyes have failed for your saying. For our Lord Jesus Christ, he means. We have him as an advocate with the Father, as the apostle says, and he is the atonement for our sins. Saying, When will you comfort me? For when the Word comes to dwell in me, then I am comforted. For I have become like a wineskin in the frost. The righteous, though living, become more like the dead through their afflictions, so that they resemble wineskins rather than human beings. They shrivel as if frost had congealed around them, though they choose [?] what is warm and active. By the same author: A man becomes a wineskin in the frost when he has wasted away his own flesh and allows nothing fiery or full of desire to remain in himself, but has, as it were, chilled it. How many are the days of your servant? For the days of human beings on earth are few. In them he prays that Satan may soon be crushed under his feet, so that his soul may be made subject, once the divine Word has come to be in it. The lawless have told me idle tales. By the teachings he means either the old wives' fables of the Jews, or the commandments of men and the nonsense of the wise of this age. All your commandments are truth; they have persecuted me unjustly; help me. He knows that at the divine tribunal he will receive recompense for the injustices he has suffered, and so he is eager to see that time. They almost made an end of me on the earth. Very nearly, through their persecution. Give me life according to your mercy, and I will keep the testimonies of your mouth. The mouth of God is the prophets, who served his testimonies, commandments and statutes. Forever, O Lord, your word endures in heaven. As he makes progress he takes hold of loftier doctrines too. He recalls the eternal Word of the Father, all but saying, In the beginning was the Word, and he recalls the ordering of the universe, clearly [declaring] the whole creation to be his servant

Your truth is from generation to generation. There are two generations that received God's truth: the Jewish people, who had the law and the prophets, and the Church. So God's truth is not for generations in general, but for the first generation and for the second. The other nations have gone astray. But when the first generation also cast out the truth and said, Away, away with such a man from the earth, the truth passed from that generation to this one. You founded the earth, and it endures. The earth has been founded on this truth.

For all who are saved from the earth are built on this cornerstone, which has been laid as a foundation. That is why the earth endures, since it has an unbreakable and secure base and foundation. Moreover, the truth enlightened the earth and made it day, when God shone forth

By your ordinance the day endures, for all things are your servants. This day does not change or come to an end, as the enlightenment under the Old Scripture did, since that was established only until the time of reformation. All these things were brought into existence by God. Since he is Creator and Provider, all things are his servants.

If your law had not been my meditation, I would have perished in my humiliation. When evil thoughts assailed me, he says, and the opposing powers made war on me, I would have perished, had your law not become my support. I will never forget your statutes, for by them you have given me life. By your laws I will see [?], he says, for I will have life in them, just as you told me: the man who does them will live by them. So only the righteous man is alive, even if he seems to have died, and the unrighteous are dead, even if they appear to be alive. For the righteous have within themselves what sustains life, namely righteousness. Those who lack it resemble lifeless things, which are moved not by themselves but from outside. I am yours; save me. With I am yours we should understand: I am your servant, I am your son by grace, I am your

Sinners lay in wait for me to destroy me; I understood your testimonies. That is, I meditated, and through meditation on you I made their plot come to nothing. I have seen the end of every consummation; your commandment is exceedingly broad. By consummation he means the plotting of the demons. I saw its end come to nothing, and then the commandment became broad for me. This belongs to someone who has passed through every stage of progress to the goal of virtue and is crossing over to the perfect good, laying down many beginnings and ends. For the completion of an earlier improvement is the beginning of the next, as in the verse: When a man has finished, then he begins. How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all day long. Whoever says and does everything according to the law meditates on the law of God. In the first psalm, however, he added the night to the day as a time of meditation for the one who will be blessed. For we said that human life here is mixed. That is why we now have day and night, but night will not follow for those who have become holy. So the one who is making progress spends the day when he lives according to the law, and the night when he does not meditate with his whole heart [and] does not do anything according to [?]. From every evil way I have kept back

my feet. For keeping the divine law means fulfilling it in deeds. I have not turned aside from your judgments. I always remembered the divine tribunal. How sweet your sayings are to my throat! They are sweet because of the rational delight they give. But [they are sweeter] than honey, and by honey all the pleasant things known among human beings are meant. Your law is a lamp to my feet. Whoever walks in the light of the divine law makes his way through life straight and without stumbling. I have been humbled exceedingly. Either by the attacks of spiritual enemies, or by the austerities he practiced privately and by his own choice. I hated the lawless, but I loved your law. He means the wise of this age and the leaders of the heretics. Depart from me, you evildoers. He means either evil thoughts or the teachers mentioned earlier. Help me, and I will be saved. For although he said, You are my helper and my protector, he still needs unceasing help. As long as we are here, the words I will be saved are not yet fulfilled. But when we live with God's angels, then our meditation on the statutes will also be face to face, not in shadow but in truth. You have set at naught all who depart from your statutes. For this is the end that awaits those who set aside God's law. I counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors; therefore I loved your testimonies. [Transgressing means] wanting to trample on the divine law. Nail my flesh with the fear of you. Nail means fix. Fix my flesh in purity, then, he says. Only in this way could anyone say with Christ: I have been crucified with him. For I was afraid of your judgments. That is, of the divine law. For no one commits sin without first placing himself outside the fear of God. My eyes have failed for your salvation. For the divine appearing, he means, through which he hoped that he himself and the whole human race would be saved. And for the saying of your righteousness. Even if some, transgressing and not keeping fear of you before their eyes, have set your law aside, I made it my one concern at all times and kept it continually in my meditation. I am your servant; give me understanding, and I will know your testimonies. Let the one who is in no way a slave to sin say: I am your servant. As the wages of his service he asks for the understanding that God gives and that is stored with him as in a treasury. For there is a spirit of wisdom and understanding, and the other gifts of good things that follow. Distinguishing it from another kind, he says in Proverbs: Good understanding gives

favor. If all understanding were good, he would not have added the word good. It is time for the Lord to act; they have scattered your law. I have done judgment and righteousness; but there will one day be a time for you, O God, to act as well, that is, to execute judgment and righteousness against those who have scattered your law. Therefore I have loved your commandments more than gold and topaz. This agrees with The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver pieces, and with Take instruction and not silver, and knowledge rather than refined gold. For wisdom is better than precious stones, and nothing valuable is worth as much as she is. Therefore I was guided toward all your commandments. What does therefore refer to, if not to meditating on the law continually? And it will give understanding to infants. By infants you should understand those held in ignorance, who are like babies. Your word, he says, fills them with understanding as they are illuminated by your light. I opened my mouth and drew in breath. The sayings need to be opened up. That is why the Savior opened the minds of the disciples so that they could understand the Scriptures. And the understanding given through the words guards against the deception that comes through pleasure or glory. Look upon me and have mercy on me, and so on. Just as you have decided, he says, to look upon those who love your name and to grant them your close care, so grant me that same care and that same mercy. Direct my steps according to your saying. According to his saying, God directs the steps of one who is passing from vice and ignorance to virtue and knowledge. For right reason guides such people. Those who do not commit sin are not slaves of sin. Redeem me from the false accusation of men. By the false accusation of men he means the teaching of the heretics and that of the wise of this age. Joseph and Susanna experienced this literally. Figuratively, however, he calls the evil powers men, and only God can redeem us from their false accusation. Make your face shine upon your servant. He longs to behold the coming of the Lord, for he is the exact imprint of the Father. And teach me your statutes. He means the New Covenant, through which God the Father has justified those on the

My eyes ran down with streams of water. I shed a flood of tears lamenting those who transgress your law. You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is upright. He gives the reason why he wept for those who transgress God's law: because God has threatened those who transgress it with punishment at the divine tribunal,

and he had already solemnly declared this from that point on. "You commanded your testimonies in righteousness," and so on. Were not the testimonies you commanded, with heaven and earth and certain others as witnesses, righteousness and the clearest truth? But not [?] … that is, the perfectly straight rules of your judgments make your righteousness known. Your testimonies, then, are the divine Scriptures: they are righteousness with respect to the moral precepts, and truth with respect to the contemplation of their words. "Zeal for you has wasted me away, because my enemies have forgotten your words." What zeal I took up whenever I saw someone who had forgotten your words! And it was not mere zeal; it made me waste away [?] with zeal for you whenever I saw people forgetting your words. The disciples remembered this zeal, which a psalm speaks in the person of the Lord: "For zeal for your house has consumed me." "Your word is thoroughly refined by fire." The word of God has been thoroughly refined by fire and tested [?], and no trial can refute it. And whoever has this fire-refined word judges all things but is himself judged by no one. "I am young and despised." He is young who is being taught the rudiments of the divine words, and despised because he humbles himself. "Your righteousness is an everlasting righteousness." For among human beings righteousness awards justice to the one on trial for a short time, but the righteousness of God renders a judgment that is everlasting. "Affliction and distress have found me." Not even in hardships, he says, did they neglect to meditate on your

"Your testimonies are righteousness forever." The testimonies you have given me, he says, are not useful for a short time only; they are righteousness forever, and they justify whoever draws near to them in his inward disposition. "Give me understanding, and I shall live." For the righteousness we practice in the present is repaid not in our few days but forever. And I shall live, he says, if you give me understanding, for the foolish person does not enter that blessed life. We must therefore ask for understanding from the one who gives it to all who ask him with their whole soul. "I cried out with my whole heart." The first time: "I cried out with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord; I will seek out your statutes." The second time: "I cried out to you; save me." For what I spoke in the ruling part of my soul was nothing other than God. So, having called on you mightily, I mightily promise to keep your testimonies. "I rose before you at an untimely hour and cried out." By "untimely hour" he means darkness, or the confusion of affairs. What he is saying is this: Although the lawless do everything in confusion, I [?] much in your law

"You are near, O Lord." God says elsewhere: "I am a God who is near, and not a God far off, says the Lord." For the power of God is everywhere, by reason of creation and providence. "Judge my cause and redeem me; give me life for the sake of your word." By "word" he means the promise, for he promised to come and save us. "Salvation is far from sinners." Which the rulers of this age greedily seized [?]. "For they have not sought out your statutes." This is why they persecute the righteous: they have set themselves far from the divine law. "Your mercies are many, O Lord." I knew, he says, that the commandments you solemnly laid on us are firm and immovable. He shows this also in the verse above: "From the beginning I knew from your testimonies." "I saw those without understanding, and I wasted away." Whenever I saw anyone who did not understand, I wasted away over such a person from zeal for godliness. "See how I have loved your commandments, O Lord." For you will see in me the marks of good works. I did not merely keep them; I loved them, with nothing forcing me toward them. Yet I beg your mercy no less, so that I may live. "The beginning of your words is truth." This was given as the first of your commandments: to be truthful in all things, in deed, in word and in thought. "Rulers persecuted me without cause." The rulers of every age, he says, afflicted me, being enemies of the truth. But I do not fear the afflictions they bring, because I fear your word. And what word is this, if not: "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna"? "I will rejoice over your sayings like one who finds much spoil." He says that he obeyed the divine words not out of fear alone but also with joy, the kind of joy one feels at great wealth. And keeping the commandments with joy is firmer. Having mentioned the enemies in pursuit, he fittingly mentioned spoils as well. For even if I had slain and despoiled them all, he says, I would not have valued it as highly as your words. (Cord.) Which words? Those Paul speaks of: "For we were the first to believe the oracles of God," meaning the Jews. "I hated injustice," and so on. For I do not, as they do, fend off a corpse [?] and then loathe the spoils I have taken. The only profitable thing is to loathe injustice. That is why I loved your law, once I had understood it as I ought, never dragging it down to

earthly things. For since we have been raised with Christ, we seek the things above, not the things on earth. "Seven times a day I praised you." Throughout his whole life the righteous person, being enlightened, will live in a perfect day that no night interrupts. And he praises God seven times because he has risen above the world, having passed beyond the world that was made in six days. Since he has also come to be in the paradise of God and has contemplated the principle of God's creation and providence, he gives thanks for the judgments of God's righteousness, according to which God fashioned and provides for each thing in its own varied way. He means unceasing praise. He says: I continually remembered your judgments, which you justly brought about, casting out the greedy rulers and redeeming those who had been wronged. "Let my supplication draw near … Let my petition come in before you, O Lord." Notice the good order of the divine words. First comes "let it draw near," then the greater thing, "let my petition come in," since drawing near comes before coming in. For someone who draws near a house goes in, if he is a friend of the master. What he called a supplication he now calls a petition (axioma), from the verb "to request" (axioun). But perhaps, just as there are worldly dignities (axiomata) of rank, so there are dignities of the soul as well? For being an apostle of Christ is a dignity, and the ranks and orders of the Church are dignities. Possessing the virtues, or even one of them, is also a dignity of the soul. Whoever has such a dignity [?] the present things

"May my lips belch forth a hymn." Belching generally happens to those who are full. The divine word, then, knows of a spiritual food. And the Word himself says that he is bread: "For I am the bread of life that came down from heaven"; and he also says: "Whoever eats my flesh has life in himself." When we have eaten him, we belch forth a hymn. Such a belching I pray to be granted. And that is impossible unless you teach me the

"May my tongue utter your sayings." He prays that whatever he says may be a word of God, as in: "Open your mouth with the word of God." Such a person speaks no idle word. That is why Paul says: "For 'You shall not murder, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal,' and any other [?] …" (Rom. 13:9).

the salvation. For most people long for salvation according to the flesh. But God's salvation is to be saved in him, to rest in him, to inherit the holy things. For this is the salvation of God: eternal life. Moreover, the name Jesus means "salvation of God," for he was sent to us for salvation. Whoever wishes to journey toward the longing for him will meditate

"My soul shall live and shall praise you." He is speaking of the life to come. For our life is hidden with Christ in God. Then I shall truly praise you, and then your judgments, now made famous, on those you judge will help me [?]: the righteous without torments, and the one who needs them through torments. "I have gone astray like a lost sheep." After speaking of himself as one who has accomplished good works, he again calls himself a straying sheep, practicing humility, according to the Lord's saying: "When you have done everything, say, 'We are unprofitable servants.'"

The people in Babylon sing the first Song of Ascents to God, distressed at the length of the captivity and praying to be set free. "In my affliction I cried out to the Lord … O Lord, deliver my soul from unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue." How could the lips of the Babylonians not be unjust, when they have professed idolatry? And that same tongue may well be called deceitful, since it says nothing straight about God. "What shall be given to you, and what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue? The sharpened arrows of the mighty one." What more do you ask to be given to you, he says, or what else do you want added to you against the deceitful lips? Arrows full of fire, kindled by the mighty one. He is pointing to the punishment that was soon to fall on the Babylonians. "Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged." He makes another request of God: to be set free from his life as a sojourner. "I have dwelt among the tents of Kedar." Kedar is a region in the desert lying to the east, stretching as far as the borders of Persia; the people of the Saracens live there. "My soul has long been a sojourner. With those who hated peace I was peaceable." It is the wickedness of the Babylonians to make war for no reason on those who live at peace. The exception would be when judicial punishment is required, such as God ordered against the Canaanites and Amorites when he forbade friendship with them. But the wicked will not be reconciled with the peaceable, because they loathe godliness. "When I spoke to them, they made war on me without cause."

between Babylon and Jerusalem. [?] … and cut off in the midst of the mountains, he prays that help may come to him. Hearing him, the prophetic Spirit declares: "The Lord will guard your coming in and your going out." "I lifted up my eyes to the mountains … My help comes from the Lord, who made heaven and earth." To show God's power, he says, "who made heaven and

"May he not let your foot be moved, and may he who guards you not slumber." Hold on to this hope, and you will be saved. The words "does not slumber" do not point to the toil of those who guard armies and cities and flocks. Rather, "he who guards Israel will neither slumber nor sleep" shows that the Divine is beyond passion. He seems to slumber when we are shaken by the unstable affairs of life and by the plots laid against us. "May the Lord guard you; the Lord is your shelter at your right hand." He said this also in Psalm 15: "I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken." And here again he says that, being at your right hand, he will shelter you, guard you, and count you worthy of all his providence. A Song of Ascents. 121.

The third song brings good news to those still on the road: their arrival at the house of God. That is why it cries out: "I was glad when they said to me, 'Let us go to the house of the Lord.' Our feet were standing in your courts, O Jerusalem." This is the voice of the old, who had also endured the captivity, recounting how their feet, now on the journey, once stood in Jerusalem long ago. "Jerusalem, built as a city." Long ago, he says, it was a true city, not scattered here and there, but so well fitted together that, through the joining and harmony of its buildings, it seemed to be a single house. "For there the tribes went up." All the tribes, he says, having come out of Egypt by the power of the Lord, hastened to this city to bear witness, that is, to give thanks to the God of Israel. "To give thanks to the name of the Lord." For these things he fulfilled his wonderful promise, and he says that thrones of the house of David were established there. For David also prophesies a kingship over all, speaking not of the rule of one person but of a shared rule exercised by the best and most godly. Through them the kingdom of David is restored by the grace of Christ, who gave it to the twelve apostles, who sit on twelve thrones judging Israel. "For there thrones were set for judgment." And according to the history, the palaces were there, and the thrones

of the priests, so that the city was adorned as if with a double crown and diadem. But now everything has fallen, and only the faintest remnants of its former prosperity remain. "Thrones over the house of David." In this city, he says, that is, Jerusalem, royal thrones were set up to judge with just judgment. David was the first to rule from them, and after him his descendants according to the flesh. That is why he calls it the house of David. "Pray for the things that make for peace for Jerusalem." Now that you have learned, my friends, what Jerusalem once was, pray for her peace, seeking nothing other than what contributes to her peace. "Let there be peace in your strength, and abundance in your towers." That is, in your palaces. I wish you good things, he says, for the sake of those who live in you, who are neighbors and brothers. For the old pray this for Jerusalem: that there may be peace within her walls. By "strength" he means the walls; or, in another sense, those within her

The fourth song contains the prayer of those who over many years were making the journey home. Worn out on the road, they ask God for mercy and compassion, since they had been despised by the nations. That is why the Spirit cries out to them in comfort, saying: "Reproach to those who prosper." "To you I lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in heaven. Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hands of their masters." The eyes of those who have the spirit of slavery that leads to fear look to the hands of master and mistress; but the eyes of one who has the spirit of adoption look to the Lord God. "Have mercy on us, O Lord, have mercy on us." The repetition shows how fervent the request is. We ask for mercy not as people who deserve it, but as people who are deeply disgraced.

Those who have set foot in the land of Judea sing the fifth song, sending up prayers of thanks for their rescue from captivity and from the enemies along the way. A Song of Ascents. 124. "Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion."

They sing the sixth song when they have reached the very mountain they longed for. Then, seeing that the city has no walls, they pray, he says, that the Lord's help may become its wall; and they are confident of escaping the plots of their enemies. And from that same help

of God once more, since he does not let the rod of sinners rest on the lot of the righteous and of his saints. "Peace upon Israel." For the peace that surpasses all understanding is given only to the one who has understanding. And also, now that their enemies have perished, these [enjoy] peace
Those who have gained the security of their redemption by coming to be in the city itself sing the seventh song. And they plead for the rest, those still in Babylon, that they too may be redeemed.

"When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted." These things are prophesied of the apostles, as said about themselves and about those among the nations. For in David's time there was no captivity. Perhaps, then, he is speaking of a spiritual captivity. For the words "they will say" show prophetically what is to come. "Then they will say among the nations, 'The Lord has done great things,'" and so on. And this has made us much talked of [?] among all. For everyone marvels at God's mighty deed in freeing us from that bitter slavery. And we too cry out, for we are not unfeeling, even though we have not yet received back the rest of our people. For them we plead, saying: "Turn back our captivity, O Lord, like torrents in the south." They are pointing to the great multitude that remained in Babylon, and to its return, likening them to the stream of the Egyptian river. For by "south" he means the desert. "Those who sow in tears shall reap with rejoicing. They went on their way weeping." To those who prayed for the remnant, the prophetic Spirit answers that if they weep for those in Babylon, those too will return. A Song of Ascents, for Solomon. 126.

The eighth song is sung when the foundations of the temple had already been laid and they hoped the fortification would be unshakable. So it covertly prophesies the temple's coming fall once again, under Roman rule. It also adds a prophecy about the Church of Christ. It is sung by Solomon in a prophetic sense, just as there are psalms of Zechariah and Haggai. And the eighth song is fittingly the beginning of the New Covenant. "Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain." He says such things because the Jews were proud of how solid the building was. "When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord is sons." Do not be proud of the temple, he says, as though your inheritance

were given to you in it. For it is not. But when he gives rest to his beloved ones from the former people, that is, the prophets, then he will give the inheritance to their sons. And who could these be but the disciples? (Cord.) For the divine promise, and the blessing concerning children, has been granted as a kind of reward to those who have hoped in him. "The reward of the fruit of the womb." The fruit of the womb would be the salvation of the spirit, as in: "We have been in labor and have given birth to a spirit of salvation, which we have brought about upon the earth." As the reward of this fruit, and as an inheritance, adoption will be given. "Like arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the sons of those who have been shaken off." By "shaken off" he means those cast away from the former people. Their sons, that is, the apostles, became arrows of the Mighty One, and through them he shot down the opposing powers. "Blessed is he who fulfills his desire from them." He calls blessed those who will benefit from their teaching. "They shall not be put to shame when they speak with their enemies in the gates." He clearly points to the coming of the preaching. A Song of Ascents. 127.

The ninth song calls blessed the one who has come in the fear of God. And fittingly, after the appointing of the apostles, it calls blessed those who believed. "Blessed are all who fear the Lord … Your wife shall be like a flourishing vine." To the one who fears the Lord is given as a gift not just any wife, but one adorned with good fruits. For a good wife is a good portion. "And may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life." The spiritual good things, clearly: "What eye has not seen," and the rest. "And may you see your children's children. Peace upon Israel." He is speaking of the promises. For just as offspring are the first fruits of a soul that loves God, so the promises are its second fruits. A Song of Ascents. 128.

The tenth song teaches about the many persecutions of Christ's people, and that they will leap over them all, always proving stronger than those who plot against them. He says this because the persecutions began at the very start of the preaching. "Many times they have made war on me … The righteous Lord has broken the necks of sinners." For all the persecutors are evil, and they will come to an evil end. A Song of Ascents. 129.

The eleventh song contains a prayer of martyrs and teaches confession to the new people. It clearly proclaims the propitiation of virtue [?], which is Christ. For it is said of him: "And he is the propitiation for our sins." "Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord …"

"Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplication." By the ears of God we understand also the angelic powers, through whom our supplications come in to God. "If you should mark iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who could stand?" Repeating "Lord, Lord" is the mark of one who marvels at the greatness of God's love for humankind. He says that propitiation comes from that love, not from our good deeds. "For your name's sake I have waited for you, O Lord." These are the words of those who come not for some spiritual need but for the sake of the holy name itself. So they run with endurance the race set before them and at no time turn away from God and from what pleases him

"From the morning watch until night let Israel hope in the Lord." For we must hope in the Lord even when things are grim. Not only at the morning watch, when present things are bright [?], but all the way through dark circumstances. And when the true light rises, the discerning mind receives from God an increase of bright things and release from grim ones. Let him hope, for mercy is with him as in a spring, and comes from him, since he is redemption itself and the propitiation that thoroughly cleanses sins with great sufficiency [?]. A Song of Ascents. 130. Argument. The twelfth song teaches one who has been counted worthy of propitiation not to grow proud, trusting in his own improvement, but to be humble. "O Lord, my heart was not lifted up … nor did I walk among great things or among things too wonderful for me," and so on. Against pride, he says, the opposite virtue is fitting, even to excess. The Savior taught this too, saying: "Unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven." He speaks of weaned children to indicate distress. For the weaned child does not leave its mother, though it grieves at being deprived of milk. In the same way, he says, when I was in misfortune I too always prayed to God. If I were not so, may I pay the utmost penalty. A Song of Ascents. 131. Argument. The thirteenth song contains a prayer for David. Since the propitiation obtains forgiveness of sins for all, the prophetic Spirit must also speak of David along with the rest of those who are saved: "O Lord, remember," repaying him according to his meekness. For just as he in his meekness forgave Saul the wrongs done to him, so forgive him his offenses as well. "Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness: how he swore to the Lord and vowed to the God of Jacob," and what follows. For he had learned from the Holy Spirit that the Lord would come to dwell among human beings.

…granting forgiveness of the many sins. Hoping that he himself would be saved through it, he hastens to learn when it will be, where it will happen, and in what manner he will come. In his longing to know these things he put himself through such hardship that he refused every bed, renounced his house, and lay on the ground before God, facing the sanctuary, having sworn an oath not to rise before he had learned them. Taking pity on his earnestness, God grants his request, as one who had sworn once and would not lie. So he went on: “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah.” This is Bethlehem. And what is “it” but the coming of the Lord that was to be? “We found it in the fields of the forest.” For the cave in which Christ was born is in the plains, that is, in the fields. “We will go into his dwellings.” This signifies the churches that would come to be in due time. “We will worship at the place where his feet stood.” He means the Mount of Olives, where everyone who passes by worships. “Arise, O Lord, into your rest.” They are urging on his ascension into heaven. “You and the ark of your holiness.” By the ark of holiness he means his holy flesh. “Your priests shall clothe themselves with righteousness.” No longer, he says, with robes according to the law, but with righteousness itself. And Christ is righteousness. “For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your anointed.” Along with your kindness to all people, remember David too, you who made him turn back on account of his sin. For the one who came from him according to the flesh is a servant, having taken the form of a servant. “The Lord swore truth to David.” And where did he swear? When he said to him: “And it shall be, when your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, that another shall arise from your seed, who shall come from your body. And I will prepare his kingdom forever. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish his kingdom forever. I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me.” “If your sons keep my covenant.” He plainly proclaims the covenant that was to come [?] — and had the sons of David according to the flesh kept it, they would not have fallen from the kingdom prepared for them. “This is my rest forever.” For even if the ancient temple lies desolate because of the madness of the Jews, yet there again the places of the cross, of the resurrection and of the ascension have been counted worthy of divine grace. “I will abundantly bless her provision.” For each one [?] of such people, being the seed of the righteous, does not

lack bread. It is also written, “Her widow,” meaning, clearly, the one without a protector. “Her poor I will satisfy with bread”: those who became poor for God's sake, and with spiritual bread. “Her priests I will clothe with salvation.” Again, Christ himself is the salvation, who was also named righteousness above. “There I will make a horn spring up for David.” At the time when salvation appears, clearly the glory of David will spring up. “I have prepared a lamp for my anointed.” This he says about John, in accordance with what was said by the Lord: “He was the burning and shining lamp.” A Song of Ascents. Psalm 132.

The fourteenth song, following upon the shining forth of the Savior, makes plain the good that he gives to human beings, saying: “Behold now, what is good, or what is pleasant.” “Like ointment upon the head, which runs down upon the beard.” When the Church is gathered, he says, and forms as it were a single harmony, then indeed the anointing of the Holy Spirit and the priesthood are applied, first to the head of the Church, which is Christ, then also to the beard, which is the comeliness of the Church's face. By this the apostles are meant. Last of all it passed to the whole body, that is, to all in the Church who have put on Christ. “For there the Lord commanded the blessing, and life forevermore.” “There,” he says, clearly meaning among the brothers themselves who dwell together; “and life,” not ordinary life but immortal life. For it was upon Zion that the life-giving dew of the all-holy Spirit was sent down upon the holy apostles, through which all who believe reap the eternal blessing. For of them the heart and the…

The fifteenth song exhorts those in the Church who are still catechumens to praise God. He calls them servants, since they have not yet been counted worthy of adoption as sons. “In the nights lift up your hands to the holy places.” He says that they still stand in night, since they have not yet been counted worthy of the illumination of the Holy Spirit…

“May the Lord bless you from Zion.” He says “from Zion” because the very name was dear to them, since it was there that all holy worship had its ground. Then he teaches them to call upon him from every side [?], saying: “who made heaven and earth.” Alleluia. Psalm 134. “Praise the name of the Lord; praise the Lord, you servants.”

This psalm too is addressed to those being initiated, exhorting them: Praise God. For “allelu” is interpreted “praise,” and “ia” “the Lord.” “Praise the Lord, for the Lord is good; sing to his name, for it is good.” He urges them to sing, [?] who had once also worshiped idols in Egypt. These were the descendants of Jacob, and they were called to hymn God. “Israel for his own possession.” That is, as his chosen one; for Israel is the mind that sees. “For I know that the Lord is great, and our Lord is above all gods.” He came to know him as Lord from his creative power. “In the seas and in all the deeps. Bringing up clouds from the ends of the earth.” He says this because the seas surround the earth on the outside, and from them he brings up the clouds. “He made lightnings for the rain.” This too would be a sign of power befitting God: to mingle in the same thing the fiery nature of lightning and water. “He who brings out the winds from his treasuries.” By the treasuries he showed that the nature of the winds is beyond human comprehension. Similar is what the Lord said: “The wind blows where it wills, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where…”

“He who struck the firstborn of Egypt, both man and beast.” He placed the last plague first, since it was after this that they received their freedom. He mentions beasts too, because these came into being for the sake of man, and are punished on his account as well, so that, to increase their fear, the plague might be shown to be sent by God. “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands.” Having shown divine providence and given glory, and speaking as to those from the nations who had just come over and were still servants, he goes on, consistently, to set beside it the refutation of the gods they formerly believed in, as he had said: “For I have known that the Lord is great, and our Lord is above all gods.” For he has done so many great things, but your former gods are only idols, dead and dumb; may those who make them become like them. For how could those who worship lifeless things not have had their souls turned to stone? And those he called gods above, following common usage, he now puts to shame and calls idols, mocking both their material and their workmanship. Alleluia. Psalm 135. “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever. To him who divided the Red Sea into parts.” An ancient account says that the sea was divided into twelve sections, giving one path to each tribe. “To him who led his people through the wilderness.” The wonder of the wilderness is no less than that of the sea.

For many things threatened death: hunger, drought, thirst, a multitude of wild beasts, the lack of every necessity. Yet they walked on with nothing to fear. And he rescued them from two mighty kings who prided themselves on their strength, their power and the size of their bodies. Og was nine cubits in length and five in breadth, and had an iron bed. “Sihon king of the Amorites.” It was not without reason that he passed over the other kings and made special mention of these: he was reminding the people of the victory God gave them. For these prided themselves on their strength, their power and the size of their bodies. “For in our humiliation the Lord remembered us.” The words “For in our humiliation the Lord remembered us” would better suit those freed from spiritual slavery, or else from physical slavery. “He who gives food to all flesh.” For the care of the God who loves mankind reaches not only to the godly but even to the irrational animals, so that he gives each suitable food; and his providence extends from the wonders in heaven down to the smallest things on earth, and from there reaches back up to heaven. That is why, after “to all flesh,” he added: “Give thanks to the God of heaven.” Though he is the maker of all things, he is especially styled the God of heaven, because he is served by those who dwell there; for it is a place pure of sin. For David, through Jeremiah. Psalm 136. “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept.” The passage teaches those who, much later, would be in Babylon because of their lawlessness to weep and be distressed, seeking to recover their own good things. “If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand be forgotten.” That is, may I not obtain help from above. “May my tongue cleave to my throat if I do not remember you.” For what use is a sound organ of speech if it is not struck for what it ought? That is why the blessed men spent their whole life in care for hymns, saying: “I will sing to the Lord as long as I live.” The city was precious to them because of the worship of God, as was said before: “For the sake of the Lord our God I have sought good things for you.” “If I do not set Jerusalem first, at the beginning of my joy.” I will set the memory of you, he says, before every joy. For in this way our other joys too turn out to be good. And the Lord also puts holy food before bodily food. “Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom.” The sons of Edom are the Idumaeans descended from Esau, who, when Jerusalem was captured, trampled bitterly upon it until they saw it torn up from its foundations. “Daughter of Babylon, you wretched one.” Prophetic

too is that saying, which signifies the sack of Babylon. “Blessed is he who will repay you what you deserve.” Blessed, he says, is the one who takes you captive in return. For David, through Zechariah. Psalm 137. Argument. The present psalm contains a prophecy of the calling of all the nations. He gives thanks for this, that not only he himself, being a king, has been counted worthy of the divine manifestation, but he says that many kings of the nations too will be counted worthy of the same grace, which came about only after the coming of Christ. “I will give thanks to you, Lord, with my whole heart.” The Savior gave this commandment to the rich man, saying: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your strength…”

“And before the angels I will sing to you; I will worship toward your holy temple.” As though the angels were present and were always watching the victory God gave him. “And I will give thanks to your name for your mercy and your truth.” I will give thanks, he says, because I have been redeemed from the shadow and counted worthy of the truth. “For you have magnified your holy name above all.” He says that he offers thanksgiving for the calling of the nations: I give thanks not only for the benefits I have received, but also because I behold your glory everywhere, as you create, do good and punish. For there is nothing in creation that does not proclaim your greatness. “You will care for me greatly in my soul by your power.” By great care he means length of days. The sense is: by your power you will transform me from corruption into…

“And let them sing in the songs of the Lord, for great is the glory of the Lord.” He has written of “songs of the Lord,” which he promises that all those from the nations will sing. “For the Lord is high, and looks upon the lowly.” Do not wonder, he says, that these things will happen among human beings; for human affairs are not estranged from God's providence. “And the lofty he knows from afar.” For, according to the divine Apostle, he foreordained from the foundation of the world the calling of the nations and their being raised up to the heights. “If I walk in the midst of affliction, you will give me life.” Similar is: “In the world you will have affliction; but take courage, I have overcome the world.” “Against the wrath of my enemies you stretched out your hands.” For the right hand of the Father, that is, the Son, was brought against them, and it also saved us. “The Lord will repay on my behalf.” For having judged the injustice done against us, he cast out the ruler of this…
The psalm is attributed to the person of Zechariah, when the sons [of Israel] were still in captivity…

“You understood my thoughts from afar; my path and my measured way you have searched out.” If God knows even the movement of our thoughts, much more does he know the course of our life. “My path and my measured way you have searched out.” A measured way is a fixed measure of a road. He means: you know every movement of reasoning; for by roads he signifies movements. “For there is no deceit on my tongue.” This too was the greatest of David's achievements: not to sin with his tongue, whether by lying, by perjury, by fraud and deceit, or in any other such way. “Behold, Lord, you have known all things, the last and the ancient.” The middle things are passed over in silence, because evil lies in between. For it was not there in the beginning, nor will it be there again at the end. “You formed me and laid your hand upon me.” Not only did you form me, he says, but you also hold me fast now that I exist. For the laying on of God's hand signifies the gift of the Spirit bestowed on us, just as the apostles imparted the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. “Your knowledge has become too wonderful for me; it is mighty, I cannot attain to it.” What he is saying is this: that there are very many other things God has done for him which he is unable to discern. For it exceeds my power, he says, and the knowledge of these things lies beyond my comprehension, so that I cannot discover them or tell them. For whatever I have said is small and slight; the comprehension of divine power escapes my littleness. “If I go up to heaven, you are there.” Similar is: “Heaven is my throne.” “If I go down to Hades, you are present.” He prophesies the descent into Hades that took place…
“If I take up my wings at dawn and dwell at the farthest parts of the sea.” That is, if I should take the wings of birds

that are not yet tired — for this is what “at dawn” signifies — fresh for flying and full of strength. The sense is something like this: You, Lord, embrace all things, know all things beforehand, are present everywhere, and fill all things as God. Then: What would become of me if I fell into some sin and needed to run away and flee, when you, the Lord, have taken hold of everything? “And I said: Surely the darkness will trample me.” “Trample” stands for “cover me and hide me from your eyes.” But even this darkness, he says, is so within your knowledge that it might as well itself be…

“As its darkness, so also is its light.” For just as the night is gloomy to me, so it is bright to you. He says the kidneys are what produce fear. And he means: I have always feared you, because I always kept your judgment before my eyes. “You upheld me from my mother's womb.” It is fitting, he says, that I acquired fear of you, since your providence guarded me while I was being carried in the womb. “I will give thanks to you, for you are fearfully made wonderful.” Fittingly, after the theology just stated, he utters his thanksgiving. “Wonderful are your works, and my soul knows it very well.” The power that is in me, he says, which is beyond words, is itself also plain to you, O God. “My bone, which you made in secret, was not hidden from you.” The woman's fall did not escape you, he says, the woman you made secretly from my bone after putting me into a deep sleep; you knew our secrets, you who brought her into being in secret. “And my substance in the lowest parts of the earth.” Even if I should be dissolved, he says, and go back to dust, this too is known to you. “Your eyes saw my unformed substance.” Before I came to be, he says, and before I was given shape, the eyes of your foreknowledge beheld me and foresaw me — not in a general way, but as already present, already numbered and written in your book. “Days will be formed, and no one in them.” Through all the days of their life they conducted themselves in good order and good form, and had not a single day that was shapeless or unformed. “But to me your friends, O God, are greatly honored.” Similar is: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet's reward.” “I will count them, and they will be more numerous than the sand.” I am full of hope, he says, since I honor your friends, that in the resurrection I will stand with them, and through them will obtain honor from you. Then indeed, he says, the sinners would also be slain, that is, they will receive the punishments due to them. “If you slay sinners, O God.” Knowing the punishments that will come upon them, he sets them apart somewhere away from himself. “Men of blood, turn away from me, for you are contentious in your thoughts.” He states the reason

for which he drives sinners away from himself. They are driven away, he says, because they speak against God and contend with him, vainly exalting themselves and swaggering over human life. “Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord?” That is: I loved and welcomed your friends, but your enemies I hated completely. The enemies of God are first and properly the unclean demons; second after them are those who champion idolatry and the leaders of heresies. For the end. A psalm of David. Psalm 139. “Rescue me, Lord, from the evil man.” He cries out to God about the injustice done by the demons to human nature, asking him to take vengeance and turn the injustice back upon the heads of the wrongdoers. These words could also be said of visible enemies…

“Who devised injustice in their heart; all day long they drew up wars.” For they not only harbored evil thoughts, but added deeds to their thoughts. For “all day long” Symmachus renders “every day.” “Beside the path they set stumbling blocks for me.” All these things, he says, they did to halt the course of his journey toward God, entangling his feet in snares so as to throw him down from his firm standing in God. “Do not hand me over, Lord, from my desire to the sinner.” I, Lord, he says, desire with longing for salvation; so do not abandon me, lest I be turned aside from it and handed over to the sinner, that is, to the devil. “They plotted against me; do not forsake me, lest they be exalted.” He asks to be sheltered under the shelter of his wings, and under his mighty hand, from which no one can snatch, so that they may not pride themselves as over some [?] other thing. “The head of their encircling.” May what they plotted, he says, come upon themselves. For this is what “the head of their encircling” means. For the head of sinners is their reasoning and their perception. So may the beginning and head of their plot against me, by which they encircled me — and indeed also their toil and labor against me — come upon themselves. He asks also that they be handed over to punishment by fire. “Coals will fall upon them in fire.” For you will consume them with your wrath as with a fire. “You will cast them down in miseries, and they will not stand.” They will fall into calamities and will not survive them. This is what happened to Saul in the war against the foreigners; for there he was slain and met the end of his life. “A man full of talk will not be directed aright on the earth.” Eternal fire awaits the ungodly. And in this life too, the man full of talk will not in the end be directed aright. For no one who is quarrelsome and abusive, being of an earthly disposition, is directed aright, since his quarrelsomeness twists him. For since such people love sin, how could they be set straight by virtue? “Evils will hunt down the unjust man to destruction.”

For just as it is destroyed by its own disease without its own wickedness, having paid the fitting penalty. [?] For wickedness is enough by itself, in place of any other punishment, to destroy the soul that has it. A Psalm of David. 140.

This psalm also resembles the one before it, but it is more doctrinal. "Lord, I have cried to you; hear me. Attend to the voice of my supplication when I cry to you." "Cry" certainly indicates the intensity of the mind. "Receive my supplication graciously, Master," he says. "Let my prayer be directed like incense before you." He likens what comes from the mind to incense, since it is fine and is offered to God alone. "The lifting up of my hands an evening sacrifice." He likens the deeds signified by the hands to a sacrifice, since they are coarser than the choices of the mind. He says "evening" because we must practise good deeds right to the end. "Set a guard, Lord, on my mouth, and a door enclosing my lips." Since he knows that guarding the tongue is a great achievement, he asks God to grant him self-control over it. "Do not turn my heart aside to words of wickedness." That is, do not allow my mind, once it has been rightly ordered, to be turned to the opposite, so that I may not, he says, entertain thoughts of lawlessness. "The righteous man will [?] me in mercy and will reprove me." May I receive every discipline from the righteous, but may I not receive the praise and flattery of the sinner, with which they anoint my head as if with oil. "For still my prayer is against their pleasures; their judges were swallowed up near the rock." Having come near a rock, he says, they will be drowned. And it signifies that Christ himself will plunge them into the abyss. "They will hear my words, that they were sweet." From the outcome of the punishment foretold against them, he says, may my words win credence for their truth and fitness. "As a clod of earth is broken up upon the ground." We have broken up, he says, all that is earthy in us, humbling ourselves for your sake, so that all our strength was brought down even to Hades. This is like the saying, "For your sake we are being put to death all day long." "For my eyes are toward you, Lord, Lord." I put my trust in nothing human; I wait for your help, and I beg that my soul may not be stripped of it. "In you I have hoped; do not take away my soul." [?] That is, do not pour out or drain away the hope I have in you. "Sinners will fall into their own net." May sinners fall, he says, into their own nets. "I am alone until I pass by."

Then, he says, I will pass by without fear and without care, when the sinners themselves fall into their own nets. And I will go on living apart from them until I reach the end of life. Of understanding, for David, when he was in the cave; a prayer. 141.

What is set before us is a prayer and nothing else. Yet it calls for understanding, so that we may learn how, when we are in difficulties, we can escape evils. "With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice I made supplication to the Lord. I will pour out my supplication before him." He has, as it were, dedicated his whole mind to the Lord, he says. "I will declare my affliction before him." Contending in the race for my very soul, he says, I offer up my supplications, praying to slip free of my afflictions. You know, he says, that I am persecuted unjustly. "When my spirit was failing within me." This I did, seeing how extreme the evils were; for I was dwelling beside death itself. "And you knew my paths": "You knew my paths" is the word of one confident in the course of his life and in his deeds. Seeing that the spiritual enemies of the soul had arranged for Saul to enter the cave in order to capture David, he fittingly said: "They hid a snare for me", which the prayer, being present, made void. For as far as human help went, once he was caught in the cave he was cut off from all escape, and there was no one to rescue him or to seek out his soul. "In this way in which I walked they hid a snare for me." If one considers the place in the cave, one will find the words fitting. "I looked to the right and gazed, and there was no one who knew me." They set the vices that lie next door beside the virtues being practised. For instance, for one journeying toward wisdom they hid a snare, a wisdom not of God; and for one seeking knowledge they set beside it the knowledge falsely so called. The saying has some likeness to "Beside the path they set stumbling blocks for me." The snares may also signify excesses, into which one who is not on guard falls; it is of these he says, "I looked to the right." For those who are more ambitious, the snares lie on the right. "Flight has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks out my soul." For it was not possible to escape from the cave, since the way out in front was held by Saul. No one, he says, [seeks] the salvation of my soul

"I cried to you, Lord." For it is on him alone that he rests his hopes of salvation. "Bring my soul out of prison." He says this with reference to the place of the cave. Symmachus has: "Bring my soul out of confinement." "That I may give thanks to your name." Once you have released me, he says, from this affliction and this imprisonment, I will send up songs of thanksgiving.

"The righteous wait for me until you reward me." If you bring me out of here, he says, repaying my good deeds, then the rest of the righteous too, keeping me before their eyes as an example and storing up lessons for their own lives from what happened to me, will offer you their supplications and run to you. A Psalm of a song, of David, when his son Absalom was pursuing him. 142.

This psalm too has a theme like the one before it. For he prays to be rescued from his pursuers. As the Apostle says, these things happened to the ancients as types, and were written for our admonition. We are taught, then, to flee to God alone in our difficulties. It should be understood that the prayer is spoken in the person of humanity, pursued and afflicted by Satan, who had gained the upper hand over it; and it prays to be rescued from him through the coming of the Only-begotten. "Lord, hear my prayer." I ask, he says, to be heard through your truth. It is as if he said: Hearken to me by sending your Only-begotten, who is truth and righteousness. "He has made me sit in darkness like those long dead." By darkness he means the ignorance it once had. For I was no different from a dead man. By "those long dead" he means the idolaters of old. "Hear me quickly, Lord; my spirit has failed." In extreme circumstances, when someone's soul is in danger, it is fitting to say this, but not necessarily to use it in ordinary human affairs. "Make me hear your mercy in the morning." He means the Lord's resurrection in the morning; or perhaps he prays that Christ's morning resurrection may come, through which we receive mercy. "Make known to me, Lord, the way in which I should walk." He prays to obtain the teaching of the Gospel. "Rescue me from my enemies." The spiritual

Of David, against Goliath. 143. "Blessed be the Lord my God." The opening springs from great joy. "Who trains my hands for battle." By hands he means the deeds done in godliness, by which we make war on Satan. "Man has become like vanity." Every human being has become like this world. "Flash forth lightning, and you will scatter them." By lightning he means the preaching of the Gospel. "Send forth your hand from on high; deliver me and rescue me from many waters, from the hand of foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity." That is, from the thoughts that have surrounded us through the plotting of the demons. Or by waters he means the people of the Jews, who surrounded the apostles

in order to confound and destroy them. And these would be the estranged sons, who also speak vain things. And what vain things, if not their saying to Christ, "How is it that you, being a man, make yourself God?" "O God, I will sing a new song to you." The song of the Gospel, clearly. The words are spoken in the person of David himself. "On a ten-stringed psaltery I will make music to you." The ten-stringed psaltery is the body, since it has five senses and five activities of the soul, each activity taking place through each sense. "Who gives salvation to our kings." To the holy apostles, whom Christ appointed as their rulers. "Who redeems David his servant from the evil sword; rescue me and deliver me from the hand of foreign sons." For the sake of your covenants with them, take every care of us. For he called the frenzied and bestial fury of the attackers an evil sword, and he called the same people foreign, as being impious. "Whose sons are like young plants grown up in their youth." The sons of the people according to the flesh, he says, are flourishing, while those of the people according to the spirit are humbled. For these are the ones who say, "Though our outer man is wasting away, yet the inner man is being renewed." "Their daughters adorned, decked out like the likeness of a temple." With earthly adornment. That is why they did not become a temple of God, as the holy souls of believers did, but only the likeness of a temple; for they made a pretence of practising the way of life prescribed by the law. But they did not have the Word within them, but the evil

"Their storehouses full, overflowing from one into another." For they stored up treasure that was not heavenly but earthly. "Their sheep prolific, multiplying in their outgoings." And their cattle fat and fruitful. "There is no breach in the wall, nor any passage through." They enjoyed great prosperity, he says, but it will not stand firm for them to the end. For he taught this in another psalm, saying, "You cast them down when they were lifted up." "They called blessed the people for whom these things are so; blessed is the people whose God is the Lord." Those who do not judge rightly, but fix their imagination on the things of the flesh, think it blessed to enjoy these things in abundance. But this is not blessedness; blessedness is to call upon the Lord as one's God. Praise of David. 144. "I will exalt you, my God, my King." He does not bestow exaltation as on one who lacks it, but shows others that he has it. It is like "Father, glorify your name on earth." For he does not ask for a glory he did not have, but that the glory he did have be shown, as is made clear by "Glorify me with the glory I had with you before the world came to be."

so that not a single day should pass without hymns. With all one's soul and mind, then, one must exalt and bless God, and glorify his name with mortal names and words. "Generation and generation will praise your works." He means the Church gathered from both peoples, from those of the circumcision and from those of the Gentiles. By his works he means those he did during his sojourn on earth; and he hymns them in many ways, calling them power, majesty, glory, holiness and wonders, and again power, greatness, goodness, righteousness and mercies. "And they will speak of the might of your terrible acts." They will speak of them in their conduct and with right understanding. Such is the saying "It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God", and "Shout to God with a voice of rejoicing, for the Lord Most High is terrible." For they will speak of these things by the very fact that they fear and revere God. And they will recount his greatness as having no limit, not circumscribing it by knowledge, but recognizing it as incomprehensible; for only the Son knows the Father, and the Father the Son. And even if he reveals the Father to whom he wishes, it is still only so far as created beings are able to see, in proportion to the preparation each one has made beforehand. "They will pour forth the memory of the abundance of your goodness." He himself, being a good God, has bestowed his goodness on all, and has compassion on all his works. But those are saved who are willing to enjoy his goodness.

Psalm 145. "Praise the Lord, O my soul; I will praise the Lord in my life." "On that day all his thoughts will perish." At the time of death, he says, all that he had in mind will be gone [?], and none of the things he imagined on earth will exist. "Who gives food to the hungry." Spiritual food, clearly, to those who will hunger for every good thing. Psalm 146. "Praise the Lord, for it is good." In the preceding psalm he exhorted himself to place his hope in God alone; in this one he shows the choir of the apostles teaching the multitude to praise God for the benefits he bestowed on the human race. "The Lord lifts up the meek." By the meek he means those who have received faith in him, who have imitated the one who said, "I am meek." But I hate the sinners, he says, who are the unclean demons, who dwell in the fire. "And green herbs for the service of men." By the service of men he means oxen and mules and the other

The psaltery, then, is a ten-stringed musical instrument which produces its sound from the upper parts of its frame, rendering its notes in harmony with the melody of the voice; among the Hebrews it is called the nabla, and among the Greeks it is named the kithara. For they constructed it of an upright, unbending piece of wood, and on this ten strings were stretched. Each of the strings was fastened separately at the far end of the psaltery, while the beginnings of the strings were let down from above. For ten kollaboi, that is, pegs, turning around the arm of the psaltery, tightened and slackened the strings according to the rhythm of the harmony and the wish of the psalmist. And this is what the great Basil says, etc.

Athanasius. Why did the kings, Herod of Ascalon and Pontius Pilate, stand up, that is, array themselves and come against Christ? And why did the rulers of the Jews, the impious, pestilent sinners, the scribes, Pharisees and lawyers, run together into one, and rage against the Lord, that is, the Father, and against his Christ, that is, his Son? For whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father either. Perhaps, then, since what they dared served rather to show the Lord's power, and their attempts turned out the opposite of what they intended, David is mocking them, as people who dared everything in vain; or perhaps he is also reproaching them. For what charge did those who gathered against Christ bring when they hung him on a cross? Is this not the one who gave wisdom to the nations, granted might to kings, strengthened rulers in their rule, and worked for the Jews the greatest wonders and the most celebrated miracles? Athanasius. (5[?]) Here the word "saying" is missing, so that the sense is: "They were gathered against the Lord and against his Christ, saying, 'Let us break their bonds.'" Whose bonds? Those of the Father and the Son; for they did not wish to be inside the sacred net. "And let us cast off the yoke", that is, the law and commandment of the Gospel, of which it is written, "My yoke is easy." Reproaching them for this, he said through Jeremiah, "You said, 'I will not serve you'"; that is, you conducted yourself so as to shake off my service.
