Either, then, these words are spoken in the person of the Jews, who rejected submission to the Lord and wished to be yoked neither to him nor to the Father; or else the Spirit exhorts believers and says: Let us not become like those who plotted against Christ, nor be bound to them in agreement; rather, let us shake off the heavy yoke of the old law, counting as nothing the things expressed in types unless they are understood spiritually. For the shadow contributes nothing to our benefit unless it portrays the mystery of Christ. Of Athanasius. (54) "Then." When? Was it when they said, "Let us burst their bonds"? And what are the things he spoke in his wrath? "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees", and "The kingdom of God will be taken from you", and to the lawyers, "Woe." Or else "Then" refers to the time of judgment, when they will look on the one whom they pierced. For then he will trouble them, saying, "Depart from me, you cursed." They also experienced divine wrath when the Roman army came upon them, burned the city, and

sacked the temple, and sent most of them to their deaths. The title refers us to the history in 2 Samuel. David had many children by different wives. Among them Amnon was the firstborn; and by another wife he had Absalom and Tamar, both of them beautiful in appearance. Amnon fell in love with her; and pretending to be ill, when David visited him, he asked that his sister come to look after him. He violated her, then came to hate her, and at once sent her away. She told her brother Absalom of the outrage. He was indignant, but hid his anger. After some time he invited Amnon to a dinner and killed him, and, fearing his father's anger, he fled; three years later he returned, once David's wrath had subsided. Even so he was not admitted to his father's presence at once, but only after two years. He then began to plot against his father: he provided himself with chariots and horsemen, and he won over those who came to the king for judgment, drawing the subjects to himself with a show of kindness and gathering a crowd of rebels to plot against his father. Finally he revolted and proclaimed himself king. Among many others he won over Ahithophel, whom David had as his counselor, a shrewd and energetic man. When David heard this, he fled barefoot with those around him; it was then that Shimei cursed him. Praying that Ahithophel's counsel might be thwarted, David sent his friend Hushai to oppose Ahithophel's advice and to report to him, through the priests Zadok and Abiathar, whatever Absalom planned. When Hushai came to this parricide and was trusted as being well disposed toward him, both he and Ahithophel were asked to say what should be done about the war. Ahithophel urged him to lie with his father's concubines, then to pursue him and attack him while he was unprepared. Hushai said nothing about the concubines, but he would not let Absalom set out against his father at once: "Lest," he said, "you fall into the mountains and into hardships, destroy your army, and be taken yourself by your father's hands." When the parricide said, "Hushai's counsel is better than Ahithophel's counsel," Ahithophel was grieved and hanged himself. Hushai reported everything to David through the priests and told him to keep fleeing. When Absalom, having made his preparations, set out in pursuit of his father, having first lain with his father's concubines in the open, David did not go out to battle himself, but entrusted the army to commanders and gave them orders, saying, "Spare the young man Absalom for my sake." When battle was joined in the forest of Ephraim, twenty thousand men of Absalom's army fell,

while he himself fled just as he was, turning his bridle. Since he wore his hair thick and long, it became entangled in an oak; the mule slipped out from under his legs, and he was left hanging in the air from the tree, until someone saw him and reported it to Joab. Joab was one of David's commanders. He took three darts in his hand, thrust them into Absalom's heart, and killed him. When David heard of it he mourned, saying, "My son Absalom, my son! Would that I had died instead of you!" And so, the tyrant having been destroyed, David took up the kingdom again. But that was later. He composed the psalm we have before us while he was still being pursued. That is why it contains laments and wailing. The psalm will also be referred to Christ, the true David; for David is interpreted as "beloved" and "strong of hand." Who could be beloved by nature and in truth but Christ, who is fairer in beauty than the sons of men? And who is strong of hand but the mighty Jesus, who by the power of his divinity routed all the alien demons? For he was pursued, as by another Absalom, by Israel according to the senses and the flesh, that is, the Jews. Of them he says through Isaiah, "I begot sons and raised them up, but they rejected me." And Judas, like another Ahithophel, joined in the pursuit, he whom the spiritual David, Christ, had as his counselor. For of him it is said in one of the psalms, "But you, O man [?], my guide and my familiar friend." Judas indeed, like Ahithophel, went off and hanged himself; while Christ, sending out his disciples as his commanders into the war against his enemies, gave orders, just as David had commanded that they spare Absalom, that they too should not neglect the Israelites. "For you shall be," he says, "my heralds and witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth." And just as the mule and the hair delivered Absalom to death, so senselessness and pride in external and bodily things deprived the Jews of true life, and allowed them to enjoy neither earth nor heaven. (55) According to the great Athanasius, the word here plainly convicts the unbelief of the Jews. That is why Moses addressed them, saying, "Sons of men, in whom there is no faith." Of Cyril and Athanasius. This too is true of the Jews: "Each one spoke vain things to his neighbor", as they gathered their plots against our Savior.

And the poets and prose-writers among the Greeks, having taken no care whatever to be truthful, composed without scrutiny whatever seemed good to them, having a single aim: to make a display of eloquence. (56) Of Athanasius. In the anagogical sense, however, in the present psalm he expressly makes clear the utter impiety and lawlessness of human practices, in order to proclaim the necessity of Christ's appearing. So says the divine Athanasius; but according to Basil the Great, etc. Athanasius and Basil, the great Fathers, say that David sings this psalm to teach what would prepare a person to attain that blessed lot. Therefore the Word, wishing to sketch for us the perfect man, the one who is to attain the beatitudes, follows a certain order and path through the things observed in him, and has made its beginning from the nearest and first. So, beginning, he says: Lord, etc. (58) Athanasius. He says that the saints here are those sanctified in the Spirit of Christ, and the earth is the Church; and "He has made wonderful" stands for "He has made manifest." The wills are those of the Father himself, so that the whole means: He made the will of the Father known to those sanctified in faith. You may also understand the verse in this way: God made the saints wonderful. Why? Because all his wills were in them and were carried out by them. (59) Athanasius. Here, however, David, as in the twenty-third psalm, singing of the works of creation, accuses those who say that things came into being of themselves and are without providence, and those who worship the creature rather than the Creator. What then does he say to those from [?] … but the earlier words, "In the anagogical sense, however," [?]

their beauty and good order are, as it were, a voice. For the heavenly narration and the word proclaimed by the day is not an articulate voice, nor speech from a mouth; rather it becomes a teaching of divine power, a silent voice, for those who know how to listen. However, by calling creation voiceless, David showed that it is neither ensouled nor rational, contrary to the opinion of the wise men of the Greeks. For they say that this whole universe is a single living being, and that its parts, from which it is made up, are likewise living beings. (61) This psalm too is entitled "For the end," since it contains a prediction of certain things to come. For according to the great Athanasius, the psalm is spoken in the person of David's companions, praying for David himself as he offers sacrifice; but it is also referred to the person of the apostles, as praying together with Christ on the day of the cross. (62) According to the great Athanasius, the cedars of Lebanon are the lofty ones of the Jewish people, since Jerusalem is often called Lebanon in divine Scripture. The calf signifies the altar. So both they and the altar among them are utterly crushed. (65) According to the divine Athanasius, the return into his bosom of Christ's prayer for the Jews would signify that they remained in their sin and gained nothing from it, since by the excess of their folly they made the prayer, as it were, turn back. For the Lord, seeing the destruction that would overtake them and their final ruin, mourned for them; but they acted in such a way that his prayer for them was not conveyed to the Father's ears, but, as if beaten back by the magnitude of their impiety, was dragged down and turned back to him. Therefore he said: And my prayer shall return into my bosom. For if they had been going to be saved and to turn away from their impieties, the Saviour's prayer, running straight, would have passed unhindered and unimpeded to the Father's ears. (64) According to the excellent Athanasius and Cyril: Since man now walks about in an image and not in truth (for the true life belongs to the age to come), the psalmist fittingly called the image vanity. Since we do not now live the true life, but one that is as in an image, and do not devote our effort to the things that are truly good, therefore we are troubled in vain,

busying ourselves with worldly desires and gathering treasures whose heirs we do not know. (65) According to the great Athanasius and Cyril: Since in the psalm before this the Saviour said to the Father, "Raise me up, and I will repay them," now the person of those who crucified him is introduced. They suffered irremediable things, though it is evident that they will later be taken back, grafted, as Paul says, into their own olive tree. So Israel, repenting, says these things. Of Athanasius and Cyril. Grieving over their fall and repenting, those who crucified the Lord say that they thirst for God and long for the fountain that is with him, of which it is said: For with you is the fountain of life. And they long to come near to God through the disposition and sanctification that come by faith in Christ. And the one whom they killed, the author of our life, and handed over to death, him they call the living God (66). The words "When shall I come?" belong to those who yearn for the later calling and seek to learn the time when they too will appear before the face of God the Father (which is the same as that of the Son), even though they are now rejected. For I will turn away my eyes from you, he says. Why? For your hands are full of blood. (67) Athanasius and Cyril. The Saviour had foretold: When you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies. When the word came to fulfillment and the Romans sacked them, they lamented: first, because they had offended God; then, because they had fallen from the salvation that comes from him; and third, because their neighbours, trampling on them, said mockingly, "Where is your God?" To the excellent Athanasius the present psalm also seems to have the same subject as the one before it. For again those of Israel come asking for salvation through Christ. Therefore they say to the Father: Send out your light and your truth. For he was going to bring them into the holy mountain, that is, into heaven and the mansions above (which he also calls tabernacles), and to the spiritual altar; and he himself was going to gladden their youth. By youth he means the gladness that also renews their soul. Therefore on the

lyre they promise to offer him their thanksgiving. And he has often taught us to understand the lyre as the body. (69) Athanasius, Cyril, Theodoret. Those of the circumcision who repent claim God as their stronghold; those of the Gentiles who have believed make him their strength; and the captives do not hope to be redeemed by anyone else. Athanasius, Cyril. He calls the body a lyre, because through it the mind is naturally set sounding, sending up melody to God as through the strings of the senses. The lyre signifies both the mortification of the body and the harmony of the virtues: the strings hint at the mortification, and the tunings at the harmony. He showed cheerfulness by adding the lyre, and love by the address repeated twice: For O God, he says, my God. This is so that you may learn that the God who is over all is the one whom those of the circumcision who repent, and those of the Gentiles who believe, claim out of zeal and faith as their own special God. In him the spiritual youth also rejoices, being the opposite of the old man. For only someone who is young in spirit and mind, akin to the new man and in newness of spirit, will go in to God, who gladdens such youth. (70) According to the great Athanasius, this psalm too keeps to the same subject: those of Israel recount the ancient benefits, repenting and asking to be taken back by Christ, because they place their hope in him and give thanks in his name; but according to the golden-tongued Father, etc. (71) Athanasius. In the past you used to fight at our side as our general; but now not only do you not go out with us, you have even turned us back and made us the lowest before every enemy, so that we became plunder for those who hate us. The shame that once held our enemies now surrounds us; we have become inferior to those whom we formerly ruled, and have been plundered by those whom we plundered. According to the great Athanasius (72), these things are said by the prophetic chorus, making the people's calamities its own; but according to the others, by the army of the Maccabees. (73) Athanasius. They compare to sleep

the great forbearance that God showed on account of their sins. And they pray that the appearing of Christ at the end of the times may be granted to them, so that they may not be deprived of the life that comes from him; and they say: Why do you hide your face and forget our affliction and our tribulation? You hide your face, O God, and turn it away so as not to look upon things that are shameful, unseemly and unworthy of your sight. But since we have boldness on account of the achievements just mentioned, why do you hide your face? And since we suffer so much and endure hardship for the sake of piety toward you, why do you forget our affliction, that is, our poverty? For even if these achievements are great as far as we are concerned, in relation to you they are all poor, small and very slight; yet as coming from us they are great. Therefore we beseech you not to forget our poverty, but to remember also our tribulation, which we endured for your sake, O Master. (74) Athanasius. The Jews too say that their soul has been brought low, since, having rejected the mind of Christ, they fell into a carnal mind. (75) Athanasius. The verses also signify the return and calling of Israel that will take place in later times. They also say: Help us, then, and show your favour. And they confess that the time of return is true faith in you. By adding "For your name's sake," they expressly confess that those who turned against Christ are not worthy to receive mercy. Yet it befits him to have mercy and to pity human failings for his own sake. For he says: It is not for your sake that I act, says the Lord, but for my name's sake. (76) The excellent Athanasius and the divine Cyril understand these words as spoken in the person of God the Father about the Word who was in the beginning with him, whom, they say, he brought forth as it were from his heart, or from his very bowels. Concerning him he also says through David: My heart has poured forth a good word. For he has been begotten as a word from a mind, good from good, God from God. Observe how the Father speaks of the Son as having become man: I speak my works to the king. For he all but promises to teach him

what kind of words he will use, leading us on to do his works. By the works of God we mean the godly way of life, which has been made manifest to us through the preaching of the gospel. And Christ, when he spoke to the Jews of the things useful for salvation, ascribed his own words to the Father, saying: I do nothing of myself; and again: The Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself does. The Father fittingly calls him king, so that he might not seem, because of the lowliness of the incarnation, to be stripped of the dignity that belongs to him by nature. For even after the dispensation he remained no less a king, being from the Father who is king; and though he is king and God, he is said to come into a king's rule because he became flesh. In the same way, the things he knows by nature as God he is again said to hear, by dispensation, on account of his humanity. For Christ is the king to whom the Father speaks his works. And the one he called Word he also calls his tongue, since he speaks nothing other than the Father's will that is in him. For among us too the tongue conveys the mind to those outside. And he is called the pen of a swift scribe because he speaks and it happens at once, as in: I say, be cleansed, and at once he was cleansed; Young man, I say to you, arise, and at once he arose. Moreover, like a pen, he swiftly writes the Father's will on our hearts. And the Father's will, as he himself says, is that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me. The Father's pen is swift. For the law of Moses indicated what was useful only dimly, through the roundabout ways of the letter, but the common Saviour showed the Father's will concisely. For he is the Angel of great counsel. And the Lord, it says, will make a concise word in the whole world. (77) The excellent Athanasius also applies to the holy Theotokos the words "Listen, O daughter" and "He is your Lord," since they are like "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you." For having spoken of Christ the Word of God, he says, David at once also indicated his human birth from a virgin. Gabriel simply calls her full of grace, being unrelated to her by birth; but David addresses her as daughter, since she was of his seed. (78) Athanasius and Cyril. The psalm signifies the calling of the nations, being sung in the person of the holy apostles, who exhort the nations to leap for joy

(79) The divine Athanasius says that the peoples and nations are Satan and the evil powers with him, of whom the Saviour said: Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions. For he subjected the nations of the demons to the feet of the apostles. (80) Athanasius. This psalm too is sung in the person of the holy apostles, who recount the persecutions they suffered because of the preaching and the victories won over them. It is entitled "Song of a psalm" because moral philosophy works together with contemplative philosophy. (81) According to the great Athanasius, what is signified here is the war waged against the apostles because of the preaching, both by the visible kings of the nations and by the invisible demons who formerly reigned. They were amazed and astonished when they saw the help given by God to the saints. For the surpassing strength of the one who saves produced wonder and amazement in them. Then they were troubled, since they had set themselves up as enemies of God, and they were as if in birth pangs. If you attend to what is said next, you will understand that the ships called ships of Tarshish brought great wealth to Solomon, as we have learned from the history of the Kingdoms. Therefore here too, through the shattered ships of Tarshish, he indicated the loss of the wealth and power of the kings already mentioned. And by the violent wind you will understand certain spiritual powers, through which he defeated the enemies of the apostles. (82) Of Athanasius. That, having judged the cause of the nations,

you drove out the demon who was hostile to them. Or, if you like, Mount Zion is those entrusted with the heights of theology, and the daughters of Judea are the Churches throughout the world, since they were founded by the apostles, who traced their descent from the Jews. He also urges the preachers to rejoice because of the just judgments of God, by which he accomplished the salvation of the world. (83) According to the great Athanasius, the Lord will make his second coming, the manifest and glorious one, from the Zion above; this he has also called [?] "the beauty of his loveliness." (85) According to the great Athanasius, he called the mind "spirit," and by "right" [?] he means its steadfastness, as if to say: Make my mind secure, so that it may no longer easily fall into sin. Of Athanasius and Eusebius. Truly every God-loving person grows weary and is distressed while spending his days in this mortal life; and he is distressed also out of love for mankind, seeing the multitude of those who are perishing. Since David too, seeing the oppression and tyranny of the demons, was filled with weariness, he beseeches the Lord to appear and deliver us from the hand of those who oppress us (85). The words "from the ends of the earth" signify that he makes his supplications on behalf of the whole world. Not only that, but they also show the great distance between the being of God and that of men, as in the saying in Ecclesiastes: God is in heaven above, and you are on the earth below. While Symmachus said more plainly, "when I was distressed," the Seventy said more vividly and expressively, "when my heart grew weary." For one is said to be distressed even over small things, but to grow weary to the point of despair only over great ones: when, because of the multitude of evils, a person is finally hemmed in by them, gives up before them and as it were despairs, casting aside the counsels of his mind, as one no longer able to bear it. (86) Athanasius. As to the sense: through Christ, who has been called a rock by the blessed Paul, we have become stronger than the demons who abuse us. And to state the whole meaning of the psalm, the passage contains a thanksgiving. For these things that I mentioned before, he says, have come to me because you yourself, O God, lifted me up

and set me high upon the rock that is with you, which is your Word; for the rock was Christ. Since then by your Word you have set me high and raised me aloft, so that I no longer dwell in the middle of the earth but have come to its ends; since you have already guided me so that I have come near to you; since you have become my hope, and because of this hope I shall not be put to shame; and since, though many spiritual enemies press upon me, seeking my soul, you alone have sufficed in place of all, having become for me a tower of strength: it is fitting that I, having obtained all these things, send up hymns to you (perhaps read σοί, "to you"), as to the one who has become the cause of all good things for me. (87) Of Athanasius and Cyril. It is proper to guides to show which way is safe and to warn which is dangerous and harmful; and Christ is found to have done this when he says: I am the way and the door. And "a tower of strength" is as if he were saying: You have become a wall and a safeguard, so that I suffer nothing from the enemies who abuse me. For Christ is a firm, unshakable tower. (88) Athanasius, Cyril. As to the sense: from the good things he has already received, he also hopes for those to come, namely that, having come to the tabernacles above, he will be under his shelter forever. For just as those who are about to celebrate a feast, when it is near and at the doors, are filled with delight beforehand and see the feast that is not yet present as already present, so also the saints, having good hopes for the life to come, rejoice in it. By "wings" he means the providential powers of God, under which the God-loving person is sheltered, never departing from God's tabernacle but dwelling in it forever. Of Eusebius and Athanasius. It should be understood, however, that these words also contain a hint of the true inheritance, which is eternal life. But this will be given in the age to come; how then did he say, "You have given"? Because, although it is awaited after the resurrection, it has already been given, by being already prepared, to those who will receive it at the proper time. And notice that the inheritance is given even to those who fear God. If, then, it is given to them, who are of lesser rank, much more to those who have risen above them, that is, to those who love God. And by saying without qualification "to those who fear," and not adding "Jews" or "Greeks," he extended the grace to all people; though Scripture is accustomed to call those who come from the Gentiles especially "those who fear the Lord." And what

is the inheritance but the kingdom of heaven, of which the Saviour spoke in the Beatitudes? (89) Of Eusebius, Athanasius, Cyril. As to the sense, the passage signifies that eternal life too is part of the inheritance. For this is what it means to add days upon days to the years of the king, since by "days" he signifies certain times and ages. Do not suppose that he says such things about some one particular king; know rather that he says them about everyone called to the kingdom of heaven, of whom he also says that he abides forever before God. For those who have been conformed to his sufferings will also reign with him forever. Having first said, "You, O God, have heard my prayers," the Prophet joined to it, by transposition, "You will add days upon days of the king." For you heard my prayers, he says; you added days upon days. The mention of those who fear the name of the Lord was inserted in between, since the prophecy promises the inheritance to them as well; and this was eternal life. (90) Athanasius. The phrase is inverted, so that it amounts to this: If anyone seeks out his mercy and truth, he will abide before God through the endless ages. Symmachus rendered this more clearly: Mercy and truth will preserve him. For these, the mercy and the truth of God, will be the causes of his immortality. But according to the Seventy: Who, it says, is able to grasp precisely God's measured and just mercy? For his judgments are a great deep. (91) Athanasius. As to the sense, he says these things because, blaspheming Jesus, they said to the apostles: Did we not strictly order you to speak to no one in this name? He called the words of slander a sharpened sword, to show how keenly they work destruction; and he likened the slanderer's tongue to a bow, because it harms even those far off. For the reviler and slanderer spares no one, whether present or absent. (92) Athanasius. Those who see, he says, the [?]

[?]… seeing so many men, and such great ones, fail and miss the mark in their schemes, they were filled with confusion and fear, and marveled at divine providence. For once they understood God's care, they feared the divine judgment, and all understood that it is God who makes their destructiveness [?] come to nothing, and that the plots against me were shown to be vain. So all proclaim, "This is your work, O Master," and credit what has happened to you. (95) For who would not fear, seeing God's visitation come upon the ungodly, and vengeance on behalf of those who are wronged? (94) Athanasius. Mixed in with the prediction about these things is a prophecy of the salvation of the Gentiles as well. For here David brings forward those from the Gentiles who believed in Christ, crying out against the wise of this age and asking forgiveness for their former ungodliness. He also sends up a prayer for them, who were once fruitless but have become fruitful through faith in Christ. It was said earlier that "psalm" denotes action, and "ode" denotes contemplation. So when the good is achieved through both, with moral philosophy running together with contemplative philosophy, there is a "psalm of an ode." For the contemplative life, achieved together with the practical life, produces a perfect man. (95) Athanasius. In its meaning it hints at the new people, chosen from the Gentiles as an inheritance for Christ. By "courts" we should understand the churches in each region. Taken another way, the Prophet calls blessed the one who has been perfected in virtues. For God chooses the one who is fit to contend and to run, but the one who has already conquered and closed his life with a good end he takes up into heaven, where he also gives him a dwelling in his own courts. Of these it is said, "There are many mansions with the Father." So being taken up by the one who chose you is more perfect than being chosen. For when the chosen one has done everything according to God's will, he is taken up with glory into the promises, and once he has moved from the earthly place he dwells there, in the courts of the one who chose him. Someone who still longed for these from here said, "My soul faints for the courts of the Lord." So those who emulate the departed and call them blessed fittingly use these words, I mean, "Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken up." (96) Athanasius. In its sense: the good things of the

house of God are the various gifts of the Spirit. Paul calls the Church the house of God. In it the virtue called righteousness is wonderfully brought to completion. So whoever believes and is filled with good works has the Lord within himself. For it is said that Christ dwells through faith in the inner man, and that he comes with the Father to the one who keeps his word and makes his home with him. Such a person becomes a temple, as in "Do you not know that you are God's temple?", and he also wonderfully achieves the righteousness that comes through faith. He is holy because he is pure, and wonderful because of his righteousness. In its meaning: "You," he says, "who prepare the mountains," that is, the opposing powers, "for punishment" (for the abyss has been prepared for them). And you will do this because you are mighty. Athanasius and Cyril. In its meaning: Christ stirs up the multitudes of the nations like the depths and expanse of the sea. He does not let them rest in their ancient deceptions, but rather moves them to the knowledge of his power, and stirs up the praises of all toward him like the roar of waves. Or here he calls the multitude of unclean spirits a "sea," which is thrown into turmoil at Christ's coming. That is why they said in fear, "Have you come here before the time to torment us?" Or he calls the multitude of tyrants a sea because of the saltiness of their idolatry, and the "roar of waves" means the plots and tortures against the martyrs. Who could have endured these unless he had been empowered and strengthened by the power of Christ? Athanasius. He also pointed to the preaching of the holy apostles. Because it was unfamiliar, and because the ancestral worship of the nations was being dissolved and their way of life changed, it immediately stirred up turmoil and storm among people, as the Lord said, separating bride from mother-in-law and father from son. But after the storm it grew calm and brought peace to all. So when, he says, the nations are troubled, that is, the hosts of demons, then indeed those at the ends of the world will fear you, having seen the great signs that took place at your coming. Athanasius, Eusebius and Cyril. And indeed, when those who inhabit the

world have seen the great signs and fear with the good fear, then for the outgoings of morning and evening, that is, at every time, there will be delight for them as they rejoice over what Christ's coming has achieved. Christ himself also has two outgoings, that is, goings forth. The morning one took place from the Father before all ages, as in "His goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity." The evening one is the one from the Virgin, which came about at the consummation of the ages. Each of them is delight and exultation. Symmachus, however, says, "They sing hymns at the approaches of dawn and of evening." He seems to mean that at both the beginning and the end of the day, those who have abandoned error and come to know the one who is God by nature will offer the hymns that please God. Athanasius. In its meaning: "You have satisfied," he says, "the whole earth with good things from above. You have filled with spiritual gifts those who live in all the world under heaven. And us, who were then wandering in error and were like a dry and waterless land, you have made fruitful, most fertile, and truly holy." Athanasius. In its sense, the river of God is the Only-begotten. For as a river comes from a spring, so he too comes from the essence of the one who begot him, and is consubstantial with him. He is full of waters, since the fullness of the Godhead dwells in him. "And we beheld his glory … full of grace and truth." The Holy Spirit too might be understood as a river, full of the waters of the various gifts. He says that the spiritual food has been prepared because the mystery of Christ was determined before the foundation of the world. Christ is the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world. "For thus," he says, "is the preparation of the true food, as you yourself prepared it, and not otherwise" (or perhaps "no one else"), meaning most providently and in a manner fitting for God. For it befits God to prepare such things that those who partake of them rise through repentance to a dignity worthy of God. Athanasius and Eusebius. Contemplatively: "Continue, O Master," he says, "watering the depths of human hearts like furrows, drenching them and rousing them to bear fruit. Then the produce of their righteousness will be multiplied, not only through the river (that is, the grace of the Spirit), but also through the drops that fall as from clouds, the teachers, that is, through the thoughts of the divine Scriptures." Athanasius. According to the letter, then, he has called the year of plenty a blessed year of goodness,

since it receives abundance through God's goodness and is filled with blessing through plenty. Theodoret and Athanasius. The age to come may also be the crown of goodness, because in it the saints are crowned with great goodness. Athanasius. In its sense, he compares the souls of believers to plains and fields. God enriches them with divine and spiritual gifts so that they can bear the fruits of godliness. (97) Athanasius. In its sense, by "the beautiful places" he means the holy apostles and evangelists, who have been well nourished with spiritual gifts. By "wilderness" he means the Church, which was once desolate of the knowledge of God. Athanasius, Cyril. In its sense: When God's goodness has appeared, the land that was once desolate will bear fruit. The hills, once defiled by idolatrous sacrifices, will rejoice once they have received those who choose the angelic life. Or he compares to hills those who in every age lead the holy churches and preside over the peoples, that is, pastors and teachers. For just as the mountains and hills rise above all the rest of the earth, so the rank of the holy initiators into the mysteries is higher than that of others. They also gird themselves with exultation, that is, the consolation of the Spirit. Gregory the Theologian and Athanasius. The valleys of the earth bear fruit that is perceptible and short-lived, but those of the souls well cultivated by the Word bear fruit that is spiritual and eternal. For the souls of the Gentiles, he says, which were once utterly destitute and barren, will be full of spiritual fruit. Athanasius. Simply put: All those mentioned before, he says, will sing hymns with all eagerness to God, who gave such a change to human nature. Athanasius. (98) Contemplatively, a "shout" is a victory hymn sung over fallen enemies. Since the rulers of this age have been destroyed through Christ's coming, he urges all the nations to send up victory hymns to God, the cause of the victory, and to his name, that is, to the Son.

For just as we are known by our name, so too the Father is known through the Son. [?] Cyril, Athanasius. That is the historical sense. In the spiritual interpretation, the works of Christ, that is, his divine signs, are very fearful, as is his command, "Be gone," to the hordes of unclean demons. His resurrection is the abundance and surpassing greatness of his power. It overthrows the might of death and renews all human nature to incorruption. The Jews saw Christ's miracles, and when they ought to have been amazed, they slandered the wonderworker and called him a deceiver. So he rebukes them and says, "Stop, and say to him instead, 'Fearful are your works.'" Then, since he saw that they would not obey, he stops speaking to them and turns to address the slandered Christ: "Great is your power, even though your enemies lied to you. They willingly shut their eyes to your divine light that appeared to the world, and not even the overwhelming greatness of the miracles brought them to believe." For when our Lord, by the abundance of his power, accomplished his own resurrection from the dead as a man, his enemies the Hebrews lied to him, that is, they slandered the resurrection. "Even if the Jews deny you," he says, "all the earth will bow down to you and worship you in their place," that is, the nations that inhabit the earth. Worship is no longer in Jerusalem, since the shadow of the law has ceased, as in "They will worship him, each from his own place." Worship now takes place in spirit and truth, with works that match the worship of God, since his name has been called upon them. These words foretell the present time, in which the God of all is praised in hymns among all the nations, and Christ the Master is called Most High by all. (2) Athanasius. Here he brings forward the apostles as speakers, teaching the nations that the one who worked divine signs when he came in the flesh is the same one who long ago dried up the Red Sea and cut off the streams of the Jordan, so that the children of Israel crossed on foot. So he says: "Turn your minds and consider each of the things done by the good God, how incomprehensible he is in his counsels. And marvel at his ineffable wisdom, by which he guides the human race
toward godliness. For he has used fearful and wonderful means for the sake of humankind's [?]

Athanasius. In its sense: There we will reign with Christ, when he reigns over the new age, and we will rejoice in him. And we rejoice in the one who made difficult things easy. Athanasius, Eusebius. In the spiritual interpretation, we will understand the eyes of God to be the apostles. The embittering ones are the Jews, whom the prophets also called an embittering house. "For who," he says, "is the embittering one, if not the house of Israel?" So through Israel's trespass the Lord looked upon the nations. Therefore let the ungodly not be exalted, as though they could destroy those who come to the Gospel. And let the arrogant people, that is, Israel, not think highly of itself, nor raise a haughty brow against the multitude of the Gentiles. Let it not say to itself, "I have become the firstborn among the children of God." Let it know instead that it embittered its Creator. That is why he took his oversight away from it. Athanasius. In its sense, the apostles say to those from the Gentiles: "When you hear from us how it is fitting to give glory, then bless with us [?], no longer the falsely named gods, but our God, the giver of life." For life was the delight of paradise, in which God placed man to work it and keep it. Athanasius, Cyril. (4) In its sense, the Spirit foretells the afflictions that came upon the apostles because of their preaching, and lists them as if the apostles were speaking. For just as silver melted in fire is thoroughly purified, so too the souls of the saints are freed from every stain when they boldly meet the assaults of temptation. Their approval comes through burning, as they are tested as if by fire. Paul applies these words to the holy martyrs. But those too who have passed through the fire of boiling anger and the water of dissolute pleasure and desire, and have not stayed in these passions, find the

(5) Athanasius. In its sense, the apostles say: "We will enter the heavenly temple, not with perceptible burnt offerings but with spiritual ones." For they dedicated themselves wholly to God as a whole burnt offering.

Athanasius, Cyril, Basil. In its meaning: Everything is spiritual, the burnt offerings, the oxen, and the goats that he promises to offer. The offering is also made with rams. The rams are movements and impulses that draw their force from the spirited part of the soul, or ruling thoughts that gore the passions. He sacrifices an ox who offers himself through action as a living sacrifice. For the ox, an animal that works the soil, corresponds to the body formed from the earth. The goats are the works of repentance, since they were offered for sin. The incense is the fragrance breathing from pure souls. Athanasius. The apostles, however, do not recall ancient stories. Instead they marvel at the new achievements of our Savior, all that he has given to the souls of us all. Athanasius. Perhaps the sinners are the demons, the inventors of sin. They vanish like smoke, driven off and scattered by the Holy Spirit, and they melt like wax, dissolving at the appearing of Christ, who is called a fire that consumes wickedness. And then those who have been justified by faith rejoice, since the tyranny of the demons has been destroyed. Eusebius, Athanasius. The Sun of righteousness took the form of a servant, drew in, as it were, the rays of his own Godhead, and set in the body, or even in death itself, and so drove away the darkness that had spread over human souls. Yet even though he entered into our poverty and, as part of his plan of salvation, veiled his own glory when he passed among humans and lived among them in the flesh, still, "the Lord is his name." For when he became man he did not cast off being God. So the word urges the holy apostles to run to the nations with dancing and hymns, and through their preaching to prepare the way of their souls for the King of all. The "settings" might also be nights, and the souls that had fallen away from the Sun of righteousness, from which Christ drove out the gloom of error by dwelling in them through faith. "I undertook to know," etc., verse 16. (6) According to the divine Athanasius: "I imagined," he says, "that I could know judgments so deep, and I threw myself into toil, since they are unsearchable. But I have found for myself the proper time for knowing them. This was the time of judgment, when you will repay each according to his works. For then the

faint-hearted will know exactly what virtue is, and what [?]" (7) According to the holy Athanasius: "Since I have nothing in heaven but you alone," he says, "of necessity I wished to receive nothing on earth from you either, since all things are perishable and [?]. I prayed to obtain one thing only, and I wore myself out on earth longing for it. This is for you alone to become my portion. For my heart failed. What, of one who seeks the [?]
